Under the Nagoya Protocol, utilisation of genetic resources means research and development on the genetic and/or biochemical composition of genetic material, so biochemical R&D is correct; cloning humans is excluded as human genetic material is not covered.
The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) is named after Cartagena, Colombia, where it was negotiated.

30x30 is the biodiversity target launched by the High Ambition Coalition to protect 30% of land and ocean by 2030, not a renewable-energy goal, so I is wrong. India was the first BRICS country to join the HAC, so II and III are correct.
The Nagoya Protocol (ABS, 2010) is a supplementary protocol under the Convention on Biological Diversity, not the UNFCCC, Ramsar or Paris Agreement.

Rashid Ali received the separate 7-year sentence, whereas the other INA officers such as Shah Nawaz were sentenced to transportation for life. Aruna Asaf Ali and Rash Behari Bose were not tried in this way.
Supercooling means cooling a liquid below its freezing point without it solidifying. The notes do not state this, so no line is linked.
Absolute humidity is the weight (mass) of water vapour per unit volume of air. Specific humidity is per unit weight of air and relative humidity is a percentage ratio.
Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation starts. The other terms are not standard measures.

Statement II is the definition of dew point. Statement I is the standard definition of saturation deficit (capacity minus actual vapour), so both are correct, although the notes only confirm statement II.

Evaporation takes place at the surface, so a larger surface area exposes more molecules and raises the rate. Higher humidity, lower wind and lower temperature all reduce it. The notes do not state this.
Steam at 100°C carries extra latent heat of vaporisation, which it releases on condensing on the skin, so it burns worse than boiling water at the same temperature.
During boiling the heat supplied goes into latent heat of vaporisation, so the temperature stays constant at the boiling point.
At high altitude atmospheric pressure is lower, which lowers the boiling point of water. A pressure cooker raises the pressure and so raises the boiling point, which makes cooking easier.
Heat absorbed during the liquid-to-vapour change at constant temperature is the latent heat of vaporisation. Specific heat concerns a change in temperature.
Air pressure is lower at altitude, and lower pressure lowers the boiling point of water.
The change from liquid to gas is vaporisation (evaporation or boiling). Condensation is the reverse, and precipitation and decantation are different processes.
Change of water into vapour only changes its physical state, and no new substance forms, so it is a physical change rather than a chemical one.
Adiabatic temperature changes occur when air expands (cools) or is compressed (warms) without exchanging heat with its surroundings. Latent heat is a separate, non-adiabatic heat source.
The notes do not give the rediscovery date of Sanchi. It was rediscovered in 1818 by General Henry Taylor, so (2) is correct, and the other years are wrong.
The notes do not cover this. Tawang Monastery in Arunachal Pradesh is the largest monastery in India and the oldest and biggest in Asia, so (1) is correct.
The capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi in the announcements of 12 Dec 1911 under Hardinge II, so 1911 is correct; 1905 was the Partition of Bengal.

Curzon revived and organised the Department of Archaeology (appointing John Marshall as Director-General in 1902). Canning only set up the ASI in 1861, but Curzon is the answer here as the organised department.
The first (non-synchronous) census was held in 1872 under Lord Mayo; the first synchronous census came in 1881 under Ripon.
The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act was passed in 1904 under Curzon, not Canning (who set up the ASI in 1861).
The Preamble secures social, economic and political justice, so option 4 is right; religious and cultural justice are not in the Preamble.
Fraternity means a sense of brotherhood among citizens, promoted by single citizenship.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held the Preamble is a part of the Constitution, overruling Berubari. Golaknath, Minerva Mills and Gopalan are distractors.
In S.R. Bommai (1994) the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution. The other cases listed are not noted for this holding.
The Preamble reflects the philosophy, ideals and objectives of the Constitution, so it is the right answer rather than FRs, DPSPs or Parliament.
The Preamble is non-justiciable, meaning it cannot be enforced in a court of law.

Article 75(5) provides that a Minister who is not a member of either House for six consecutive months ceases to be a Minister. 75(3) is collective responsibility, 75(4) the oath, 75(2) the President's pleasure.
The President appoints the PM and the other Ministers on the PM's advice, and Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure (Art 75(2)), so the President determines their membership and term.

Statement I is wrong because the Council is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha, not to both Houses. Statement II is right because the President appoints other Ministers only on the PM's advice, so only II is correct.

A is true: under Art 75(3) the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. R is also true, since members of either House can be Ministers. But R does not explain A: responsibility to the Lok Sabha holds even for Rajya Sabha Ministers.
The 91st Amendment (2003) inserted Art 75(1A), capping the Union Council of Ministers at 15% of Lok Sabha strength. The 90th and 92nd amendments dealt with other matters.
Sulphur dioxide is a gaseous air pollutant (cause of acid rain), whereas zinc, copper and nickel are heavy metals that contaminate water.

Chemical fertilisers (nitrates, phosphates) and excessive pesticides are the agricultural practices that pollute water; deforestation is not an agricultural practice, and the notes do not list livestock manure as a primary cause, so II and III is correct.
Coliform count indicates faecal contamination, i.e. contamination by human (and animal) wastes, not hydrocarbons or phosphorus.
BOD is the oxygen bacteria need to decompose organic matter, so high BOD means heavy organic or microbial pollution, as with sewage.
IS 10500-2012 specifies 500 mg/L for TDS in drinking water.
BIS IS 10500 gives the desirable pH range of drinking water as 6.5 to 8.5.
The BIS (IS 10500) desirable pH range for drinking water is 6.5 to 8.5.
Eutrophication is nutrient (N, P) enrichment of a water body. Algae then bloom (not get destroyed) and DO falls, so the other options are wrong.
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment, and algal decomposition uses up dissolved oxygen, so both statements are correct.
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of a water body, and decomposition of the algal bloom depletes dissolved oxygen, so both statements are correct.
Mandamus literally means "We command"; the other options are the meanings of Quo Warranto (by what warrant), Habeas Corpus (to have the body) and Certiorari (to be certified).
Quo Warranto means "By what authority (or warrant)?", i.e. it asks what authority a person has to hold a public office. Habeas Corpus, Certiorari and Prohibition have different meanings.

Certiorari is issued by a higher court calling for the subordinate court's record for review. Stopping proceedings is Prohibition, showing authority to hold office is Quo Warranto, and producing a detained person is Habeas Corpus.

Prohibition is issued by a higher court to stop a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction while proceedings are pending. Option 2 describes Certiorari, option 3 Quo Warranto and option 4 Habeas Corpus.
Mandamus compels a public official to perform a public legal duty that has been refused or neglected. Prohibition only restrains lower judicial bodies.
Prohibition is issued by a higher court to stop a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction. Certiorari acts after an order has been passed, so it is the tempting wrong option.
Habeas Corpus literally means "To have the body (of)". The other writs have different literal meanings.
Habeas Corpus is the writ for release from unlawful detention, with the detained person produced before the court. Mandamus, Certiorari and Prohibition do not secure release.
Certiorari is nicknamed the "postmortem" writ because the higher court reviews an order or record after it has been passed. Prohibition acts while proceedings are pending.
Certiorari quashes an order already passed by a lower body or authority. Mandamus commands a duty, Quo Warranto tests a claim to office, and Habeas Corpus secures release from detention.
Mandamus means "We command", which is closest to "order" among the options. Prohibition means to forbid, Certiorari to be certified, and Quo Warranto by what authority.

Mandamus cannot force the Government to make a law or policy, but it can enforce the terms of a policy once laid down. So (A) is true, and (R), that mandamus cannot lie in the absence of policy, is true and explains (A).

Art. 32 covers only Fundamental Rights. Right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right (it is a statutory/legal right), so it cannot be enforced by a writ under Art. 32, though Art. 226 covers other legal rights.
Old NH-1 ran from Delhi to Amritsar (now part of NH-44), while Delhi–Kolkata was old NH-2, so option 3 is wrong.
The notes give NH-44 as about 4,112 km, which differs from the 3,745 km option (the older figure); no line supports 3,745 km.
National Highways make up about 2% of road length but carry about 40% of road traffic.
Maharashtra has the longest National Highway length among States (17,756.6 km).
Old NH-1 was Delhi–Amritsar; Delhi–Kolkata was old NH-2.
Old NH-7 is now mostly part of NH-44, which passes through Nagpur, Hyderabad and Bengaluru; Pune is on NH-48 and NH-65, not NH-44, so NH-7 does not pass through Pune.
Declaring the commencement or cessation of a state of war is notified by the Ministry of External Affairs, which handles India's relations with other states. The notes do not state this.
Mossad is Israel's intelligence agency. GRU is Russian, NSIS is South Korean and CISEN is Mexican.
CISF is a Central Armed Police Force under the Ministry of Home Affairs, so option 3 is right.
The Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy is in Hyderabad. Dehradun is a tempting but wrong option.
The Indian Army commands include Northern, Western, Eastern, Southern, South-Western, Central and the Army Training Command (ARTRAC). There is no South-Eastern Command.
Project Seabird is the Indian Navy's base at Karwar on the west coast, a greenfield naval base project.
The National Defence Academy is at Khadakwasla, Pune. Mount Abu houses the Internal Security Academy, which is a different institution.
The Southern Naval Command has its headquarters at Kochi (Kerala). Karwar is a naval base but not the command HQ.
Kuroshio is a warm current of the North Pacific off Japan, so it is the one that is not cold. Canary, California and Oyashio are all cold currents.
The East Australian Current is a warm current of the South Pacific. West Australian, Benguela and Peru (Humboldt) are cold currents.
The South Atlantic Drift is a cold current in the South Atlantic, as the West Wind Drift flowing eastward there is cold. Mozambique and East Australian are warm currents.
The Canary Current off NW Africa is a cold current of the North Atlantic. Brazil, Gulf Stream and Kuroshio are warm currents.
The Canary Current is cold, so it is the one that is not warm. Brazil is a warm current, and the North Pacific Drift and North Equatorial currents carry warm water.
North Atlantic Drift and Brazil are both warm currents. California, Canaries, Benguela and Falkland are cold, which rules out the other options.
The Gulf Stream is a warm current of the North Atlantic that starts in the Gulf of Mexico as the Florida current. It is not cold and not in the Pacific.

Groundwater depletion comes from deep bore tubewells, topsoil loss from brick production, and habitat loss from agricultural expansion, which gives A-2, B-1, C-3. Urban construction on water bodies matches land for buildings (D-4).
Plants, animals and micro-organisms are living resources, so they are biotic. Abiotic resources are non-living, and renewable is a different basis of classification.
The notes do not give the data needed to judge these statements.
The notes give no figures for forest cover by country.
Forests are renewable, so A is true. R is also true, but improving the environment is not why forests are renewable, so R does not explain A.
The notes say Andhra Pradesh ranks first in tank irrigation, with Tamil Nadu at over 23%. They do not support the given answer, Tamil Nadu.
Afforestation adds vegetation and helps groundwater recharge rather than depleting it. Excessive pumping and loss of forests or recharge area are depletion causes.
Zing is Ladakh, Zabo is Nagaland, Johad is Rajasthan, Phad is Maharashtra and Eri is Tamil Nadu. This gives A-III, B-V, C-II, D-IV, E-I.
The notes give 2004-05 to 2012-13 as the highest average growth period (boom peak ~8.5%), while the 1980s were only about 5.1-5.2%, so option 4 is right.
The Tenth Plan (2002-07) targeted 8% GDP growth (cut to 7% at the mid-term review), so 8.0 is correct.
The Eleventh Plan achieved 8.0% growth, the highest among plans, above the Eighth (6.8%), Ninth (5.4%) and Tenth (7.6%).
The Twelfth Plan targeted 4% average annual growth for agriculture, forestry and fisheries (agriculture and allied sectors), so 4.0 percent is correct.

Bauxite in Chhattisgarh occurs in Bastar, Bilaspur, Dantewada, Jashpur, Mainpat and Amarkantak. Kondagaon was carved out of Bastar, so it is the correct choice; Raipur, Durg and Dhamtari are not listed.
Khetri (Jhunjhunu, Rajasthan) is a major copper mining centre, so copper mining is correct.
Chhattisgarh (Dantewada) is the only tin-producing state and holds a major share of tin resources, so tin ore is correct; coal, iron and limestone are not its distinguishing largest national deposit.
Rajasthan is the sole producer of lead-zinc ores, selenite and wollastonite. Copper is not solely Rajasthan's, so options with II are wrong.
Kolar Plateau is known for gold; the Kolar gold mines (closed 2001) are in Karnataka.
Gypsum is used in cement (as a setting regulator) and is produced mainly in Rajasthan. Lignite and graphite are not cement inputs.
Gypsum is hydrated calcium sulphate, CaSO4·2H2O. 2CaSO4·H2O is plaster of Paris and CaSO4 is anhydrite.
Gypsum is CaSO4·2H2O (dihydrate), used in cement as a setting regulator; the other formulas are not gypsum.
Gypsum has the formula CaSO4·2H2O, i.e. calcium sulphate dihydrate. Limestone is CaCO3.
Gypsum is a Rajasthan mineral used in cement, fertiliser (soil fertility) and plaster (building). It fits the clues, while limestone, lignite and fuller's earth do not match all three.
The Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh–Munger belt is the main mica belt, the 'Capital of Mica'.
Makrana in Rajasthan yields the finest marble, used for the Taj Mahal and Victoria Memorial.
The Jalakaranda instrument is mentioned in the Dharmasagara (Dharmasagaram) inscription, not in Chebrolu, Malkapuram or Pillalamarri.
Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) built the Thousand Pillar Temple in 1163. Ganapatideva and Rudramadevi came later and did not build it.
The C. Rangarajan Committee (formed 2006, report 2008) was the Committee on Financial Inclusion; the other committees listed are not associated with financial inclusion.
LBS stands for Lead Bank Scheme (Lead Banking Scheme), which is a financial inclusion measure; the other options are not real schemes.

Financial inclusion covers financial literacy, credit for weaker sections and formal services, so the listed elements fit together and 'All of the above' is the best answer. The notes do not explicitly list consumer protection or grievance redressal.
Swabhimaan (10 February 2011) was a financial inclusion campaign taking banking to the doorsteps of the rural poor, so it is associated with rural banking.
PMJDY, launched in August 2014, aims at a bank account for every household, making it the 2014 financial inclusion reform. GST, Make in India and PMFBY do not aim at universal banking access.
PMJDY was launched on 28 August 2014, having been announced on 15 August 2014.

The MUDRA loan limit was ₹10 lakh at launch and the question's wording matches that original limit. It has since been raised to ₹20 lakh (Tarun Plus), so the ₹20 lakh option is the tempting alternative.
The limit was ₹10 lakh at launch and is now ₹20 lakh after the Tarun Plus category was added (from 24 Oct 2024).
Shishu, Kishore and Tarun are the loan categories under PM MUDRA Yojana, with MUDRA being the refinance agency. They are not schemes of RRBs, SIDBI or IDBI.
India is the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses, so option 4 is correct. The USA, China and England are not leaders in pulses.
Kentucky is nicknamed the 'Blue Grass State' because of the bluegrass grown in its pastures. The notes do not cover this nickname, so the other states are wrong by general knowledge.
Lapland spans Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola Peninsula, and its reindeer-herding inhabitants are the Lapps (Sami). The other options are unrelated peoples.

Bushmen (San) are hunter-gatherers of the Kalahari, so option 4 is correct. Eskimos belong to the Arctic tundra, not the Amazon; Pygmies live in the Congo rainforest, not the Irrawaddy basin; and the Sahara is home to Tuareg and Bedouin.
The Inuit live in the tundra of Canada, Alaska and Greenland. Sweden is Lapland (Sami) territory, so the Inuit are not found there.
Inuit (Eskimo) live in the tundra of Canada, Alaska and Greenland, so Canada is correct. Mongolia, Malaya and Sri Lanka are not their homes.
Blood group AB has both A and B antigens and no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so it is the universal recipient; O negative is the universal donor.
The pancreas is both endocrine (insulin from Islets of Langerhans) and exocrine (digestive enzymes). Liver, testis and pituitary are not described this way.
The adrenal glands sit above the kidneys, so the adrenal gland is the one on the kidney. The pituitary, thyroid and hypothalamus are in the brain or neck.
The adrenal glands sit above the kidneys, so the adrenal gland is the one on the kidney. The pituitary, thyroid and hypothalamus are in the brain or neck.
The lacrimal gland secretes tear fluid that is spread over the eye by blinking. The thyroid, salivary and pituitary glands have no such role.
Insulin promotes glucose uptake and fat storage and lowers blood sugar, including by slowing glycogen breakdown in the liver, so all of the listed functions are correct.
Normal human body temperature is about 37°C (98.6°F). 98°C is far too high; 367 K is about 94°C, not 37°C (310 K).
The eye's lens focuses light to form the image on the retina, which holds the photoreceptors. The cornea, iris and pupil do not form the image.
Kaivalya (Kevala jnana) is the Jain term for omniscience, i.e. perfect or complete knowledge. Jina means conqueror of passions and Nirvana is not the Jain term for this.
The Triratna (Ratnatraya) of Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct is the Jain path to moksha. Buddhism's three jewels are Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.
The Jain Triratna is Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct. 'Right view' is not one of them (it belongs to the Buddhist Eightfold Path), so it is the answer.
Triratna (Ratnatraya) is the Jain doctrine of Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct, so the philosophy is Jain.
Anuvratas are the milder vows for Jain householders (shravakas). Anuvrata is a Jain term.
Samadhi Marana is another name for Sallekhana/Santhara, the Jain ritual fast unto death at the end of life. It is therefore related to Jain philosophy.
Anuvratas are the limited vows for Jain householders, whereas ascetics follow the Mahavratas. The concept is therefore Jain.
The Sthanakvasi are a sect of Svetambara Jainism that does not worship idols. The notes do not mention this sect.
Self-mortification is not common: Jainism practises severe penance, while Buddhism follows the Middle Way. Ahimsa, indifference to the Vedas and rejection of rituals are shared.
Jainism stresses severe self-mortification, while Buddhism follows the Middle Way, so this is not common. Non-violence, indifference to the Vedas and rejection of rituals are shared.
Indifference to the Vedas and denial of rituals are common to both. Avoiding the extremes of penance and pleasure is Buddhist only, so statement I is wrong and the answer is II and III.
Summer solstice is 21 June, winter solstice 22 December, vernal equinox 21 March and autumnal equinox 23 September, giving A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3, which is option 2.
Day equals night at the vernal equinox (21 March) and the autumnal equinox (23 September), when the Sun is overhead at the Equator. The other date pairs are not equinoxes.

Statements I and II are correct: the vernal equinox is on 21 March and the Sun is overhead at the Equator. Statement III is wrong because the Earth's tilt is fixed; the tilt gives seasons and unequal day length, and day length changes because the Sun's overhead position shifts.
Pingali Venkayya, the designer of the tricolour, served as a soldier in the British Army in South Africa during the Anglo-Boer War. The other options are not linked to this service.
Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka I, so 1336 is correct; 1346 is the year of the Sringeri visit/Hoysala annexation.
The Sangama dynasty (1336-1485) was the first of the four Vijayanagara dynasties; Hoysala was not a Vijayanagara dynasty, and Saluva and Tuluva came later.
One origin tradition says Harihara and Bukka were treasurers under Prataparudra of Warangal, and they founded Vijayanagara in 1336. So the place is Vijayanagara.
Vijayanagara lay on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra, a tributary of the Krishna, with its ruins at Hampi.
The four Vijayanagara dynasties were Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu in that order. Hoysalas, Yadavas and Poligars are not among them.
The Cholas are best known for village autonomy, with each village having its own assembly (sabha). Religion, wars and trade are not the distinguishing hallmark.
Autonomous village administration through local assemblies is the special hallmark of Chola polity. Monarchy and mandalam divisions were not unique to the Cholas.
The Cholas of south India were known for village autonomy and elaborate local self-government, so Chola is correct; the Chalukyas were highly centralised.
The Cholas are the dynasty famous for elaborate local self-government with elected assemblies and committees. The Chalukyas, Solankis and Parmars are not known for this.
Variyam is a committee system, kudumbu a ward, kudavolai a lottery and perumakkal members of the village assembly, giving a-IV, b-I, c-II, d-III.
Thotta variyam was the committee for gardens and orchards. Samvatsara was annual, eri handled tanks and pon handled gold and finance.
The Khilafat Movement aimed to protect the Ottoman Sultan as Khalifa and the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire after World War I; the other options are not its aims.
Gandhi saw the Khilafat cause as a golden opportunity for Hindu-Muslim unity and merged it with Swaraj, so he backed it to win Muslim support against the British.
The Ali brothers (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali) were leading Khilafat figures. Jinnah did not support the movement, and Kidwai is not listed as a leader.
Gandhi presided over the All-India Khilafat Conference at Delhi in November 1919, where non-violent non-cooperation was first proposed.
Shaukat Ali and Mohammad Ali (the Ali brothers) were the initiators of the Khilafat Movement. Shariatullah (Faraizi movement) and Azad are not credited as its starters.
M.A. Jinnah did not support the Khilafat-Non-Cooperation movement and criticised Gandhi's participation, unlike the Ali brothers and Azad.
The notes do not mention Malaviya's stance on Khilafat. Nehru, Mohammad Ali and Shraddhanand supported the movement, while Malaviya is the one who did not.

The movement aimed to save the Ottoman Empire and the Khilafat, which was directed against British policy and so aroused anti-British feeling. Separate electorates and social reform were not its objectives.
The Khilafat Movement arose after the First World War, not the Second, so A is false. Gandhi did preside over the 1919 Khilafat Conference, so R is true.
The Non-Cooperation Movement was launched on 1 August 1920.
The Non-Cooperation Movement, linked to the Khilafat issue, was launched on 1 August 1920.
Gandhi promised Swaraj within a year if non-cooperation was followed, so the slogan belongs to the Non-Cooperation Movement.
Mycorrhiza is an association of fungi with plant roots: the fungus absorbs water and minerals for the plant while the plant feeds the fungus. Algae are involved in lichens, not mycorrhiza.
Plants of warm dry climates have tiny, waxy, thick leaves with a thick cuticle to cut water loss, so small and thick is correct. Large thin leaves would lose too much water.
Cryptophytes are the plants listed as growing on the ice surface. Lithophytes grow on rocks and xerophytes in dry habitats.
Halophytes are plants of saline habitats, i.e. salt-loving, with adaptations such as pneumatophores and salt glands. Xerophytes live in dry places and mesophytes in moderate conditions.
An ecotone is the transition zone where two communities meet. An ecotype is a genetic race of a species, not a zone.

A uniform stand of one forest type, such as teak forest, is a single community and not an ecotone. River bank, marshland and mangroves are transition zones between dry and wet or marine and terrestrial areas.
Tropical rainforest has the highest NPP per unit area. Swamps and reefs are also high but lower than tropical forests.
Triratna, the three jewels or refuges of Buddhism, are the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha. Tripitaka is the set of scriptures, not the Triratna.
The Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha together form the three refuges, called the Triratna. Trivarga, Trisarga and Trimurti are unrelated terms.
Women were admitted to the Sangha at Vaishali at Ananda's request, with Mahaprajapati Gautami as the first nun. Shravasti is the tempting wrong option.
Birth was at Lumbini, enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, first sermon at Sarnath and death (Mahaparinirvana) at Kushinagar, giving A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3.
The eight limbs of Ashtanga Yoga are Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana and Samadhi. Anusmriti is not among them, so it is the odd one out.
Syadvada is the Jaina doctrine (associated with Kundakundacharya), not a Charvaka, Bauddha or Samkhya teaching.
Astika and nastika are distinguished by whether the authenticity of the Vedas is accepted. Belief in God, rebirth or heaven and hell is not the criterion.
Nyaya, the school of logic, was founded by Gautama (Akshapada). Kapila is linked with Samkhya and Jaimini with Purva Mimamsa.
Materialism is called Lokayata or Charvaka, so the Charvaka system is also called the Lokayata system. It is a nastika school, not an astika one.

Samkhya holds that the world was formed by the blending of nature (Prakriti). Vaisheshika treats the atom as the basis of the world, Lokayata is materialist, and Ajivika upholds Niyati (predetermined fate). This gives a-II, b-III, c-IV, d-I.
Golden Rice is engineered to produce beta-carotene (pro-vitamin A) in the grain, which addresses vitamin A deficiency. Thiamine, ascorbic acid and calciferol are not what the modification targets.
Golden Rice is a genetically engineered (transgenic) rice carrying foreign genes for beta-carotene (carotene) synthesis. It is not a wild, stored or regional variety.

Both statements are true: Golden Rice is a biotech achievement that supplies beta-carotene (pro-vitamin A) against vitamin A deficiency, and the beta-carotene gives the golden colour and is the reason for its benefit, so R explains A.

Religious freedom is not unlimited: Art. 25 is subject to public order, morality, health and other Part III provisions, and Art. 26 to public order, morality and health. So option 1 is the incorrect statement.
Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, i.e. freedom of religion. Protection of minorities is Art. 29.

Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work, so it deals with exploitation of children. Art. 23 covers trafficking and forced labour, and Arts. 17 and 19 are unrelated.
Article 24 bars employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous work. Art. 25 concerns religion, and Arts. 17 and 19 are unrelated.
Explanation I to Article 25 says that wearing and carrying kirpans is part of the profession of the Sikh religion, so the right comes under Article 25.

Art. 25 is subject to public order, morality and health (I), and the State may make laws for social welfare and reform and throw open Hindu public religious institutions to all Hindus (II, III). Defamation or incitement to an offence is an Art. 19 restriction, not Art. 25, so IV is wrong.
Art. 26 is limited by public order, morality and health only. National security, education and secularism are not listed grounds, so I, IV and V are right.
The Jewish place of worship is the synagogue. Kaaba is the Islamic shrine at Mecca, and Ahura Mazda is the Zoroastrian supreme god, not a place of worship.
Nobel Prizes are given in Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature and Peace, with Economics added in 1968. Mathematics is not among them (it has the Fields Medal and Abel Prize instead).
Economics was not in Nobel's will; it was added in 1968 and first awarded in 1969. It was not established by Alfred Nobel, so the option naming the Central Bank of Sweden is the one that fits.
Röntgen received the first Physics Nobel in 1901, for the discovery of X-rays.
Alfred Nobel was Swedish and his will (1895) set up the prizes, so the Nobel Prize was instituted in Sweden.
Khorana's 1968 Medicine prize was shared, not won alone, so statement 3 is wrong. Banerjee's 2019 prize was shared with Duflo and Kremer.
C.V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for the Raman Effect.
Tagore won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first Indian laureate. The other options did not win in 1913.
Homi J. Bhabha never won a Nobel Prize, whereas Raman (1930) and Tagore (1913) did. Bhabha is linked to nuclear energy, not the Nobel.
Tagore was the first Indian Nobel laureate, in Literature in 1913.
S. Chandrasekhar became a US citizen in 1953, so he was not an Indian citizen when he won the 1983 Nobel Prize.
White phosphorus has a very low ignition temperature and catches fire in air, so it is stored under water.
Butane is a saturated alkane (only single bonds), whereas acetylene, pentene and benzene contain double or triple bonds and are unsaturated.
Methylpropane (isobutane) has formula C4H10, the same as n-butane but with a branched chain, so they are structural isomers.
In v = u + at, u is the initial velocity and v is the final velocity.
Only statement I is correct: in equilibrium the net moment is zero. Momentum is conserved only when no external force acts, and kinetic energy is not conserved in inelastic collisions.
Sound is a mechanical wave produced by vibrations and needs a medium, so it is mechanical energy, not an electromagnetic wave.
By the first law, ΔU = Q - W. With W = 0, ΔU = Q, so the change in internal energy equals the heat flow.
The photoelectric effect is explained by light as photons (particles). Diffraction, interference and polarisation show its wave nature.
In photosynthesis, plants convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.
Both gain the same kinetic energy (qV), as the charges are equal in magnitude. Since KE = ½mv², the lighter electron gets the higher speed.
A wave transmits only energy through the medium; the particles just oscillate about their mean positions and the material is not carried along.
By kinetic theory, the average kinetic energy of ideal gas molecules is (3/2)kT, proportional to the absolute temperature.
Mitochondria, chloroplasts and the nucleus contain DNA. Golgi bodies, plasma membrane and ribosomes do not.
Light consists of packets of energy called photons, as in the quantum theory of light.
Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and hence similar chemical properties.
Radioactivity depends on nuclear stability, not on electron arrangement, so it shows no periodic trend. Atomic size, valency and electronegativity vary periodically.
Mercury (Hg) is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary temperature. K, Ag and Pb are solids.
In a BJT the base is thin and lightly doped, the emitter is heavily doped and the collector is moderately doped.
Insects breathe through tracheae that open to the outside by pores called spiracles.
The Rowlatt Act was passed on 10 March 1919, so 1919 is correct; the other years are unrelated to it.
The Rowlatt Act aimed to curb national and revolutionary activities and punish dissent. It had nothing to do with agrarian reform, trade balance or WWII trials.
The Act allowed arrest without warrant and detention without trial for up to two years, which caused popular indignation. It did not concern religion, education or trade unions.
The Act allowed arrest without warrant and detention without trial and aimed to punish dissent, so it limited individual liberty, which is why Congress opposed it. It did not ban the Congress.
Satyapal was arrested on 9 April 1919, the massacre came on 13 April 1919, and the Amritsar Congress session was in December 1919. So the order is II, I, III.
The Act was based on the Sedition (Rowlatt) Committee and Gandhi tried to use the Home Rule League, so I and II are correct. The Simon Commission came in 1928, so III is wrong.
The gathering was to protest the arrest of Kitchlew and Satyapal and the Rowlatt Act, though Baisakhi was also being celebrated. Gandhi and Lajpat Rai were not the leaders whose arrest prompted it.
The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place at Amritsar, Punjab, on 13 April 1919.

The notes do not mention Farkhor. Farkhor Air Base is in Tajikistan, near the Afghan border, so Tajikistan is correct. Afghanistan is the tempting wrong option because the base sits close to its border.
The notes state that the 2016-17 budget raised the irrigation allocation by about 57.6% over the 2015-16 BE, so 57.60 per cent is correct.
The notes give the 2018-19 revenue receipts of AP as ₹1,57,599 crore. The similar figure of ₹1,57,768 crore belongs to 2022-23.
Before GST, sales tax/VAT made up about 73% of AP's own tax revenue (2016-17 RE), so 73 per cent is correct.
Mines and minerals is the largest non-tax revenue source in AP, ahead of forests, interest receipts and education (2016-17 RE).
Both statements are supported by the notes: AP's capex stayed below 15% of total expenditure during 2016-21, and capex shows commitment to infrastructure. So both are true.
The notes give AP's debt-GSDP ratio as 32% in December 2022, so 32% is correct.
The Indian Association of Calcutta was founded in 1876 by Surendranath Banerjee and A.M. Bose, so 1876 is correct; 1884 is the Madras Mahajana Sabha.
The British Indian Association was formed in 1851 at Calcutta by merging the Landholders' Society and the Bengal British India Society. The Landholders' Society dates from 1838.
The East India Association was founded by Dadabhai Naoroji in London in 1866, unlike the other bodies which were Indian-based.
Bombay Association (1852) came first, then the Indian League (1875), the Indian Association of Calcutta (1876) and the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884), giving I, IV, III, II.
Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha (1836) came first, then the Landholders' Society (1838), the Bengal British India Society (1843) and the Indian League (1875), giving I, II, III, IV.

The Madras Native Association (1852) and Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884) are correct pairs. The Krishna District Association was founded in 1892, not 1900 (the Angalur conference year), so only A and B are correct.
Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty was the founder and first president of the Madras Native Association (1852).
The notes list reducing FD and RD as FRBM aims, but nothing states a public-debt cap of 50% of GDP from 2011, so no notes line settles option (4).
The FRBM Act prescribes deficit limits and statements laid with the Budget, but it has no penal provisions for missing targets. So option (3) is the thing it does not do.
The FRBM Act does not make the Centre answerable for States, which have their own fiscal responsibility laws. So including the States' failure in the Centre's targets is not mandatory.
N.K. Singh chaired the FRBM Review Committee. Urjit Patel, Sumit Bose and Rathin Roy were only members.
Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka led the confederacy of chiefs against Tughluq rule; Kolani Rudra and Prolaya Vema Reddi only took part, and Annayadeva was not the leader.
Kapaya Nayaka was the first holder of the title Andhra Suratrana, and with no Anavema-popularity framing here, Kapaya is the answer; Anavema Reddi bore it later.
Sangeeta Sudhakaram, a commentary on Sarngadeva's Sangita Ratnakara, was written by the Velama king Singabhupala II, not Singabhupala I or a Reddi.
Rekapalli on the Godavari was the capital of the Musunuri Nayaks founded by Prolaya Nayaka, not of the Recherlas, whose capitals were Rachakonda and Devarakonda.
The Damerla Velama family ruled from Sri Kalahasti; the other options are not their seat.
The Preamble reads Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic, so the sequence is C, A, D, B. The 42nd Amendment placed Socialist and Secular between Sovereign and Democratic.
The words 'We, the People of India' open the Preamble, showing the people's sovereignty. They are not part of the Directive Principles, Fundamental Rights or citizenship provisions.
The Preamble describes India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic, in that exact sequence. The other options scramble this order.
Adult franchise is among the words that do not appear in the Preamble. Justice, Fraternity and Equality of status all do appear in it.
'Sovereign' means supreme authority, internally and externally free, so India is not subject to any external authority. Socialist, Liberty and Fraternity do not carry this meaning.

A Republic has an elected head of State, not a hereditary one, so the absence of hereditary elements makes India a republic. An elected Parliament, adult franchise or a bill of rights do not define a republic.
In a socialist economy, productive resources are owned and controlled by the government. A mixed economy combines public and private ownership, and a capitalist economy relies on private ownership.
Rousseau is associated with the concept of popular (political) sovereignty through his idea of the general will.
Aristotle gave the concept of distributive justice, the proportional allocation of honours and goods according to merit.
The Preamble opens with 'We, the People of India', so the people are the main source of political authority. Parliament and State Legislatures derive their power from the people.
The Preamble secures justice of three types: social, economic and political. Religious and Natural justice are not mentioned.
Bhaskaracharya (Bhaskara II) was a mathematician and astronomer who wrote the Siddhanta Shiromani, not a medical figure. Dhanvantari, Charaka and Sushruta are all linked with Ayurveda and medicine.
The pillar's inscription names king Chandra, identified as Chandragupta II, so it is a Gupta work.
The Sarnath school of Buddha images belongs to the Gupta period, with polished Chunar sandstone and little decoration. The notes do not name the Bhumi Sparsha mudra specifically.
The Mehrauli iron pillar has not rusted for over fifteen centuries because its high-phosphorus iron forms a protective layer, which is why scientists study it.
The Wildlife (Protection) Act was enacted by Parliament in 1972; the other years are not associated with it.

The degree of protection runs Reserved > Protected > Village forest; reserved forests are strictest, protected forests allow activities unless prohibited, and a village forest is a reserved forest assigned to a village.
The National Forest Policy targets one-third (33%) of the geographical area under forest or tree cover. Two-thirds applies only to hills.
The 1952 policy classed forests as National, protected and village forests and tree-lands; National Parks were not a class, so National Park is the answer.
The Act bars hunting of the gharial, Indian wild ass and wild buffalo except as the law permits, so all three statements are correct.
The Wildlife (Protection) Act was enacted in 1972, which is the correct option.

Human society is distinguished from animal groups by culture, the shared learned knowledge, values and norms transmitted across generations; economy, religion and science are only parts or products of culture.
The Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya, the large national museum of human evolution and culture, is located in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
Pongal is the harvest festival of Tamil Nadu, celebrated in January; it is not a festival of the other listed states.

The Manifesto presents history as a history of class struggle between bourgeoisie and proletariat, which is the central theme; the state and production tools are secondary to it. This matches Marx's conflict perspective based on class struggle.

Statement I is true: agriculture still employs 46.1% of the workforce. The notes give nothing showing that volatility of agricultural growth has not declined, so Statement II is the false one and (3) is the answer.
Commercialisation means growing crops for the market rather than for own consumption (subsistence), so the answer is Consumption.
The rise in output came mainly from better technology, irrigation and improved methods, not from expanding the cultivated area. Option (3) is therefore correct.
The notes give no 2017-18 net area sown percentage for AP. The correct figure is 37.29%.
The notes do not give AP's gross irrigated area as a share of gross cropped area. The correct value is 52%.
Holdings of 1-2 ha are classed as Small farmers. Marginal holdings are below 1 ha.
Mustard is a Rabi crop, sown in Oct-Nov. Cotton, maize and arhar (tur) are Kharif crops.
Cotton is called the "white gold" of Andhra Pradesh and is an expanding commercial crop there. Rice and wheat are food crops, and rubber is not known as white gold.
The Agricultural Renewal Action Plan covers soil health, irrigation and water augmentation, and credit and insurance. Boosting capital formation was not part of it, so (1) is the exception.

Hiuen Tsang was not sent as an emissary by anyone. The Tang emperor Taizong had banned foreign travel, and he travelled on his own via the Silk Route. The keyed answer (Taai-Sunga, i.e. Taizong) is the Tang emperor, and the notes only support that this emperor was not the sender.
Hiuen Tsang, the 'Prince of Pilgrims', visited India in the time of Harsha and was at his court in 631 CE. Ashoka, Vishnugupta and Samudragupta belong to other periods.

Statement II is right: ordeals by water, fire, weighing and poison were used. Statement I is wrong because Hiuen Tsang was robbed twice, so the roads were not completely safe. The notes do not cover the ferry duties in III.
Harsha wrote Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda, so 1, 2 and 4 are right. Harshacharita was written by Banabhatta, which is why options including 3 are wrong.
Pal toured Andhra towns in April 1907 and the Tenali bomb case was in April 1909, so A and B are correct. The notes do not support C, so the answer is A and B only.

I is correct: the modified Objectives Resolution became the Preamble. II is correct: the Preamble is non-justiciable. IV is correct: it is neither a source of power nor a limit on powers expressly granted, so it cannot override specific provisions. III is wrong because the Preamble is amendable under Art. 368 (it was amended once, by the 42nd Amendment).

The 42nd Amendment (1976) added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble. Sovereignty and dignity of the individual were already in the original text, and privacy is not in the Preamble.
The 42nd Amendment added Socialist, Secular and Integrity. Sovereign was in the original text, and Gram Swarajya is not in the Preamble at all, so only I and III are correct.
The Preamble has been amended only once, by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. The other amendments listed did not change it.
The 42nd Amendment changed 'unity of the Nation' to 'unity and integrity of the Nation', so 'Integrity' was inserted. Economic, belief and political were already in the original text.
'Socialist' was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), not by the 41st, 43rd or 44th.
The original 1949 Preamble described India as a 'Sovereign Democratic Republic', so Socialist, Secular and Integrity were absent. Republic was already present, so IV is wrong.
'Secular' was absent from the 1949 text and was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Democratic and Republic were in the original Preamble, and 'Liberal' is not in the Preamble at all.
The word 'Socialist' was inserted into the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976), which is the Forty-second Constitutional Amendment.
K.M. Munshi described the Preamble as the 'horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'. Palkhivala's phrase was 'identity card', and Ambedkar's 'heart and soul' referred to Article 32.
East Timor was a Portuguese colony until 1975, which is outside these notes on Europeans in Andhra, so no line states the fact.
This is a current-affairs question: Vijay Mallya is reported to be living in England. The notes do not cover it.
The Golden Farman was granted by Abdullah Qutb Shah, Sultan of Golconda, to the English in 1632, so 1632 is correct.
The Dutch set up their first factory in Andhra at Machilipatnam (Masulipatnam) in 1605. Nizampatnam came second (1606) and Pulicat later (1610).
The notes list the CM order as Sanjivayya (1960-62), Brahmananda Reddy (1964-71), P.V. Narasimha Rao (1971-73), then T. Anjaiah (1980-82), which gives B, D, C, A.
Damodaram Sanjivayya was CM from 11 Jan 1960 to 1962, the first Dalit CM in India.
Nadendla Bhaskara Rao was CM from 16 Aug to 16 Sep 1984, i.e. 31 days, the shortest tenure.
e-Pragati was launched under Chandrababu Naidu's government. The notes do not state this fact.
Kasu Brahmananda Reddy was CM from 1964 to 1971; Vengala Rao served 1973-78 and Sanjivayya 1960-62.
The 1956 understanding between Andhra and Telangana leaders is known as the Gentlemen's Agreement, a moral and political understanding signed on 20 Feb 1956.
The 1956 understanding between Andhra and Telangana leaders is known as the Gentlemen's Agreement, a moral and political understanding signed on 20 Feb 1956.
The Gupta age is famed as the Golden Age for art and culture (sculpture, painting, first structural temples), not for imperialism or land reform.
No age gave women equality with men; the notes record the falling status of women in the Gupta period, so 'None of these' is correct.
Janaki-haranam was written by Kumaradasa, not Kalidasa; the other three are Kalidasa's works.
Kalidasa was one of the Navaratnas of Chandragupta II, so he belonged to Chandragupta II's period.
The Panchatantra, a collection of animal fables, was written by Vishnu Sharma; Kalidasa wrote poems and plays.
In Sanskrit plays of the period, women and lower-class characters spoke Prakrit while kings and Brahmins spoke Sanskrit.
Amarakosha (Amarasimha, a Navaratna), Kamasutra (Vatsyayana), Meghaduta (Kalidasa) and Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta) are all Gupta-era works, so all four are correct.
The Panchatantra is a set of animal fables on statecraft that teach through illustration what should and should not be done; it is not a philosophical, linguistic or scientific text.
Sanskrit was the court language of the Gupta rulers, and the period saw the peak of Sanskrit literature; Pali and Prakrit were not the court language.
Under Art. 53(1) the executive power of the Union vests in the President. The PM and Council of Ministers exercise it in practice, but formal vesting is in the President.

The parliamentary system makes the President a nominal head, while the real executive is the Council of Ministers under the PM, responsible to the Lok Sabha. Federalism, franchise and a representative legislature do not indicate this.
The President is the nominal or constitutional Head of State, not the Head of Government. The PM heads the government.

Statement I is correct (Art. 53(1)) and III is correct (Art. 53(2), Supreme Commander). Statement II is wrong because the President may exercise power directly or through subordinate officers, not only through them.
Art. 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor. Arts. 153, 155 and 156 deal with other matters such as appointment and tenure.
Art. 258A lets a State entrust its functions to the Union with the Union's consent. Art. 356 is President's Rule, so it is not the answer.
The notes do not give this fact, so no line is linked.
Thrombin is the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin in blood clotting; the notes link clotting to vitamin K, but they do not mention thrombin, so the answer rests on general knowledge.
Group B donates to B and AB. AB is the universal recipient, so B can donate to AB. Group B cannot donate to A or O.
Oxygenated blood from the lungs returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium (auricle). The notes do not cover heart chambers.
Haemophilia is a genetic disorder in which blood fails to clot because clotting factors are missing. The notes do not state this.
Wilson's disease is copper accumulation, causing neurological symptoms, liver problems and fluid build-up. Night blindness is caused by vitamin A deficiency, so it is not a symptom.
Haemophilia A is the X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of clotting factor VIII. The others are blood cancers or a clotting disorder (thrombosis), not factor VIII deficiency.
The ciliary muscles of the ciliary body change the lens curvature and so adjust its focal length (accommodation). The notes do not cover this.
Bile is made in the liver but stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. The notes mention only that the liver produces bile.
Lymphocytes are formed from stem cells in the bone marrow of long bones. The notes do not state this.
The left ventricle has a thick wall and pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for the whole body. The notes do not cover heart chambers.
AB is the universal recipient, so A can donate to AB. A cannot donate to O, B cannot donate to A, and AB cannot donate to O.
Urine is made in the kidneys and passes through the ureters to the bladder, then out through the urethra. The notes mention only that the kidney filters urea.
The pituitary is the smallest of the listed glands, about pea-sized. The notes call it the master gland but give no size.
The pituitary is the master gland and controls other endocrine glands through hormones such as TSH and ACTH.
The thymus lies behind the sternum, between the lungs, and trains T cells. The pituitary and pineal glands are in the brain.
Cortisol is a steroid hormone from the adrenal gland, so it has no peptide chain. Oxytocin, corticotropin (ACTH) and insulin are peptide hormones.
Thyroxine (T4) from the thyroid regulates the metabolic rate. Blood glucose is controlled by insulin, not thyroxine.
Cretinism results from thyroid hormone (thyroxine) deficiency, as stated for the thyroid in the notes.
The adrenal gland is called life-saving because adrenaline and cortisol help the body cope with stress and emergencies. The notes list these hormones but do not use the phrase.
Adrenaline from the adrenal gland is the emergency hormone, used in fight-or-flight situations.
The Godavari is the 2nd-largest basin of India (about 10% of the country) after the Ganga, so Godavari is correct.
The Water Resource Information System gives the total length of the Godavari as 1,465 km.

The notes do not state that the Krishna forms the Telangana-AP border from Srisailam to Pulichintala, so no line settles this. The other options match the notes: Godavari ~250 km in AP, Tungabhadra 58 km boundary. Option 4 is the one marked incorrect.
The Penna (Pinakini) rises in the Nandidurga/Nandi hills of Karnataka, so Nandi hills is correct.
Vamsadhara rises in the Jayapur hills, Machkund in the Madugula (Mudugal) hills, Gundlakamma in the Nallamala forests and Pennar in the Nandidurga hills, which gives a-III, b-IV, c-I, d-II.
In 2025 the Godavari stretch near Rajamahendravaram was named among India's most polluted river stretches because of untreated factory and sewage waste.
The Basava Sagar Dam is on the Krishna river.
The Tungabhadra is the largest right-bank tributary of the Krishna; Bhima is only the longest.
The Tungabhadra joins the Krishna at Sangameswaram in Kurnool, so it is a tributary of the Krishna.
Vijayawada is on the Krishna river.
Gandikota Fort stands on the banks of the Pennar, which cuts the Gandikota gorge.
The Penna's mouth is at Utukuru in Nellore district, so Nellore is correct.

For an object between F and P of a concave mirror, the image is virtual, erect and magnified, and it is formed behind the mirror. It is not formed at infinity (that happens when the object is at F), so option 3 is not correct.

The centre of curvature is at 32 cm (R = 2f). Moving the object 8 cm toward the focus puts it at 24 cm, which is between F (16 cm) and C (32 cm). The image is then real, inverted and magnified, beyond C.
A magnifying glass is a convex lens. An object within its focal length gives a virtual, erect, magnified image.
For a real image from a convex lens, the object-image distance is u + v. Its minimum is 4f, reached when the object is at 2f and the image is at 2f.
Power P = 1/f, so f = 1/2 = 0.5 m. A positive power means a convex (converging) lens, so option 3 is correct.
Rain drops spread sunlight into its colours by refraction and dispersion, as in a rainbow. A plane mirror or lens alone does not do this.
In long-sightedness (hypermetropia) the eyeball is short or the lens is too weak, so the image of a near object forms behind the retina. A convex lens corrects it.
Presbyopia is age-related loss of near vision, and in many cases distance vision also needs correction. Bifocal lenses, which combine concave and convex parts, are commonly used for it.
The notes give 1 C as the unit of charge (1 C = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons). The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb.
Potential difference is defined as the work done per unit charge in moving it between two points in a circuit. Current, power and resistance are defined differently.
Direct current flows steadily in one direction and does not alternate. Its frequency is therefore zero, unlike AC (50 Hz in India).
Ohm's law relates potential difference (V) and current (I) through a conductor: V = IR at constant temperature.
Ohm's law is not universal. Many materials and devices (semiconductors, diodes, strong fields) deviate from it, so the claim that all homogeneous materials obey it is wrong.
Resistance is measured in ohms. Volt is potential difference and ampere is current.
Resistivity is the inverse of conductivity, and R = ρl/A. With the same l and A, aluminium has lower conductivity, so it has higher resistivity and higher resistance than copper.
Manganin and constantan have resistivity that is almost unchanged with temperature. This is why they are used in standard resistors.
Superconductors offer zero resistance to current below a critical temperature. Option 3 states this property.
Resistors in parallel are connected across the same two points. They therefore have the same potential difference, while the current divides.
The metal cap of a dry cell is its positive terminal, and the zinc case is the negative terminal.
An ammeter, connected in series, measures electric current. A voltmeter measures potential difference. A galvanometer only detects small currents.
Notes state that between 2011 and 2015 more than 90 million people were lifted out of poverty, so option 3 is right and the options showing no change or an increase are wrong.
The Tendulkar estimate of all-India poverty for 2011-12 is 21.9% (rural 25.7%, urban 13.7%), so option 3 is correct.
Uttar Pradesh had the largest number of poor in 2011-12 (about 5.98 crore). Bihar is the tempting wrong option because it has the highest MPI, not the most poor people.
IKP stands for Indira Kranthi Patham, the name given to Velugu, which works through women's organisations and livelihoods for BPL households. The other spellings are not the correct full form.
SERP stands for Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty, which mobilises the rural poor into women's SHGs and livelihoods. The other options are invented expansions.
Alfred Weber proposed the least-cost theory of industrial location (1909). Christaller is known for central place theory, not industrial location.
Lorraine is in France and Midland is in the UK, which fixes options with A-4 and B-3. Kiruna is in Sweden (C-1) and Kokshetau in Kazakhstan (D-2), giving 4 3 1 2.
Chelyabinsk is an iron and steel centre in the Ural region of Russia, not a shipbuilding centre; shipbuilding centres are Glasgow, Yokohama and Hamburg. The other pairs are correct.
Camden is a shipbuilding centre in New Jersey, not Florida, so this pair is incorrectly matched.
The Industrial Revolution began in England around 1750, helped by coal, iron ore, canals and rail, as seen in the Midlands.
The iron industry symbolised the British industrial revolution from the 1780s is the statement marked not correct; the notes do not settle the date, but the other statements are standard facts.
Japan is a leading industrial country through high technology despite imported minerals and energy, so it lacks abundant minerals.
The Ruhr lies in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, and is known for coal, steel and chemicals.
Southern New England is in the USA (the oldest US industrial region), not the United Kingdom, so this match is wrong.
The Ruhr is a major industrial region with coal, steel and chemicals, so industrial activity is its main activity.
The objectives of procurement and PDS are price stability, assured MSP, affordable grain and protecting consumers and farmers. Controlling the production of foodgrains is not among them.
OSM stands for Online Storage Management, the digital system launched from 1 April 2022 for storage, movement and distribution under TPDS.

FCI's missions are procurement at MSP, storage and distribution, buffer stocks and grain at reasonable prices via TPDS. Regulating agricultural markets is done by State APMC laws, so it is not an FCI mission.
MSP is a floor price fixed before sowing, so it is an example of a price floor. A ration-shop price is a subsidised issue price and an MRP is a ceiling, so neither is a floor.
The procurement price is the price at which the government actually buys grain. MSP is the floor price announced before sowing and the issue price is what the Centre charges States.
The ONORC rollout target date was 1 June 2020, so the answer is 1st June.

AP ended MDU door delivery and restored distribution from fair price shops from 1 June 2025. Door delivery remains only for those above 65 and the disabled, so doorstep delivery is not a prominent feature.
AP has 29,796 fair price shops, which is approximately 29,000 (option 2).
The Mother Goddess (Devi Mata) cult, shown by terracotta female figurines and probably the main deity, belongs to the Indus Valley Civilisation and later continued as Shakti cults.
The Indus people worshipped a proto-Shiva figure (Pashupati), so Shiva is correct. Indra and Varuna are Rig Vedic gods, not Harappan.
The notes do not state which bird was worshipped; the answer is pigeon (dove) per the exam key.

BoP is a systematic record of all economic transactions between residents and the rest of the world over a period, normally a year; of the options, the import-export record is the closest fit, while the others cover only parts (goods exports, government dealings, capital movements).
BoP is a systematic and complete record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world in a period. Exports minus imports is the balance of trade, not BoP.

The current account covers goods, services, income and transfers, while capital receipts and payments (loans, FDI, portfolio investment) belong to the capital account, so option 4 is not part of the current account.
Foreign loans, FDI and portfolio investment are capital account items. Private remittances are current account transfers (invisibles), so any option including III is wrong.
CAD arises when payments exceed receipts on the current account, i.e. total imports exceed total exports (goods, services, transfers and income).

In 2013-14 India had a trade deficit and positive net invisibles, and the capital account was in surplus (net inflows) financing the CAD. So the claim that the capital account balance was negative is incorrect.
Hampi, the Vijayanagara capital on the Tungabhadra, preserves the empire's monuments and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site; Bijapur and Golconda were Deccan sultanate centres.
Hampi lies on the Tungabhadra's southern bank in Vijayanagara district, Karnataka.
The Virupaksha temple is at Hampi in Karnataka, not Thiruvananthapuram, so this pair is wrongly matched; the other pairs are correct.
The Virupaksha (Pampapati) temple is the first and largest temple of Hampi.
During free fall from 20 m, after 5 m the body has lost 5/20 = one-fourth of its initial potential energy, which has become kinetic energy while total mechanical energy stays constant.
In free fall, potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, so the decrease in potential energy equals the increase in kinetic energy.
As a swing rises from rest position it slows down, so kinetic energy decreases while its height, and thus potential energy, increases.
A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy; a generator converts mechanical to electrical, and a transformer only changes voltage.
A dry cell stores energy in chemical bonds and converts that chemical energy into electrical energy.
Rogun Dam in Tajikistan (about 335 m) is the world's highest dam, taller than Bhakra and the other options.
Silent Valley is in Kerala, associated with the movement led by Salim Ali and others to save it.
Medha Patkar led the Narmada Bachao Andolan against the Sardar Sarovar dam.
Kiru Hydroelectric Project (624 MW) is on the Chenab in Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir.
Idukki is a hydroelectric project in Kerala, not a thermal station, so I is wrong; Sabarigiri (hydro), Ghatprabha (irrigation) and Ramganga (multipurpose) are correctly matched.
Koyna in Maharashtra is a major hydroelectric station (1,960 MW); Neyveli and Trombay are thermal.
Chutak Hydro Power Station (44 MW) is on the Suru river in Kargil district, Jammu and Kashmir.
Tapovan-Vishnugad and Vishnugad-Pipalkoti hydroelectric projects are on the Alaknanda/Dhauliganga in Chamoli, Uttarakhand.
Hotspots are defined by high plant endemism together with a high degree of threat (habitat loss), so option 1 is right; the other options ignore the threat criterion.

The hotspot concept originated with Norman Myers and was adopted by Conservation International, not BirdLife International, so statement II is wrong. Statements I and III (BirdLife is a global partnership that identifies Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas) are correct, giving I and III only.
Eastern Himalayas and the Western Ghats are both global hotspots in India (the older two-hotspot framing). Eastern Ghats, the Deccan Plateau, the Sundarbans and the Thar Desert are not hotspots.
The Andaman Islands fall in the Indo-Burma hotspot and the Nicobar Islands in Sundaland, so Andaman and Nicobar is a hotspot region. The Gangetic plains and Central India are not hotspots.
The Eastern Himalayas is a hotspot in India. The Mediterranean Basin is a hotspot, but North-Western Australia is not, so the question's options II and III are not both correct and only I stands.

On a conflict between Union/Concurrent and State law, the order of predominance is Union > Concurrent > State, so the Concurrent List prevails (Art. 254(1) makes the repugnant State law void). No referral to the Speaker or President is involved.
Parliament's legislative power is limited by the distribution of powers under Art. 246 and the Seventh Schedule lists. UNO constitution, conventions and public opinion are not legal limits.
Legislative relations (Arts 245-255) fall in Part XI, which covers Arts 245-263. Part XIII deals with trade and commerce, and Art. 248 is in Part XI, not XII.

The notes do not cover Jammu and Kashmir's special status, so no line settles it. Option 4 is the wrong statement because residuary power did not vest in Parliament for J&K as it does for other States.
Art. 248 together with Union Entry 97 vests residuary powers exclusively in Parliament. The States hold them only in the USA and Australia.
Under Art. 250, during a National Emergency Parliament can legislate on State List matters, and such laws lapse 6 months after the Emergency ends. So option 3 is right, and options 2 and 4 are wrong.

Under Art. 252, Parliament may legislate on State List subjects when the legislatures of two or more States pass resolutions requesting it. So a resolution passed by the States is the correct option. The President's assent, or any situation, is not the trigger.
Dastar-bandan (turban-wearers) denotes the Ulema, whereas Kulah-daran (cap-wearers) were the Sayyids; the two should not be swapped.
Sone is the unit of perceived loudness, whereas the decibel measures sound level (intensity), not perceived loudness. The notes do not state this fact.
Noise is measured in decibels (dB); hertz measures frequency and nanometer is a unit of length.
Rustling leaves are about 20 dB, so option 2 is correct.

GloLitter Partnerships is an IMO-FAO initiative, not UNEP, so statement I is wrong; statement II is also not supported as stated, since the project targets sea-based litter from shipping and fisheries rather than all sources. Hence neither is correct.
Radioactivity causes DNA damage and mutations (hereditary changes) and carcinogenesis. The mineral imbalance in soil in statement II is not a recognised effect, so the answer is I, III and IV.
Chernobyl (1986) was a nuclear reactor accident that released radioactive material, so it is radioactive pollution, not oil spill, acid rain or CO2.
MRDS stands for Mobile Radiation Detection Systems, the NDMA plan to detect orphan radioactive material in metros and State capitals.
MRDS stands for Mobile Radiation Detection Systems, the NDMA plan to detect orphan radioactive sources.

India's first Dark Sky Reserve is Hanle in Ladakh (not Himachal Pradesh), so IV is wrong. II is wrong because Mont-Mégantic is in Canada, and the certifier is DarkSky International, so none of the statements is correct as given.
Land Degradation Neutrality (no net loss of land health) is targeted by 2030 under SDG 15.3, so 2030 is correct.
Heavy sand mining lowers the riverbed and the water table and can pollute groundwater, so II and III are correct; it does not decrease salinity (statement I is wrong).
Gully erosion in clayey soil creates badlands, called ravines in the Chambal basin, so Chambal basin is known for bad land topography.
Deforestation causes soil erosion, loss of fertility and desertification, whereas urbanisation is a cause of land-use change rather than an impact of deforestation.
The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is observed on 17 June (UNGA 1994).
Chipko was a forest/tree-protection movement in Chamoli, Uttarakhand (1973), so it relates to plant conservation, not tigers, crocodiles or plant reproduction.
The notes list both Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna as Chipko leaders, so Bahuguna is an accepted answer here, though the question is ambiguous.
Veeresalingam is called the Father of the Andhra Renaissance and wrote Rajasekhara Charitra (1878), the first Telugu novel. Venkataratnam Naidu was a Brahmo/anti-nautch leader, not its author.
In 1906 Veeresalingam founded the Hitakarini Samajam and gave it all his property.
Veeresalingam is listed as the founder of the Brahmo Samaj in united Andhra, with Venkataratnam Naidu spreading it.
Veeresalingam founded Vivekavardhini in 1874, the first Telugu social-reform journal, to promote reform and women's education.

Veeresalingam promoted education for all, including girls' schools, a night school and co-education, so universal education fits his philosophy. The other options contradict his scientific and cultural reform aims.
Veeresalingam founded the Rajahmundry Social Reform Association in 1878, the first organised reform body in Andhra, which aided widows. Vidyasagar worked in Bengal.
The notes do not mention the 'Apna Van Apna Dhan' scheme. It was launched by Himachal Pradesh, so option (3) is correct.
Gandhara art, with its Greek-style Buddha images, developed under the Kushanas, so Kushans is correct. The Guptas, Akbar and the Mauryas are not linked with the Gandhara school.
The Manusmriti called foreigners such as the Shakas and Kushans who did not follow priestly customs 'Fallen Kshatriyas'.
Vima Kadphises was the first to issue gold on a large scale, for regular use. Menander only issued gold coins rarely, so he is the tempting wrong option.
Kujula Kadphises (Kadphises I) was a Kushan ruler. Vikramaditya, Dantidurga and Pushyamitra belong to other dynasties.
The Kushanas came from Central Asia and held Kabul valley and Bactrian regions beyond India. They traded across Han China, Rome and India, so their empire extended outside India.
The Fourth Buddhist Council was patronised by Kanishka. Ashoka patronised the Third Council.
The Fourth Buddhist Council at Kashmir was held under the patronage of Kanishka. Ashoka patronised the third, Kalasoka the second and Ajatasatru the first.
Ashvaghosha, Parshva and Vasumitra were scholars of Kanishka's court. Vishakhadatta is expressly listed as not in his court.
The Buddhacharita was composed by Ashvaghosha, not Nagarjuna.
Charaka was Kanishka's court physician and wrote the Charaka Samhita. Vasumitra and Nagarjuna were Buddhist scholars, and Patanjali belonged to the Shunga period.
Ashvaghosha was Kanishka's court poet and vice-president of the Fourth Council held under him, so he was Kanishka's contemporary.
The Kushana period is best known for art, notably the first Buddha images in the Gandhara and Mathura schools.

Errana wrote the Nrusimha (Narasimha) Puranam, along with the Harivamsam and the completion of the Aranya Parva. Potana and Srinatha wrote other works, and Bana (Vamana Bhatta Bana) wrote Sanskrit and Telugu works such as the Vema Bhupala Charitra.

Errana (Errapragada) was the court poet of Prolaya Vema Reddi and dedicated his Harivamsam to him. The Vidyadhikari post belonged to Srinatha under Pedakomati Vema, not Errana, but the option that fits Errana's patron is Prolaya Vema.

Statement I is correct: Ayyavole-500 originated from Aihole in Karnataka. Statement II is wrong: the notes describe Manigramam as a foreign/long-distance trade corporation, and nothing says it was subordinated to the Anjuvannam, a guild of West Asian merchants.

Kyrgyzstan's President Sadyr Japarov signed a decree on 30 December 2023 recognising the snow leopard as the country's national symbol. Kazakhstan, Mozambique and DR Congo are not linked to this decree.
Papua New Guinea's PM James Marape became the first Pacific leader to address Australia's Parliament on 8 February 2024.
GLONASS is owned by Russia, not the United Kingdom, so the pair GLONASS-United Kingdom is wrongly matched. The other pairs (GPS-USA, Galileo-EU, NavIC-India) are correct.
Galileo belongs to the European Union, not the USA, so USA-Galileo is the incorrect match. India-IRNSS, China-BeiDou and Russia-GLONASS are correct.
NavIC stands for Navigation with Indian Constellation; it was formerly called IRNSS.
Statement I is correct: IRNSS has 3 GEO and 4 inclined GSO satellites. II is wrong because coverage extends about 1,500 km beyond India's borders. III is wrong because NavIC is regional, not global.
Elena Geo Systems launched India's first NavIC-based device, which gives precise directions for infrastructure projects.
Elena Geo Systems launched India's first NavIC-based device, which gives precise directions for infrastructure projects.
GPS-type satellite navigation and timing is used in telecom (mobile phone networks), banking and power systems, so all three areas apply.
Muslims (Islam) grew 24.6% between 2001 and 2011, the highest of any religious community, against 16.8% for Hindus, 15.5% for Christians and 8.4% for Sikhs. So Islam is correct.
A podcast is a radio-style programme shared as digital audio over the internet for streaming or download. Internet radio and digital broadcast refer to live transmission, not shared programmes.
FCP is Final Cut Pro, Apple's professional non-linear video editing software, so it is used for video production.
Disney bought most of 21st Century Fox's film and TV assets, including the studio, in a deal completed in 2019. The notes do not cover this.

Friendster and Flickr are social networks, while Funny or Die is a comedy video site that is also commonly counted as social media. Since none of the three is wrongly listed here, the answer is 'None of these'.

Article 21 secures the right to life and personal liberty, and in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) the Supreme Court held privacy to be intrinsic to them. So option 4 is correct, while options 1-3 each leave something out.

The Inter-Creditor Agreement (July 2018, under Project Sashakt) covers loans of ₹50 crore+ with multiple lenders and binds all lenders once 66% approve, so it speeds up resolution of stressed assets under consortium lending; it is not a regulator or a fiscal measure.
The Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) uses the single emergency number 112. The other numbers are not the ERSS number, and CSCs have no link with it.

CARD (Computer-aided Administration of Registration Department, 1998) computerised the registration of land and property deeds. MeeSeva is a G2C service centre and Spandana is a grievance-status platform, so neither fits.

At the 20th NCeG (Visakhapatnam, Jan 2017) AP won Gold in citizen-centric service delivery for the Aadhaar-enabled PDS. The Loan Charge Creation project won Gold in a different category, process re-engineering.
After one half-life (10 days) half remains; after two (20 days) a quarter remains, so 3/4 has decayed. The element never fully disintegrates, so options 1 and 2 are wrong.
Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few mm of aluminium, and gamma only by lead or concrete. Penetrating power therefore increases in the order alpha, beta, gamma.
A gas-cooled reactor uses graphite as the moderator and carbon dioxide gas as the coolant. The notes do not cover this reactor type.
A moderator slows fast neutrons so that U-235 can fission. Absorbing neutrons and controlling the rate is the job of the control rods.
Control rods absorb neutrons and regulate the reaction rate. Without them the chain reaction goes out of bounds, so it would not stop or slow down.
A fast breeder reactor breeds more fissile material than it burns, as U-238 is converted to Pu-239. It is Stage II of the programme, not Stage I, so statement III is wrong.
Thorium is more abundant than uranium, gives more energy per unit mass mined, and produces less harmful waste. All three statements are therefore correct.
The PFBR was designed by IGCAR but built and commissioned by BHAVINI. The question asks who developed it, and the key is BHAVINI.
A breeder reactor produces more fissile material than it burns. Fast neutrons convert the fertile U-238 blanket into Pu-239.
A fast breeder reactor generates electricity by nuclear fission, while its fertile blanket breeds more fissile material. It does not use solar cells, fossil burning or hard water as fuel.
Fast breeder reactors, including the FBTR at Kalpakkam, use liquid sodium as the coolant and have no moderator.
A velodrome is a track built for cycling events, so the answer is Cycling.
Triples is a newer format in badminton, played as one player against two, so the answer is Badminton.
The Melbourne Cricket Ground is the largest cricket stadium in the world by capacity. Perth Stadium, Lord's and Eden Gardens are smaller.
Virat Kohli scored double hundreds in four consecutive Test series (2016-17 to 2017-18), a record no other batsman has matched.
Baseball is regarded as the national pastime or national game of the USA.
India won its first World Cup in 1983 under captain Kapil Dev.
Switzerland minted a commemorative coin for Roger Federer, the Swiss tennis star.

Lionel Messi won the FIFA Best Men's Player award in 2019, ahead of Virgil van Dijk and Cristiano Ronaldo.

A flagrant foul is a basketball term. Uppercut belongs to boxing, penalty corner to hockey and bicycle kick to football.
Tiger Woods is a famous professional golfer.

Kolinda Grabar-Kitarović was President of Croatia and attended the 2018 World Cup final.

Libero is a defensive specialist position in volleyball.

Nicolo de Conti was an Italian who visited under Devaraya I (1420-21); the question's Devaraya II premise is loose, but Conti is the only Italian among the options linked to Vijayanagara's early rulers (Varthema came under Krishnadevaraya).

Abdur Razzaq was the Persian envoy of Shah Rukh who visited Devaraya II in 1443; Conti was Italian, Barbosa Portuguese and Nikitin Russian.
Caesar Frederick, a Venetian, visited in 1567 and saw the ruined capital after Talikota. Razzaq, Conti and Nuniz came earlier.
After Uttar Pradesh, the most populous State is Maharashtra (about 11.24 crore), followed by Bihar, West Bengal and undivided AP.
