Santos in Brazil is the world's chief coffee-exporting port; São Paulo and Rio are not known by this name.
San Francisco is known as the city of the Golden Gate, named for the Golden Gate Bridge and strait.
Venice is not a shipbuilding centre. Detroit is the motor city and Cuba (Havana) is known for cigars. Notes list Glasgow, Yokohama, Hamburg and St. Petersburg for shipbuilding.
Anshan is an iron and steel centre, Detroit is the motor city (automobile), Havana (Cuba) is known for cigars, and Nagoya (Japan) is a textile centre. This gives A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1.
In a tornado, air spirals inward toward the centre and, by conservation of angular momentum, its rotational (angular) speed increases as the radius shrinks.

Thunderclouds (cumulonimbus) develop in unstable, warm, moist air with strong convection; condensation, high temperature and humidity, orographic lifting and vertical winds all contribute, so all four apply.
North Atlantic tropical cyclones are called hurricanes; typhoons belong to the NW Pacific and tornadoes are small land funnels.
The Philippines' local name for tropical cyclones is Baguio (Bagyo); typhoon is the broader NW Pacific term and willy-willy is Australian.
Tornadoes are rated on the Fujita scale, now used as the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale, the current standard. Beaufort measures wind force and Saffir-Simpson hurricanes.
IMD calls a system a Cyclonic Storm when winds are 62-88 km/h (the exam option 63-88 is the matching range); the other ranges are higher categories.
A tropical cyclone has winds at or above 62 km/h (34 knots), the threshold for a cyclonic storm and naming.
Tornadoes are rated on the Fujita scale, now used as the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale, the current standard. Beaufort measures wind force and Saffir-Simpson hurricanes.
The Saffir-Simpson scale (Cat 1-5) categorizes hurricanes by wind speed; Richter and moment magnitude measure earthquakes.
Hathras and Kanpur are known as styles of Hindi folk theatre (Nautanki), so the answer is Theatre; the notes do not cover this.
Alibaksh Khyal is a Rajasthani khyal theatre tradition of Alwar, so Alwar is correct; the notes do not cover this.

Kuchipudi, named after Kuchipudi village in Krishna district and founded by Siddhendra Yogi, is Andhra's classical dance. Kathakali is Kerala's, Kathak is North Indian and Bharatanatyam is Tamil Nadu's.
Polycot (polyester-cotton), polywool (polyester-wool) and terrycot (terry-cotton) are all polyester blends, so all three may contain polyester.
Soap molecules form micelles, with dirt trapped in the centre. Micelles are colloidal in size and do scatter light, so statement II is wrong.
Chlorine bleaches by oxidation: it forms hypochlorous acid, which releases nascent oxygen that oxidises coloured matter. Redox is tempting, but oxidation is the bleaching step.
Cement sets and hardens through hydration of its compounds, so the answer given is hydration and dissociation of water.
UV radiation only inactivates or kills microorganisms. It does not remove odours or speed sedimentation, so only statement I is correct.
The refrigerator releases heat at the condenser outside, and the compressor also adds heat. With the door open, the room is heated rather than cooled.
In a pressure cooker the higher pressure raises the boiling point of water (~120 C), so food cooks faster.
The tungsten filament slowly evaporates (sublimes) when hot, so it thins and the bulb dims.
Tungsten (W) has the highest melting point of the metals, so it is used for bulb filaments.
Silica gel absorbs moisture and is the standard desiccant. Polystyrene is a plastic, and NaCl and sodium carbonate are not used as desiccants.
Iodine (tincture of iodine) is a standard antiseptic; potassium nitrate and potassium chloride are not.
On strong heating, sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) decomposes to sodium carbonate, water and CO2.
Baking soda is NaHCO3, whose chemical name is sodium hydrogen carbonate. Sodium carbonate is washing soda.
Slaked lime is Ca(OH)2, calcium hydroxide, formed when quicklime (CaO) reacts with water.
Washing soda is Na2CO3, sodium carbonate. Sodium bicarbonate is baking soda.
Toothpaste is basic (alkaline) and neutralises the acid produced by bacteria in the mouth, which prevents tooth decay.
Soft soap is made with potassium hydroxide, so it contains potassium. Hard soaps use sodium.
Slaked lime is calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2. CaO is quicklime and CaCO3 is limestone.
Lawsone, the dye in henna, binds to keratin proteins and amino acids in skin and hair, giving the orange-red stain.
Overloading is prevented by all of these: a fuse, limiting the number of appliances on one circuit, and keeping faulty appliances out. So all options are correct.

Section 85 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 provides for the Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards, so Section 85 is correct. Sections 95, 80 and 60 deal with other matters (e.g. Sec. 95 covers admission quotas).
Section 46(2) of the AP Reorganisation Act provides for Central grants to meet the resource gap of residual Andhra Pradesh. The other sections do not deal with this.

The 2014 Bill proposed consequential amendments to the Representation of the People Act, 1950, which governs electoral rolls and seat allocation. This is why 1950 is correct; the 1951 Act is not among the options.

Statement I is correct: Tilak's Indian Home Rule League was founded on 28 April 1916 and based at Poona, before Besant's League of September 1916. Statement II is not supported: the notes record no Congress resolution demanding Home Rule at Bombay in 1915, and Home Rule supporters only showed their strength at Lucknow in 1916. So only statement I is correct.

Residuary powers lie with the Union in India and with the States in the USA, so I and II are not common to both. Statement III (pocket veto) is the only common feature, so the answer is 'Only III'. The notes do not cover the pocket veto or nominated members.

The quote about a daily as well as a periodic assessment of the Government is by B.R. Ambedkar, who argued in the Constituent Assembly that the parliamentary system gives responsibility, with the executive assessed daily by the legislature and periodically by the electorate. The notes mention only his preference for responsibility over stability, not this quote.
Digital India was launched on 1 July 2015 (it completed 11 years in 2026), so option 3 is correct; the other dates do not match its launch.

PURVODAYA is a development plan for five eastern States and includes the Buxar–Bhagalpur expressway, so I and II are correct. Its focus is eastern India, not Gujarat, so IV is wrong; the notes do not mention a New Delhi–Kolkata corridor, so III is not supported.
The programme launched on 10 October 2019 to nurture talented children is Dhruv. The notes do not cover it, so no line is linked.

Merz, the 10th Chancellor (6 May 2025), failed to win in the first Bundestag round and was elected only in the second round, which had not happened since World War II. He was not elected by popular vote; the Chancellor is chosen by the Bundestag.
Pasupu Kumkuma was an Andhra Pradesh scheme giving one-time financial assistance to women members of Self-Help Groups (SHGs). The notes do not mention this scheme, so no line is linked.
Robotics is the exam-keyed technology most closely associated with artificial intelligence; biotechnology, nanotechnology and space exploration are not.
Pratham, the world's first no-code computer-vision platform, was launched by Assert AI; the other companies are not linked to it.
Oncology.ai was developed by AIIMS with C-DAC for early detection of breast and ovarian cancer. CAIR is a DRDO lab and is not the partner.
Oncology.ai was developed by AIIMS with C-DAC for early detection of breast and ovarian cancer. CAIR is a DRDO lab and is not the partner.
Pratham, the world's first no-code computer-vision platform, was launched by Assert AI; the other companies are not linked to it.
Indrajaal, India's first AI-powered anti-drone system, was developed by Grene Robotics of Hyderabad, so the city is Hyderabad.
Kevlar is an aramid (para-aromatic polyamide) fibre used in bulletproof vests. Nylon 6,6, rayon and Dacron are not used for this.
Kevlar, a strong aramid fibre, is used in bulletproof jackets and vests. Nylon, Terylene and Tweed are not used for this.
Kevlar, an aramid fibre, is used in lightweight bulletproof helmets and jackets. Terylene and nylon are not used for this.
The 3D-printed cornea came from IIT Hyderabad with LV Prasad Eye Institute and CCMB. The 3D-printed human liver tissue came from Pandorum Technologies, Bengaluru.
One carbon credit equals one tonne of CO2e avoided or removed; one tonne is 1000 kg of carbon dioxide, not carbon, so option 4 is correct.

New Zealand was the first country to propose a tax on agricultural (livestock) emissions. Denmark was the first to actually levy one, from 2030, so it is the tempting alternative, but it is not among the options.

Parliament's control tools include questions, resolutions and no-confidence motions, but dissolution of the House is not one of them; it is not a device of legislative control over the administration.
Zero Hour is an informal Indian innovation (1962) and is not in the Rules of Procedure. Calling attention, half-an-hour and short-duration discussions are all formally provided for.
Parliament controls the administration mainly through Parliamentary Committees. Consultative Committees are not parliamentary committees, and Parliament cannot issue writs.
Zero Hour is the time right after Question Hour, when members raise matters without prior notice. Option 3 describes this.
No time is fixed for Zero Hour in the Rules; it lasts at most one hour, so the maximum is one hour.
In the Lok Sabha Zero Hour comes immediately after Question Hour (12 noon to 1 PM), when matters are raised without prior notice.
The notes give 20 starred questions a day and 30 Rule 377 matters, but no figure for Zero Hour matters. By the usual practice, 20 matters per day are taken up in Zero Hour by ballot priority.

The White Paper is the official Government of India document explaining policy, so 'White Book' as official reports of India is the wrongly matched pair. India does not use the 'White Book' label in this way.
Rule 193 covers a short-duration discussion with no formal motion and no vote. Rule 184 is the one involving a motion and a vote.
Rule 377 allows matters that cannot be raised under any other device to be raised in the Lok Sabha, with the Speaker's consent.
The notes list the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act as 1856, so option (1) is correct. 1850 is the Lex Loci/Religious Disabilities Act, which is a different law.
The revolt began as a sepoy mutiny: Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore, the 19th NI at Berhampur and then the Meerut sepoys on 10 May 1857. Zamindars, peasants and plantation workers joined later.

The Enfield cartridges, rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, made sepoys suspect British interference in their religion, and this triggered the revolt. The Doctrine of Lapse, military discontent and economic exploitation were long-term causes, not the immediate one.

Under Section 30 of the PHRA, the State Government, with the concurrence of the HC Chief Justice, notifies a Court of Session in each district as a Human Rights Court for speedy trial. Collectorates, Panchayats and Gram Sabhas are not courts.
Arasavalli (Srikakulam) is the Sun (Surya) temple; Amarkantak and Omkareshwar are not known for Sun temples (Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga), so only I is correct.
Shiva has 12 Jyotirlingas in tradition (e.g. Srisailam in Andhra Pradesh), so 12 is correct.
Shiva has 12 Jyotirlingas in tradition (e.g. Srisailam in Andhra Pradesh), so 12 is correct.
FAO stands for Food and Agriculture Organisation (headquartered in Rome); the other options are not real organisations.
IAAF (now World Athletics) is headquartered in Monaco; the notes do not cover it.
Angkor Wat is in Cambodia (formerly Kampuchea), so option 4 is correct.
Jesus Christ is traditionally held to have been born in Bethlehem, not Jerusalem.

Manipuri Sankirtana is a song-and-dance performance narrating the life and deeds of Lord Krishna, so I and III are correct. Statement II is wrong because it uses the pung (drum) along with cymbals, not cymbals alone.
Cabo Verde was certified malaria-free by WHO in 2024; the other options were not certified that year.
INTERPOL stands for International Police Organisation (International Criminal Police Organization), headquartered in Lyon.

Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and UAE joined BRICS on 1 Jan 2024. Argentina declined its invitation and Indonesia joined only in 2025. Saudi Arabia was invited and was counted by the question as a member, so option 4 (I, IV, V) is the answer key's choice.

Guntupalli is the centre of the Rajagirika sect, while the Siddharthaka chaitya is at Gudivada. So pairing Guntupalli with Siddharthaka chaitya is the wrong match; the other three sect–centre pairs are correct.
Guntupalli has rock-cut chaityas and viharas, so I is correct. Eastern Deccan chaityas and viharas are usually structural, with Guntupalli the rock-cut exception, so II is wrong.

The notes do not say which religious groups imitated the Buddhist rock-cut chaityas later, or where their temples stood, so no line settles this. Statement I (the Buddhists excavated first and others imitated them later) is the one accepted as correct.
ICRISAT, the international crops research institute, is at Patancheru, Hyderabad, so Hyderabad is correct.
The lumpy skin disease vaccine developed by two ICAR institutes is Lumpi-ProVacInd, so option 2 is correct.
NRCWA is located at Bhubaneswar, so option 3 is correct.
IVRI is at Izatnagar, Bareilly, so Bareilly is correct.
NDRI (dairy) is located at Karnal (since 1955), so Karnal is correct.
The Central Institute of Agricultural Engineering (CIAE) is at Bhopal. The notes do not state this.
CAZRI, the arid zone research institute, is at Jodhpur.
The Central Rice Research Institute (CRRI/NRRI) is at Cuttack, so Cuttack is correct.
The Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) is at Shimla, so Shimla is correct.
The citrus research centre is at Nagpur, so Nagpur is correct.
The Plant Protection Directorate is at Faridabad (NPPTI is at Hyderabad), so Faridabad is correct.
The Bay of Bengal forms Andhra Pradesh's eastern boundary. Telangana and Chhattisgarh lie to the west and north, and Odisha to the north.
The alluvial deltas of the Godavari and Krishna form the coastal plain called the 'Rice Bowl'. The other regions listed are not the deltaic Rice Bowl.
Sriharikota island, home to the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, lies in Andhra Pradesh. It cuts off Pulicat Lake from the Bay of Bengal.

The Eastern Ghats are cut by the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, and they run on to join the Western Ghats near the Nilgiris. So they stretch from the Mahanadi valley to the Nilgiris. Mahendragiri is only the northern start within AP.
The Tirumala, Kalvarayan, Garhjat and Shevaroy hills are all parts of the Eastern Ghats.
AP's bauxite reserves lie mainly in the Eastern Ghats, in the khondalite hills.
The Tirumala, Kalvarayan, Garhjat and Shevaroy hills are all parts of the Eastern Ghats.
Velikonda is an Eastern Ghats range in the Nellore–Tirupati (Prakasam side) area of AP. Javadi hills lie in Tamil Nadu, so option 3 is wrong.
Red Sanders is endemic to the Seshachalam range, which includes the Tirumala hills and the Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve.
The Velikonda range lies in the SPSR Nellore–Tirupati (Prakasam side) area of Andhra Pradesh. It is the easternmost of the southern ranges of the Eastern Ghats.
Arma Konda, Gali Konda and Sinkram Gutta are peaks of the Eastern Ghats, in the northern Ghats of AP.
Arma Konda (1,680 m) at Chintapalli in ASR district is the highest peak of AP. Galikonda and Sinkram Gutta are lower, and Jindhagada is often treated as the same summit.
The Human Poverty Index was introduced in the Human Development Report of 1997 (and was later replaced by the MPI in 2010). 1995 relates to GDI/GEM, not HPI.
India's GII rank was 108 in the 2023-24 report (HDR 2025 notes 102nd, 'up from 108'), so 108 is correct for 2022; 102 is the later HDR 2025 rank.
HDI covers health (long, healthy life), knowledge and a decent standard of living. Discounting for loss due to inequality is done by the separate IHDI, so option 4 is not part of the HDI itself.
UN Women proposed partnering with Kerala's Gender Park (in Kozhikode) to promote gender parity in South Asia; the notes do not cover this.
Distribution of revenues between the Union and States (Arts 268-281) is based on Finance Commission recommendations, not the Finance Ministry, RBI or NABARD.
Non-agricultural income tax is levied by the Union and shared with the States under Art. 270 (divisible pool); it is not wholly kept by the Centre nor wholly given away.
Excise on liquor is a State subject; States levy it and keep the revenue.
Under Art. 268, stamp duties are levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States; estate duty and newspaper taxes were moved to the Art. 270 pool.
The GST Council under Art. 279A is chaired by the Union Finance Minister.
The Finance Commission (Art. 280) recommends the sharing of tax revenue between the Centre and States; NITI Aayog, the Inter-State Council and the NDC do not.
Ibn Battuta was born at Tangiers in Morocco (1304), so Morocco is correct; Persia and Afghanistan are not his origin.
Al-Biruni, a scholar from Khwarizm, came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni and wrote Kitab-ul-Hind. Ibn Battuta, Khusrau and Ferishta belong to other periods.
Al-Biruni wrote Tahqiq-i-Hind, Minhaj-us-Siraj wrote Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi and Ibn Battuta wrote the Rihla. This gives a-II, b-IV, c-I, d-III.
Ibn Battuta's Rihla was written during his stay in India (1333-1342) under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, so it throws light on that reign. Bernier, Manucci and Tavernier were Mughal-era travellers.
The chronological order is Kitab-ul-Hind (c. 1030), Prithviraj Raso (late 12th c.), Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (c. 1260), then Fatawa-i-Jahandari (14th c.), which gives III, II, IV, I.
Khazain-ul-Futuh, on Alauddin Khalji's conquests, was written by Amir Khusrau. Hasan Nizami wrote Taj-ul-Maasir and Minhaj wrote Tabaqat-i-Nasiri.
Amir Khusrau is called the Father of Khari Boli, as his Hindavi verses and riddles led to Rekhta/Urdu. So Khari Boli is correct.
The notes do not mention reserved seats for women. The 1935 Act reserved seats for women in the legislatures in line with the communal allocation, while the 1909 and 1919 Acts did not.

The federal scheme of the 1935 Act, with its Union-State structure, is the source of the Constitution's Centre-State distribution of powers. The 1919 Act only separated central and provincial lists within a unitary set-up.

The Atlas range lies in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, i.e. north-western Africa, so this pair is correct. The Abyssinian Plateau is in Africa (Ethiopia), the Guiana Highlands in northern South America, and the Okavango Basin in Botswana, not Patagonia.
The Caucasus lies between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, forming the Europe-Asia divide with Elbrus as its highest peak.
The Darling Range is a low escarpment in Western Australia running near the south-western coast (near Perth), so the South-Western Coast is correct.
Black Mountain is a name used in the USA (e.g. the Black Mountains of North Carolina, with Mount Mitchell, and Black Mountain in Kentucky), so USA is the answer.
Mount Titlis is a peak in the Swiss Alps in central Switzerland, near Engelberg.
Rajasuya, Ashvamedha and Vajapeya are the royal sacrifices by which kings asserted supremacy; Muvendavelan is not a sacrifice but a title, so it is the odd one out.
Bali was the regular, compulsory tribute paid to the king in this period (earlier it was voluntary). Vidatha was an assembly that vanished, not a tax.
The term 'ecosystem' was coined by the British botanist A.G. Tansley in 1935, so option 4 is correct.
Air is part of the atmosphere, a physical (abiotic) component; plants, bacteria and animals are biotic components.
Crop fields, parks and villages are artificial ecosystems, whereas ponds and forests are natural ones, so a field is the artificial ecosystem.
Phytoplankton, seaweeds and chemosynthetic bacteria (vents, active volcanoes) are producers, which occupy the first trophic level.
The notes state that the marine ecosystem (ocean) is the most stable overall, as it stays unchanged for long periods, unlike forests, mountains or deserts.
Primary consumers are herbivores, which occupy the second trophic level. Ants and deer fit here, whereas fox and tiger are carnivores (higher levels).
Humans are omnivores, eating both plants and animals, so in a food chain man acts as both a primary and a secondary consumer.
Light stays inside the fibre because it undergoes successive total internal reflections at the core boundary, giving the zig-zag path. The other options do not explain this guiding.
Diamond has a very high refractive index and so a small critical angle. Light entering it undergoes repeated total internal reflection, which produces its brilliance.
TIR needs light to go from a denser to a rarer medium. Diamond has a higher refractive index than air, so diamond to air qualifies, while air to water or glass goes rarer to denser.
A desert mirage occurs when light from the sky passes from denser to rarer, hotter air layers near the ground and undergoes total internal reflection. The notes do not cover this.
A sonic boom is the shock-wave bang produced by an object travelling faster than sound, such as a supersonic aircraft. Lasers, radar and reflection are unrelated.
Western education in Andhra was first spread by Christian missionaries, who contributed the most; the Company, officials or public philanthropy did not play this lead role.
Nizam College was founded in 1887 by merging Hyderabad School and Madrasa-i-Aliya, so 1887 is correct; 1885 is the year Fergusson College was founded.

Statements I and III are stated in the notes: TIME named him the world's richest man (about US$2 billion, early 1940s) and he donated to AMU and BHU. Statement II (Santiniketan in Hyderabad) is not supported, so the answer is Only I and III.

Statements I and III are stated in the notes: TIME named him the world's richest man (about US$2 billion, early 1940s) and he donated to AMU and BHU. Statement II (Santiniketan in Hyderabad) is not supported, so the answer is Only I and III.
Joule's law of heating gives H = I²Rt: heat grows with the square of current, with resistance and with time. Options 1 and 3 omit a factor, and option 2 uses I instead of I².
Covering unequal distances in equal time intervals means the velocity is changing, which is non-uniform motion. Uniform motion covers equal distances in equal intervals.
Lateral meristem (vascular cambium and cork cambium) divides sideways and so increases the girth of the stem. Intercalary meristem only increases length.
Persistence of hearing is about 0.1 s, so an echo needs a gap of at least 0.1 s to be heard as distinct from the original sound.
In the taxonomic hierarchy, an order is an assemblage of related families. Species and genus are lower categories, and class is a higher category that groups orders.
For a body at rest the distance stays constant as time passes, so the distance-time graph is a horizontal line with zero slope.
The projectile range R = u²sin2θ/g is maximum when sin2θ = 1, i.e. θ = 45°.
The magnetic meridian is the vertical plane passing through the magnetic axis, that is, through the magnetic north and south poles of the Earth. It is not just a line.
The hierarchy runs Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species, so Phylum-Class-Order-Family-Genus is the correct descending order.
The term meiosis was coined by Farmer and Moore in 1905. Fleming described mitosis.
The stamens (male) and carpels (female) are the reproductive parts of a flower. Sepals and petals are accessory, non-reproductive whorls.
Complex tissues such as xylem and phloem contain more than one cell type, so Statement I is correct. Meristems are dividing tissues, not permanent tissues, so Statement II is wrong.
A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it (Oersted), and this field deflects a nearby compass needle. So II correctly explains I.
The arrangement of leaves on a stem is called phyllotaxy. The other terms are not botanical terms for this.

Equal weights in water means W - buoyant force is equal for the two pieces. Both pieces have the same volume, so the buoyant force is equal, and the weights in air would be equal. The question seems to describe pieces of different volume, though: the denser gold piece has smaller volume, experiences less buoyancy, so it needs a smaller air weight than silver for equal water weights. Hence silver weighs more in air.
The 5th period begins with Rb and ends with Xe and includes the 4d transition series, giving 18 elements.
With no friction, he cannot push against the ground. Sneezing expels air and, by conservation of momentum, pushes him in the opposite direction. Jumping, running and rolling all need friction.
Thomson's atomic model is called the plum pudding model, with electrons embedded in a positively charged sphere like plums in a pudding.

In orbit there is effective weightlessness, so a hanging mass does not stretch the spring. The oscillation period T = 2π√(m/k) depends on mass and not on gravity, so only the oscillation method works.
By Newton's law of cooling, for a small temperature difference the rate of heat loss is proportional to that difference. Doubling the difference doubles the rate.
China denied visas to the Arunachal members of India's delegation to the 1995 Beijing women's conference, since it claims Arunachal as 'South Tibet'. So the state is Arunachal Pradesh.
Doklam (2017) is the standoff at the India-Bhutan-China tri-junction. Aksai Chin is a disputed territory, not a standoff site, and the other options are not listed standoffs.

The Belt and Road Initiative, which includes CPEC passing through PoJK, is the project India objects to on sovereignty and territorial integrity grounds. The other options are not projects India opposes on these grounds.
One Belt One Road (OBOR), now the BRI, was launched by China's Xi Jinping in 2013, so it relates to China.
The UN definition of absolute poverty was set at the World Summit for Social Development held in Copenhagen in 1995, so Copenhagen is the venue.
The UN defined absolute poverty in 1995 at the Copenhagen World Summit for Social Development, so 1995 is correct.
Sirr-i-Akbar (1657) was the Persian translation of about 52 Upanishads by Dara Shikoh, Shah Jahan's eldest son. Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama, so he is the tempting wrong option.
The notes do not state this fact. Ghalib was born in Agra, but he later settled in Delhi, which is the tempting wrong option.

Jadunath Sarkar is the historian best known for his research on Mughal history, especially his multi-volume work on Aurangzeb. Sumit Sarkar and S. Gopal are known for other fields, and Sushobhan Sarkar for Bengal history.

Statement I is right: the Akbarnama's third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari. Statement II is wrong because Abul Fazl wrote all of it, not Akbar. Statement III is right: the Akbarnama and Baburnama are well-known illustrated works.
The notes do not say who gifted the Padshahnama to King George in 1799. The Nawab of Awadh is the correct answer, while Abdul Hamid Lahori only wrote the work.
Dara Shikoh's Persian translation of about 52 Upanishads (1657) was called Sirr-i-Akbar, 'The Great Secret'. Majma-ul-Bahrain is his separate work on Sufism and Vedanta.
Hitopadesha was translated into Persian by Taj-ul-Din Maliki (Tajul Mali) as Mufti-al-Mufarrih-al-Qulub. Dara Shikoh translated the Upanishads, and Faizi and Badauni worked on other texts.
Tulsidas, author of the Ramcharitmanas, was a contemporary of Akbar and Jahangir, so the work belongs to Akbar's reign.
The notes list the Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha, CPI, Unionist Party and princely states as not supporting Quit India, so each named party stayed away and 'All of the above' is correct.
The Muslim League and Hindu Mahasabha did not support Quit India (the League condemned it), so the claim that they actively participated is the incorrect statement.
The notes do not state which historian called the movement a spontaneous revolution. F.G. Hutchins is the historian known for describing Quit India as a 'spontaneous revolution'.
MoEFCC is the Government of India's nodal ministry for UNEP and for environmental policy, which is why option 1 is correct. The other ministries do not handle UNEP matters.
The CPCB was constituted in 1974 under the Water Act, so 1974 is correct.
APPCB was set up in 1976 under the Water Act, and its head office is at Vijayawada with 3 Zonal and 13 Regional offices. Both statements are therefore correct.
Davis Instruments Airlinks is not among the machines in the APPCB scientific division. The UV-Visible Spectrometer, Specific Ion Analyser and AAS are, so option 4 is correct.
The NGT was established for the effective and expeditious disposal of environmental protection and pollution-control cases. Monitoring and standard-setting are CPCB functions, not the NGT's.

Statement I is wrong because the CPCB is a statutory body created under the Water Act 1974, not by an executive order. Statement II is right because the NGT gives environmental justice and eases the litigation burden on higher courts, while the CPCB sets standards and monitors.
The National Environment Tribunal Act was enacted in 1995, but it was never brought into force and was repealed by the NGT Act 2010.

Governors' emoluments are charged on the State fund (Art. 158(3)), not on the Consolidated Fund of India under Art. 112(3). Debt charges, SC judges' salaries and HC judges' pensions are all charged on the CFI.
SC judges' salaries, allowances and pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 112(3), Art. 125).
State PSC expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art. 322). The notes do not state this.
A vote on account is needed when the regular Budget will not pass in time, for example during elections, so that money can be withdrawn from the CFI before the Budget is passed (Art. 116).
Greenland has been Danish territory since 1380, although it is geographically part of North America. Finland, Canada and the UK do not rule it.
Borneo is the largest island in Asia. Indonesia is a country, not an island, so it cannot be the answer.
Honshu is Japan's largest island, at about 228,000 sq km. Hokkaido, Shikoku and Kyushu are smaller.
Greenland, at about 2.17 million sq km, is the world's largest island. Madagascar is only fourth.
Madagascar (587,041 sq km) is the largest island in the Indian Ocean.
New Guinea (785,753 sq km) is larger than Borneo, Madagascar and Sumatra.
Diego Garcia is an island in the Indian Ocean, held by the UK after being part of Mauritius until 1965.
The span from Aceh in northern Sumatra to the Torres Strait describes Indonesia.
Angel Falls, the highest waterfall, is 979 m or 3,212 ft high.
The notes do not cover this fact. The 131 ft indoor waterfall is at Jewel Changi Airport in Singapore.
Wular Lake in J&K is listed as the largest freshwater lake by volume. Vembanad and Chilika are not the largest freshwater lakes, and Chilika is brackish.
Among the four States, UP has the lowest density (829 per sq km in 2011) compared with Bihar 1,106, West Bengal 1,028 and Kerala 860.
Indian textiles faced heavy duties in Britain, which shut them out of the British market and caused their decline. Quality, raw material and craftsmen did not fall short.
The notes do not name Dhaka. Dhaka, a muslin centre, declined as Indian textiles collapsed under British trade policy, while Calcutta, Madras and Bombay grew as colonial ports.
The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly and brought one-way free trade, so British goods flooded India and deindustrialisation intensified. Both statements are correct.
Railways opened Indian markets to cheap British machine goods, accelerating the ruin of town handicrafts. Handicrafts is the broad category that collapsed.
After the Industrial Revolution India shifted from exporting manufactures to supplying raw materials such as raw cotton to British mills. So raw cotton exports rose.
Textiles were the second-largest employer after agriculture in British-period Andhra.
Bihar was the main opium-producing region under British rule (with Bengal and Malwa). Assam was known for tea and Gujarat for cotton.
Peasants were made to grow cash crops to pay cash revenue, which commercialised Indian agriculture. Handicraft exports fell and urban growth was not rapid.
The Opium Wars arose from the opium trade, in which Indian opium was sent to China, so they were fought between Britain and China.
The notes do not state this. Commercialisation tied peasants to markets, where merchants and middlemen exploited them, which deepened rural poverty.
Aditya-L1 was launched on 2 September 2023 on PSLV-C57, so option 2 is right; the other dates do not match.
India's first solar mission, launched in September 2023, is Aditya-L1, named for its position at the Sun-Earth L1 point.
H3 is the next-generation rocket of Japan's space agency JAXA, which had its first success on 17 Feb 2024. The other agencies listed do not operate it.
H3 is the next-generation rocket of Japan's space agency JAXA, which had its first success on 17 Feb 2024. The other agencies listed do not operate it.
Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so every 15° of longitude corresponds to 1 hour (60 minutes). 4 minutes is the time for just 1°.
6.30 a.m. is 5.5 hours behind noon, which is 82.5° of longitude west of 82°30'E, i.e. 0° (the Prime Meridian). The other options do not match 5 h 30 min of difference.
The Treaty of Yandabo (Yandabu) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War under Amherst and was signed in 1826, not 1824 (when the war began) or 1825.

States kept internal administration but had no international life, and the British intervened only to give effect to their international commitments (or for misgovernance). So option 2 is right; the other options are not recognised grounds.
Assam is the biggest tea-producing state in India, ahead of West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
Coffee production ranks Karnataka first, then Kerala, then Tamil Nadu, which matches option 1.

Statements I and III are correct: Assam is the biggest tea state and Andhra Pradesh is a major tobacco producer (30.22%, second to Gujarat). Coffee's main state is Karnataka, not Tamil Nadu, and jute is grown in West Bengal, Bihar and Assam rather than Chhattisgarh, so II and IV are wrong.
Non-plan expenditure covered defence, interest and loans to States/UTs/PSUs, so interest payments are correct, whereas science and technology and agriculture were developmental plan items.
Economic Survey 2016-17 put combined Centre and State spending at about 28% of GDP, so option 2 is right.
Interest payments are the largest single item of Union expenditure, ahead of defence, subsidies and pensions, which makes interest the largest non-plan item too.
Interest is the largest item of Union revenue expenditure (about 26% of total spending and 40% of revenue receipts), larger than defence, subsidies or grants.
Interest payments are the biggest single item in Union expenditure, at about 26% of the total, ahead of defence and subsidies.
Interest payment creates no asset, so it is revenue expenditure, and it is also non-developmental. It is not capital expenditure.

The notes list rice subsidy among revenue items, but they do not name the scheme under the targeted PDS, so this link is only partial. Rice is the foodgrain subsidised under the TPDS for food security, unlike sugar or oil.
Hidden subsidies arise from under-pricing of public services such as higher education in public universities. Food, fertiliser and petroleum subsidies are explicit budget items.

Krishnadevaraya's reign saw Albuquerque as the Portuguese contact (Goa 1510), and the Portuguese were allowed a fort at Bhatkal in 1510. Vira Narasimha was linked to Almeida, so he is the tempting wrong option.
Andhra Bhoja is a title of Krishnadevaraya, reflecting his literary patronage. Andhra Kavita Pitamaha is Peddana's title, not his.
Amuktamalyada is a Telugu work, his only Telugu work, so the claim that it was written in Sanskrit is incorrect.
Rourkela steel plant was built with German collaboration (Krupp and Demag), not the USSR or Britain.
Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur were set up after independence. Jamshedpur (1907), Bhadravati (1923) and Burnpur (IISCO) were pre-independence plants.
TISCO at Jamshedpur lies in Singhbhum district of Jharkhand, at the confluence of the Subarnarekha and Kharkai. The other districts listed are not where it is located.
Hard (high-carbon) steel contains about 0.5 to 1.5% carbon, whereas mild steel has about 0.1 to 0.4%.
Mission Purvodaya aims to develop Eastern India as an integrated steel hub.
BALCO, NALCO and HINDALCO are aluminium producers. TELCO (Tata Motors) makes vehicles, not aluminium.
BALCO is at Korba, Chhattisgarh, not Raipur, so the pair BALCO – Raipur is wrong.
SAIL has its headquarters in Delhi (A-4), Hindustan Zinc is at Udaipur (B-2), HEC is at Ranchi (C-3) and Instrumentation Ltd is at Kota (D-1). This gives 4 2 3 1.
The Global Competitiveness Report and its Index are published by the World Economic Forum (WEF). UNDP publishes the HDR and the IMF publishes the WEO and GFSR, so they are wrong.
The Ease of Doing Business report/index was published by the World Bank (Group), not the WTO, UN or EU.
The Global Gender Gap Report is published by the World Economic Forum (first in 2006). It is not a UNDP or World Bank report.
India was 100th in the 2017 report and 77th in the 2018 (DB 2019) report, a climb of 23 ranks.
DB 2020 placed India 63rd, and in DB 2019 (released 2018) India was 77th, so both statements are correct.
Mudrarakshasa is a play by Vishakhadatta on Chandragupta Maurya and Kautilya overthrowing the Nandas; it is not by Kalidasa, Bhasa or Ashvaghosha.
Kshapanaka is listed among the Navaratnas as the astrologer (Jyotishyashastra). Vararuchi was a grammarian, Shanku a sculptor/architect and Amarasimha a lexicographer.
The Romaka Siddhanta, one of Varahamihira's five siddhantas, deals with astronomy (with Roman-Greek influence), not chemistry, mathematics or medicine.
Decimal place value is credited to Aryabhata, who used zero and place value; Brahmagupta is known for the rules of zero arithmetic and Bhaskara I for the circle-zero in 629 CE.
State Lokayuktas submit a yearly consolidated report to the Governor, who appoints them, not to the CM, Chief Justice or Speaker. Uttar Pradesh follows this pattern.
BhashaNet was unveiled by NIXI together with MeitY on Universal Acceptance Day, 21 March 2024. CSIR and NITI Aayog are not involved.
SWAYAM stands for Study Webs of Active-Learning for Young Aspiring Minds, the free MOOCs platform for higher education. The notes do not give this expansion, so no line is linked.
Khasi and Garo are the languages of the Khasi and Garo tribes of Meghalaya, where they are official languages alongside English. Neither is spoken mainly in the other listed states.
Article 371A relates to Nagaland, 371B to Assam, 371C to Manipur, 371F to Sikkim and 371G to Mizoram. This gives AQ, BP, CR, DT, ES, which is option 3.

Roy's work was not limited to the middle class: he campaigned against sati, child marriage and polygamy, for women's rights, and for peasants (fixed maximum rents). So 'exclusively middle class' is wrong.
The Brahmo Samaj banned idols and rejected the need for a priestly class, so I and II are correct. It did not hold the Vedas faultless, so III is wrong.
The Tattvabodhini Sabha was founded by Debendranath Tagore in 1839 in Calcutta. The other options give the wrong founder or year.

The notes say religious reforms in Bombay were started by the Paramahansa Mandali (Poona, 1849). The Prarthana Samaj came later (1867) and the Brahmo Samaj and Deoband are not Bombay's starting point.
Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj, not the Brahmo Samaj, which was founded by Rammohan Roy. So this pair is wrongly matched.
The notes give the order Rammohan Roy, then Vidyasagar, then Jyotiba Phule, then Dayanand Saraswati, which is C – A – D – B.
Macdonald's Communal Award (2), Linlithgow's August Offer 1940 (3), Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse (1) and Chelmsford's Dyarchy under the GoI Act 1919 (4) give A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4, which is option (3).
The provisional Census 2011 figure, the most-quoted one, is 74.04%. The final figure is 73.0%, which is the tempting alternative.
The notes say that 'UP has the lowest female literacy' is wrong. NSS 2017-18 puts the lowest female literacy in Rajasthan, and Bihar is lowest in Census 2011, so option 4 is the incorrect statement.
In NSS 75th round (2017-18), AP female literacy was about 59.5%. The 71.4% option is the PLFS 2025 total figure, not this one.
Undivided AP female literacy in Census 2011 was 59.15%. 67.02% is the overall final literacy figure for undivided AP, not the female figure.
Undivided AP female literacy in Census 2011 was 59.15%. 67.02% is the overall final literacy figure for undivided AP, not the female figure.
Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu was launched in AP on 14 Nov 2019 to improve school facilities. The other options are not AP programmes from that date.
The Ramamurti Committee (1990) reviewed the National Policy on Education (NPE 1986).
Punjab had the highest FLN Index score in the 2nd edition, so statement I is correct. The notes do not support statement II, which is the tempting wrong part.
Punjab had the highest FLN Index score in the 2nd edition, so statement I is correct. The notes do not support statement II, which is the tempting wrong part.

The Home Rule Movement was the popular movement during the First World War, launched in 1916 by Tilak and Annie Besant to demand self-government. Swadeshi and the Swaraj Party belong to other periods.
Tilak's Indian Home Rule League was founded on 28 April 1916 at Belgaum (Bombay Provincial Conference), though it was based at Poona; so Belgaum is correct.
The notes name Tilak, Besant and S. Subramania Iyer as associated with Home Rule; C.R. Das is not mentioned in connection with it, so he is the odd one out.
The Home Rule Leagues were launched in 1916 by Tilak (April) and Annie Besant (September). Aurobindo, Lajpat Rai and Pal were not the Home Rule leaders.
Annie Besant is chiefly associated with the Home Rule Movement, which she launched in 1916 with her All India Home Rule League. The other movements were Gandhian or Khilafat-related.

LIC was set up in 1956, IDBI and UTI both in 1964, and SEBI became statutory in 1992, so the order is LIC, IDBI, UTI, SEBI (1, 2, 4, 3). Options placing SEBI before UTI are wrong because SEBI is the latest of the four.
Hepatitis is a viral infection of the liver, and the notes link hepatitis A and E to jaundice (a liver symptom). So the liver is the organ affected.
Measles is a viral, airborne disease that antibiotics cannot cure, so the causative agent is a virus.
AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus, so it is a viral disease, not bacterial or fungal.
AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus, so the answer is virus.
Hepatitis B is a DNA virus spread by blood, sex and mother-to-child, so it is viral, not bacterial or protozoan.
Chickenpox is listed among the viral diseases and is caused by the varicella virus; the other options are not its cause.
Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis and affects livestock and other animals, so goats, sheep, cows and buffaloes all get it. 'All animals' is therefore the best answer.
The SEZ policy was announced on 1 April 2000; the SEZ Act came later, in 2005, so 2000 is correct and 1991 and 2005 are wrong.
The SEZ Act was passed in 2005 (SEZ Rules followed in 2006). The 2000 date refers to the SEZ policy, not the Act.
The WTO's 13th Ministerial Conference (MC13) in 2024 was held in Abu Dhabi.
India had a trade surplus only twice since independence, in 1972-73 and 1976-77, so option 2 is correct.
AMRUT focuses on renewing urban infrastructure (water supply, sewerage, drains, parks, transport), so urban infrastructure is correct; sanitation is only one component.
AMRUT stands for Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation.
JNNURM was a mission for urban infrastructure and basic services in mission cities, not rural housing, marketing or employment.
Swachh Vayu Survekshan 2023 ranked Indore first among million-plus cities.
Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on 2 October 2014, so the launch month is October 2014.
The mission was launched on 2 October 2014, Gandhi Jayanti.
The notes do not state the number of Water Plus certified cities in Andhra Pradesh.
Dausa was not an AMRUT mission city of Rajasthan until March 2024, unlike Jaipur, the State capital.
The World Wide Web is the collection of linked information on computers that is available through the internet. A web server only stores and serves pages.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the WWW in 1989 at CERN.
WWW stands for World Wide Web, the information system for sharing content over the internet.
The WWW was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989.
WWW stands for World Wide Web, an information system for sharing content over the internet.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the WWW at CERN in 1989.
MAN stands for Metropolitan Area Network, which covers a city.
A modem (modulator-demodulator) converts digital signals to analog and back. Cables and satellites only carry signals.
A modem links a microcomputer with the telephone line to send and receive data. VDU is a display and UNIX is an operating system.
The Badami (Chalukya) capital was Vatapi, modern Badami in Bagalkot district. Shravasti, Kanchi (Pallava) and Kannauj were not Chalukya capitals.
Pulakesin II (610-642) was the zenith and greatest ruler of the Badami (Vatapi) Chalukyas, not of the Kalyani Chalukyas, Pallavas or Cholas.
The Aihole inscription of Pulakesin II, composed by Ravikirti, names Kalidasa and Bharavi, claiming fame like theirs. The other inscriptions listed do not mention Kalidasa.
The notes do not state anything about Mauryan land grants on a religious basis or a peasant revolt. Statement A is true and R is false, so option (3) is correct.
The Mauryan silver coin was the Pana (karshapana). Niska, Kakini and Shatamana are not the Mauryan silver coin.
Mauryan coinage was mainly the silver Pana, with copper Mashaka and Kakani as smaller coins. So silver and copper is correct; gold (Suvarna) was not the standard metal.

Buddhism is credited with starting image worship, as the Buddha came to be represented and venerated in images. The Vedic religion did not practise idol worship, and Jainism and the Ajivikas are not credited with laying its foundation.

The notes do not directly say where stupas stood. They link stupas to merchants' and guilds' patronage, which fits sites near trade routes, so the claim that they were in rural areas is the incorrect statement.
Sanchi Stupa has Ashoka's brick core, so Ashoka built it. Chandragupta, Kautilya and the Buddha had no role in building it.
Murshid Quli Khan was the last Subahdar of Bengal appointed by the Mughal Emperor; later Nawabs such as Shuja-ud-din acted independently, so the other options are wrong.
Siyar-ul-Mutakherin was written by the contemporary historian Ghulam Husain (Ghulam Hussain Khan Tabatabai); Salabat Jung, Qasim Khan and Ram Mohan Roy did not write it.
The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757, so 1757 CE is correct.

Census 2001 defines an urban area by three tests: population of at least 5,000, at least 75% of male workers in non-agricultural work, and density of at least 400 per sq km. There is no minimum area criterion, so statement 4 is wrong and the answer is 1, 2 and 3.
Census 2011 recorded India's urban population at 31.16% of the total, which is about 31%.

India's urban population (28.6 crore in 2001) exceeded the total population of the USA (28.14 crore), so A is true. The USA also has a higher level of urbanisation, so R is true. But the higher urbanisation level in the USA does not explain why India's urban population is larger; that is due to India's much larger total population. So R is not the correct explanation.
Under Article 75(4) the President administers the oath of office and secrecy to the PM and Union Ministers; the PM, CAG and CJI do not.

The President's oath is in Article 60, not the Third Schedule, so statement III is wrong; the Union Minister's, the Chief Justice's (as a Supreme Court judge) and the MP's oaths are in the Third Schedule, so I, II and IV are correct.
The notes do not state the order of precedence. Per the Warrant of Precedence, the PM ranks above a former President, who ranks above the CJI, so option 1 is correct.

DRDO is a network of about 52 laboratories (it grew from 10 labs at the start), so the claim that it is a network of only 10 labs is the incorrect statement. The other statements (1958, Ministry of Defence, missiles and armaments) are correct.
Dr G. Satheesh Reddy served as Scientific Adviser to the Defence Minister from 2015 (and was DRDO Chairman 2018-22), so he is the answer among the options.

The Ministry of Defence includes the Department of Defence, the Department of Defence R&D and the Department of Defence Production. There is no 'Department of Defence Finance', so option IV is wrong and I, II and III is correct.
JCBCAT at Jadavpur University, Kolkata, was set up with DRDO, not ISRO, NASA or BARC.
JCBCAT at Jadavpur University, Kolkata, was set up with DRDO, not ISRO or BEL, so 'All of the above' is wrong.
Lakshya, developed by DRDO's ADE, is India's first unmanned aircraft (a pilotless target aircraft). INS Viraat is a ship and Sukhoi is a fighter, so they are wrong.
The College of Military Engineering (CME) is at Dapodi, Pune, and is affiliated to JNU. The notes do not cover this fact.
The list of 16 Mahajanapadas appears in the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya and the Jain Bhagavati Sutra, so (ii) and (iv) are right. The Arthashastra and Digha Nikaya are not listed as sources.
Panini's Ashtadhyayi names Magadha, Ashmaka and Kamboja among its 22 janapadas. Chedi and Vatsa are not the ones named.
The Anguttara Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka gives the list of the sixteen Mahajanapadas.
Mathura was the capital of Shurasena (Surasena). Vajji's capital was Vaishali, Vatsa's was Kaushambi and Kashi's was Varanasi.
Magadha covered the Patna, Nalanda and Gaya region of Bihar. Anga lay in east Bihar around Bhagalpur and Munger.
The Buddha attained parinirvana at Kusinara, which belonged to the Malla Mahajanapada. So the answer is Malla.
Fiscal deficit equals the (old) budget deficit plus borrowings and other liabilities (market borrowings), which is option 4. Options 1 and 2 describe budget deficit and revenue deficit.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments, so adding interest payments back to primary deficit gives the fiscal deficit.
The effective revenue deficit was introduced in Union Budget 2011-12 (and added to FRBM by the 2012 amendment), so option 2 is correct.
Primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments, so removing interest from fiscal deficit leaves the primary deficit. Revenue and budgetary deficits are different measures.
Fiscal deficit equals the budget deficit plus borrowings and other liabilities, i.e. budgetary deficit plus net increase in borrowings, matching option 1.
Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts, so the item subtracted is revenue receipts.
Fiscal deficit is always greater than revenue deficit in practice, because it also includes the borrowing for capital expenditure.
Fiscal deficit is the largest deficit in the GoI budget (fiscal > revenue > primary), as it measures the total borrowing requirement.
Hugli (1651) was the first English factory in Bengal, set up on Shah Shuja's farman; Calcutta came later, in 1690.
Surat (1613) was the Company's first permanent factory in India. The other options were never EIC factories, and Machilipatnam (1611) was only a temporary one.
The English first set up a permanent factory at Surat in 1613. Bombay, Madras and Sutanuti (Calcutta) came later.
The British factory in Nellore district was at Armagaon (Dugarajapatnam), set up in 1626.
The ship Globe under Captain Hippon reached Machilipatnam in 1611, where the first English factory in Andhra was founded.
The Company's settlement at Madras was Fort St. George, founded in 1639 and the seat of the Madras Presidency. Fort William is at Calcutta.
Job Charnock founded Calcutta in 1690, and Fort William was built there in 1700 as its nucleus. Job Carnock is a variant spelling of Charnock.
Job Charnock, chief of the Qasim Bazar factory, chose Sutanuti and arrived in 1690, so he is regarded as the founder of Calcutta. John Surman led the 1717 farman mission.
Fort William (1700) was the fort built by the British at Calcutta, and it was the nucleus of the city. Fort St. David is not the Calcutta fort.
The main business of the English settlements in Andhra, including Fort St. George, was trading locally woven piece-goods. The Company was a trading body, not a military or agricultural one.

The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee proposed democratic decentralisation, with all planning and development work entrusted to the Panchayati Raj bodies. Ashok Mehta and Gadgil came later and Mahalanobis is not a PR committee.
Balwant Rai Mehta is called the Architect or Father of Panchayati Raj because his committee recommended the three-tier system. Singhvi and G.V.K. Rao are other PR committee heads.
Panchayati Raj was adopted as democratic decentralisation, transferring genuine power and resources to local bodies. It was not meant merely to make people politically aware or to educate peasants.
The Panchayati Raj system followed the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957). It recommended democratic decentralisation, later known as Panchayati Raj.
Rajasthan was the first State to set up Panchayati Raj, at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. Andhra Pradesh was second, though first across the entire State.
The Panchayat Samiti is the block-level tier, and the block is the basic unit of planning. The Gram Panchayat is at village level and the Zila Parishad at district level.
Balwantrai G. Mehta chaired the committee whose report led to Panchayati Raj, so he is called its architect. The other names are unrelated to it.
POCSO stands for the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, drafted by the MWCD. The other options are invented expansions.

The notes record as true that the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs recommended lowering the age from 18 to 16, so A is true. The reason, that serious sexual crimes warrant trying those above 16 as adults, explains the recommendation and matches the JJ Act idea of transferring 16-18 year olds for heinous offences.

The MP High Court asked the Centre to lower the consent age to 16, citing early puberty caused by exposure to social media. The other options (fast food chemicals, climate, safe sex) are not the reasons it gave.
PENCIL (Platform for Effective Enforcement for No Child Labour, 2017) is the MoLE portal for enforcing the child labour law. SPARC, SRIJAN and YUKTI are wrong options.
ILO Convention 138 deals with the minimum age for employment and Convention 182 with the worst forms of child labour, so both relate to child labour.

Statement V is right: HDR 2021/22 ("Uncertain Times, Unsettled Lives") describes a new uncertainty complex. Statement II is wrong because HDI equals IHDI when there is no inequality. The notes give no basis for IV being false, so the answer is IV and V.
The Minimum Needs Programme is the same as investment in the human approach, i.e. spending on people's basic needs.
The notes do not state the four pillars of human development (equity, productivity, empowerment, sustainability), so no line is linked. The correct option is the standard UNDP set.
The first HDR was published by UNDP in 1990 and contained the HDI, so 1990 is correct.
The HDI was introduced by UNDP in its first HDR in 1990, so UNDP is correct.
HDI covers life expectancy, schooling and per capita income. Ownership of basic assets is explicitly outside HDI.
HDI dimensions are a long and healthy life, knowledge and a decent standard of living. Access to banking and financial provisions is not one of them; it belongs to financial inclusion.
HDI rests on three dimensions: health (long and healthy life), education (knowledge) and standard of living. Employment is not a dimension.
The Medium band is 0.550-0.699, and 0.685 falls in it, just below the 0.700 threshold for High.
The Second Plan (1956-61) followed the Mahalanobis model, stressing heavy industry, so it is called the Mahalanobis Plan. Harrod-Domar was the model of the First Plan.
Krishna Menon was Defence Minister during the 1962 war and resigned after the Chinese attack, so option 3 is correct.
Air India was nationalised in 1953, the Imperial Bank became SBI in 1955, the first elected Communist government came in Kerala in 1957, and Goa joined India in 1961. So the order is III, II, I, IV.
Residuary Andhra Pradesh received about 46% of the estimated revenue at bifurcation, while carrying a larger share of the debt. So option 1 (46) is correct.

The notes do not cover these location-and-news associations, so no line is linked. The matching in option 2 (Kakinada-bio-diesel plant, Dundigal-Indian Air Force Academy, Margao-Skybus Metro rail test-run, Bhadrachalam-ITC paper board unit) is the correct one.

The founder of the imperial Chola line was Vijayalaya, who captured Thanjavur in 850 CE, not Parantaka I. The other three statements are true: Parantaka I was Madurai-konda, Rajaraja I took the Maldives, and Rajendra I founded Gangaikondacholapuram.
Vijayalaya, a Pallava feudatory at Uraiyur, captured Thanjavur in 850 CE and founded the imperial Chola line in the 9th century.
Thanjavur in the fertile Kaveri delta is known as the Granary of South India, but the notes do not state this.
Aditya I succeeded the founder Vijayalaya. The 'Victor of the Ganges' title belongs to Rajendra I, not Aditya I, and Rajendra I was not the founder.
Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda Chola after his Ganga expedition of 1022, in which he beat the Pala king Mahipala I.
Rajendra I's titles included Gangaikonda, Kadaram Kondan and Pandita Chola. Tyagasamudra is not among the titles listed for him in the notes, so it is the exception.
Rajendra I conquered the whole of Sri Lanka by defeating Mahinda V. Rajaraja I took only the north.
Rajendra I conducted the Ganga expedition in 1022 and defeated the Pala king Mahipala I of Bengal.
K.A. Nilakanta Sastri said the Cholas turned the Bay of Bengal into a 'Chola Lake'. This is linked to Rajendra I's 1025 Srivijaya naval expedition, not to Rajaraja I.

Statement I is correct because the Cholas defeated the Pandya and Chera rulers and dominated peninsular India. Statement II is correct because Rajendra I defeated the Sailendra king and took Kadaram and parts of Sumatra. So both are correct.
Gravity pulls the atmospheric gases toward the Earth and holds them around it; winds, clouds and rotation do not retain the air.
The exosphere is the outermost layer with light gases, and in the heterosphere the gases are layered by weight, with hydrogen the lightest at the top. So hydrogen dominates the exosphere.
CO₂ is a greenhouse gas because it is a good absorber of long-wave (infrared) radiation, trapping heat. Its abundance or role in photosynthesis does not make it a greenhouse gas.

Rising greenhouse gases cause global warming and a CO₂ fertilisation effect, and are linked with ozone depletion in the stratosphere. There is no 'oxygen fertilisation effect', so that is the exception.
The greenhouse effect is the warming of the atmosphere as CO₂ and other gases absorb outgoing long-wave (infrared) terrestrial radiation. The other options are unrelated to this process.
Carbon dioxide is a major greenhouse gas that absorbs long-wave radiation, and its rising levels enhance the greenhouse effect. Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas.
Meteors burn up in the mesosphere (50–80 km). The thermosphere/ionosphere and exosphere are higher and are not where meteors burn.
Arsenic-74 is a positron emitter used to locate brain tumours. Iodine-131 is for the thyroid, Co-60 for radiotherapy and Na-24 for blood flow.
Cobalt-60 emits powerful gamma rays, which is why it is used in radiotherapy and sterilisation.
Radon is the radioactive noble gas used to treat cancer. Xenon, krypton and argon are not used for this.
Radon is the radioactive noble gas used in cancer treatment; the other gases listed are not.
X-rays and gamma rays are both electromagnetic waves. Beta rays and cathode rays are electron streams, and alpha rays are helium nuclei.
Radon is the radioactive noble gas used to treat cancer; helium, krypton and neon are not.
Lead is dense and absorbs gamma rays and X-rays effectively, so it is used for shielding against nuclear radiation.
The becquerel (1 decay per second) is the SI unit of radioactivity (activity). The ampere is current and the decibel is sound level.
Carbon-14 dating is used for once-living remains such as animal bones, wood and younger fossils. Uranium dating is for very old rocks.
Carbon-14 dating applies to once-living remains such as fossils, up to about 50,000 years. Rocks and the Earth's age need uranium-lead dating.

Commercial and trade bills are instruments of the organised money market, not unregulated non-bank intermediaries. Indigenous bankers, moneylenders and unregulated loan companies are unorganised intermediaries.
An indigenous banker accepts deposits and lends, combining banking with trade or commission business. One who lends only in kind is not an indigenous banker.
IFCI, set up in 1948, was the first DFI, and its setting up began the era of development financing. ICICI, IDBI and SIDBI came later.
SIDBI is an all-India financial institution (DFI) for MSME finance. UTI is an investment institution, and ECGC is not listed as an AIFI.
SIDBI is the DFI for MSME (small industry) finance. IDBI and IFCI serve medium and large industry, and NABARD serves agriculture and rural credit.
IFCI (1948), ICICI (1955), IDBI (1964) and NABARD (1982) is the chronological order, so option 1 is right.
NHB was wholly RBI-owned until 2019, so statement I is correct. SIDBI began as an IDBI subsidiary, so statement II is correct. Both are correct.
SIDBI was established on 2 April 1990 under the SIDBI Act 1989, so April 1990 is correct.
The notes do not state SIDBI's head office location. SIDBI's head office is at Lucknow.
NHB RESIDEX is India's first official housing price index, so it relates to residential property (land) prices. Share and mutual fund prices are unrelated.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own DNA and ribosomes and make some of their own proteins, so they are semi-autonomous. The endoplasmic reticulum has no DNA, so it is not.
Sound waves are longitudinal (compressions and rarefactions), not transverse, so the statement that they are transverse is the incorrect one.
Zone melting is the method used to obtain ultra-pure metals such as germanium and silicon. Slugging, smelting and leaching are not ultra-purification methods.
In SHM, a = -ω²x, so the magnitude of acceleration is greatest at the extreme positions (amplitude) and zero at equilibrium.
Quality (timbre) of a musical note depends on the harmonics (overtones) present. Pitch depends on frequency and loudness on amplitude.
Euglena, Amoeba and Paramecium are all single-celled organisms, so all the options listed are correct.
Capillarity lets oil rise in a lamp wick, ink be absorbed by blotting paper, and water reach the tops of tall trees. A straw works by suction (air pressure), not capillarity, so II is wrong.
Sound-type pressure waves from an underwater explosion travel through the water as longitudinal waves, because a fluid cannot support transverse waves.
EM waves are non-elastic, travel in vacuum, and have mutually perpendicular E and B fields. Their speed is 3×10^8 m/s (3 lakh km/s), not 3 lakh m/s, so IV is wrong.
The apparent bending of a pencil in water and the sun appearing before sunrise are refraction effects. The blue sky is due to scattering, not refraction.
In a compound microscope the eyepiece has a longer focal length than the objective. The final image seen is virtual, inverted and magnified.
The electron is a negatively charged constituent of cathode rays. Its mass is about 1/1836 of a proton's, and it is deflected by both electric and magnetic fields.
Only acids turn blue litmus red. Base and neutral salt solutions do not, so II and III are the answer.
q + W gives the change in internal energy, a state function, and H - TS is the Gibbs free energy, also a state function. q and W individually are path functions.
Viruses lack the enzymes for energy generation. They cannot be cultured in synthetic media because they need living host cells, and they are not transmitted only by biological vectors.
Xylem conducts water and minerals and also gives mechanical support through its fibres, so all three are correct.

DNA is the hereditary material of most organisms (some viruses use RNA, so I is generally accepted by the key), nuclear DNA is an antiparallel double helix, and mitochondria contain DNA. Not all DNA segments code for proteins, so II is wrong.
For a concave mirror, an object between C and F gives a real, inverted, magnified image beyond the centre of curvature.
Specific heat is a property of the material. It does not depend on the mass or shape of the body, and it is not dependent only on temperature, so only II is correct.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image. Its magnification is less than 1, so it is never enlarged or real.

Gulf of Mannar is a World Network BR (2001), and the notes list the World Network examples; the option with Gulf of Mannar, Nokrek, Pachmarhi and Simlipal was given as correct, while Nilgiri, Panna options contain Seshachalam or are not matched.

Agasthyamalai BR covers Neyyar, Peppara and Shendurney sanctuaries and Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve in Kerala and Tamil Nadu; the other options are parks of the Nilgiris, Andhra Pradesh or Telangana.

Agasthyamalai BR covers Neyyar, Peppara and Shendurney sanctuaries and Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve in Kerala and Tamil Nadu; the other options are parks of the Nilgiris, Andhra Pradesh or Telangana.
Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve (1999) lies in the Satpura range of Madhya Pradesh, covering parts of Betul, Narmadapuram and Chhindwara districts.
Sundarbans, Keoladeo and Kaziranga are natural World Heritage Sites, whereas Gir (Asiatic lion, Gujarat) is not on the list.
Keoladeo (1985), Sundarbans (1987) and Kaziranga (1985) are World Heritage Sites, but Ranthambore is not, so I, II and III is correct.
Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim was inscribed in 2016 as a mixed site; Kaziranga was listed in 1985 and Valley of Flowers in 1988, and Corbett is not listed.

Under the original 1993 Act the NHRC Chairperson had to be a former Chief Justice of India; only since 2019 can a Supreme Court Judge also be Chairperson. So the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court is the expected answer.
The statement that members are not eligible for reappointment is the wrong one, since members can be reappointed (the 5-year limit was removed in 2019). The other statements reflect the original Act.
Under the original Act the term was 5 years, which is the expected answer here. Since 2019 it is 3 years or age 70, whichever is earlier.
Under the original Act the term was 5 years, which is the expected answer here. Since 2019 it is 3 years or age 70, whichever is earlier.
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is not on the selection committee; the Deputy Chairman is. The PM, Speaker and Lok Sabha LoP are members.
SHRC Chairperson and members are appointed by the Governor, though removal is only by the President.

Macaulay's Minute of 1835 promoted English education, producing an English-educated middle class that was the first to be shaped by Western influence. This makes the educated Hindu middle class correct, not landlords, merchants or Muslims.
Article 243P (74th Amendment, Part IXA) defines a metropolitan area as one with a population of 10 lakh or more, so option 1 is correct.
Khurja (Bulandshahr, UP), Karnal and Rohtak (Haryana) are NCR towns, while Ambala is not in the NCR. So only II, III and IV are correct.
The VV Giri National Labour Institute is located in Noida, Uttar Pradesh (Sector 24), so option 1 is correct.
Mahavira died at Pavapuri (Pava) near Rajgir in 527 BCE, aged 72. Rajgir is only the nearby town, not the place of death.
Vardhamana Mahavira was a contemporary teacher of Gautama Buddha. Parshvanatha lived about 250 years before Mahavira, and Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta Maurya came later.
Somadeva Suri held the title Syadvadachala Simha. Kundakundacharya is the one who preached Syadvada, so he is the tempting wrong option.
Syadvada, the doctrine of conditioned predication (seven-fold predication), is a Jain doctrine. It is not a doctrine of Lokayata, Saivism or Vaishnavism.
The notes do not state this. Jainism has no creator god, and the world is eternal and runs by its own law, which is why 'Universal Law' is the answer rather than a universal soul.
The Eleventh Schedule, added by the 73rd Amendment, lists 29 subjects for Panchayats (Article 243G); 18 is the Twelfth Schedule figure for Municipalities.
The State Finance Commission (Art. 243I) recommends to the Governor how the net proceeds of State taxes, duties, tolls and fees are shared between the State and local bodies.
Under Article 243K(4), the State Legislature may make provision by law on all matters relating to Panchayat elections; the SEC only conducts them and the ECI has no role.
The notes do not give the Chhattisgarh notification date; the keyed answer is 23 December 2019.

The Haryana Panchayati Raj (Amendment) Act 2015 required a functional toilet, cleared power bills and no cooperative loan default, so I, II and III apply. The matriculation condition varied by category, so statement IV is wrong.
Haryana and Rajasthan prescribe minimum educational qualifications for Panchayat candidates, whereas Punjab and Karnataka do not.
The 73rd Amendment came into force on 24 April 1993, so National Panchayati Raj Day is observed on 24 April.

The 2018 Standing Orders Rules introduced fixed-term employment across all sectors, which makes hiring and exiting workers easier for firms, and they provide that no termination notice is needed for temporary workmen. Both statements are therefore correct.
The GST regime was enabled by the 101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016, which inserted Article 246A and created the GST Council. The 102nd, 103rd and 104th Amendments deal with other subjects.
The National Wildlife Genetic Resource Bank at Nehru Zoological Park received two giant tortoises gifted by Seychelles in 2018, so Seychelles is correct.
Before the Constitution of 1950, India was governed under the Government of India Act 1935, whose provincial autonomy came into force in 1937 while the Centre ran under the 1919 Act till 1947.
The 1935 Act proposed dyarchy at the Centre as part of its federal scheme, so 1935 is the answer; 1919 introduced dyarchy only in the provinces.
The Federal Court was a creation of the 1935 Act and was set up in Delhi in October 1937.
The federation never came into being because too few princely states acceded, so states were not compelled to join; the other statements are features of the Act.
The notes do not state this fact, so no line is linked.
Punjab was ruled by the Unionist Party of Sikandar Hayat Khan, so no Congress ministry was formed there; Bihar, Madras and Orissa had Congress ministries.
The Congress ministry formed in Madras on 14 July 1937 was headed by C. Rajagopalachari as Premier; Prakasam was only Revenue Minister.
The Viceroy Linlithgow declared India at war with Germany in September 1939 without consulting Indian leaders, so the Congress ministries resigned in protest in Oct-Nov 1939.

Vinegar is made by Acetobacter fermentation (e.g. of sugarcane juice) and its acid is acetic acid, so A and B are correct. Benzoic acid is not the acid in vinegar, so C is wrong; D (preservative) is correct, giving A, B, D.
Vinegar's sour taste is due to acetic acid, which is not among tartaric, lactic or citric acid, so 'None of these' is correct.
Wine is made by yeast fermenting sugars in grape juice into ethanol. Conjugation, catalysation and displacement are not wine-making processes.
Vinegar's major component is acetic acid (CH3COOH), formed by Acetobacter fermentation. Citric, lactic and nitric acids are not its main component.
Biogas (methane) is produced by methanogens through anaerobic fermentation of organic matter. Oxidation and aerobic respiration need oxygen and do not yield methane.
Lactobacillus bacteria convert lactose in milk into lactic acid, which sours and sets it into curd. Yeast is a fungus and the other bacteria listed do not make curd.
Amylase is the enzyme that breaks down starch into sugars, as used in bread-making. Invertase acts on sucrose, not starch.
AMTZ is the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone at Visakhapatnam, devoted to medical equipment manufacturing.
The notes do not state this fact.
The notes do not state CCMB's headquarters, though CCMB is known to be in Hyderabad.
Tropical rain forest has the highest land species richness, so the number of species per unit area is greatest there, unlike temperate, deciduous or taiga forests.
The ocean (marine ecosystem) covers about 71% of Earth's surface, making it the largest ecosystem, larger than desert, grassland or mountain ecosystems.
Lentic habitats are still-water bodies such as ponds, lakes and swamps, whereas rivers, springs and waterfalls are lotic (flowing), so only ponds and swamps fit.

Upwelling brings nutrient-rich deep water to the surface, which fuels phytoplankton growth and raises productivity. It does not bring decomposers or bottom-dwelling organisms to boost productivity, so only statement II is correct.
Cotton, groundnut and rice are kharif crops, while wheat is a rabi crop, so I, II and III is correct; options with wheat are wrong.
Aman rice is sown in June-July and harvested in Nov-Dec, so June-July is the sowing period. November-December is the harvest time, which makes it the tempting wrong option.

The freedom to own, acquire and dispose of property is not in Art. 19(1); 19(1)(f) was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978). The other three freedoms (movement, assembly, trade or profession) are still in 19(1).
Article 19 gives the six freedoms (originally seven, until property was deleted). Arts. 18, 20 and 21 deal with other rights.
Freedom of the press is not named in the Constitution; it is read into Art. 19(1)(a). Trade, residence and association are expressly listed in 19(1).
Freedom of speech and expression is in Art. 19(1)(a). Arts. 15, 16 and 17 deal with equality and untouchability.
Press freedom is not named in the Constitution; it is read into the freedom of speech and expression in Art. 19(1)(a). Arts. 16, 22 and 31 do not cover it.
Freedom of speech and expression is guaranteed by Art. 19(1)(a). Arts. 14, 21 and 22 deal with equality, life and liberty, and arrest.
In Anuradha Bhasin (2020) the Supreme Court read speech and trade over the internet into Art. 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g). So internet access is linked to Art. 19, not 14, 17 or 21.
Press freedom is not named in the Constitution; it is implied in the freedom of speech and expression under 19(1)(a). It does not come from a Parliament law or executive power.
Rajkumar Shukla, a local indigo cultivator, met Gandhi at the 1916 Lucknow Congress and persuaded him to come to Champaran. Rajendra Prasad and the others were lawyers/associates who joined later.
Under the Tinkathia system tenants had to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land for European planters, so option 1 is correct.

Gandhi reached Champaran with Brajkishore Prasad, Rajendra Prasad, Anugrah Narayan Sinha and Kripalani, who were Bihar lawyers/associates. Patel, Nehru, Vinoba and Maniben are not listed among them, and Mahadev Desai joined later in 1917 without Maniben.
The Champaran Agrarian Committee was appointed by the Bihar and Orissa government by agreement between the Government and Gandhiji, so option 1 is correct.
The Champaran struggle was against forced indigo cultivation and illegal exactions, to solve the problems of indigo workers. The other options do not relate to Champaran.
Tinkathia was the system in Champaran under which tenants had to grow indigo (neel) on 3/20th of their land for European planters.

Champaran was the first satyagraha in India and Rajendra Prasad and Kripalani worked with Gandhi there, so I and II are correct. Statement III is wrong because Satyagraha was already formulated in South Africa.

Champaran connected peasant grievances (indigo cultivators) with Gandhi and the national movement, which is its significant aspect. It did not involve all-India participation of lawyers, students and women, and the decrease in plantation crops was a result.
The 2024 double cicada emergence (Brood XIII and Brood XIX together, first in 221 years) is the correct answer. The notes do not mention cicadas or this phenomenon, so no line supports it.
India launched the national family planning programme in 1952, the first country in the world to do so.
NPP 2000 set the long-term goal of a stable population by 2045; 2070 is only the later revised target.
The current target year for population stability is 2070, revised from the original 2045 in NPP 2000.
World Population Day is observed on 11 July each year.
JSY gives a cash incentive for institutional delivery, so statements I and II are correct. It is not a wage-loss compensation scheme, so III is wrong.
JSY aims to cut both maternal and neonatal mortality among poor pregnant women through institutional delivery, so option 1 is right and the 'only' options are wrong.

Nokrek is in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya, so pair I is correct. Namdapha lies in the Dapha bum (Mishmi)–Patkai area, not the Dafla Hills, and Loktak is in Manipur (the notes do not place it in the Barail Range), so II and III are wrong.
Indravati National Park is in Bastar, Chhattisgarh. Betla is in Jharkhand and Gugamal is in Maharashtra.
Vansda National Park is in Gujarat (Dangs/Navsari). The notes do not mention it.

Desert National Park is a natural habitat of the Great Indian Bustard, so III is correct. It spans two districts (Jaisalmer and Barmer), so I is correct. It has human habitation inside (villages), so II is wrong.
Rajiv Gandhi National Park is the other name of Nagarhole in Karnataka. The notes list a Rajiv Gandhi NP in Andhra Pradesh (Rameswaram), which is the tempting wrong option.
Bajirao, the last captive white tiger, died at Sanjay Gandhi National Park (Mumbai). The notes do not cover this.
The Godavari flows through Papikonda National Park in Andhra Pradesh.
Kanha National Park received the Green Guard Award for 2001-02.
Kanha lies in the Tropical Dry Forest biogeographic zone (dry deciduous). The notes do not state this.
Karl Marx was born in Trier, Prussia (Germany), so Germany is correct; he later lived in France and Britain but belonged to Germany.
Nicosia is the capital of Cyprus. The other pairs are wrong: Bogota is Colombia's capital, Caracas is Venezuela's, and Wellington is New Zealand's.
