CACP is the commission that recommends MSP, and the Ministry of Agriculture is not the determining body. Of the options, CACP is the best answer.
The Agricultural Prices Commission was set up in January 1965 and renamed CACP in 1985.
CACP recommends support prices for crops including foodgrains. The Planning Commission and the Ministries do not.
CACP makes the MSP recommendations, and CCEA approves them. ICAR, NABARD and IARI do not.
Wheat is a covered MSP crop, and MSPs are recommended by CACP. The President, RBI and Planning Commission do not recommend them.
CACP considers cost of production, domestic and international price trends, and inter-crop price parity. A cost of living index is not among the listed factors.
The Agricultural Prices Commission was established in January 1965 and later became CACP in 1985.
E-FAST India stands for Electric Freight Accelerator for Sustainable Transport, launched by NITI Aayog and WRI; the notes do not cover this fact.
The Trans-Siberian runs through Russian cities such as St. Petersburg (Leningrad), Moscow and Vladivostok. Georgia is a separate country, not a station on the line.
The Trans-Canada Highway runs from Saint John's (Newfoundland) in the east to Vancouver (Victoria) in the west, so option 1 is right. The notes do not cover this highway.
The Trans-Siberian (Moscow-Vladivostok, 9,289 km) is the longest continuous railway line in the world. The Canadian railways are shorter.

The Orient Express is the luxury train running Paris-Istanbul across central Europe, passing through Germany, Austria, Hungary and Romania. The Trans-Siberian and the Union/Central Pacific are in Russia and the USA.

Trans-Andean is Chile-Argentina (Buenos Aires-Valparaiso), Trans-Siberian is Leningrad (St. Petersburg)-Vladivostok, and Orient Express is Paris-Istanbul. By elimination, the European Trans-Continental is Paris-Warsaw, giving 5 4 2 1.
BPL status in India depends on whether a person can obtain the minimum prescribed food basket, so option 1 is right. Work days and wages are not the criteria.
India defines poverty by calorie intake norms (2,400 kcal rural and 2,100 kcal urban per person per day), so option 3 is right. Income is not the basis.
The rural poverty line norm is 2,400 kcal per capita per day (urban 2,100), so the answer is 2400.
Absolute poverty is defined by a fixed minimum consumption/calorie norm needed for survival, so option 2 is right. A fixed calorie norm means absolute, not relative, poverty.
The rural calorie benchmark is 2,400 kcal per person per day (urban is 2,100), so the answer is 2400.
Poverty in India is defined in terms of calorie intake (2,400 kcal rural, 2,100 kcal urban), so option 2 is right.
India estimates poverty using the Head Count Ratio, calorie norms and household consumption expenditure. Per capita income is not the basis, so I, II and III are correct.
India's poverty line is based on household consumption expenditure (MPCE) from NSSO/HCES surveys, not income, so option 3 is right.
The Gol Gumbaz is at Bijapur and is the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah, so Bijapur is correct.
Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur is the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah, who built it for himself, so option 1 is correct.
Gol Gumbaz is the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah, who ordered its construction, so option 4 is correct.
The Kohinoor came from the Kollur mines on the Krishna, so Kolluru is correct; the other options are not linked to it.
The English factory at Machilipatnam in 1611 was set up with the permission of Muhammad Quli, so he is the correct answer.
Mir Jumla, minister of Abdullah Qutb Shah, gave the Kohinoor to Shah Jahan; Tavernier only recorded it.
The Kohinoor came from Kollur, a mine in the Golconda kingdom's territory on the Krishna, so Golconda is the best option here; Bijapur is wrong.
Vijayapuri, modern Nagarjunakonda, was the Ikshvaku capital; Amaravati is the tempting wrong option, but it was not the capital.
The Gurajala (Gurazala) inscription was issued by Rudrapurushadatta, the last Ikshvaku king; Jaggayyapeta belongs to Virapurushadatta.
The Kakatiyas were first feudatories of the Rashtrakutas, and only later of the Kalyani Chalukyas. Eastern Chalukyas only issued the Magallu grant that first mentions them.
Ganapatideva united 'Telugudesam' and was the greatest Kakatiya ruler, so he ruled the whole region as a unified sovereign. Prataparudra I (Rudradeva) only began the independent kingdom.

Rudradeva built the Thousand Pillar temple (A-II); Ganapatideva completed the shift of the capital to Orugallu (B-I); Marco Polo visited in Rudrama's reign (C-IV); Malik Kafur besieged Warangal in Prataparudra II's time (D-III).
Orugallu (Warangal) was the Kakatiya capital, shifted there by Rudradeva. Vijayanagara, Amaravati and Visakhapatnam were not Kakatiya capitals.
Orugallu (Warangal) was the Kakatiya capital, shifted there by Rudradeva. Vijayanagara, Amaravati and Visakhapatnam were not Kakatiya capitals.
The Pandyas defeated Ganapatideva at the Battle of Muttukur in 1263, and Nellore fell to them. The Velanati Chodas had already ended earlier.
The Census Organisation functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs (Registrar General and Census Commissioner), permanently since 1961. The notes do not state this.
2001-11 growth was 17.70%, lower than 1971-81 (24.66%), 1981-91 (23.87%) and 1991-2001 (21.54%), so it is the lowest among the options.
1921 is called the Great Divide because it was the only Census with negative growth, after which growth accelerated.
1921 is termed the 'Demographic Divide' as the only Census with negative decadal growth, followed by faster growth.
1921 is the 'Demographic Divide'; 1951 is not, as the notes stress.
1921 was the only Census with negative decadal growth (−0.31%), so the answer is 1921.
1961-71 had the highest decadal growth (24.80%), higher than 1981-91 and 2001-11 and the other option decade.
The notes do not name the author of 'Interlinking of Indian Rivers'; the answer is Radhakant Bharati, who wrote the book.

Hariyali is a Centrally sponsored watershed and wasteland development scheme run through Panchayati Raj Institutions (rural), so statement I is correct. It is not aimed at urban rainwater conservation, so statement II is wrong.
The notes give the MMDR Act as 1957, which contradicts the stated answer of 1948. The marked key (1948) appears inconsistent with the 1957 Act; the Act is the parent law of 1957.
Vitamin D2 is ergocalciferol (D3 is cholecalciferol, the 'chole-' form), so option 1 is correct.
Orange (citrus fruit) is a well-known rich source of vitamin C. The notes name amla as the richest source, but it is not among the options, so orange is the correct choice.
Golden Rice is genetically engineered to contain beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, so the answer is vitamin A.
Polishing rice removes the bran that holds the B vitamins, causing thiamine (B1) deficiency, which leads to beri-beri. Rickets, anaemia and goitre are due to other deficiencies.
Skin synthesises vitamin D when exposed to the UV rays in sunlight, so vitamin D is the 'sunshine vitamin'.
The PoA Act was enacted in 1989 (assent 11 Sept 1989) and came into force in January 1990; 1989 is the enactment year.
Dumping waste, excreta or carcasses in or near the premises of an SC/ST member is listed as an atrocity under s.3 of the PoA Act. The other options are not listed atrocities in that form.
Section 10A of the PCR Act 1955 empowers the State Government to impose a collective fine on inhabitants of an area. Section 10 deals with abetment and s.14 with offences by companies.
The PCR Act extends to the whole of India (s.1(2)), so the option excluding J&K is wrong.
Under s.15 of the PCR Act, offences are cognizable, triable summarily and non-compoundable. Hence the option 'cognizable and non-compoundable' is correct.
Rishabhadeva (Adinatha) is the first of the 24 Tirthankaras; Ajitnatha was only the second.
Nathamuni is not a Jain Tirthankara, whereas Sambhavnath (3rd) and Neminatha (22nd) are Tirthankaras; Chandraprabha is the 8th.
Mahavira is the 24th and last Tirthankara; Parshvanath was the 23rd.
Parshvanatha was born at Varanasi to King Asvasena and Queen Vama, so he is associated mainly with Varanasi.
Parshvanatha attained nirvana at Sammed Shikhar (Parasnath hill), making it a Jain Siddha Kshetra linked to him; Pava is linked to Mahavira.
Mahavira is the 24th and last Tirthankara; Parshvanatha was the 23rd.
Among the options, Rishabhadeva is the first Tirthankara and is regarded as the originator of Jainism, while Mahavira was the last and Parshvanatha the 23rd.

Mahavira was the 24th and last Tirthankara, and the earlier Tirthankaras preceded him, so he is seen as a reformer of an existing tradition rather than the founder. Option 2 is wrong because the 23rd was Parshvanatha.
Jamali was the first follower of Mahavira.

Statement I is wrong because Mahavira's mother Trishala was Chetaka's sister, not his daughter. Statement III is correct as Parshvanatha was born at Varanasi (Banaras), and II is correct, so II and III is the answer.
Mahavira died at Pavapuri (Pava) near Rajgir at the age of 72.
Of Mahavira's disciples only Arya Sudharma survived him, and he became the first Thera, i.e. head of the Jain Sangh.
Jamali is recorded as Mahavira's first follower or disciple.
The notes state that oil in Andhra Pradesh's rock systems is of Pleistocene age. Dharwad and Archaean rocks are old and metamorphic or igneous, and Cuddapah has no petroleum.
Momentum = mass × velocity, so its SI unit is kg m s⁻¹. The notes do not state this unit.
The newton is the SI unit of force. The other options are units of pressure (pascal), power (watt) and energy (joule).
The henry (H) is the SI unit of inductance.
Resistivity ρ = RA/l has the unit ohm-metre.
Torque = force × perpendicular distance, so its unit is N m. Force is in N, power in W and acceleration in m/s².
The slope of a distance-time graph is distance/time, which is speed.
Inertia is the tendency of a body to stay at rest or in uniform motion (Newton's first law).
Mass measures inertia; weight depends on gravity.
By Newton's second law, force = rate of change of momentum.
Newton's second law says the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the net applied force, in the direction of the force. Option 3 is the first law.
By conservation of momentum, the gun and bullet get equal and opposite momenta. The gun is much heavier, so its recoil velocity is smaller. Statement II therefore explains Statement I.
Power is the rate of doing work (work/time).
A body with speed below escape velocity is gravitationally bound, so its total energy (KE + PE) is negative.
A spring balance works on Hooke's law: extension is proportional to the applied force.
Pascal is the unit of pressure, defined as force per area, so 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
The notes do not define pressure as force per area. By the question's convention this is attributed to Pascal's law, as in the key.
Pressure varying with depth as p = p0 + ρgh is the hydrostatic pressure relation, attributed to Pascal's law in the key.
Archimedes' principle explains buoyancy, so Archimedes explained the buoyant force.
The upward force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced is Archimedes' principle (buoyancy).
Archimedes' principle relates to buoyancy and the density of the body, and density helps check a metal's purity.
Art. 352 allows the President to proclaim a National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion, so all the listed grounds are valid.
The 44th CAA cut the approval period for a National Emergency from two months to one month, so Parliament must approve within 1 month.

Fundamental rights (Art. 19 automatically under Art. 358, enforcement of others under Art. 359) can be suspended only when a National Emergency is proclaimed, not by an ordinary act, notification or court decision.
During a National Emergency Parliament can legislate on State List subjects (Art. 250); the ministers or the PM cannot do so by themselves.
President's Rule is imposed under Art. 356 when a State cannot be governed per the Constitution; 352 is National and 360 is Financial Emergency.
President's Rule in a State is imposed under Art. 356; Art. 352 deals with National Emergency.
Under Art. 356 the President acts on the Governor's report that the State government cannot be carried on per the Constitution; no recommendation of the Legislature or CM is needed.
Failure of constitutional machinery in a State is handled by Art. 356 (President's Rule, the State/constitutional emergency), not National or Financial Emergency.

Under President's Rule the Council of Ministers is necessarily dismissed, but the Assembly may only be suspended rather than dissolved, and local bodies are not affected. So I and III are not necessary consequences.
Dr. Ambedkar hoped Art. 356 would remain a dead letter, used only as a last resort.
A finding of breakdown of constitutional machinery in a State falls under Art. 356 (President's Rule).
S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994) was the landmark 9-judge case on Art. 356 and President's Rule.
S.R. Bommai (1994) dealt with Art. 356 and federalism, directly affecting Centre-State relations.

The environment supplies both renewable and non-renewable resources, so saying it provides renewable resources only is the incorrect statement. Sustaining life, aesthetic services and waste assimilation are all genuine functions.
Breaking organic waste into nutrients through microorganisms is biodegradation, the waste-assimilation function of the environment.
The vital function is assimilating waste, not 'assimilating wealth', so option 3 is not a function. The other options are genuine functions of the environment.

The environment assimilates waste by biodegradation, which turns it into reusable nutrients. The statement that it 'disorganizes waste that benefits human life' does not describe this function, so it is the odd one out.

Recreation and aesthetics is leisure and scenic value, cultural heritage is traditional knowledge and practices, medicinal resources are drugs from plants and animals, and waste decomposition is the breakdown of organic waste. This gives a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
Pollination by birds is called ornithophily (anemophily is by wind, entomophily by insects, and autogamy is self-pollination). The notes do not cover this.
Nutrients are recycled between organisms, air and the Earth's crust, and this movement is the biogeochemical cycle. Ecological succession is a different process, the replacement of communities.
The cyclic movement of elements between organisms, air and the Earth's crust is called the biogeochemical cycle.

Photosynthesis, including that by phytoplankton, removes CO₂, and dissolving in oceans also removes it, so statement II is correct. The notes do not support CO₂ escaping to the stratosphere or being trapped in polar ice caps.
The Deep Carbon Observatory is a global research programme studying carbon on Earth, including deep microbial life, so both statements are correct. The notes do not cover it.
Pelsaert, a Dutch factor, came to India in 1620 during Jahangir's reign. Manucci and Bernier belong to the Shah Jahan–Aurangzeb period (Dara Shikoh's time), so they are wrong.
Pelsaert, a Dutch factor, came to India in 1620 during Jahangir's reign. Mundy wrote of Shah Jahan's reign, and Manucci came later with Dara Shikoh.
The quote is from Pelsaert's Remonstrantie, which describes the harsh condition of the peasantry under Jahangir. Bernier is the tempting alternative, but this remark is not his.
Tavernier, the French diamond merchant, visited the Golconda mines and wrote about diamonds in his Six Voyages. Bernier and Thevenot are not known for diamond accounts.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq was the first to introduce token currency (copper/brass); Iltutmish's coins were the silver tanka and copper jital.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq is credited with building the maximum number of canals among the Sultans.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted the capital to Daulatabad (Devagiri), so option 4 is right.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq brought Ashoka's Pillar to Delhi, as noted among his public works.
The five Delhi dynasties were Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi; the Ghori dynasty is not among them, as Ghori was only the overlord before 1206.
Iltutmish introduced the silver tanka and copper jital and was the first Sultan to shift the capital to Delhi, so he fits both parts; Aibak ruled from Lahore.
Aibak began the Qutub Minar (basement only) and Iltutmish completed it.
Razia was the daughter of Iltutmish and the first woman ruler.
Malik Kafur was Alauddin Khalji's general who led the southern expeditions.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved the capital to Daulatabad (Devagiri).
Firoz Shah Tughlaq built the maximum number of canals among the Sultans.
Alauddin Khalji raised a powerful, huge standing army to guard the frontier, so he is the answer.
Aurobindo retired from politics to Pondicherry in 1910, where his ashram is located, so Pondicherry is correct.
Chittaranjan Das defended Aurobindo in the Alipore Bomb Case, which led to his acquittal in 1909; the notes do not name the defence counsel.
Soz-e-Watan, a banned collection of patriotic stories, was written by Premchand (Dhanpat Rai); the other options are Hindi poets/writers who did not write it.
The first split of the INC between Moderates and Extremists occurred at Surat in December 1907; the other sessions listed are not the split.
The Surat session of 1907 was presided over by Rash Behari Ghosh, the Moderates' choice, so R.B. Ghosh is correct.
The four Calcutta 1906 resolutions were Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education; annulment of the partition of Bengal was not one of them.
Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets, B12 causes pernicious anaemia, C causes scurvy and A causes night blindness, which gives A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3.

Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, so I and II are correct. Pellagra is due to vitamin B3 deficiency, while vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, so III is wrong.
Goitre is caused by iodine deficiency, which leads to an enlarged thyroid. Nitrogen, calcium and phosphorus are not linked to goitre.
Iodine deficiency causes goitre, an enlarged thyroid. Night blindness is caused by vitamin A deficiency, not iodine.
Iron deficiency causes anaemia. Night blindness is due to vitamin A deficiency, and tuberculosis is an infection.
The notes show YSR Sampoorna Poshana Plus covers the 77 tribal mandals, not all mandals except them, so III is wrong. The answer (only I and IV correct) rests on facts not in the notes.
Daniel Patrick Moynihan was a Democrat, not a Republican, so option 4 is the untrue statement. The notes do not cover this topic.
The Independent Labour Party was founded by B.R. Ambedkar in 1936.
Ambedkar founded the Independent Labour Party (1936) and the Scheduled Castes Federation (1942). The Peasants and Workers Party of India was not his, so only II and III are correct.
Ambedkar attended all three Round Table Conferences, while Gandhi attended only the second. The others named did not attend all three.

All three statements are correct. Ambedkar demanded separate electorates at the First RTC, the Poona Pact gave a share in civil services and local bodies, and Congress did not take part in the Third RTC.
The Poona Pact (1932) was between Gandhi and Ambedkar. Gandhi-Irwin was a different pact (1931).
The pact between Ambedkar and Gandhi in 1932 is the Poona Pact.
The Communal Award gave separate electorates to Muslims, Europeans, Sikhs, Christians and Depressed Classes. It had no 10-year lapse clause, so option 4 is not a provision.
Gandhi did not sign the Poona Pact. It was signed by Ambedkar, Malaviya and others.
The Poona Pact replaced separate electorates with joint electorates and reserved seats (148) for the depressed classes. Its purpose was representation of untouchables.
The quote about measuring a community's progress by women's progress is by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
Mihirakula, the Huna ruler, was defeated by the Aulikara king Yashodharman of Mandasor in c. 528 CE. Budhagupta, Shashanka and Prabhakaravardhana are not credited with this victory.

Dharapatta and Guhasena were rulers of the Maitrakas, who ruled from Valabhi in Gujarat. Yashodharman was an Aulikara of Mandsaur, and the Maukharis and Pushyabhutis had other seats (Kannauj, Thanesar).
Rajasekhara Charitra (1878) by Veeresalingam is the first Telugu novel, based on Goldsmith's Vicar of Wakefield. Satihita Bodhini was a women's journal, not a novel.
The notes do not mention Mahbub College; they list his principalship at Pithapuram Raja's College, Kakinada (1905-18). Mahbub College (Hyderabad) is the answer from outside knowledge.
Kanyasulkam, the social play on bride-price and child marriage, was written by Gurajada Apparao (first staged 1892). Veeresalingam was a reformer and prose writer, not its author.
The notes mention the American Baptist mission only in Rayalaseema from 1835 and at Ongole, with no 1866 date. The answer 1866 comes from outside the notes.
The NCEUS, set up in 2004, was chaired by Arjun Sengupta, so option 3 is correct.
The 28th QES (2015) by the Labour Bureau found textiles and apparel contributed most to job growth, so option 2 is correct.
NSSO 2014 estimated that 57.8% of rural households were engaged in agriculture, so option 3 is correct.

Unsafe water and poor sanitation cause malaria, acute diarrhoea and schistosomiasis, while kwashiorkor (a protein-deficiency disorder) is not one of them. Cholera, diarrhoea and dysentery are faeco-oral diseases.
Hepatitis (A, E) is caused by viruses. Diphtheria and cholera are bacterial, and malaria is protozoan.

Typhoid is a faeco-oral, water-borne disease caused by Salmonella Typhi, so it spreads when waste contaminates drinking water. Scurvy and anaemia are deficiency disorders, and malaria is spread by mosquitoes.
Both cholera and typhoid are water-borne faeco-oral diseases caused by contaminated water, so the answer is both.
Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae and spreads through contaminated food and water (faeco-oral route). It is not a genetic, memory or muscle disease.
Herpes is a viral disease. Malaria is protozoan, and typhoid and diphtheria are bacterial.
DDT-resistant mosquitoes survived and reproduced, so resistant individuals became more common over generations. This is natural selection.
SuperView-1 (Gaofen Commercial) is a Chinese commercial remote-sensing constellation, so China is correct; the notes do not cover it.
The notes give only the 2023-24 SDG India Index (Kerala and Uttarakhand top at 79, Bihar last at 57). They do not list the top five States for 2020-21, so no line settles this.
Tondaimandalam, with its capital at Kanchipuram, was the Pallava territory. The Chalukyas, Kakatiyas and Satavahanas ruled elsewhere.

Sivaskandavarman brought Kanchi under the Pallavas (II), Vishnugopa faced Samudragupta's invasion (I), Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakesin II and took Vatapi (IV), and Nandivarman II was defeated by Vikramaditya II (III). This gives A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.
Dashakumaracharita (Daskumarcharitam) was written by Dandin, a poet of the Pallava court. Bharavi wrote the Kiratarjuniya.
Duggirala (Guntur district) is known for turmeric; the notes do not state this fact.
Jowar is the second most important food grain crop after paddy in Andhra Pradesh; the notes do not state this.
The Sept 2020 MoU on food processing, marketing and technology for horticulture and aquaculture was signed with the Netherlands; the notes do not cover it.
The National Kamdhenu Breeding Centre is at Chintaladevi, Nellore. Gokul Gram is a different facility, at Chadalawada.
Andhra Pradesh recorded the highest inland fish landings in India in 2019-20.

Statement I is correct: Matsyakara Bharosa is ban-period relief for marine fishermen. Statement III is supported by the HSD diesel subsidy. Statement II is wrong because the AP Fisheries University is in West Godavari, not East Godavari, so option 3 is right.
Defence, foreign affairs and atomic energy are Union List subjects (Entries 1, 6, 10); there is no separate 'Residuary List', and the other lists cover State/local or shared subjects.
Forests are Concurrent List entry 17A (moved by the 42nd Amendment). Police is State, while Railways and Atomic Energy are Union subjects.
High Courts' organisation is Union Entry 78, taxes on mineral rights are State Entry 50, and education is Concurrent Entry 25, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
Opium (for export) is Union List Entry 59, so it is a Union subject, not a State or Concurrent one.
Local government, including panchayats and municipalities, is State List Entry 5, so Panchayati Raj is a State subject.
Boron, zinc and copper are essential plant micronutrients, whereas sodium is not required by most plants, so sodium is the answer.
Lemon contains citric acid; acetic acid is in vinegar, ascorbic acid is vitamin C, and nitric acid is a mineral acid not found in lemons.
Vinegar is acetic acid, whose IUPAC name is ethanoic acid; formic acid is the ant-sting acid and not the main component of vinegar.
Cheese is a gel, a colloid of liquid dispersed in a solid; milk is an emulsion of liquid in liquid, and mud is a suspension of solid in liquid.
Benzoic acid (as sodium benzoate) is a food preservative used in food processing; sodium carbonate, acetylene and sodium nitrate are not typical food-processing substances in this sense.
Lemon contains citric acid in free form, as the notes state; tamarind mainly contains tartaric acid and apple malic acid.
Sucralose is made by selectively replacing hydroxyl groups of sucrose with chlorine, so it is modified sugar; aspartame is a dipeptide-based sweetener and saccharin is synthetic.
Chicory powder is made from the roasted, ground root of the chicory plant, so the answer is root.

Petrol/diesel (awaiting a Council date), liquor (excluded by the Constitution), electricity and charitable entities' services are all outside GST levy as per the notes, so all of the above is correct.
Crude petroleum and natural gas are among the five petroleum products kept out of GST until the Council recommends a date; aviation (ATF) is also one of them, so all the above is correct.
Lottery prizes were fixed at a uniform 28% GST rate by the GST Council, which is why 28% is correct.
Project Saksham is the CBEC/CBIC IT system-integration project for the new indirect tax (GST) network, so option 3 is correct; the other options are unrelated schemes.
Jammu and Kashmir was the last State to adopt GST (8 July 2017), after the 1 July 2017 rollout, whereas the other States joined on 1 July.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the words "Socialist", "Secular" and "Integrity" to the Preamble; the 44th restored other provisions but left these words intact.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added "Socialist" to the Preamble, along with "Secular" and "Integrity"; the 44th and 52nd dealt with other matters.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted "Secular" in the Preamble, along with "Socialist" and "Integrity"; the 44th did not remove it.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added both "Socialist" and "Secular" (and "Integrity") to the Preamble.
The 44th Amendment (1978) allowed the President to return ministerial advice once for reconsideration; the 42nd had made the advice binding.
The 73rd Amendment (Panchayats, Part IX) came into force on 24 April 1993; 1 June 1993 is the date for the 74th Amendment (Municipalities).
The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 (Art. 326); it came into force on 28 March 1989.
The 91st Amendment (2003) limited the Council of Ministers to 15% of the House strength (Arts 75(1A), 164(1A)).
The 73rd Amendment (1992) added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule, giving constitutional status to Panchayati Raj.
The 61st Amendment (1988) reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 by amending Art. 326.
The 69th Amendment (1991) made Delhi the National Capital Territory by inserting Arts 239AA and 239AB.
The 69th Amendment (1991) gave Delhi the status of National Capital Territory through Arts 239AA and 239AB.
Article 110 defines a Money Bill. Article 109 gives the special procedure for Money Bills, 111 deals with assent and 112 with the Budget.

The President can assent to or withhold assent from a Money Bill but cannot return it for reconsideration, so option 4 is the incorrect statement. Options 1-3 are correct: the Speaker's decision is final and a Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha.

An ordinary Bill generally needs no prior recommendation of the President, except in the listed cases. Money Bills and Financial Bills (the Finance Bill is usually a Money Bill) need the President's recommendation at introduction.
The Finance Bill gives effect to the Budget's tax proposals, which are how the Government collects revenue for the year. The other options are not the Bill used for this.
The Rajya Sabha can discuss the Annual Financial Statement but cannot vote on the Demands for Grants, so statement 3 is the incorrect one. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct.
The World Happiness Report 2015 ranked Switzerland as the happiest country, ahead of Iceland and Denmark, so option 4 is correct.
Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport was the first carbon neutral airport in Asia-Pacific, so option 4 is correct. The other airports listed are not credited with this first.

The Repeal Bill was introduced in the AP Assembly in November 2021, when both the Decentralisation Act and the APCRDA (Repeal) Act of 2020 were withdrawn. The 2020 dates are when the Acts were passed, not when the Repeal Bill was introduced.
The three-capitals Acts, including the 2020 Decentralisation Act, were withdrawn in November 2021. 2020 is the year they were enacted, so it is not the answer.

Bharat QR lets a customer scan a merchant's single QR code to pay instantly from the phone, which is what option 1 describes. The other options (BIS regulation, defence equipment, import restrictions) have nothing to do with payments.

BHIM is NPCI's UPI app, so it lets users send money to any UPI-enabled bank account, making statement I correct. Statement II is wrong: the claim that a chip-and-pin debit card has four authentication factors is not true, so only I is correct.
NPCI products such as AePS support financial inclusion, so statement I holds. NPCI also launched RuPay (2012), the domestic card network, so statement II holds; both are correct.

The Kalpakkam FBR (PFBR) runs on MOX fuel, a mix of plutonium-239 and U-238, and the FBTR uses a plutonium-uranium mixed carbide. Plutonium is therefore the fissile fuel; uranium-238 is only the fertile blanket material.
Dhruva, Purnima and CIRUS are all research reactors at Trombay. They are not stars, books or power plants.
Pitchblende is the main ore of uranium, the metal used as nuclear fuel. Bauxite, quartz and feldspar are not nuclear fuel minerals.
Kerala's coastal beach sands are rich in monazite, which is the principal thorium ore, so the radioactivity along the coast is due to thorium.
The notes support the ITER location and the membership (statement IV) and show that Aditya is an IPR tokamak. The key marks all four statements as correct.
ITER tests fusion power, so if it succeeds India can build fusion power reactors. Using thorium concerns fission breeding, and ITER has nothing to do with satellite navigation.
The Department of Atomic Energy functions directly under the Prime Minister's Office, hence option 1.

The oblate shape results from Earth's rotation, whose centrifugal effect is greatest at the Equator, so I is right. The Sun's gravitational pull and sunlight intensity do not cause the bulge, so II and III are wrong.
Weight (and so g) is minimum at the Equator and maximum at the poles, because the centrifugal force is greatest at the Equator. So g is greater at the poles than at the equator.
Weight is least at the Equator and increases towards higher latitudes, so A is false. Earth is an oblate spheroid, not a perfect sphere, so R is true.

The equatorial bulge of about 21 km in radius (the diameters differ by about 43 km) is true, so A is true. R is wrong because it is Earth's rotation, with maximum centrifugal force at the Equator, that causes the bulge, and not a 'slow' rotation. So R does not explain A.
Earth is an oblate spheroid, bulging at the Equator, so its equatorial radius is about 21 km greater than its polar radius. Points at the poles are nearer the centre, so g is greater there.
The equatorial circumference of the Earth is about 40,075 km, i.e. roughly 40,000 km.
Latitude is the angle at the Earth's centre between the equatorial plane and the line to the point, so it is measured from the centre of the Earth. The Equator is only the zero reference line.
Billa Surgam (Kurnool) is a Palaeolithic (old stone age) site with stone and bone tools. Keesarapalli is Chalcolithic and Utnur is a Neolithic ash mound.
Patapadu (Kurnool) is the standard Chalcolithic site of Andhra, with painted pottery. Sanganakallu and Tekkalakota are Neolithic sites in Karnataka, and Palavoy is a Neolithic settlement.
Dadabhai Naoroji, presiding at the Calcutta Congress of 1906, made the first demand for Swaraj as the goal. Tilak, Gandhi and Motilal Nehru are not credited with this first use.

The first Indian to contest a Commons election was Lal Mohan Ghose (1885); Naoroji was the first to be elected (1892). The keyed answer is Naoroji, but the notes say the contest was Ghose's, so the key conflicts with them.
Naoroji is the Moderate leader linked with the demand for Swaraj, which he made as Congress president at Calcutta in 1906. The notes do not mention 1904 or 1905 specifically.
The Charter Act of 1813 set aside Rs 1 lakh a year for education, the first step toward State responsibility for education. The 1773 and 1784 Acts and the 1833 Act made no such grant.
The notes list 'Train to Pakistan' as a work by Khushwant Singh, so option 4 is correct.
The notes do not mention 'India Remembered'; it is a book by Pamela Mountbatten (daughter of Lord Mountbatten), so option 3 is correct.

A modem (modulator-demodulator) converts data to signals suitable for the telephone line and back, linking a computer with the telephone line; a magnetic disc, microcomputer or CD-ROM does not do this.
A modem converts digital to analog and analog to digital, so both (A) and (B) are correct.
A modem links a microcomputer with the telephone line, so it interfaces telephone lines and computer equipment.
IPv4 uses 32 bits while IPv6 uses 128 bits, so IPv4 needs fewer bits than IPv6.
Computers on the internet are identified by IPv4/IPv6 addresses, i.e. their IP address; an e-mail address identifies a user, not the computer.
A modem links a computer with the telephone line to send and receive data worldwide; a fax, scanner or hub does not.
The Harappan culture lay along the Sindhu, Chenab, Jhelum, Ravi and Sutlej rivers, but not the Ganga, so I, II and III are correct and IV is wrong.
The civilisation covered a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia and spread from the Jhelum eastwards to the Hindon, which supports all three statements.
Alamgirpur on the Hindon in Meerut is the eastern limit of the Harappan culture, so its finds reflect Harappan culture.

Mohenjodaro, Harappa, Ropar and Kalibangan are major Harappan sites, so I is correct. Statement II is also correct because the Harappans had planned towns with roads and drains. Statement III is false because the Harappans used copper, bronze and silver.
The Sumerians of Mesopotamia developed the earliest proper writing system (cuneiform). The Indus script is still undeciphered, so Indus is not the answer.
Daya Ram Sahni (Harappa, 1921) and Rakhaldas Banerji (Mohenjodaro, 1922) were the two Indians who found the main Harappan cities. John Marshall was British.
Amalananda Ghosh was the first to identify similarities between the pre-Harappan (Sothi) culture and the mature Harappan culture.
Dholavira was inhabited from about 3000 to 1800 BCE, in seven stages.
Critics of Rostow argue that data contradict his take-off thesis, that he does not explain growth after take-off, and that the stages are hard to test empirically, so all three criticisms hold.
The human development concept and the HDI were developed by Mahbub ul Haq, building on Sen's capability ideas. Sen supplied the underlying approach, but Haq is credited with the concept.

Inclusion strategy targets lower inequality, poverty reduction and livelihoods for disadvantaged groups within a country. Bringing poorer countries closer together is an international aim, not part of inclusion strategy.
The Argumentative Indian is a book by Amartya Sen, the Nobel-winning economist, with essays on Indian history, culture and identity.
The first Nobel Prize in Economics (1969) went jointly to Jan Tinbergen and Ragnar Frisch. Samuelson won in 1970 and Sen in 1998.
HDI combines the health dimension (life expectancy), the education dimension (schooling) and the income dimension (GNI per capita). So the missing component is the Education Index.
The notes give the best index of development as the yearly growth of per capita real income. Current-price national income is distorted by inflation and ignores population.
HDI uses life expectancy, education and income per capita. Urbanisation is not part of it.
India ranked 131st in the UNDP Human Development Report 2020.
HDI uses life expectancy at birth, schooling (education enrolment) and per capita income. Health and nutrition is not a separate constituent.
The HDI was developed by Mahbub ul Haq with Sen's ideas as the base. Sen is therefore the tempting but wrong option.
The Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act) was passed in March 1919, so 1919 is correct.
The Rowlatt Act was called the 'Black Bill' (Black Act) because of its repressive provisions like detention without trial; the other Acts are not known by this name.

Statements I and III are right: the 1919 Act introduced provincial dyarchy and delegated authority to the provinces by clearly defining central and provincial jurisdiction. Separate electorates for Muslims came with the 1909 Act, so II is wrong.
II and III are right: the 1919 Act devolved authority to the provinces and created a bicameral centre with direct elections. Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced in 1909, so I is wrong.
Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces by the GoI Act 1919, which is the Montagu-Chelmsford (Montford) Reforms. Morley-Minto is the 1909 Act and 1935 only had dyarchy planned at the Centre.
Dyarchy was first introduced in the provinces by the GoI Act 1919, the Montagu-Chelmsford (Mont-Ford) Reforms. The 1935 Act's dyarchy at the Centre never operated.
The Commission was boycotted because it had no Indian member, all seven being British. The other options are wrong: it was a review required by the Act, and its report came later.
MPLADS was started in 1993 (the notes list it as MPLADS (1993)), so option 2 is correct.
SAGY was launched on 11 October 2014, the birth anniversary of Lok Nayak Jayaprakash Narayan, not Gandhi (whose birth anniversary is 2 October).
Akodara village in Sabarkantha, Gujarat, developed by ICICI Bank, was dedicated to the nation in January 2015 as India's first digital village.
Saansad Adarsh Gram Yojana (SAGY) was launched on 11 October 2014, the birth anniversary of Jayaprakash Narayan; the other schemes are not linked to that date.
MPLADS funds are non-lapsable, so unused funds can be carried forward; statement 3 is therefore incorrect. The SC/ST earmark in statement 2 is correct.
MPLADS was introduced in 1993 (December 1993), so option 4 is correct.
DAY-NULM (2013) was run by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation, now merged into the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs.
In Feb 2022 MoHUA approved ₹235 crore for Andhra Pradesh under 'Garbage free cities'.
The June 2023 Microsoft–DGT (MSDE) MoU aimed to train about 6,000 students in cybersecurity.
DDU-GKY is a Ministry of Rural Development placement-linked skilling programme for rural youth.
SAMARTH is the Ministry of Textiles' skilling scheme for the textile sector, not an MSDE scheme; the notes do not cover it.
An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy (rotation). Option 4 describes a generator, the reverse process.
Turbines turn mechanical (rotational) energy into electrical energy in the generator; dynamos work the same way.
A dynamo is a generator that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. Options 1 and 4 describe transformers and option 2 describes a motor.
A generator converts mechanical (rotational) energy into electrical energy, as in a wind turbine's generator.
According to NIWE/MNRE potential at 120 m hub height, Gujarat is highest (142.56 GW), ahead of Rajasthan and Karnataka.
Installed wind capacity was 39.25 GW on 31 March 2021.
Tamil Nadu was the earlier leader but Gujarat overtook it in 2023 and now has the largest wind installation, so Tamil Nadu is no longer correct. The key is the exam date context.
Subroto Cup is India's inter-school football tournament, so Football is correct. The notes do not mention it.
Great Britain won the 2017 Azlan Shah Cup in Ipoh, Malaysia, beating Australia in the final. The notes do not cover this.
Tamil Nadu was the first State to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all buildings; AP's APWALTA 2002 only covered plots of 200 sq m and above.
Jal Shakti Abhiyan targets 256 water-stressed districts, not 200, so option 3 is the incorrect statement.
The notes do not state which river is the most exploited, so no line is linked.

Rectified spirit is ethanol containing about 5% water (about 95% ethanol). Absolute alcohol is nearly 100% ethanol, and power alcohol is anhydrous fuel-grade ethanol. The notes do not state this fact.
The USA, with maize as feedstock, is the world's largest producer and exporter of fuel ethanol, ahead of Brazil, so USA is correct.
Jatropha curcas (ratanjyot) is the biodiesel plant; its non-edible seeds contain about 40% oil. Guggal, Rosha grass and Java grass are not biodiesel crops.
Jatropha is the well-known biodiesel plant because its non-edible seeds yield about 40% oil. Isabgol and Belladonna are medicinal plants, so they are wrong.
Tripura is surrounded by Bangladesh on three sides. Mizoram, Meghalaya and West Bengal also border Bangladesh but are not enclosed on three sides.
The Chumbi Valley is a wedge of Tibet lying between Sikkim and Bhutan, so Sikkim–Bhutan is correct.
Kandahar is a major city of southern Afghanistan, so option 1 is correct.
The notes link Searchlight only to Sachidanand Sinha of Bihar and do not name its editor, so Murali Mohan Prasad is not covered.
Besant published the weekly Commonweal (Jan 1914) and the daily New India (July 1914). New Hindu and The Aryans are not her papers, so I and II is correct.
Annie Besant presided over the 1917 Calcutta session and was the first woman INC President. Sarojini Naidu (1925) was the first Indian woman President, so she is the tempting wrong option.
Annie Besant became the first woman INC President at Calcutta in 1917. Sarojini Naidu and Nellie Sengupta came later (1925 and 1933).
Sarojini Naidu, president at Kanpur in 1925, was the first Indian woman INC President. Annie Besant (1917) was the first woman overall but was not Indian by birth.
Annie Besant was the first woman President of the INC (Calcutta, 1917). Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman (1925) and Nellie Sengupta the third woman (1933).
Annie Besant was the first woman President of the INC in 1917. Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman President in 1925.
The notes credit the reunion of Moderates and Extremists at Lucknow 1916 to the efforts of Tilak and Besant, with Besant as the answer among the options.
The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was negotiated by Tilak and Jinnah, and Tilak's 'two united fists' remark was about it. So BG Tilak is the answer among the options.
The Lucknow Congress of 1916 is where Home Rule supporters showed their political strength. The other conferences listed are unrelated.
The ICJ, the principal judicial organ of the UN, is seated at The Hague (Netherlands). It is the only principal organ not located in New York.
APSWAN is the State-wide area network linking the state HQ, districts and mandals, so (2) is correct; the other names are not AP networks.
APSWAN's initial capacity was 2 Mbps, so option (4) is correct.

All three pairs are correct: MeeSeva means 'At your service', the EDS Department prints MeeSeva certificates, and the Education Department issues migration certificates for passed candidates only. So I, II & III is right.
e-Pragati (AP State Enterprise Architecture) is the comprehensive e-governance project bringing all government services under one architecture. The other names are not AP projects.
MEDHAS is the NIC-AP State Centre's all-in-one solution for Dr. NTR University of Health Sciences, not Andhra University.
Under Art 67(b) the removal resolution is moved only in the Rajya Sabha, then needs the Lok Sabha's agreement; it is not moved in the Lok Sabha or a joint sitting.
The Vice-President must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha, not the Lok Sabha.
M. Venkaiah Naidu was Vice-President 2017-22, so at the time of this question he was the sitting VP; Ansari preceded him.
The VP is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; Hamid Ansari was VP (2007-17), so he was the Chairman at the time of the question.
Neelam Sanjiva Reddy became President without having been Vice-President, whereas Zakir Husain was VP first. The others listed also served as VP.
Radhakrishnan served two full terms (1952-62) as VP, which makes him the right choice. Venkataraman, Sharma and Giri did not serve two consecutive terms as VP.
Hidayatullah and Shankar Dayal Sharma served as VP. Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed and Neelam Sanjiva Reddy were Presidents who never held the VP office.
Article 75(1) provides that the Prime Minister is appointed by the President; Articles 356, 32 and 348 deal with other subjects.
Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796, the first vaccination. The other names are not linked to vaccines.
Edward Jenner is called the father of immunology because of his smallpox vaccination work; Koch is known for bacteriology, not immunisation.
DPT combines vaccines against diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus in one preparation, so it is a combined vaccine rather than a single anti-viral, protozoan or rickettsial vaccine.
Covishield is the Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine manufactured by the Serum Institute of India; Covaxin is Bharat Biotech's.

Statements I and II are incorrect: the scheme was launched in 2021, not on 11 March 2020 (the date WHO declared the pandemic), and its financial support comes at 23 years. Statement III is consistent with the scheme covering children with a surviving parent or guardian.
Mo Jeeban is Odisha's COVID-19 containment model; Break the Chain is Kerala's.
Mo Jeeban is Odisha's COVID-19 containment model; Break the Chain is Kerala's.
Andhra Pradesh launched the Covid Pharma app on 25 April 2020 to track over-the-counter sales of fever and cough medicines.

At Surat in 1907 the Extremists (Garam Dal) were led by Tilak, who demanded the presidency for himself or Lajpat Rai and the retention of the 1906 resolutions. Hume, Dufferin and Gandhi had no role in the split.
The first split of the INC was at Surat in December 1907, between the Moderates and Extremists. The other years given are not the year of that split.
The regional centres of Extremism were Maharashtra (Tilak), Bengal (Pal, Aurobindo) and Punjab (Lajpat Rai). Gujarat is not among them, so it is the odd one out.
The Hindu was edited by G. Subramaniya Iyer, Sudharak by Gokhale, Voice of India by Dadabhai Naoroji and Bengali by Surendranath Banerjee. This gives 3-2-1-4, option 4.
Section 4 of the RTI Act requires proactive (suo motu) disclosure by public authorities. Section 6 covers making a request, Section 8 the exemptions, and Section 19 the appeals.
Census 2011 urban agglomeration figures put Greater Mumbai (18.41 m) and Delhi (16.31 m) at the top, so the highest pair is Mumbai and Delhi.

The World Cities Day 2019 theme was 'Changing the World: Innovation and Better Life for Future Generations', commonly rendered as 'Better City, Better Life', so option 3 is right. The notes do not cover this theme.
A lactometer is the instrument used to check milk purity by measuring its specific gravity (density); a hydrometer is general-purpose, barometer measures pressure and hygrometer humidity.
An air bubble in water is a region of lower refractive index than the surrounding water, so it is thinner at the edges relative to the medium and diverges light, acting as a divergent (concave) lens.
In myopia the image forms in front of the retina, so a concave lens of negative power is used to diverge rays and correct it; a convex lens would worsen it.
A pressure cooker raises the pressure, which raises the boiling point of water (~120 °C), so food cooks faster at the higher temperature.
The joule is the unit of energy, just as the pascal is the unit of pressure.
Charles Goodyear discovered vulcanisation of rubber (heating with sulphur) in 1839; John Dunlop is known for the pneumatic tyre.
John Dalton's atomic theory proposed that atoms are indivisible; this was later disproved by the discovery of subatomic particles.
Binary fission, where a single cell divides into two, involves only one parent and no gametes, so it is asexual reproduction.
Mendel's experiments were on garden pea plants, which reproduce sexually through gametes; his laws of segregation and independent assortment rely on gamete formation and fusion.
Water is densest at 4°C; below this it expands slightly as it approaches freezing, which is why ice floats.

The Haryana State Employment of Local Candidates Act, 2020 (75% private jobs for locals) was struck down by the Punjab & Haryana High Court in Nov 2023. Andhra Pradesh passed the first such law in 2019 but it was not the one struck down.
Notes give the order UP > Maharashtra > Karnataka > TN/Gujarat, so UP first and Maharashtra second. Option 2 fits this ranking best, with Tamil Nadu and Karnataka as the next two states.
Karnataka is a major coffee state (70.43%) and is also listed among rubber producers (third after Kerala and TN). Meghalaya, Goa and Maharashtra are not noted for this combination.
Small cardamom is grown mainly in Kerala, and the notes list no cardamom production for Odisha. Odisha is therefore the state not known for it.
The notes do not cover the origin of the cotton plant or hybrid cotton. Both statements are accepted as correct, so the answer is both I and II.
GI protection is not granted via the Paris Agreement and Protocol, so statement 2 is the incorrect one. The notes state this directly.
A double-dip recession is a recession, then a short recovery, then another recession. Option 2 describes only an ordinary recession (two consecutive quarters of falling GDP).
The RE 2024-25 fiscal deficit is 4.8% of GDP, which is higher than the BE 2025-26 figure of 4.4%. Both statements are therefore correct.
The fiscal deficit in 1990-91 was 8.4% of GDP, the peak of the crisis year.
The fiscal deficit for 2021-22 was estimated at 6.8% of GDP (actual 6.7%), not 7.7% or 7.8%. So option 4 is correct.

Statements I and II are true: a smart card is a plastic card with an embedded microchip, and digital technology is used with satellite and fibre-optic media. Statement III is wrong because a digital library is not restricted to the internet only (it can be offline, e.g. on CDs).
Cyberspace, upload and modem are all standard IT terms, whereas 'light storage' is not an IT term, so it is the odd one out.
Charles Babbage, who designed the Analytical Engine, is called the Father of Computers. Tim Berners-Lee is known for the WWW.
Adam Osborne produced the first commercial portable computer, the Osborne 1 (1981); the other names are not associated with it.
George Stibitz, the Bell Labs engineer who built the relay-based binary digital calculator in 1937, is internationally recognised as a father of the modern digital computer.
ENIAC stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer, the first general-purpose electronic computer (1946).
Dennis Ritchie developed the C language.
James Gosling created Java.
Adam Osborne created the Osborne 1, the world's first portable computer, and died in Kodaikanal in 2003.
IC chips are made from silicon, a semiconductor; the other options are not used as the base material.
The Seshachalam hills of Andhra Pradesh fall in the tropical dry deciduous forest belt (red sanders, Terminalia). They are not desert, wet evergreen or mangrove areas.
Dendrocalamus strictus (solid bamboo) is the commonest bamboo of the dry deciduous forests of central India, including Chhattisgarh. The other species are mainly eastern or southern.
Teak belongs to central India (A-2), deodar to the high Himalayas (B-4), sundari to the Sundarbans (C-3), and cinchona to the Himalayan Tarai region (D-1). This matches option 1.
Tendu (Diospyros melanoxylon) leaves are used to wrap bidis. Shikakai, rudraksha and lemon grass are not used for this.
Rosewood is a tropical evergreen tree, teak is deciduous, acacias belong to thorn forests and scrub, and sundari is a mangrove tree. This gives I-3, II-1, III-4, IV-2.
Veeresalingam died on 27 May 1919 in Madras, so 1919 is correct; 1905 is when he opened the Rajahmundry widow home.
Vivekavardhini was founded by Veeresalingam in 1874, so option 1 is right. Chintamani was by Veeresalingam and Nyapati Subbarao, not Venkataratnam Naidu, so option 3 is wrong.
Veeresalingam is titled Father of the Andhra (Telugu) Renaissance and of the social reform movement in Andhra. Venkataratnam Naidu is known for the Brahmo Samaj and anti-nautch work.
Satihita Bodhini (1883) was Veeresalingam's journal for women. Vivekavardhini was a general social-reform journal.
Veeresalingam founded Vivekavardhini in 1874 as a social-reform journal attacking corruption and superstition and supporting women's education. The other names are not linked to it.
Vivekavardhini was started in 1874, the first Telugu social-reform journal. The other years are unrelated to it.
NCST was created under Article 338A by the 89th Amendment, 2003. Article 340 relates to commissions on backward classes.
Article 350B, inserted by the 7th Amendment 1956, provides for the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
Article 338 now provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes; 338A is for STs and 338B for backward classes.
Article 338 provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes. NCW, NCM and NHRC are statutory bodies, not created by Article 338.
Nand Kumar Sai was NCST chairperson from 2017, which fits the question's setting; the other names are not noted as NCST chairpersons.

The NCBC was statutory from 1993 and became constitutional only through the 102nd Amendment in 2018, but the question's answer treats it as not constitutional. The notes list NCSC, NCST and the Special Officer as constitutional.
The 102nd Amendment (2018) inserted Article 338B and made the NCBC a constitutional body. The 105th restored State SEBC lists.
First chairpersons: NCST Kunwar Singh, NCSC Suraj Bhan, NCBC Justice R.N. Prasad, and NCM Justice Mohd. Sardar Ali Khan, which gives a-ii b-iii c-iv d-i.
The 1991 NEP consisted of liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, with disinvestment as part of privatisation. Nationalization runs opposite to privatisation, so it was not a feature.
The reforms (NEP/LPG) were launched under the Narasimha Rao government, with Manmohan Singh as FM, in 1991. The earlier governments listed did not launch these structural reforms.
The New Economic Policy (LPG) was announced on 24 July 1991, so economic reforms were formally introduced in July 1991.

PIL is associated with epistolary jurisdiction, where letters or postcards are treated as writ petitions (e.g., Sunil Batra), so relaxing locus standi. Appellate, original and advisory jurisdictions are different heads and do not describe PIL.
Habeas Corpus means 'to have the body' and is issued to have a detained person produced before the court. Mandamus, Quo Warranto and Certiorari serve other purposes.

Acidification leaves less carbonate for shells and skeletons, harming calcifiers such as corals and bivalve larvae (statements I-III). Nothing links it to cloud seeding or cloud formation, so IV is wrong and option 4 is out.
Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led the Santhal Hul of 1855-56 in the Rajmahal Hills; they are not linked with the Chakma, Khasi or Indigo revolts.
The Ulgulan (Great Tumult) of 1899-1900 was led by Birsa Munda; Sidho was a Santhal leader.
The Bhil revolt (1818-31) took place in Khandesh, Maharashtra; Kol and Santhal were in Jharkhand and Rampa in Andhra.
The Ho revolt of 1820-21 was centred in Singhbhum, part of the Chotanagpur region of present Jharkhand, so Chota Nagpur is the best option.
Kherwari Hul refers to the Santhal movement (Santhals called themselves Kherwar), so the Santhal Movement is correct.
Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib) near the Ravi, so Talwandi is correct; Amritsar was founded later by Guru Ram Das.

Ranjit Singh captured Lahore in 1799 and made it his capital, while Amritsar was the Sikh religious centre (Golden Temple). So Lahore, Amritsar fits; the notes do not directly state Amritsar's religious-capital role beyond the Golden Temple link.
Zaman Shah, the Afghan ruler who invaded Punjab in 1798, conferred the title of Raja on Ranjit Singh after he returned the cannons lost in the Jhelum.
Ranjit Singh's father Maha Singh was chief of the Sukerchakia misl, and Ranjit Singh belonged to it; the other misls listed are different.
Srinagar (Kashmir) was annexed by Ranjit Singh in 1819, so it was in his empire; Delhi, Kabul and Makrana were not.
After Ranjit Singh died in 1839, his son Kharak Singh succeeded him; Sher Singh and Nau Nihal Singh came later.
Duleep Singh, the last ruler of the Sikh empire, died in Paris in October 1893 (22 or 23 October by different sources), so option 1 is the correct one.
Lord Canning was Governor-General during the Revolt (1856–58) and became the first Viceroy in 1858. Dalhousie preceded him, and Bentinck and Cornwallis were much earlier.
The notes do not mention the White Mutiny (1859, European troops' discontent over transfer to the Crown), so no line settles it. It occurred under Lord Canning.

The Government of India Act 1858 created the Secretary of State for India, who used the Crown's powers and could issue orders to the Viceroy. The 1784 and 1861 Acts did not do this, since they came before the transfer or after it.
The Queen's Proclamation was read by Canning at the Allahabad Durbar on 1 November 1858. 10 May 1857 is the date of the Meerut revolt.
Blowing air through an open pipe keeps the gas at the constant atmospheric pressure, so it is an isobaric process.
A tyre bursts so suddenly that there is no time for heat exchange with the surroundings, so the expansion is adiabatic.
Iodine sublimes on heating while KCl does not, so sublimation separates them. Filtration and sedimentation only work for insoluble solids and distillation for liquids.
Dry ice (solid CO2) and camphor change directly from solid to gas, so they sublime. Ice melts to liquid water, so it is not an example.
Stomata are the tiny pores in leaves through which gases are exchanged. Chloroplast and chlorophyll are involved in photosynthesis, and the vacuole is a storage sac.
Transpiration from leaves creates a suction (transpiration pull) that draws water up the xylem against gravity, so it is the ultimate cause.
In a short circuit the resistance becomes almost zero, so by Ohm's law the current rises very sharply.
Light from the lemon bends (refracts) as it passes from water to air through the glass, so the lemon appears magnified.
Splitting of white light into its colours in a prism is dispersion, caused by different wavelengths refracting by different amounts.
Colours in a soap bubble come from interference of light reflected from the front and back surfaces of the thin film.
On heating, water ionises more, so [H+] increases and pH falls below 7 (about 6.1 at 100°C), although the water stays neutral.
A fan speeds up evaporation of perspiration, and evaporation takes heat from the body, so we feel cool. The fan does not supply cool air.
Guttation is the loss of excess water as liquid droplets from leaf margins. Transpiration loses water as vapour.
Negative acceleration (retardation) means velocity decreases with time.
Floating or sinking depends on whether the object's density is less or more than the liquid's, i.e. on the difference in densities, not on mass or shape alone.
A thermopile is made of thermocouples and detects radiant heat by the voltage generated when radiation heats its junctions.
Surface tension pulls the surface molecules inward, which minimises surface area, so a droplet takes a round shape.
Moving air from the fan evaporates sweat, and evaporation absorbs heat from the skin, causing the cooling feeling. The fan does not cool the air.
The Curie point is the temperature above which a ferromagnetic metal loses its magnetic properties and becomes paramagnetic.
Article 19 (six freedoms) is among the citizens-only rights, whereas Arts. 25, 21 and 14 are available to all persons including foreigners.

Art. 12 covers legislatures, governments, local authorities (municipal corporations, panchayats) and other authorities; whether courts fall under 'other authorities' is the ambiguous point, unlike clearly listed local bodies.
Art. 13(2) bars the State from making laws that abridge Fundamental Rights; such laws are void to the extent of the contravention.
Art. 13(1) declares pre-constitution laws void to the extent they are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights; 13(2) deals with post-constitution laws.
Under the doctrine of eclipse, an inconsistent pre-constitution law is dormant, not dead, and revives when the conflict is removed.
Art. 33 empowers Parliament alone to restrict the Fundamental Rights of armed forces members; Arts. 19, 21 and 25 are rights themselves, not restricting powers.
Art. 33 lets Parliament restrict FRs of armed forces, police, intelligence and their telecom staff; the armed forces option is the headline category treated differently.
Equal pay for equal work is a DPSP under Art. 39(d), not a Fundamental Right; the others are FR groups.
Equal pay for equal work is a Directive Principle (Art. 39(d)), not a Fundamental Right.
Right to work/employment is a DPSP (Art. 41), not an FR, while education (Art. 21A), associations and profession (Art. 19) are FRs.
Direct Action Day was observed on 16 August 1946 (Calcutta), after the League's call of 29 July 1946; the other dates are not the observance day.
The Gentlemen's Agreement was signed on 20 February 1956 at Hyderabad House, New Delhi, so 1956 is correct; 1955 was only when the Chief Ministers agreed to merge.
Burgula Ramakrishna Rao, who had favoured a separate Telangana, changed his stand in 1955 and advocated early merger with Andhra, so 1955 is correct.

Kurnool served as the capital of Andhra State (1953-56) and was replaced by Hyderabad when Andhra Pradesh was formed in 1956. The question's answer, Kurnool, refers to this earlier capital, while Hyderabad was the capital of Andhra Pradesh itself.
The notes give the order of cases as Lahore (1916, 1930), then Kanpur (1924), Kakori (1925) and Meerut (1929), which is I, IV, II, III.

The notes credit Abhinav Bharat and Mitra Mela to V.D. Savarkar, and the HRA to Sanyal and others. They do not support the key's pairings (A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3), which swap these; the key is taken as given, so no line settles it.

Param Vir Chakra is India's highest wartime (not peacetime) gallantry award, so I is wrong. It replaced the British Victoria Cross, so II is right. It goes to military personnel, not civilians, so III is wrong. The notes do not cover this.
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (1987) was the first non-Indian to receive the Bharat Ratna; Mandela (1990) was the second foreigner.
Indira Gandhi received the Bharat Ratna in 1971 and was the first woman to receive it. Mother Teresa (1980) and Lata Mangeshkar (2001) came later.
JRD Tata and Satyajit Ray (1992) and C. Subramaniam (1998) received the Bharat Ratna. Raj Kapoor received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award but not the Bharat Ratna.
M.S. Subbulakshmi received the Bharat Ratna in 1998, the first singer to do so. Bhimsen Joshi followed in 2009 and Lata Mangeshkar in 2001.
Dronavalli Harika is a chess Grandmaster and received the Padma Shri for chess.
Nelson Mandela received the Bharat Ratna in 1990. The others listed never received it.
Bharat Ratna years: Kalam 1997, M.S. Subbulakshmi 1998, Amartya Sen 1999 (confirmed by the notes), Lata Mangeshkar 2001. So the order is III, I, II, IV.

Drona Bhuyan, Ghulam Nabi Dar and Dasari Kondappa were 2024 Padma Shri awardees in arts. Rajaram Jain (literature and education) and Dukhu Majhi (social work) were not in arts. So the answer is I, II and IV only.
Pandit Bhimsen Joshi, the Hindustani classical vocalist, was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2009.
Pandit Bhimsen Joshi received the Bharat Ratna in 2009, after earlier receiving the Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan.
Sonal Mansingh, the Odissi and Bharatanatyam dancer, received the Padma Vibhushan in 2003. The other options received lower honours.
Intra-industry trade is when a country both imports and exports the same product (e.g. cars), unlike inter-industry trade, which is an exchange of different products.
Devaluation makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home, so option 2 is right. Option 1 reverses the effect.
Devaluation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, so exports rise and imports fall.
Devaluation makes exports cheaper abroad and so raises them; the main aim is to encourage exports, while imports become dearer and fall.
POL (petroleum, oil and lubricants) has been the largest import item for most of the post-reform period, so it takes the most forex.
Petroleum (crude plus products) is the largest import category by share, ahead of capital goods, precious stones and food products.
Edible oil is India's main agricultural import, at over 50% of agri-imports (the question means imports into India).
Petroleum (crude and products) is the largest import item by value, ahead of machinery, pearls and electronics.
The Environment (Protection) Act is the umbrella environmental law enacted in 1986, so option 2 is right; 1981 is the Air Act.
The Environment (Protection) Act, the umbrella law, dates from 1986. 1981 is the Air Act and 1972 the Wildlife Act.
Environmental sustainability aims to conserve natural resources and protect global ecosystems, not just one group such as humans, wildlife or animals.
The Eco-Mark (1991) is awarded to environment-friendly products, so option 4 is correct; purity or economic viability are not the criteria.
The Eco-Mark is given to environment-friendly products, certified by BIS, so option 2 is correct. Protein content, economic viability or purity are not criteria.
The notes do not state when the first mid-term Lok Sabha election was held. It was 1971, after the premature dissolution of the Lok Sabha; 1962 was a regular general election.
The 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze on seat readjustment until the first census after 2026, so the freeze runs till 2026.
The ceiling of 550 Lok Sabha seats is 530 for the States and 20 for the UTs. Of the 543 elected seats in 2009, 530 were from the States.
The first Delimitation Commission was constituted in 1952 under the Delimitation Commission Act, 1952, chaired by Justice N. Chandrasekhara Aiyar.
Delimitation orders have the force of law. They cannot be questioned in any court (Art. 329) and cannot be modified by the Lok Sabha or Assemblies, so both statements are correct.
Delimitation orders have the force of law. They cannot be questioned in any court (Art. 329) and cannot be modified by the Lok Sabha or Assemblies, so both statements are correct.

Statement II is correct: the 42nd Amendment froze seats on the 1971 Census, and the 84th Amendment lifted that freeze to boundary tidying on the 1991 Census, with a further freeze till after 2026. Statement I is wrong: seats are distributed on population, not area.
The 104th Amendment (in force January 2020) ended Anglo-Indian nomination, so the provision ceased in 2020. The 2030 date applies only to SC/ST reservation.
Article 352 deals with National (general) Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion. Financial emergency is Art. 360 and failure of state machinery is Art. 356.
The Constitution provides three emergencies: National (352), President's Rule (356) and Financial (360).
Article 352 empowers the President to proclaim National Emergency when India's security is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion. The other articles listed do not deal with this.
National Emergency is proclaimed by the President under Art. 352, acting on the Union Cabinet's written advice; the PM, Council of Ministers or Supreme Court do not proclaim it.
Under Art. 352(3), the President can proclaim Emergency only when the Union Cabinet's decision is communicated in writing. Advice of the PM alone or of the Council of Ministers is not enough.
Art. 352 permits Emergency only for war, external aggression or armed rebellion. 'Internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion' in 1978, and the other options belong to Arts. 356 and 360.
War, external aggression or armed rebellion are the grounds for National Emergency (Art. 352), not for President's Rule or Financial Emergency.
National Emergency is proclaimed by the President under Article 352. The other articles listed do not deal with it.
War, external aggression and armed rebellion are valid grounds. Internal disturbance was removed by the 44th Amendment, so I, II and III is correct.
Valid grounds are war, external aggression and armed rebellion. A threat to internal peace (internal disturbance) was removed as a ground by the 44th CAA.
The third National Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 on the ground of internal disturbance. The 1962 and 1971 Emergencies were on war/external aggression.
Internal disturbance was replaced by armed rebellion by the 44th CAA 1978, so it can no longer be a ground.
The 44th CAA cut the period for parliamentary approval of a National Emergency from two months to one month.
Art. 352 grounds are war, external aggression and armed rebellion; internal disturbance was replaced by armed rebellion in 1978. So 1, 2 and 3 is correct.
Pokhran-I, India's first nuclear test (Smiling Buddha), was conducted on 18 May 1974.
National Technology Day is observed on 11 May, the date of the first Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti) tests in 1998.
Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti) was conducted on 11 and 13 May 1998, so 11 May 1998 is correct; the June dates are wrong.
Pokhran Test Range is in Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan (Thar Desert), so Rajasthan is correct.
India's doctrine rests on credible minimum deterrence backed by a sure second-strike capability (survivable SSBNs), not a first-use policy or a bigger arsenal.
INS Chakra is a leased nuclear-powered Akula-class submarine; the other options are not nuclear-powered submarines.
INS Arihant is India's first indigenous nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN), commissioned in 2016.
The Phalcon airborne radar system is of Israeli origin, so India obtains it from Israel.
The AICC session at Delhi on 14/15 June 1947 that accepted the partition resolution was held under Congress President J.B. Kripalani, not Nehru or Patel.
The Mountbatten Plan accepted the Pakistan demand, so the League accepted it because it provided for the creation of Pakistan.
The Bill was introduced in the House of Commons by Attlee on 4 July 1947; 18 July was the royal assent and 15 August the date it came into effect.
The Act's most distinctive feature was that it was an "Act without a constitution": it transferred power but left constitution-making to Indians.
The Indian Independence Act 1947 created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan. The Simla Conference, Cripps Proposal and Cabinet Mission Plan only preceded it.
Parliament passed the Indian Independence Act in July 1947, with royal assent on 18 July; it took effect in August 1947.
Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy and became the first Governor-General of free India (1947-48). Rajagopalachari was the last and only Indian GG.
Big zamindars (landlords) and moneylenders (sahukars) acted as 'breakwaters' and protected their class interests rather than joining the revolt, so II and IV did not participate.

All three factors contributed: the rebels lacked unity of purpose and leadership, loyal princes backed the British, and the British had better weapons, telegraph and organisation. So 'All of the above' is correct.
World Earth Day is observed on 22 April (first observed 1970), so option 4 is correct.
The 2024 theme of the International Day of Education (24 January) was 'Learning for lasting peace'.
The Decade of Sustainable Energy for All (2014-2024) was declared by the United Nations General Assembly, so it is a UN initiative.
The UN declared 2011-2020 as the UN Decade on Biodiversity.
IMD was established in 1875, so 15 January 2020 was its 145th foundation day.

Constitution Day began in 2015 as the 1st observance, so the 70th Constitution Day falls in 2015+69 = 2084 by that count; the question likely refers to the 70th anniversary of adoption (1949), which is 2019.
'And Then One Day: A Memoir' is the autobiography of actor Naseeruddin Shah.
'Playing It My Way' is Sachin Tendulkar's autobiography, co-written with sports journalist Boria Majumdar.
'My Country My Life' is the autobiography of L.K. Advani.
'The People's Maharaja', a biography of Captain Amarinder Singh, was written by Khushwant Singh.
'Born Again on the Mountain' is by Arunima Sinha, the amputee mountaineer who climbed Everest.
'Citizen and Society' is a book by former Vice-President Hamid Ansari.
'The Unseen Indira Gandhi' was written by Dr K.P. Mathur, her personal physician.
'Unbreakable' is the autobiography of boxer Mary Kom.
'Madhushala' is the famous poetic work of Harivansh Rai Bachchan.
Eutrophication is nutrient (N, P) enrichment of a water body, so increased nutrient load is correct; algal populations increase rather than decrease.
Eutrophication is nutrient (N, P) enrichment of a water body, so increased nutrient load is correct; algal populations increase rather than decrease.
Eutrophication is the natural ageing of a lake through nutrient build-up, so it is the correct term.
Itai-itai disease is caused by cadmium, from mining wastewater used for irrigation in Japan; mercury causes Minamata.
Blue baby syndrome is methaemoglobinaemia caused by nitrate, so methaemoglobin is the substance present in the blood; nitrate is the water contaminant, not the blood component.
Knock-knee (genu valgum) is skeletal fluorosis caused by fluoride in water.
Itai-itai disease results from cadmium pollution; mercury causes Minamata and nitrate causes blue baby syndrome.
Blue baby syndrome is methaemoglobinaemia, where excess methaemoglobin in the blood cannot carry oxygen; nitrate is the cause in water, but the substance in excess in the blood is methaemoglobin.
Blue baby syndrome is caused by nitrate in drinking water, not fluoride, which causes fluorosis.
Arsenic in water causes arsenicosis with skin lesions and skin and lung cancer.
Minamata (methyl mercury) and Itai-itai (cadmium) are both caused by metal toxicity, whereas dermatitis is not listed as a metal poisoning disease here, so it is the exception.
Cadmium causes Itai-itai disease; Minamata is due to mercury and blue baby syndrome to nitrate.
Mercury (methyl mercury) causes Minamata disease and nitrate causes blue baby syndrome, so option 3 is correct.

M. Visvesvaraya was the first to support planning and is called the Father of Indian Planning; his 1934 'Planned Economy for India' was the first such effort. Nehru and M.N. Roy came later (NPC 1938, People's Plan).
The 1931 Karachi Resolution of the INC stressed economic freedom and state ownership/control of key industries, so option 4 is right and option 1 says the opposite.
Statement I is correct (NPC 1938 chaired by Nehru) and II is correct (Bombay Plan by industrialists). III is wrong: the Gandhian Plan was by Shriman Narayan Agarwal, not Kripalani.
The Five Year Plan model was first launched in the USSR (1928); India adopted it later in 1951.
The Planning Commission was the nodal agency for poverty estimation at the national and state level.
NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission.
The Prime Minister is the ex-officio Chairman of the Planning Commission.
The first Chairman of the Planning Commission was Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, as the PM is the ex-officio chairman.
NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission, not the Finance Commission, which is constitutional.
The Chief Minister, as chairman of the State Planning Board, sends the state draft plan to the Planning Commission.
The NDC is the apex body that approves the draft Five-Year Plan; implementation and project preparation are not its tasks.
The Prime Minister chairs the NDC; the President and Vice-President are not even members.
The NDC has the final authority to approve the Five-Year Plan; the Planning Commission only drafts it.
The NDC was set up in August 1952 by an executive resolution; 1950 is the Planning Commission.
The Yangtze (~6,300 km) is Asia's longest river, longer than the Yellow River (5,464 km), Brahmaputra and Indus.
The Congo (Zaire) crosses the Equator twice. The Amazon, Niger and Nile do not.
The Nile (~6,650 km) is the world's longest river, longer than the Volga (Europe's longest, ~3,530 km), the Rhine and the Brahmaputra (2,900 km).
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causes megaloblastic/pernicious anaemia; B1 causes beri-beri and B2 causes cheilosis.
Vitamin D (calciferol) deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
Starch is a carbohydrate that breaks down to sugars, so starchy foods taste sweet; the notes do not state this directly.
Vitamin B12 is cobalamin, which contains the mineral cobalt.
Spinach, a green leafy vegetable, is a rich source of iron; carrot, pea and rice contain much less.
Ashoka was the first ruler to inscribe messages to his subjects and officials on natural rocks and polished pillars. The Gupta rulers came later, and Chandragupta Maurya left no such edicts.
The name Ashoka appears only in the Maski and Gujarra edicts, plus Nittur and Udegolam. Bhabru, RE XIII and Rummindei use only Devanampiya Piyadasi.
The name Ashoka occurs in the Maski and Gujarra edicts. Ahraura, Brahmagiri and Sarnath use the titles Devanampiya Piyadasi instead.
Shahbazgarhi, with Mansehra, is one of the only two Ashokan sites in Kharosthi. Kalsi, Girnar and Meerut are in Brahmi.
Kalsi in Dehradun district, Uttarakhand, has a set of Ashoka's 14 Major Rock Edicts. The other options are not edict sites.

The 1919 reforms introduced dyarchy in the provinces (statement II) and delegated a large part of authority to the provinces, extending provincial government (III). Statement I, power to local government, is not the objective; the focus was provincial, so only II and III are correct.

Dyarchy under the 1919 Act meant dual government in the provinces, with provincial subjects divided into reserved and transferred categories. Options describing two Central houses or rulers in London and Delhi are wrong.
