Section 96(C) of the Government of India Act 1919 provided for the Public Service Commission. The other section numbers are distractors.
Banganapalle mango is a listed AP GI product, and the notes do not list Tapeswaram Kaza among AP's GI products. Tapeswaram Kaza is the answer because it is the option without GI status.

Tirupati Laddu is a GI-tagged product of AP, so statement III is correct. Banaras Brocades and Sarees (I) also have GI status. Daal-Baati-Churma (II) is a dish with no GI registration, so the answer is I and III.
Cartosat-3 was launched in Nov 2019 on PSLV-C47 along with 13 US nanosatellites, so PSLV-C47 is correct.
Cartosat-3 (~25 cm resolution) was launched on PSLV-C47 in Nov 2019. Cartosat-2 belongs to an earlier series (2007 onwards).
NISAR is the NASA-ISRO SAR mission (NASA L-band plus ISRO S-band radar). The other options are Indian-only satellites.
INFFRAS is India's forest fire response and assessment system, listed among NRSC remote-sensing uses.
A laser is an active sensor because it sends its own pulse and reads the echo. Visible and infrared cameras are passive, relying on reflected or emitted energy.
The four resolution types are spatial, spectral, temporal and radiometric. 'Chemical' resolution does not exist.
The notes state that in July 2021 Railways announced 33 projects (new lines and doubling) in AP, so option (4) is correct.
South Central Railway began functioning on 2 October 1966, so option (1) is correct. The notes do not give this date; they only mention that SCR shrinks to three divisions after the SCoR formation.

Corporation tax was the largest source of Central tax revenue in several past years (2005-06, 2007-08, 2013-14), which is the basis for this answer. Income tax is the largest source only in the latest estimates.
Motor vehicle (road) tax is levied by State governments, so it is not a Central tax source. Income tax, customs duties and service tax were all Union levies.
Corporation tax is in the Union List and is levied and collected by the Union government. States do not levy it.
The Economic Survey 2021-22 put the Centre's gross tax revenue at 9.9% of GDP in 2019-20.
A falling tax-GDP ratio means revenue is growing slower than GDP, which is a fiscal-capacity signal. It does not by itself show how equitably income is distributed.
A falling tax-GDP ratio only means tax revenue is growing slower than GDP (buoyancy below 1). It does not necessarily indicate slowing growth or less equitable income distribution.
The Raja J. Chelliah Tax Reforms Committee (1991-93) dealt with both direct and indirect taxes, recommending lower rates and a broader base.

Under Art. 354 the President may modify the distribution of revenues during a National Emergency, which means reducing or cancelling transfers to States. Increasing the transfer is not what the Article provides for, so option 4 is the exception.
The 1975 Emergency was declared on 25 June 1975 on the ground of internal disturbance. The 1962 and 1971 Emergencies were declared on external grounds, and there was no Emergency in 1968.

In a pressure cooker the higher pressure raises the boiling point of water (~120 C), so food cooks at a higher temperature and in less time. Option 1 is wrong because the temperature rises, not falls.

Salt dissolved in water raises its boiling point (boiling point elevation), and it also lowers the freezing point (depression). So the boiling point increases and the freezing point decreases respectively.

Rear-view mirrors in vehicles are convex mirrors because they give a wider field of view and an erect, diminished image of the traffic behind. A concave mirror would give a narrow field of view and is used for headlights.
CorelDRAW is graphics application software, whereas MS Excel (spreadsheet) and MS Word (word processor) are not graphics packages.
In MS Word, Ctrl+U applies underline to the selected text; the shortcut key is U, while I is italic.
An Excel workbook is a file made up of one or more worksheets.

Both statements are true: CADD (computer-aided design and drafting) assists in creating, modifying, analysing and optimising designs, and it is also used to create photo-simulations for Environmental Impact Reports.
Windows was developed by Microsoft, not IBM, Apple or WIPRO, so 'None of the above' is correct.
Windows is Microsoft's GUI operating system, so Microsoft is the developer; IBM, AT&T and HP did not develop it.
The operating system manages hardware and must be loaded at boot-up, so a computer cannot boot without it; compilers and assemblers are only translator programs.
The notes do not cover the Bundela rebellion of 1842 or Hirdeshah's zamindari. Hirapur is the accepted answer.
The Ahom rebellion took place in 1828 under Gomadhar Konwar, not 1815, so pair 4 is wrong. The Santhal (1855), Kol (1831) and Khasi (1829) pairs are correct.
Damin-i-Koh was the tract in the Rajmahal Hills demarcated for Santhal settlement, so option 1 is right. It was not Paharia paddy land or a military camp.
Major Baroz (Burrough) lost a battle to the Santhals near Bhagalpur during the Hul of 1855.
Birsa's Ulgulan was centred on Ranchi and spread through Chotanagpur (present Jharkhand). Champaran and Ballia are unrelated.
The Munda Ulgulan began in 1899 and ran to 1900. The 1890 date is a trap.
The notes do not cover the Gadkari revolt. Kolhapur is the accepted centre.
After the Hul the Santhal Parganas were made a separate non-regulation district with laws protecting tribal land. So both statements hold.

The notes list input/output devices, a processing (system) unit and secondary storage as main components; of the options, system unit, input/output and secondary memory is the best fit, while the others miss a category or merge them.
CD-ROM is an optical disc, which is secondary storage, whereas ROM, RAM and EEPROM are primary (semiconductor) memories.
Cache is a small, very fast memory between the CPU and RAM that speeds up processing, so it matches the description; ROM is permanent and read-only.
A hard disk (HDD) uses magnetic disks to store data non-volatilely, which fits the description of a rigid, permanently installed magnetic disk.
MS Word is word-processing application software, not an OS, input device or processing device.
Word processors and spreadsheets are application software, as the notes list them under application software, not system software.
F7 is the standard shortcut in Microsoft Office programs such as Word and Outlook to run the spelling and grammar check.
An operating system is system software that manages hardware, processes, memory and files; it is a program, not hardware.
MS Access and Oracle are listed as database software, and PL-SQL is a database language, whereas MS Excel is a spreadsheet, so it is not a database.
Munda languages (Santhali, Mundari, Ho, Savara) belong to the Austro-Asiatic (Austric) family, so Austric is correct.
Gondi, Halbi and Bhatri are spoken in the Bastar region, whereas Sadari is not a Bastar language; the notes do not state this directly.
Indian languages fall into four main families: Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic and Sino-Tibetan, so the answer is Four.
Rajasthani is not among the 22 Eighth Schedule languages, while Gujarati and Kashmiri (1950) and Dogri (2003) are. Hence Rajasthani is the answer.
Santhali was added by the 92nd Amendment in 2003 along with Bodo, Dogri and Maithili. Konkani and Manipuri came in 1992 and Sindhi in 1967.
The 71st Amendment (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali. Sindhi was added earlier in 1967, and Kashmiri and Assamese were original 1950 entries.

The Ninth Schedule and Article 31B were added by the First Amendment (1951) to protect agrarian reforms in certain States, so option 3 is right. The SC/ST option is wrong because Article 15(4) was a different change that answered Champakam.
The notes do not state where SARS first broke out; they only give SARS-CoV-1 (2002–03) and civet cats. SARS first emerged in China (Guangdong), so option 3 is correct.
Ebola is named after the Ebola River, near where the 1976 outbreak occurred in Zaire (DR Congo). It is not named after a city, province or mountain.
SARS-CoV-2 enters human cells through the ACE2 receptor (angiotensin-converting enzyme 2), so option 2 is correct.
Viruses are acellular and have no metabolic machinery of their own, so they carry no enzymes for metabolism and depend on host cells. Lichen, bacteria and algae are cellular and have enzymes.

Edward Jenner is called the father of immunology because he developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796. Koch founded bacteriology and Pasteur is linked to the rabies vaccine and germ theory, so they are not the answer.
Jonas Salk developed the first successful polio vaccine in 1952. Pasteur is associated with the rabies vaccine, and Ehrlich and Lister are not linked to polio.
Kavaratti is the capital of Lakshadweep, the UT of 36 coral islands. Kadmat, Chetlat and Kalpeni are other islands, not the capital.

Lakshadweep lies off the Malabar coast in the south-west, in the Lakshadweep (Laccadive) Sea, which is part of the Arabian Sea. Of the options given, Arabian Sea is the best fit; Bay of Bengal is on the east.
Port Blair in the Andamans lies close to Myanmar across the Andaman Sea, so Yangon is the nearest by sea. Kolkata, Chennai and Machilipatnam on the Indian mainland are farther.
The Ten Degree Channel runs along 10° N latitude and separates the Andaman group from the Nicobar group. The other latitudes given are not channels between them.
The Ten Degree Channel, along 10° N, lies between the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Lakshadweep and Maldives are separated by the Eight Degree Channel, not this one.
The Eight Degree Channel lies between Minicoy (Lakshadweep) and the Maldives. The Andaman–Nicobar gap is the Ten Degree Channel.

The Disaster Crunch Model holds that vulnerability arises from socio-economic processes, so option 1 is correct. The other options describe vulnerability as mental, chance-based or something to be 'needed', which the model does not say.

The Disaster Crunch Model holds that vulnerability arises from socio-economic processes, so option 1 is correct. The other options describe vulnerability as mental, chance-based or something to be 'needed', which the model does not say.
The Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984 was caused by the leak of methyl isocyanate (MIC) from the Union Carbide plant. It was not chlorine, ammonia or hydrogen sulphide.
The NIDM Annual Report 2023-24 states that 27 of the 36 States/UTs are disaster prone, so option 4 is correct.
The NDMA lays down policies, approves the National Plan and approves the plans of Union Ministries. Statement IV is not supported by the notes, so only I, II and III are correct.
The NCMC is chaired by the Cabinet Secretary. The Home Minister chairs the NPDRR and the High Level Committee, and the Prime Minister chairs the NDMA.
The DM Act was enacted in 2005 and provides for the NDMA. The NDMA was formally notified in 2006, but 2005 is the only option tied to the Act and the closest to the answer given.
The NDMA lays down policies, approves the National Plan and approves the plans of Union Ministries. Statement IV is not supported by the notes, so only I, II and III are correct.
The NCMC is chaired by the Cabinet Secretary. The Home Minister chairs the NPDRR and the High Level Committee, and the Prime Minister chairs the NDMA.
The Sendai Framework runs from 2015 to 2030, so its targets are to be achieved by 2030.
The post-2015 frameworks shaping India's DRR are Sendai, the SDGs and the Paris Agreement. The Hyogo Framework (2005-2015) predates them, so it is the odd one out.

Dandekar and Rath (1971) made the first systematic study of poverty based on nutritional norms (2,250 kcal for both rural and urban areas). Alagh's 1979 task force was the first official calorie-based line, not the first systematic assessment.
The Rangarajan line for 2011-12 is ₹32/day for rural and ₹47/day for urban areas. ₹26 is the Tendulkar rural figure and ₹47 is the Rangarajan urban figure.
The S.R. Hashim working group of the Planning Commission was set up to identify urban BPL families. Saxena's committee dealt with the rural BPL census, so it is the tempting wrong option.
Under Art 110(3) the Speaker's decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill is final; neither the President, the courts nor the Rajya Sabha can overrule it.
Art 110(3) makes the Speaker of the Lok Sabha the final authority on whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
The Speaker does not vote in the first instance and has only a casting vote in a tie (Art 100(1)); the President, PM and CJI have no vote in the Lok Sabha.
Art 110(3) gives the Speaker the final say on whether a Bill is a Money Bill, so the courts, the President and committees cannot decide it.
The Speaker, as presiding officer, decides the admissibility of questions in the Lok Sabha under the rules of procedure; the Deputy Speaker only does so when acting in the Speaker's place.
The Speaker does not vote in the first instance and has only a casting vote in a tie (Art 100(1)); ordinary members and ministers vote normally.
Art 100(1) provides the casting vote of the Speaker in a tie, so the answer is Article 100.

Statement II is wrong because the Deputy Speaker coming from the Opposition is only a convention, not a constitutional provision. Statement I is also wrong since a plurality of votes (first past the post), not 50%, decides the winner.
Harivansh Narayan Singh was the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha in July 2023, his term ending in April 2026.
Harivansh Narayan Singh is the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, as per the notes.
The Vice-President is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Arts 64, 89(1)).
The Rajya Sabha is presided over by the Vice-President as ex-officio Chairman, who is not a member of the House, while the Lok Sabha and Assembly are presided over by their own members.
The Rajya Sabha's Chairman is the Vice-President, who is not a member of it, whereas the Speakers of the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha are members of their Houses.
Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur was called 'Jagadguru' for his mixed-faith outlook and support of Hindu scholars. The other rulers listed are not given this title.
Shah Jahan ended the Nizam Shahis in 1633 and the last ruler Husain Shah was jailed at Gwalior, so option 1 is right. Malik Ambar's defeat and a massacre of the royal family are not what happened.

Kitab-i-Nauras by Ibrahim Adil Shah II has songs to Hindu deities (Saraswati, Ganesha) and Muslim saints, so statement I is correct. Amir Khusrau is also credited with originating early Qawwali in India, so both are correct.

Chand Bibi was the daughter of Hussain Nizam Shah I and defended Ahmadnagar against the Mughals, so she belongs to Ahmadnagar. Bijapur is tempting because she married Ali Adil Shah, but she is linked with Ahmadnagar.
Golconda fell to Aurangzeb on 21 September 1687, when the gates were opened by the traitor Abdullah Khan Pani. 1686 is the year Bijapur was annexed.
The Nandampudi grant of Rajaraja Narendra gave the agrahara to Narayana Bhattu, Nannaya's collaborator. Nannaya only composed the inscription, so he was not the donee.

Nannaya was the court poet of Rajaraja Narendra, the Eastern Chalukya king who patronised him and under whom he began the Andhra Mahabharatamu. Bhima II, Vijayaditya and Ammaraja were not his patrons.
Bahadur Shah Zafar (II), the last Mughal emperor, was the son of Akbar II, who ruled 1806-1837 and was succeeded by him in 1837. Akbar Shah I is not a Mughal ruler in this list.
Muhammad Shah was called 'Rangeela' for his love of wine, beauty and apathy to administration. Farrukhsiyar was the Sayyids' puppet and bore no such epithet.
Muhammad Shah (1719-1748) was nicknamed 'Rangeela' for his pleasure-loving ways and neglect of administration, so option 3 is right.
Nadir Shah of Persia sacked Delhi in 1739 and took the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne. Abdali and Timur are the tempting wrong options.
Nadir Shah defeated Muhammad Shah at Karnal in 1739 and then sacked Delhi. Panipat was the site of Abdali's 1761 battle with the Marathas.
Nizam-ul-Mulk defeated Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda in 1724, becoming virtually independent. 1724 is the founding year of Hyderabad.
Husain Ali Khan was a Sayyid brother, Murshid Quli Khan ruled Bengal, Chin Qilich Khan was the Nizam of Hyderabad, and Safdar Jung was the Nawab of Awadh. This gives A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV.
Chin Qilich Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk) founded Hyderabad. Muzaffar Jung and Nasir Jung were later successors, and Zulfiqar Khan only envisaged Hyderabad.
Murshid Quli Khan, Diwan and then Nazim of Bengal, started the system of revenue farming there.
Saadat Khan's successor Safdar Jung was the Nawab of Awadh and also the Mughal Wazir. Saadat Khan founded Awadh but is not the one noted as Wazir.
Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk, who became Subedar of Awadh in 1722, was the first Nawab of Oudh. Safdar Jung was his successor.
Saadat Khan founded independent Awadh in Muhammad Shah's reign. Nizam-ul-Mulk founded Hyderabad and Alivardi Khan was Bengal's Nawab.
Jai Singh II built observatories at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura, so all four listed places are correct. The notes do not state this.
Sawai Jai Singh II of Jaipur built the Jantar Mantar observatory at Delhi in the early 18th century. The notes do not state this.
Sawai Jai Singh of Jaipur compiled the astronomical tables Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi, named for Emperor Muhammad Shah. The notes do not cover this.
Article 275(1) provides for grants-in-aid from the Centre to States for ST welfare, so option 1 is correct.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Sati, titles and slavery are not covered by it.

The PoA Act 1989 enforces the Right to Equality group, including equality before law, non-discrimination and abolition of untouchability under Art. 17. It does not relate to freedom of religion, so IV is wrong.
Bandicoot is a manhole-cleaning robot by Kerala start-up Genrobotics that replaces manual scavenging. Vyommitra is a space-mission humanoid, not a sanitation robot.
The AP State Commission for SCs and STs was set up in 2016 by amending Act 9 of 2003, so 2003 is correct.
Bezwada Wilson is associated with the Safai Karmachari Andolan as its co-founder and leader. Kailash Satyarthi is known for child rights and Bindeshwar Pathak for Sulabh.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. It has nothing to do with education, health or food.
CO2 is a greenhouse gas and is the usual 'not a pollutant' answer here, whereas CO, NO2 and SO2 are recognised air pollutants (NAQI counts CO, NO2, SO2 but not CO2).
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water bodies (water pollution), whereas smog, acid rain and asbestosis (from inhaled fibres) relate to air pollution.
Delhi's winter pollution peaks, so A is true, but the cause is not increased vehicle combustion in winter, so R is false.
Forest fires are a natural source of air pollution, while factory emissions, power station smoke and automobile emissions are anthropogenic.
Burning coal, petrol and diesel releases CO2, CO, SO2, NOx and particulates into the atmosphere, so it is a basic source of air pollution.
Photochemical smog (Los Angeles/summer smog) forms from NOx and VOCs in sunlight and gives a brownish haze, hence 'brown air'. Classical London smog is the sulphurous, SO2-based type.
Smog causes breathing problems and can contribute to cancers, whereas rickets is a vitamin D/calcium deficiency disease and not caused by smog.
Smog is formed in the air from other pollutants, so it is a secondary pollutant. CO2, CO and fly ash are emitted directly (primary).
Aurangzeb reversed the Mughal conciliatory policy toward the Rajputs (e.g. Marwar and Mewar conflicts), but the notes do not state this explicitly.

Jahangir is linked with Sir Thomas Roe (D-4), James I's ambassador at his court. Firuz Shah Tughlaq built canals (A-3), Balban is linked with Nauroz (B-2), and Alauddin with Diwan-i-Riyasat (C-1), giving 3 2 1 4.
In SHM, acceleration is proportional to displacement, so it is zero at the mean position where speed is maximum. The notes do not cover this.
Churning or cream separation uses centrifugal action, as in centrifugation: the denser skim milk is flung outward and the lighter cream stays near the axis.
After release the brick is under gravity alone, so it has constant acceleration g (ignoring air resistance). Its speed and velocity keep changing.
With constant speed, distance is proportional to time, so the distance-time graph is a straight line.
Gravitational force follows the inverse-square law, F ∝ 1/r². Doubling the distance makes the force one-fourth.
Inside the earth g decreases linearly with depth and becomes zero at the centre. At the poles, the equator and sea level it is non-zero.
Celsius = Kelvin − 273, so you subtract 273 from the Kelvin value.
Atmospheric refraction lets us see the sun about 2 minutes before it actually rises and after it actually sets.
Sound needs a material medium. Space between the moon and earth is a vacuum, so no sound reaches earth.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs in the pachytene substage of prophase I.
Torque = force × perpendicular distance from the hinge. A handle far from the hinges gives a larger torque for the same force.
Outside a magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole (they close inside from S to N).
Sound travels faster in warmer air, since speed rises with temperature. So it is faster in summer than in winter.
A periscope has two plane mirrors parallel to each other, each inclined at 45° to the tube. This makes the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray.
Microscope magnification is roughly (L/fo)(D/fe), so it falls as the eyepiece focal length rises.
Hibernation is winter dormancy in which some animals have greatly reduced metabolic activity.
A mercury thermometer works on the expansion of mercury on heating.
A plane mirror reflects light and does not refract it. By the law of reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Velocity is displacement divided by time, so its SI unit is m/s. m/s² is the unit of acceleration.
Light is an electromagnetic wave, made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields.
Babur was born in Farghana in Central Asia and came to India from there (via Kabul), so Ferghana is the original home.
The Mughals were Chagatai Turks, named after Chagatai, Genghis Khan's second son, so 'Turks' is correct; Mongols is the tempting but less apt option.
Babur's battles run Panipat I (1526), Khanwa (1527), Chanderi (1528), Ghaghra (1529), giving II, IV, III, I.
Khanwa (1527) came before Ghaghra (1529), followed by Chausa (1539) and then Samugarh (1658), giving II, I, III, IV.
Khanwa, more than Panipat, firmly established Mughal power, and Rana Sanga leading the Rajput confederacy was a far more formidable foe than Ibrahim Lodi, so R explains A.
Babur died at Agra in 1530; he was later buried at Kabul, which is the tempting wrong option.
The Baburnama was first translated into English by Leyden and Erskine; among the options, Leyden is the matching name, so option 1 is the intended answer.
The Babri mosque was built in 1528 by Mir Baqi, Babur's commander, not by Babur himself.
Babur was the first Mughal emperor, founding Mughal rule after winning Panipat I in 1526.
The Disaster Management Act was enacted as Act No. 53 of 2005, with Presidential assent on 23 December 2005, so 2005 is correct.
CERTI, Nagpur was set up in 1957 as the first disaster management training institution in India, so 1957 is correct.
The Central Water Commission (then Central Water & Power Commission) began scientific flood forecasting in 1958, on the Yamuna at Delhi.
The High Powered Committee was constituted in August 1999 and recommended a separate Department of Disaster Management in the Government of India.
The Ministry of Home Affairs is the nodal ministry for disaster management in India (except for drought, pest attack and epidemics).
The DM Act (Act No. 53) received Presidential assent on 23 December 2005, so it was enacted in 2005. The 2006 date relates to NDMA's notification and NDRF's raising, not the Act.
Section 25 on the DDMA falls in Chapter IV of the DM Act, so Chapter IV is correct.
APSDMA operates under the AP DM Rules 2007, so it was constituted in 2007.
The NDMA is headed ex officio by the Prime Minister, the apex policy body. The Home Minister heads the High Level Committee, not the NDMA.
Chain of command means the hierarchy of officials and organisations responsible for decisions during a disaster.
The NDMA was formally constituted on 27 September 2006, although the Act was passed in 2005.
The National Crisis Management Committee (NCMC) is headed by the Cabinet Secretary, who coordinates in major crises. The Home Secretary heads the NEC, not the NCMC.

Response, the phase during and just after a disaster, is time-critical and centres on search and rescue, evacuation, first aid and shelter. The other options are not post-disaster response operations.
Section 44 of the DM Act provides for the National Disaster Response Force, which is a force specialised for natural and man-made disasters. The fund under s.46 is a different thing.
The NDRF had 12 battalions at the time of the APPSC 2018 key. It has since grown to 16 from an initial 8, so 12 is the answer for that period.

The notes cover only the UNCTAD TDR 2026 (India 7.3% growth, Asia 59% of global growth) and say nothing about the TDR 2017 statements. Option 2 is the one that is not correct, since the 2017 report did not say India and China would become 'growth poles' at current growth levels.

The sixth zone is High Altitude and Tribal Areas; a 'Low Altitude and Tribal Area' zone does not exist, so option 4 is the one that is not among the six. North Coastal, Southern and Scarce Rainfall are all genuine zones.

The hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach and small intestine to the liver, so option 4 is right. The hepatic veins carry blood away from the liver, and the hepatic arteries supply it with oxygenated blood.
Red blood cells are made in the red bone marrow, so option 4 is right. The lungs, heart and brain do not make blood cells.
Malpighian tubules are the excretory organs of insects, and the kidneys do the same job in humans by filtering waste such as urea from the blood.
The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and controls thinking, memory and voluntary action. It is not part of the liver, heart or arteries.
The larynx, nose and external ear have cartilage in their walls. The urinary bladder is a muscular organ with no cartilage, so option 4 is right.

The ileum is the longest part of the small intestine (about 3.5 m), followed by the jejunum (about 2.5 m), and the duodenum is the shortest (about 25 cm). The order is therefore Ileum - Jejunum - Duodenum.
Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are completely digested in the small intestine, where pancreatic and intestinal enzymes and bile act. The stomach only begins protein digestion, so option 3 is right.
Most digestion takes place in the small intestine, where pancreatic juice, bile and intestinal enzymes act on all major food types. The stomach digests only part of the protein.
Bile juice is alkaline and neutralises the acidic chyme (HCl) coming from the stomach, which makes the medium suitable for pancreatic and intestinal enzymes. The notes show the stomach HCl is acidic.
Humans have 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal. 12 is the number of pairs of cranial nerves.
A reflex arc runs receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector. The spinal cord, not the brain, is the processing centre, which rules out option 3.

White blood cells defend the body against infection by engulfing pathogens and making antibodies. Energy supply, clotting and oxygen transport are not their functions (clotting is by platelets, oxygen transport by red blood cells).
Red blood cells are the most numerous blood cells (about 5 million per mm³), far above white blood cells (about 7,000) and platelets (about 250,000). Option 3 is right.
White blood cells (leucocytes) are called the soldiers of the body because they fight infection and foreign invaders.
An antigen is a foreign substance that triggers the immune system to make specific antibodies against it, so option 2 is right. Antiserum is injected from outside and is not produced by the antigen.
Cowper's (bulbourethral) glands are accessory glands of the male reproductive system that secrete a lubricating fluid into the urethra, so they belong to the reproductive system.

The liver converts glucose to glycogen, makes urea and breaks down old red blood cells. Absorption of food and water from undigested matter is done by the intestines, especially the large intestine, so option 4 is not a liver function.
Ureters, the iris and the bronchi all have smooth (involuntary) muscle. Biceps is a skeletal (striated, voluntary) muscle, so option 4 is right.

Antibodies are formed by lymphocytes (B cells), and the thymus is the organ where T lymphocytes mature. Of the options, thymus by lymphocytes is the best fit; RBCs and platelets do not make antibodies.
Haemoglobin, the iron-containing pigment in red blood cells, binds oxygen and carries it in the blood. The red blood cell is only its container, and chlorophyll is in plants.

Statement I describes the uniformity of the Mature Harappan phase, so it is correct. Statement II is wrong because in the Late Harappan phase seals, script, weights and bricks lost their uniformity, so construction techniques did not stay the same as in the mature phase.
Humayun besieged Chunar Fort in 1532 for four months, after which Sher Khan accepted his supremacy. The 1531 date belongs to the Kalinjar invasion, so option 1 is wrong.
The Battle of Chausa (26 June 1539) was fought between Humayun and Sher Khan, and Sher Khan won. The other pairings belong to different battles.
Humayun's rival brothers were Kamran, Askari and Hindal. Usman is not one of his brothers, so he is the answer.
Humayun was the first Mughal emperor to campaign against Bengal. The notes do not state this fact; they only mention Sher Khan taking Gaur in 1538.
Sher Shah said this after the Battle of Samel (1544), where Maldeo's generals Jaita and Kumpa fought bravely. He said he almost lost the empire of Hindustan for a handful of bajra (millet).
Sher Shah took the titles Hazrat-e-Ala and then Sultan (Sher Shah). Zille-e-Ilahi and Raiyat-e-Ala are not among the titles listed for him, so only I and II are correct.

Sher Shah's administration had Sarkars divided into Parganas, so statement I is correct. Each level was run through officers such as the chief shiqdar, shiqdar, amin and fotedar, so statement II (no officials) is wrong.
CDRI, the drug research lab of CSIR, is at Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh.
CSIR-NCL, the chemistry laboratory, is located in Pune.
NBRI is a CSIR laboratory in Lucknow; the notes do not state this, but Lucknow is the correct answer.
CFTRI, the food technology institute, is at Mysuru (Mysore).
The National Institute of Oceanography is in Goa, and Panaji is the capital of Goa (Dona Paula), so Panaji is correct.
CEERI is in Pilani, Rajasthan. The notes do not cover it; CMERI at Durgapur is a different institute, so don't confuse the two.
The Central Institute of Mining and Fuel Research (CIMFR) is at Dhanbad, Jharkhand. The notes do not mention it.
The Microbial Type Culture Collection (MTCC) gene bank is at IMTECH, Chandigarh.
NEERI (the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute) is at Nagpur.
Oneer is a CSIR-IITR low-cost drinking water disinfection technology for rural areas, so option 2 is correct.

Alps are young fold mountains, Vosges is a block (horst) mountain, and Fujiyama is a volcanic cone. Vindhya is matched with residual mountain by elimination (the notes do not list it), giving 3-1-4-2.
Kerala has made no formal autonomy demand, whereas Tamil Nadu (Rajamannar Committee), Punjab (Anandpur Sahib Resolution) and West Bengal (CPI(M) memorandum) all did.
The notes only say that the AP Reorganisation Act amended the ST Order, 1950. They do not say which Schedule this relates to, so no line settles the Sixth Schedule answer.

After bifurcation on 2 June 2014, the Governor constituted the State Election Commission for residuary Andhra Pradesh on 30 January 2016, so option 3 is correct. The other years (2012, 2014, 2018) are distractors.
Yellow Revolution (began 1986 with the Technology Mission on Oilseeds) concerns oilseeds and edible oils, so 'oil seeds' is correct. Poultry/eggs relate to the Silver Revolution, not Yellow.

The Yellow Revolution relates to oilseed production, and rapeseed-mustard is the main oilseed crop associated with it. Floriculture, pisciculture (Blue Revolution) and wheat (Green Revolution) are not Yellow Revolution areas.
The IMD report identifies the South-western region (Rayalaseema) as receiving the least rainfall; the other regions are wetter coastal or plains areas.
The IMD report describes AP's climate as hot and humid, so even in the summer months (March to June) the moisture level is quite high, not low or zero.
The Ongole to Machilipatnam stretch of the AP coast is the most cyclone-vulnerable, as stated in the notes, not the northern or southern stretches.
The Diviseema cyclone of 19 Nov 1977 hit the Krishna delta and caused the maximum loss of life in AP; the 1990 cyclone killed about 1,000, fewer than 1977.

Challenger Deep (Mariana) is the Pacific's deepest point, Sunda (Java) Trench is the Indian Ocean's deepest, and the Atlantic's deepest is Puerto Rico (Milwaukee Deep). So all three are the deepest points of their oceans, not trenches of one ocean.
The Diamantina Trench lies in the SE Indian Ocean, about 1,500 km west of Perth, so the answer is Indian Ocean.
Coral reefs occur in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Mannar. The Sunderbans are a mangrove and muddy delta area with no coral reefs, so IV is wrong.
The notes say the annual range is smaller in the Pacific than the Atlantic, so statement I is wrong. Statement II is right: the Northern Hemisphere has more land, so its range is larger.

Kharavela, of the Chedi (Mahameghavahana) line, was a Jaina, so he leaned heavily towards Jainism. Dashratha and Brihadratha were Mauryan rulers, and Huvishka was a Kushana, so none of them is the Jain-leaning king here.
The Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri is the year-by-year record of Kharavela of Kalinga, so the answer is Kharavela. It has no link with Ashoka, Harshavardhana or Kanishka.
The 2030 Agenda adopted in 2015 has 17 goals and 169 targets, so 17 is correct.
The UN member states adopted 17 SDGs (with 169 targets) under the 2030 Agenda.
SDG 1 is No Poverty; 'No Hunger' is not the title (Goal 2 is Zero Hunger).
SDG 1 is No Poverty; 'No Hunger' is not the title (Goal 2 is Zero Hunger).
Statement II is correct as MoSPI develops the National Indicator Framework. Statement I is wrong because the Agenda was adopted by all UN member states (193), not 198.
The 15-year 2030 Agenda (2015–2030) set 17 goals and 169 targets.
The UN member states adopted 17 SDGs (with 169 targets) under the 2030 Agenda.
The 2030 Agenda adopted by UNGA in September 2015 includes 17 SDGs.
Goal 1 is No Poverty; Quality Education is 4, Gender Equality 5, Clean Energy 7.
The universal call to action to end poverty and protect the planet comprises 17 goals.
The 2030 Agenda adopted in September 2015 has 17 goals (169 targets); the '203' in the question is a garble of 2030.
The SDGs run 2015–2030, so 2030 is the target year, not 2035.
The USDG vision holds that universal access to clean water, sanitation and healthcare is essential for human dignity.
SDG 8 is Decent Work and Economic Growth; Zero Hunger is 2, Reduced Inequalities 10.
'Life in sky' is not an SDG; the life goals are Life Below Water (14) and Life on Land (15), and Reduced Inequalities is Goal 10.
SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) aims to end hunger, achieve food security and promote sustainable agriculture.
SDG 7 is affordable, reliable, sustainable, modern energy (1); SDG 12 is responsible consumption and production (2); SDG 15 is Life on Land (4); SDG 13 is Climate Action (3). So A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3.
Goal 4 is Quality Education and lifelong learning for all.
SDG 6 is Clean Water and Sanitation, covering availability and sustainable management of water.

Lake Baikal is the deepest lake (1,642 m) and holds the largest freshwater volume, so it is the only option meeting both conditions.
Lake Victoria is shared by Tanzania (51%), Uganda (43%) and Kenya (6%), so it forms the boundary between Tanzania and Uganda. Chad, Malawi and the Zambezi are not on that border.
The Caspian is the world's largest lake by area (~371,000 km²) and volume. Superior is only the largest freshwater lake by area, and Victoria Fall is a waterfall, not a lake.
Finland is called the 'Garden of lakes' or 'Land of a Thousand Lakes' because of its roughly 187,888 glacial lakes.
Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake by area (~82,100 km²). Baikal is the largest only by volume.
The first Census (1872, under Lord Mayo) was non-synchronous, while the first synchronous Census was held in 1881, so 1881 is correct. 1871 is the tempting option but it was not synchronous.

The Cripps proposals provided for Indians to frame their own constitution through a body elected by provincial lower houses plus princely-state nominees. The August Offer only promised a representative body after the war; the Cripps draft set out the elected body's composition.
Cripps offered an Indian Union with Dominion Status after the war, not complete independence. Partition was not offered outright, only a provincial opt-out.
The Cripps draft proposed an Indian Union with Dominion Status after the war. Full independence was not offered.
Nehru and Maulana Azad (then Congress President) were the Congress negotiators with Cripps.
Gandhi called the Cripps offer a post-dated cheque, popularly quoted as on a crashing bank.

Congress objected that there was no immediate transfer of power, with defence and Governor-General's powers retained by the British, so effective power was not handed to Indians. The partition option was one objection, but the main ground was the lack of real power.
The Cripps Mission arrived in March 1942 (Delhi, 22-23 March), and returned in mid-April after talks failed.
The Cripps Mission came to India in March 1942.
The notes record 26 operational cement plants in AP in 2014-15, located in YSR Kadapa, Kurnool and Guntur.
APIIC was set up on 26 September 1973, so option 2 is correct.
The IDP 2020-23 was not applied within Vijayawada Municipal Corporation limits, so Vijayawada is the answer.
IDP 2023-27 reserves 33% of land in new industrial parks for MSMEs.
The IDP (4.0) and MSME & Entrepreneur Development (4.0) policies were notified on 26 Oct 2024 and cover 2024-29.
The IDP 2020-23 provides for 30 skill development centres and 2 skill universities. All three statements are correct, so 1, 2 and 3 is the answer.
Under IDP 2020-23 a mega project is defined by 2,000 jobs.
The notes do not cover the Aerospace and Defence Manufacturing Policy 2015-20 targets.
IDP 2020-23 reserved 16.2% of APIIC plots for SC entrepreneurs.
The Single Desk Portal gives pre-establishment and pre-operation approvals within 21 days.
SDP stands for Single Desk Portal, launched in April 2015 under the Single Desk Policy.
Pre-establishment and pre-operation approvals under the Single Desk Policy are given within 21 days.

The APEDB Resource Mobilisation Division administers the Investment Facilitation, Innovation, Viability Gap, Project Development and Capacity Development Funds. There is no 'Capacity investment project fund'.
Pepper Motion's EV bus and truck unit is at Punganur, Chittoor. The earlier 2023 plan of Rs 4,640 cr was at Badvel, YSR Kadapa, which is the tempting wrong option.
AP ranked 14th in FDI inflows as of Dec 2021.
For Oct 2019-Mar 2021, AP's FDI rank was 12th.

Raitu Bandhu is the AMC pledge loan scheme: the farmer pledges produce in market-yard godowns and borrows against it, which avoids forced sales. So option 2 is right; the notes give no support for the interest-free or 8% claims.
Rythu Bazars began functioning from January 1999, so option 2 is correct; the other dates are distractors.
The Ryot Bazar (Apni Mandi) scheme first came in Punjab, and Andhra Pradesh was the second State to adopt it.
The First Schedule lists the names and territories of the States and Union Territories, so the answer is First.
Admission of new States from outside India comes under Article 2, not Article 3. Article 3 covers only forming new States and altering the areas, boundaries or names of existing States.
The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed on 22 December 1953, after Andhra State was formed.
The Fazl Ali Commission (SRC) members were Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru. Pattabhi Sitaramayya belonged to the JVP Committee, so he was not a member.
The SRC reported in 1955, and the States Reorganisation Act came into force on 1 November 1956, so the States were reorganised in 1956.
Kurnool was the capital of Andhra State when it was formed in 1953. Hyderabad became the capital only in 1956.
Andhra State, the first linguistic State, was formed in 1953 (1 October 1953). The 1956 date is when Andhra Pradesh was formed by merging Telangana.
Amma Vodi gives ₹15,000 a year to the mother of a child who enrols and attends school, so it encourages parents to send children to school. The other schemes are not school-attendance incentives.
The notes do not state the 2019-20 budget allocation for YSR Rythu Bharosa. The keyed answer is Rs. 8750 crore.
Amma Vodi provides ₹15,000 a year to the mother of a school-going child.
YSR Rythu Bharosa gives ₹13,500 a year per family, including ₹6,000 from PM-KISAN.
YSR Rythu Bharosa promised ₹13,500 per farmer family per year, including the ₹6,000 PM-KISAN share.
Rythu Bharosa is the first-listed pillar of Navaratnalu and gives farmers financial assistance. The other options are not the farmer-support pillar.
YSR Rythu Bharosa was started in October 2019 for farmers. Navratna is not a farmer scheme.
YSR Rythu Bharosa was started in October 2019 for farmers. Navratna is not a farmer scheme.
The notes do not cover the Raithu Runa Mafi scheme. The keyed answer is a maximum relief of ₹1,50,000.
In January 2022 the YSR Pension Kanuka old-age pension was raised from ₹2,250 to ₹2,500.
The May 2025 insurance model gives cover up to ₹25 lakh per family per year for about 1.65 crore poor and middle-class families.
YSR Aasara repaid women SHGs' bank loans outstanding on 11 April 2019. Cheyutha is a yearly cash benefit, not loan repayment.
Cheyutha is for women aged 45-60, and an annual income of ₹10,000 is not a condition. Option 4 is therefore the one that is not an eligibility criterion.
YSR Cheyutha gives ₹18,750 a year, which is ₹75,000 over 4 years.
YSR Cheyutha gives ₹18,750 a year, which is ₹75,000 over 4 years.
Adarana gives modern tools to BC artisans at subsidised prices through the BC Corporation. Chandranna Pelli Kanuka is a marriage-aid scheme.
The opening line "The battle to feed all of humanity is over" belongs to Paul Ehrlich's The Population Bomb (1968), not Malthus's Essay.
The opening line "The battle to feed all of humanity is over" belongs to Paul Ehrlich's The Population Bomb (1968), not Malthus's Essay.

Under the older UN edition (WUP 2014) Tokyo was the most populous city, ahead of Delhi and Shanghai, so Tokyo is the keyed answer. Newer data (WUP 2025) lists Jakarta first, but it is not among the options.
The Inter-State Council is created under Article 263 of the Constitution, so the Constitution is its source; it is not a statutory or executive body.
The Planning Commission was set up by an executive resolution in 1950 and is not in the Constitution, whereas the Finance Commission, PSC and Election Commission have Articles.
NITI Aayog was created by a Cabinet Resolution in 2015, so it is extra-constitutional. The Finance Commission, Election Commission and Inter-State Council are constitutional.
The Planning Commission was created by executive resolution and is not in the Constitution. The Election Commission, Finance Commission and Inter-State Council have constitutional Articles.
The Planning Commission came from a 1950 executive resolution and is not constitutional. UPSC, FC and ECI are constitutional bodies.
Not covered in the notes; Justice S.N. Phukan was appointed to replace Justice Venkataswamy on the Tehelka inquiry commission.
The 21st Law Commission under Justice B.S. Chauhan issued the Uniform Civil Code questionnaire on 7 October 2016, so the answer is the Law Commission.
Article 84 fixes the minimum age for the Lok Sabha at 25 years (30 for the Rajya Sabha).
A Lok Sabha member must be a citizen and at least 25 years old (Art 84). Holding an office of profit is a disqualification, not a qualification, so III is wrong.
Under Art 101(3)(a) the seat falls vacant immediately when an Art 102 disqualification is incurred, with no decision by the House needed.
Under Art 103 the President decides disqualification questions on the binding opinion of the Election Commission.
Under Art 101(4), a House may declare a member's seat vacant if he is absent from all meetings for 60 days. The other options give wrong periods.
Statements I and II are correct: the 1959 Act exempts posts and was amended five times. III is wrong because 'office of profit' is not defined in the Constitution.
Art 103 makes the President the decider of disqualification disputes, acting on the Election Commission's binding opinion. So the answer is the President in consultation with the Election Commission.

The 15th Lok Sabha (2009) was the first with women above 10%, and the 17th (2019) had the highest share, so I and II are correct. Statement IV (assent on 28 Sept 2023) is also correct, which makes option 3 right.
The first sitting of the first Lok Sabha was on 13 May 1952, after it was constituted on 17 April 1952.
Art 100(3) fixes the quorum at one-tenth of the total membership of the House.
The Asaf Jahi (Nizam) dynasty was founded by Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I in 1724; the Qutb Shahi dynasty (Golconda) is a different, earlier dynasty.
The Razakars, the militant force of the Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen, were led by Kasim (Qasim) Razvi.
Hyderabad was ruled by the Asaf Jahi dynasty (the Nizams) in 1947-48, not the earlier Qutb Shahi dynasty.
After Operation Polo (13-17 September 1948) the Nizam surrendered and acceded in 1948.
The Hyderabad police action of September 1948 had the code name Operation Polo; Operation Vijay was Goa 1961.
The notes attribute this book to Swami Ramananda Tirtha, but the keyed answer is V.H. Desai and C. Sudarshan; the notes do not state the keyed authorship.
Operation Vijay (December 1961), led by Maj. Gen. K.P. Candeth, freed Goa, Daman and Diu from Portuguese rule.

Article 137 gives the Supreme Court the power to review its own judgments and orders, subject to Parliament's laws and Art. 145 rules. Art. 142 is the complete-justice power (and the basis of curative petitions), not the review provision.
The Supreme Court can review its own judgments under Article 137. Neither the President nor the Cabinet has such a power.

Statement I is wrong because the Speaker/Chairman may admit or reject the motion under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Statement II is wrong because the Constitution does not define misbehaviour or incapacity. III and IV are correct: the Act lays down the procedure, and removal needs a special majority in each House.
Under Art. 124(4) a judge is removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Violation of the Constitution is not a listed ground, so II and III are correct.

I is correct because the President must consult the CJI when appointing judges. III is correct because SC salaries and pensions are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India. II is wrong because neither the CJI nor the President alone can remove a judge. IV is not supported by the notes: the CJI appoints SC staff without executive interference, so it is incorrect.

I is correct as SC and HC judges are both removed under Art. 124(4)/218, the same mode. II is wrong because a retired HC judge can still practise in the Supreme Court and other High Courts (Art. 220).

Malik Baqbaq, an amir/governor under Balban, was publicly flogged on his orders for cruelty to a servant, which fits Balban's harsh 'blood and iron' discipline. The notes do not state this incident, so no line is linked.
On accession in 1266 Balban took the regnal title Ghiyasuddin Balban, so option 2 is right; his earlier name was Bahauddin.
Nauroz, the Persian festival, was brought into the Indian court by Balban, who copied Iranian kings. The other rulers listed did not introduce it.
Srisailam Dam is built on the Krishna river in Nandyal district (erstwhile Kurnool); Tungabhadra is only a tributary of the Krishna.
Srisailam Dam is built on the Krishna river in Nandyal district (erstwhile Kurnool); Tungabhadra is only a tributary of the Krishna.

Both statements are true: Pattiseema was recorded in the Limca Book of Records (2017), and it linked the Godavari to the Krishna (India's first river-linking initiative). The linking is the achievement that earned the record, so R explains A.
The Rayalaseema Lift Irrigation Scheme draws water from Srisailam, and this is the subject of the AP–Telangana dispute.

The Telugu Ganga route runs Srisailam → Somasila → Kandaleru → Poondi to supply drinking water to Chennai. The other options are wrong: it is not for Tirupati, and it irrigates Rayalaseema and Nellore rather than Nellore exclusively.
The Babli barrage in Maharashtra lies on the Godavari upstream of Sriramsagar, so it reduces inflow to the Sriramsagar reservoir.
Under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014, sharing of Srisailam water is handled by the Krishna River Management Board, not the tribunal or the Godavari board.
The one-by-six scheme made return filing compulsory on lifestyle signs, and the telephone connection criterion was dropped in Budget 2002-03. The other options were not the criterion removed.
The K.N. Raj Committee (1972) examined taxation of agricultural wealth and income. Kaldor dealt with expenditure, wealth, gift and capital gains taxes, and Wanchoo with black money.
The Vijay Kelkar Task Force on direct and indirect taxes recommended abolishing rebates under Section 88. Chelliah focused on lower rates and a broader base, and Shome on GAAR.

The notes do not name the convener of the 2017 task force (they mention only the Akhilesh Ranjan task force), so no line supports this answer. Arbind Modi was the convener of the task force drafting the new direct tax law.

The equalisation levy was introduced through the Finance Act 2016 as a separate levy, not as part of the Income Tax Act, so I is wrong. It is outside the income tax, so no foreign tax credit under DTAA is available, so II is wrong. Hence neither is correct.
J.J. Thomson received the 1906 Physics Nobel for discovering the electron (the neutron, proton and positron were found by others); the notes do not cover this.
Oliver Hart shared the 2016 Economics Nobel (with Bengt Holmström) for contributions to contract theory; the notes do not state this.
Einstein's 1921 Nobel Prize was for the photoelectric effect, not relativity, which is the tempting wrong option.
Norman Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize; the Borlaug Award is in agriculture, which is the tempting wrong option, but his Nobel was not in agriculture.

The Fields Medal, awarded to mathematicians under 40, is regarded as the mathematics equivalent of a Nobel Prize because there is no Nobel in mathematics. The notes list its Indian-origin winners but do not state this equivalence.
The 2016 Medicine Nobel went to Yoshinori Ohsumi for his work on the mechanisms of autophagy; the notes do not cover this.
The notes list five original Nobel categories (Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature, Peace), so 5 is the answer in this framing. Economics was added later and is not in the will.

I is right (ADB part-funds VCIC), II is right (aligned with the Golden Quadrilateral, ~800 km), and IV is right (Donakonda is a long-term VCIC node). III is wrong because VCIC has three nodes in AP, not four, so option 3 is correct.
Kopparthy (YSR Kadapa) hosts the YSR Jagananna Mega Industrial Hub, spread over 3,155 acres.
Kopparthy (YSR Kadapa) hosts the YSR Jagananna Mega Industrial Hub, spread over 3,155 acres.

APIIC (1973) is the nodal agency for industrial land, parks and SEZs, so it provides industrial infrastructure. APSEZ is a single SEZ at Atchutapuram-Rambilli and APGIC is a gas JV, so they are wrong.
A Citizen's Charter is a written commitment on service standards whose main purpose is time-bound service delivery and grievance redress. The other options have nothing to do with it.

Social audit is the process used in MGNREGA to raise accountability: Gram Sabhas and communities check funds and works (Section 17). Financial, political and legal audits are not the MGNREGA accountability process.
Startup India Yatra is meant to hunt for entrepreneurial talent in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, so option 2 is right; it is not about villages.
Start-up India was launched on 16 January 2016 (now National Startup Day) to build the start-up ecosystem, so the answer is Start-up India.
The notes describe Startup India Hub as a single online platform for stakeholders but give no year of operationalisation. The Hub was operationalised in 2016, alongside the Startup India launch.
Stand-Up India targets SC/ST and women entrepreneurs aged 18+, so option 4 is correct.
Walmart acquired a majority stake in Flipkart in 2018. Shop Clues, Yepme and Snapdeal were not the target of this deal.
Among the options, only the Satavahana kings put their mother's name before their own (Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra, Halamiputra), so they were identified through metronymics.
The Kodavali inscription (East Godavari, Pithapuram) is the record of Chanda Satakarni; Kanheri, Amaravati and Karle belong to other rulers.
The Peshwas' seat was Poona (Pune), where power shifted from the Chhatrapati at Satara; Nagpur was the Bhonsle seat.
Baji Rao I followed the ideology of Hindu Pad Padshahi, striking at the Mughal centre.
Balaji Vishwanath restored order after Sambhaji and was made Peshwa in 1713, securing the 1719 Mughal grant, so he streamlined the administration.
Nana Phadnavis was known as the 'Maratha Machiavelli' (Chanakya of Maratha politics) for holding the confederacy together as regent.
The Third Battle of Panipat (Marathas vs Abdali) was fought on 14 January 1761; 1526 and 1556 were the first and second battles.
Ibrahim Khan Gardi commanded the Maratha artillery at Panipat.
Sadashiv Rao Bhau was the overall Maratha commander at Panipat III; Vishwas Rao was the Peshwa's son and was also killed.

The notes list heavy baggage and non-combatants and lack of allies and supplies as causes; tactical errors and Abdali's generalship are also accepted causes, but Gardi was the artillery chief, not a traitor, so IV is wrong.
The battle took place on 14 January 1761.
Ibrahim Khan Gardi, the Muslim commander of the Maratha artillery, fought for the Marathas at Panipat III; the other names belong to Bengal.
National income is measured as NNP at factor cost, the standard measure. GNP and market-price aggregates are not national income proper.
NNP = GNP − depreciation, so depreciation is what is deducted from GNP. Interest, tax and subsidy are not the gross-to-net bridge.

GDP minus depreciation gives NDP at market price; moving to factor cost also needs removing net indirect taxes. So NDPFC = GDPMP − Depreciation is incorrect, while the other three follow MP = FC + indirect taxes − subsidies.
NNP = GNP − depreciation, so the answer is Net National Product.
Shadow prices are prices based on imputed values of costs and benefits, used where market prices do not reflect true social cost or benefit.
Factor cost = market price − indirect taxes + subsidies. So national product at factor cost equals national product at market prices − indirect taxes + subsidies.
GDP at market price and at factor cost differ by indirect taxes and subsidies, not direct taxes. Of the options, indirect taxes is the answer.
The law of diminishing returns says that adding more of a variable factor to a fixed factor eventually makes the marginal product fall.
Per capita income is the average income of a country, so it reflects the standard of living. Total national income ignores population size.
Per capita income = National Income ÷ Population, and National Income is NNP at factor cost. So it is NNP divided by total population.
Personal disposable income = personal income − personal direct taxes − non-tax payments such as fines and fees.

Role play lets participants act out situations and take on others' viewpoints, so they can re-examine their own and others' feelings, behavior and experiences. Group discussion, story telling and demonstration do not give this same chance. The notes do not cover this.

Both statements are correct. Binodini Dasi helped set up the Star Theatre in Calcutta in 1883, and she serialised her autobiography Amar Katha between 1910 and 1913. The notes do not cover Bengali theatre.
The number of public sector undertakings was 5 at the start of the First Plan (1951) and rose to 244 by 1990, so 5 is correct.
RINL (Rashtriya Ispat Nigam) is a Navratna CPSE. Indian Oil is a Maharatna, while Bharti Airtel and Renuka Sugars are private companies.
BEL is only a Navratna and has not been elevated to Maharatna, whereas SAIL, ONGC and NTPC are Maharatnas.
Sri Bagh was the residence of Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao in Madras, where the 1937 pact was signed; the other options are not where it was.
The Sri Bagh Pact was signed on 16 November 1937, so 1937 is correct.
P. Anandacharlu presided over the Nagpur INC session in 1891, making him the first Telugu INC president; Pattabhi Sitaramayya came later, in 1948.
The notes do not mention this MoES Life Time Excellence Award. Ashok Sahni, a palaeontologist, received it in July 2020.
The notes do not give the Survey of India headquarters. It is headquartered at Dehradun; the Hyderabad entry in the notes is only NIGST, its training institute.
The notes do not cover NATMO. It is headquartered in Kolkata, under DST.
SERB stands for Science and Engineering Research Board, the statutory board set up by the SERB Act 2008. The other options distort the name.
The notes record that the SERB Women Excellence Award 2020 went to Dr. Niti Kumar of CSIR-CDRI, Lucknow.
Dakshin Gangotri was India's first Antarctic research station, set up in 1983-84. It is not a river valley, a source of the Ganga or an island.
India's Antarctic stations are Dakshin Gangotri (first), Maitri (second) and Bharti (third, 2012). Bharti is therefore the third.
NIMHANS is in Bengaluru, Karnataka. The notes do not cover it.

NIPER Mohali, SCTIMST Thiruvananthapuram and Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha are Institutes of National Importance by Acts of Parliament. LNIPE Gwalior is a deemed university, so statement IV is wrong.
The Indian Institute of Ecology and Environment is located in New Delhi. The notes do not cover it.
NRLC is headquartered in Lucknow, under the Ministry of Culture. The notes do not cover it.

Moinuddin Chishti came to India with Muhammad Ghori in 1192 and settled at Ajmer, which was the time of Prithviraj Chauhan's Ajmer/Delhi region (his defeat came in 1192). The other rulers belong to later Mewar history.

Nizamuddin Auliya was the main disciple of Baba Farid (Sheikh Farid) and the one who stayed aloof from the court. Nasiruddin Chirag was Nizamuddin's disciple, and Salim Chishti was a later saint at Fatehpur Sikri.
Baba Farid (Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar) is the Sufi whose verses are included in the Adi Granth/Guru Granth Sahib. The other saints listed have no compositions in it.
Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi was imprisoned by Jahangir at Gwalior Fort for his orthodox stance. The other options are not connected with imprisonment by Jahangir.
Gunaga Vijayaditya (Vijayaditya III) is named as the greatest Eastern Chalukya king; Danarnava, Bhima I and Rajaraja Narendra were not.
The Vipparla inscription was issued by Jayasimha I (Jayasimha Vallabha), who also shifted the capital to Vengi.
Tripura Martya Maheshwara was the title of Gunaga Vijayaditya (Vijayaditya III), not of Vishnuvardhana I or III or Vijayaditya I.

At the Lahore session of 1929 Congress adopted Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence) as its goal. Self-Government as an objective, the NCM launch and RTC participation do not fit this session, which boycotted the RTC.
Nehru hoisted the tricolour at midnight on 31 December 1929 on the banks of the Ravi at the Lahore session, so 1929 is correct.
Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the 1929 Lahore session and moved the Purna Swaraj resolution.
Jawaharlal Nehru was the president of the 1929 Lahore session, which proclaimed Purna Swaraj.
The Dandi March began on 12 March 1930, not 15 March, so statement 4 is incorrect.
The Dandi March was a protest against the salt tax and monopoly, culminating in breaking the salt law on 6 April 1930.
The 1930 CDM was launched through the Salt Satyagraha against the salt tax and monopoly, Gandhi's main demand to Irwin. Complete independence was the ultimate goal, not the immediate issue.
Lord Irwin was Viceroy (1926-31) during the Dandi March of 1930.

Statement I is right as the salt tax and monopoly were the target. The Viceroy was Irwin, not Ripon, so III is wrong. Gandhi completed the march, reaching Dandi, so IV is wrong. Time coverage (II) is accepted as correct per the answer.
The Dandi March took place in 1930 (12 March to 5 April, salt law broken 6 April).
The ₹1 note is issued by the Government of India (Ministry of Finance) and signed by the Finance Secretary, unlike other notes, which carry the RBI Governor's signature.
India's note issue follows the Minimum Reserve System, adopted in 1956 and amended in 1957, which replaced the Proportional Reserve System (used until 1956).
Notes other than the ₹1 note are issued by the RBI and signed by the RBI Governor, so the ₹100 note carries the Governor's signature. The Finance Secretary signs only the ₹1 note.
The notes do not cover polymer notes, so no line settles this. Polymer notes last longer, are harder to counterfeit and reduce replacement costs, so all three objectives apply.
FICN stands for Fake Indian Currency Note, meaning counterfeit rupee notes.
The four mints are at Mumbai, Noida, Kolkata and Hyderabad. Option 4 is the only one listing only places that have mints, whereas Delhi and Bangalore have none.
The Bank Note Press is at Dewas (Madhya Pradesh), not Hyderabad. Hyderabad has a mint, not a press, so statement 4 is incorrect.
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 gives the RBI powers of licensing, branch control, management, amalgamation, inspection and audit of banks.
The notes state that the DIGIT e-Governance platform belongs to the Municipal Administration and Urban Development (MA&UD) department of AP.
Sarpanch heads a Village (Gram) Panchayat, a Chairperson heads a Municipality, a Mayor heads a Municipal Corporation, and a Councillor is the elected member for a ward. This gives A-2, B-3, C-1, D-5.
The notes say the State Government controls ULBs in legislative, financial and personnel matters, so A, B and C are correct. Control over citizens' grievances is not listed, so D is excluded.
Under Article 243S, Ward Committees are mandatory in municipalities with a population of 3 lakh or more. The 10 lakh figure applies to metropolitan areas, not ward committees.
Toto is a small tribe of Totopara in Jalpaiguri district, West Bengal. The notes do not mention it.
The Khas are found in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, not Arunachal Pradesh, so pair 3 is wrong. The notes do not cover the Khas.

The Jarawa live in South and Middle Andaman, so they are an Andaman and Nicobar tribe, not one of the NE states. Of the options, Nicobar Island is the nearest, though strictly they live in the Andaman group.
The Nyishi (formerly Dafla) are the largest tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, so option 2 is right. The notes list Dafla only under Arunachal and do not name the Nyishi.
The Bhil are found in Rajasthan, MP, Gujarat and Maharashtra, so Maharashtra is the only listed option that fits. Assam, Jharkhand and West Bengal are not Bhil areas.
Onge and Shompen are native to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The Rengma are a Naga tribe of Nagaland, so they are not native to the islands. The notes do not mention Halchu or Rengma.
The Todas live in the Nilgiris of Tamil Nadu, not Kerala, so Todas-Kerala is wrongly matched.
Limboo-Sikkim and Dongaria Kondh-Odisha are correct. Karbi belong to Assam, not HP, and Bonda are from Odisha, not Tamil Nadu, so II and IV are wrong.
The Changpa live in Changthang, Ladakh, not Uttarakhand, so I is wrong. They rear Pashmina goats and have been ST since 1989, so II and III are correct.
Bhutia-Sikkim, Toda-Tamil Nadu and Sentinelese-Andaman (North Sentinel) are in the notes. Birhor-Jharkhand is the remaining pairing, so the code is 4 3 2 1.
The 'Lal Bangala' kitchen is a Bhunjia custom: it is a sacred kitchen that no outsider may enter. The notes do not cover this.
The Tharu live in the Terai of UP, Bihar and Uttarakhand, and are Uttarakhand's largest tribe, so option 1 is correct. Bhutia belong to Sikkim.
Toda-Tamil Nadu, Lepcha-Sikkim and Garo-Meghalaya are in the notes. Birhor-Jharkhand is the remaining pair, giving 3 1 4 2.
The Hornbill Festival is celebrated in Nagaland, showcasing Naga cultural heritage.
The Advocate General is the State counterpart of the Attorney General (Art. 76 vs Art. 165), serving as the highest law officer and legal adviser of the State Government.
The Solicitor General is the second law officer who assists the AG and tenders legal advice and appears in courts for the Union, so he is a legal adviser, not an administrative officer.
Under Art. 88 the Attorney General may speak and take part in proceedings of either House without being a member. CEC, CJI and NSA have no such right.
The Advocate General is the official legal adviser to the State Government (Art. 165(2)); the AG and SG serve the Union.
Under Art. 165(1) the Advocate General of a State is appointed by the Governor, not the Chief Minister or the Law Minister.
The Attorney General is the highest law officer of India; the Advocate General is only the State's highest law officer.
The Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President (Art. 76(4)). The CAG, CEC and Speaker have fixed tenures or different removal procedures.
Statement I is correct: the AG must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. Statement II is wrong: remuneration is determined by the President, not Parliament.
Under Art. 88 the Attorney General can take part in parliamentary proceedings without being a member, whereas the Solicitor General has no such right.
Art. 88 lets the Attorney General attend and speak in either House without being a member, though he cannot vote.
Art. 88 gives the Attorney General the right to speak and take part in either House, joint sittings and committees he is named to, but not to vote.
Amitraghata (Greek Amitrochates), meaning 'slayer of foes', was the title of Bindusara, not Chandragupta or Ashoka.
The Mauryan court under Bindusara received envoys from Syria (Deimachus of Antiochus I) and Egypt (Dionysius of Ptolemy II), showing diplomatic ties with these distant lands.
Megasthenes was sent by Seleucus I Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya and wrote Indica.
The Tamil poet Mamulanar refers to the Mauryas' southward push; he is a Tamil poet, not a Greek writer.
Devanampiya and Piyadasi were the titles of Ashoka, as seen in his inscriptions.
AIIMS Delhi opened its first skin bank in June 2023, so skin is correct; eye, liver and blood are not the bank it opened at that time.
Dengue causes platelet count to fall sharply, leading to internal bleeding; red and white cells are not the main targets.
Filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) affects lymph vessels, causing fever and swelling of the lower limbs (elephantiasis). Ascariasis, amoebiasis and TB do not cause this.
Dengue (a flavivirus) mainly causes platelets to fall, leading to internal bleeding, so platelets are the correct answer.
Japanese encephalitis is caused by JEV, a flavivirus, so it is a viral disease and not bacterial, protozoan or fungal.
Dengue is spread by the female Aedes aegypti mosquito. Anopheles transmits malaria, and the tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus) is a less typical choice, so Aedes is the answer.
The name Dharmasoka occurs in the Sarnath inscription, whereas the Maski edict carries the name Ashoka (Buddhashakya Ashoka).

The remorse after the Kalinga War (RE XIII) led Ashoka to replace conquest by war (bherighosha) with conquest by dhamma (dhammaghosha), changing his policy. Buddhism and the missions came later or were consequences.
Ashoka did conquer Kalinga in c. 261 BCE, and its control of land and sea routes to the south explains its strategic importance, so R explains A. The notes, however, do not state the route fact.
Turamaya in RE XIII is Ptolemy II, the king of Egypt. Syria is Antiyoka (Antiochus II) and Macedonia is Antikini.
Kubja Vishnuvardhana, brother of Pulakeshin II, founded the Eastern Chalukya line of Vengi. Vijayaditya I was a later ruler and Pulakeshin IV is not the founder.
The Bezawada inscription records the Kartikeya temple built by Yuddhamalla, so it belongs to his reign rather than Vijayaditya, Vimaladitya or Chalukya Bhima.
The notes do not expand CDMA. CDMA stands for Code Division Multiple Access, a multiple-access method used in 2G/3G mobile networks.
The notes do not expand GSM. GSM stands for Global System for Mobile Communications, the standard behind 2G digital cellular networks.

LTE is designed to raise the capacity and speed of mobile networks, so statement I is correct. Statement II is wrong because original LTE did not meet the IMT-Advanced 4G requirements; only LTE-Advanced did, so LTE is only loosely called 4G.
Martin Cooper of Motorola made the first handheld mobile phone call in 1973, so he is credited with inventing the mobile phone.
Using mobile and wireless technologies such as SMS, apps and wearables for health purposes is m-health. Tele-medicine is only remote clinical care, and e-health is the broader term.
BCC stands for blind carbon copy: it sends copies while hiding recipients' addresses from one another. The colour-based options are made-up expansions.
The Economic Survey is published every year by the Ministry of Finance (prepared by the Economic Division of its Department of Economic Affairs); NDC, Institute of Finance and ISI do not publish it.

The Aspirational Districts Programme is built on Convergence (of schemes and funds), Collaboration and Competition, so effective use of funds and services of different departments is called convergence.
BRGF was delinked from central support in 2015-16 and is now defunct, which is consistent with it being merged into RGSA from 2015-16. The other schemes listed continue as separate schemes.

Export-led growth (import substitution to export promotion) came with the LPG reforms of 1991, so 1991 is correct. The later years (1993, 1994) mark exchange-rate and convertibility steps, not the start of the strategy.

Export-led growth (import substitution to export promotion) came with the LPG reforms of 1991, so 1991 is correct. The later years (1993, 1994) mark exchange-rate and convertibility steps, not the start of the strategy.
Fishes are cold-blooded gill-breathing vertebrates, whereas bats, whales and humans are mammals (warm-blooded, with mammary glands), so fishes is the odd one out.
In the presence of an iron (Lewis acid) catalyst, benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution with chlorine to give chlorobenzene. Benzene hexachloride forms only by addition under UV light.
Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes such as catalase that detoxify harmful substances like hydrogen peroxide; lysosomes hold hydrolytic enzymes instead.

A leaf's primary functions are photosynthesis (food manufacture), gas exchange and transpiration. Conduction of food and water is done by the vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), not the leaf's primary function.
Sound is a mechanical (elastic) wave that needs a material medium, so it cannot travel through vacuum. Statement II is therefore the correct explanation of Statement I.
Pitch depends on frequency and loudness depends on amplitude. Both are true, but they are independent facts, so II does not explain I.
A compound consists of two or more elements chemically combined, so Statement I is true. Compounds are homogeneous and are not mixtures, so Statement II is false.
Glass is an amorphous supercooled liquid, a mixture of silicates, with no sharp melting point. Because it lacks a definite melting point it is not a true compound, so II explains I.
Sound needs a medium and cannot travel through vacuum, so Statement I is false. Light is an electromagnetic wave that can travel through vacuum, so Statement II is true.
Evaporation happens at the surface, so a larger surface area speeds it up. This is why clothes are spread out to dry, so II explains I.
Mortar is a paste of cement, sand and water used as a binder in masonry. Concrete also contains coarse aggregate (gravel), and RCC is concrete reinforced with steel.
German silver is an alloy of copper, zinc and nickel, so copper is its major component. It contains no silver.
Dentalium is the genus of tusk shells (class Scaphopoda), named for their tusk-like shape. Chiton and Chaetoderma belong to other molluscan classes.
For a spherical mirror the focal length is half the radius of curvature, so R = 2f.
By the Bohr-Bury rule, the maximum number of electrons in the nth shell is 2n².
Concave mirrors are used in headlights, torches and shaving mirrors. Rear-view mirrors are convex, giving a wider field of view.
1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m = 10⁻⁷ cm, since 1 m = 100 cm.
Wolves form long-lasting monogamous pairs. Walrus, seals and deer are polygynous.
The yellow dust in the anthers of a flower is pollen, which carries the male gametes. Zygote, sperm and stomata do not fit.

The three elements of Dicey's Rule of Law are absence of arbitrary power (limitation of powers), equality before law, and primacy of individual rights (liberty and civil rights). 'People's responsibility to the Government' is not an element, so III is wrong and I, II and IV are correct.
Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia and rational nexus, so option 1 is correct and option 3 is wrong.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Article 15 only prohibits discrimination on specified grounds, so it is not the answer.
Article 16(4A), added by the 77th Amendment (1995), provides for SC/ST reservation in promotion. Option 3 is too broad, since 16(4A) concerns promotions specifically.

Articles 17 and 18 deal with abolition of untouchability and of titles, which end social distinctions, so they provide social equality. Economic equality lies in the DPSP (Art. 39) and political equality in Arts. 325-326.
Akash Prime is the Akash version with an indigenous active RF seeker, first tested on 27 Sep 2021. Akash Next, Apex and Blaze are not variants in the notes.
Dr Tessy Thomas is called the 'Missile Woman' or 'Agniputri' for her work on Agni-V. The other options are not known by this title.
APJ Abdul Kalam, the 'Missile Man', led the IGMDP, so he is regarded as the father of India's missile technology. The other scientists are linked to space or nuclear work.
Pinaka is a rocket launcher, not a missile. Agni, Akash and Nag are all IGMDP missiles.
Aluminium smelting uses bauxite as its principal ore, whereas cement uses limestone and fertiliser uses other feedstocks; ferro-manganese uses manganese ore.
Maharashtra, with the Mumbai-Pune region as its industrial core, is generally regarded as India's most industrially advanced state.
Bhagalpur in Bihar is famous for its silk (Tussar) textiles, which is why it is called the Silk City; the other options are not silk centres.
Korba in Chhattisgarh is known for the BALCO aluminium plant, along with coal-based thermal power.
Iron and steel is at Jamshedpur, jute is in the Hugli belt around Kolkata, the Barauni refinery is in Bihar, and the Integral Coach Factory is at Perambur, Chennai. This gives a-II, b-III, c-IV, d-I.
Visakhapatnam is ship-building, Muri is aluminium, Gurgaon is automobiles and Panki is fertiliser. This gives 2, 4, 1, 3.
'Life of Pi' is a novel by the Canadian author Yann Martel; the notes do not cover it.
'A River Sutra' is a novel by Gita Mehta; the notes do not cover it.
'The Scent of God' (2019) is a novel by Saikat Majumdar; the notes do not cover it.
'The Hungry Tide' is a novel by Amitav Ghosh set in the Sundarbans; the notes do not cover it.
'A Passage to India' (1924) was written by E.M. Forster; the notes do not cover it.
'Gora' is a novel by Rabindranath Tagore; the notes do not cover it.
'Post Office' (Dak Ghar) is a play by Rabindranath Tagore; the notes do not cover it.
'Flood of Fire' is the third book of Amitav Ghosh's Ibis trilogy; the notes do not cover it.
'One Night @ the Call Centre' is a novel by Chetan Bhagat; the notes do not cover it.
The book 'Don't Laugh: We are Police' was written by IGP Bishan Lal Vohra; the notes do not cover it.
'Pride and Prejudice' (1813) is Jane Austen's novel; the notes do not cover it.
'Revolution 2020' is a novel by Chetan Bhagat; the notes do not cover it.
'The Pakistan Paradox: Instability and Resilience' is by the French political scientist Christophe Jaffrelot; the notes do not cover it.
'Hope in a Challenged Democracy' is by Ashwani Kumar, a former Law Minister; the notes do not cover it.
'The Great Indian Novel' (1989) is by Shashi Tharoor, a satirical retelling of the Mahabharata; the notes do not cover it.
'Freedom from Fear' is a collection of essays by Aung San Suu Kyi; the notes do not cover it.
'Asian Drama: An Inquiry into the Poverty of Nations' by Gunnar Myrdal is an economics work on South Asian development; the notes do not cover it.
'My 51 Poems' is a collection of poems by Atal Bihari Vajpayee; the notes do not cover it.
'A Bend in the River' (1979) is a novel by V.S. Naipaul; the notes do not cover it.
'No Full Stops in India' is by the BBC journalist Mark Tully; the notes do not cover it.

NTPC's 25 MW floating solar project at Simhadri, Visakhapatnam, became operational on 1 July 2022, so Simhadri is correct. Srisailam, Rajamahendravaram and Vijayawada have no such floating solar project in the notes.
South Africa was the 'laboratory' where Gandhi turned passive resistance into satyagraha (first used in 1906 against the Black Act), not England or India.
The notes do not cover this film; it is a 1996 film directed by Shyam Benegal, based on Gandhi's South African years, unlike Attenborough's 'Gandhi'.
The Sabarmati Ashram was also called the Satyagraha Ashram, so (3) is the answer; the question asks for the other name of the ashram on the Sabarmati's banks.
Gandhi founded the Phoenix Settlement near Durban in 1904 after reading Ruskin's Unto This Last; the others had no link with it.
