Alauddin needed a large cash-paid standing army on low fixed salaries, so he fixed prices of daily goods so soldiers could live comfortably on low pay. The other options (farmers' returns, direct purchase) were not the aim.
Price control was introduced for the large standing army: soldiers on low, fixed cash salaries could live comfortably on low pay.
Market control and rationing was the Khalji Sultan Alauddin's system, set up to support his large army; neither Balban nor the Tughluqs did this.
Alauddin was the first Sultan to measure land (masahat) for revenue assessment, so masahat is the term for land measurement.
Alauddin required royal permission for nobles' feasts and marriage alliances, as an ordinance to prevent their gatherings and intermarriage from fuelling revolt.
Madras had the first Municipal Corporation, set up on 29 September 1688 (now Greater Chennai Corporation); Bombay and Calcutta got corporations later, in 1726.
Mango showers are the pre-monsoon thunderstorm showers of Kerala and coastal Karnataka. Kalbaisakhi belongs to West Bengal and the NE, and Loo is a hot dry wind, not rain.
Pre-monsoon summer rains are convectional: strong heating makes air rise, and it cools adiabatically, condenses and gives thunderstorms. So both A and R are true and R explains A.
The notes say dust storms commonly occur in May, in the hot pre-monsoon season, so May is correct.
Kerala gets the monsoon first (1 June). It then advances to the east and north, reaching West Bengal, then Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan last, giving the order III, II, I, IV.

The monsoon strikes the Malabar coast first, so I is correct. Withdrawal comes as the STJ and wind belts shift back south, so III is correct. Rajasthan does get some SW monsoon rain, though little, so II is wrong.
Mawsynram in the Khasi Hills is the wettest place in India, with about 1,187 cm. Cherrapunji is second.
Leh is among the driest places in India, with rainfall under 60 cm, and the notes name it the driest. Meghalaya, the Coromandel Coast and the Konkan Coast are all wet.
The SW monsoon season (June–September) gives about 75% of annual rainfall, so it is the largest source.
The high Western Ghats lie across the SW monsoon winds and force them to rise, giving heavy orographic rain on the windward west coast.

Mumbai on the windward Konkan coast gets heavy rain, and Pune lies in the rain shadow. Vidarbha is semi-arid in the rain-shadow interior. Statement III is not supported by the notes, so only I and II are correct.
A feeble winter high over NW India sends dry winds outward and makes the northern plains cold, so I and II are correct. Loo and thunderstorm rains belong to the hot summer season, not mid-winter.
The Gandhi-Irwin (Delhi) Pact was signed on 5 March 1931, so 1931 is correct.
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931, not 1930, so option 2 is correct.
Sarojini Naidu called Gandhi and Irwin the 'Two Mahatmas' after the Pact.
Under the Pact Gandhi agreed to suspend the Civil Disobedience Movement in return for Irwin's concessions; the RTC was something Gandhi agreed to attend, not to suspend.
The Karachi Session (March 1931) was presided over by Vallabhbhai Patel.
The notes do not state Bose's view of the Karachi Session; it was reportedly Subhas Chandra Bose who described it as the peak of Gandhi's popularity and prestige.
Gandhi was the sole Congress representative at the Second RTC (1931), not Nehru.
After the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Gandhi attended the Second RTC in London as the sole Congress representative, so the conference followed the Pact.
The order is Chauri Chaura (1922), Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931), Poona Pact (1932), Cripps Mission (1942), so III, II, IV, I.
Samarendra Kumar Mitra designed India's first analog computer (built in the 1950s); the notes do not cover this, and the other names are not credited with it.
National Science Day is on 28 February, marking the Raman Effect discovery of 1928. 22 December is National Mathematics Day, a tempting wrong option.
28 February commemorates the Raman Effect (1928), so National Science Day is Raman-effect day, not a satellite launch or Bhabha's birthday.
National Science Day is observed on 28 February, the day in 1928 when the Raman Effect was discovered.
Rabindranath Tagore was born in 1861, so the 150th birth anniversary was celebrated in 2011. The notes do not state this.
Homi J. Bhabha is called the Father of India's Atomic Energy/Nuclear Programme, so he is the right answer, not Dhawan, Raman or Bhatnagar.
Homi Bhabha was the first chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, set up in 1948, so he is the right answer.
Bardoli (1928) was led by Patel, not Gandhi; the Mehta brothers and Dayalji Desai began it and Patel led it.
Patel led the Bardoli Satyagraha, whereas the Dandi March was led by Gandhi, and Bijolia and the Ahmedabad strike are not Patel's campaigns in these notes.
The title 'Sardar' was conferred by the women of Bardoli in 1928 for his leadership in the Bardoli Satyagraha, not Kheda or Salt.
Bardoli was led by Patel, not Gandhi.
Patel is called the Iron Man of India for integrating about 565 princely states.
Patel held Home and Information & Broadcasting in the 1946 Interim Government, making him India's first I&B Minister.
The 182 m Statue of Unity was opened in October 2018; 2014 is when Ekta Diwas was announced.
The 182 m Statue of Unity was opened in October 2018; 2014 is when Ekta Diwas was announced.
Liquid nitrogen is a cryogenic liquid (below about -150°C), so it is used to store bull semen for artificial insemination; ice is not cold enough, and liquid oxygen is unsuitable.
Cryogenic engines use LOX (-183°C) as the oxidiser and LH2 (-253°C) as the fuel. Chlorine, fluorine and sulphur are not used.

Statement I is correct: India fully tested the cryogenic stage (full stage test 2006, GSLV-D5 with indigenous CE-7.5 in 2014). Statement II is wrong: India is the 6th country, after US, Russia, France, Japan and China, and not the only one after the three.
Cryogenic engines (LH2 + LOX) are used in rocket upper stages and the space shuttle, not in Boeing aircraft, rapid rail or nuclear reactors.
Statement I is correct: jet engines use atmospheric oxygen, so they cannot work in space. Statement II is wrong: a rocket carries its oxygen as a liquid (LOX) or solid oxidiser, not as a gas.
Monsoon rainfall is unsteady, uneven and variable with breaks, so 'equally distributed' is not a characteristic; the other options are genuine features.
Monsoon rainfall is unsteady, uneven and variable with breaks, so 'equally distributed' is not a characteristic; the other options are genuine features.
Climate is controlled by latitude (distance from equator), relief/physiography and the Himalayas among other factors, so all the listed factors influence it.
India's climate is described as tropical monsoon type, dominated by seasonal reversal of winds, so option 1 is correct.

Both statements are true: the Asian landmass's size creates the heating contrast, and upper-air circulation (jets, Tibetan anticyclone) is also involved, but R does not explain how the landmass drives the monsoon, so R is not the explanation of A.
Heat-wave season in north India runs from March to June, so option 4 is correct; the shorter periods omit part of it.

South India has a maritime climate with small diurnal and annual ranges and high temperatures all year, so extreme climatic conditions are not found there; extremes belong to the continental interior.
The anti-arrack agitation by rural women began at Dubagunta village in Nellore district (1992 in the notes). Renigunta, Domalamadugu and Rajupalem are not associated with it.
Bhu Poratam was a joint CPI–CPI(M) land-occupation campaign launched in Andhra Pradesh in 2007, so Andhra Pradesh is correct.
All India Service appointments are made by the President on the UPSC's recommendation. The UPSC only recommends, so option 3 is wrong.
Dismissal or removal of an AIS member lies only with the Union Government, even if the officer serves under a State. So option 1 is correct and the State-government option is wrong.
IPS is an All India Service, common to the Union and States, so it is not a Central Service. IFS and IRS are Central Services.
The existing All India Services are the IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service, so all three statements are correct.
BSE is Asia's oldest exchange (1875), its brokers are at Dalal Street, and its index is the SENSEX, so all statements are correct.
Dalal Street is where the Bombay (Mumbai) brokers moved in 1874 and where the BSE is located, so the answer is Mumbai.
BSE GREENEX includes 25 companies (20 at launch), so 25 is correct.
The SENSEX comprises 30 blue-chip companies listed on the BSE.
The BSE Sensex covers 30 blue-chip companies, so 30 is correct; 50 is the Nifty.
Order: Bombay Congress (1904), Partition of Bengal (1905), Muslim League (Dec 1906), Surat Split (Dec 1907), i.e. I, III, II, IV. The Bombay session is not in the notes but precedes 1905.
Partition of Bengal (1905), Surat Split (1907), capital shift to Delhi (1911), Home Rule League (1916): III, II, I, IV.
The Swadesh Bandhab Samiti was founded at Barisal by Ashwini Kumar Dutt. The other names are Bengal revolutionaries, not the founder of this Samiti.
H.W. Nevinson, a British journalist, covered the Swadeshi movement and the Surat Congress of 1907 and wrote about it in 'The New Spirit in India', so the answer is the Swadeshi Movement.
Sardar Patel headed the States Department (Ministry of States) and led the integration of the princely states; the other options had no such role.
Vijay Singh Pathik publicised the Bijolia peasant movement through the Kanpur newspaper Pratap (edited by Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi); Kesari and Maratha were Tilak's papers from Pune.

The Nawab of Junagadh announced accession to Pakistan in September 1947 although most of his people wanted India. Hyderabad's Nizam sought independence, and Bhopal delayed but did not accede to Pakistan.
The Dewan of Travancore was C.P. Ramaswami Iyer, who declared Travancore independent and ran an autocratic administration that the State Congress opposed.
Prince Akbar, Aurangzeb's son (called Akbar II in the option), joined the Rajputs in 1681, which weakened Aurangzeb's position against them. The other sons named did not rebel in this way.

The Jat revolt (Gokula, 1669) was a peasant revolt against heavy revenue, and the Satnami revolt (1672) was by peasants and artisans. So the Satnami and Jat revolts were rooted in agrarian distress, unlike the Rajput, Sikh or Maratha conflicts.
Jat leader Rajaram plundered Akbar's tomb at Sikandra in the 1680s. Gokula and Churaman are linked to other episodes.
The Satnami revolt took place in 1672 at Narnaul, during Aurangzeb's reign (1658-1707).
Aurangzeb spent his last 25-27 years campaigning in the Deccan, conquering Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687). Earlier emperors did not devote so much of their reign to this.

Under Aurangzeb the Mughal empire reached its greatest extent, after the conquest of Bijapur and Golconda and the pursuit of the Marathas to Jinji in the far south. Earlier emperors did not reach Tamil territory.
Bijapur fell to Aurangzeb in September 1686 after a long siege, so the answer is 1686.

Burning contaminated soil is thermal treatment (incineration), not a biological process, so it is not bioremediation. Bacterial oil clean-up, plants absorbing pollutants (phytoremediation) and composting are all bioremediation.

In-situ bioremediation treats the contaminated material at its original site without excavation. Ex-situ is the one that excavates and treats elsewhere, so the other options describe ex-situ or are wrong.
Using living organisms such as bacteria to break down organic waste and pollutants is bioremediation. Desalination, fossilisation and incineration are not biological clean-up processes.
Removing pollutants such as oil spills using micro-organisms is bioremediation. Biomagnification is the rise of toxins up the food chain, which is not a clean-up process.
Bioremediation is the removal of pollutants from the environment by biological processes using organisms or their enzymes. The other options describe biocontrol, transplantation and diagnosis.

Statements I and III are right: bioremediation uses natural biodegradation and engineered microbes can be used. Statement II is wrong because heavy metals complicate treatment and reliability varies with pollutant and site, so they cannot be readily and completely treated.
The National Planning Committee was set up in 1938 at the Haripura session under Bose's presidency, so 1938 is correct.
Although the NPC was set up under Bose's presidency, its chairman was Jawaharlal Nehru. The other options were not its chairman.
The 51st Haripura session in 1938 was presided over by Subhas Chandra Bose, not Nehru or the others.
At Haripura in 1938 the National Planning Committee was set up under Bose, introducing the idea of planning. It did not declare war or appoint Nehru as future PM.
Bose was Congress President in 1938, presiding over the Haripura session.
After Bose resigned in April 1939, Dr. Rajendra Prasad became Congress President. Pattabhi Sitaramayya was the candidate Bose defeated, not his successor.
The notes only say Bose defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya at Tripuri in 1939; they do not support a contest against Nehru.
Reliance Industries was the first Indian company to reach a market valuation of ₹10 lakh crore; the notes do not state this, so it rests on general knowledge. Jio and Airtel were not the first.
Bull and Bear are share-market terms: a bull expects prices to rise and a bear expects them to fall. They are not related to trade, banking or production.
A broker only executes trades for clients and is not a speculator, whereas Stags, Bulls and Bears are speculators. So the broker is the one that is not a speculator.
The notes do not cover ETFs. Option 3 is the incorrect statement because ETFs typically have high liquidity and low fees compared with mutual funds, and they trade throughout the day.
A bear expects prices to fall and sells to buy back lower. The option about an investor expecting a rise describes a bull.
SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) regulates stock exchanges and the primary and secondary securities markets. The other options are not real bodies.
SEBI regulates stock exchanges, brokers and depositories. SAIL, SIDBI and Stock Holding Corporation do not regulate stock exchange operations.
Goncha is the Bastar region's festival (the Rath Yatra of Bastar Dussehra tradition), so Bastar is correct; the notes do not state this.
Jaunsaris and Todas practise polyandry, so III and IV is correct; Gonds and Nagas are not noted for it.
Mundu is the traditional dress of Kerala, not Chhattisgarh, so this pair is wrong. Bokhu (Sikkim), Mekhla (Assam) and Pheran (Kashmir) are correct.
The 2013-14 PMO High-Level Committee on tribal socio-economic, health and educational status was chaired by Virginius Xaxa.
Shompen live in Great Nicobar, so they belong to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, not the mainland states listed.
Korwa (Pahadi Korwa) is a Particularly Vulnerable (primitive) Tribal Group, whereas Kawar, Kora and Karmali are not. The notes do not state this.
Baiga is the PVTG with the largest population in Chhattisgarh, compared with Abujhmadia, Kamar and Pahadi Korwa. The notes do not state this.

Tsunamis are caused by sudden vertical displacement of the ocean floor: undersea earthquakes, submarine landslides, volcanic eruptions. Hurricanes (cyclones) are not a cause; they produce storm surges instead.
Tsunamis are not tidal waves; tides come from the gravity of the Moon and Sun and play no role in generating them. So the statement about tides is the incorrect one.
The Pacific Ocean, ringed by subduction zones (the Ring of Fire), has the most undersea earthquakes and so the most tsunamis. The notes do not state this.
Operation Phuktal (2015) used controlled blasting by the Army and NDMA to drain a landslide lake on the Phuktal river in Zanskar, Kargil, preventing flash floods.
An avalanche (snow plus steep slope) is classed as a hydro-geological disaster, not purely geological or hydrological.
The Mana avalanche of 28 Feb 2025 hit a BRO labour camp near Mana village, about 4 km from Badrinath, so the cause was a snow avalanche.
The TAC for Landslide Mitigation was formed by the Ministry of Mines, which is the nodal ministry for landslides.
Landslide causes include unregulated construction, road building, deforestation and heavy rain. Increased forestation is not a cause; it stabilises slopes.
Landslide causes include unregulated construction, road building, deforestation and heavy rain. Increased forestation is not a cause; it stabilises slopes.
Flood forecasting is done by the CWC under Jal Shakti, not by IMD, so the Floods–IMD pairing is incorrect.
The Bhopal gas tragedy was caused by methyl isocyanate (MIC) leaking from the Union Carbide plant.
The Bhopal gas tragedy was caused by methyl isocyanate (MIC) leaking from the Union Carbide plant.
The Bhopal plant was a Union Carbide pesticide plant, and MIC was used in making pesticides.
The money market is the short-term market for loans and funds (up to 1 year), so loans of money are obtained there, whereas the capital market deals in long-term debt and equity.
Finance companies that are unregulated belong to the unorganised money market, whereas money market mutual funds are organised. CDs and T-bills are money market instruments controlled by RBI.
The call money market is repayable on demand and is the most unstable (volatile) part of the organised money market.
The organised money market comprises RBI, commercial banks, DFHI, mutual funds and similar bodies. SEBI is the capital market regulator and is not a participant in the organised money market.
Treasury bills are issued by the Centre in three tenors: 91, 182 and 364 days. The 14-day option is wrong because that relates to notice money.
The gilt-edged market is the market for government securities such as Treasury Bills and government bonds, with almost zero default risk. It is not corporate paper or bank CDs.
Gilt-edged securities are government securities (Treasury Bills and government bonds), as repayment and interest are sure. Company shares and mutual fund stocks are not gilt-edged.
The NeGP approved in 2006 listed 27 MMPs (9 Central, 11 State, 7 Integrated); 31 and 44 are later expansions (NeGP expanded, e-Kranti).
e-Courts is an integrated MMP for judiciary ICT under implementation since 2007, so 2007 is correct.
The notes give about 11,079 MeeSeva centres and authorised agents in January 2023, so option 3 is correct.
APAAR stands for Automated Permanent Academic Account Registry, launched in Feb 2024 through CSCs; the other options alter words like 'Permanent' or 'Account'.
Aaykar Setu is the Income Tax Department's mobile app for tax payment and tax-related services. The notes do not cover it.
Bharti Airtel runs the DIKSHA app and website end to end; DIKSHA belongs to NCERT/Ministry of Education, so the other telecom/companies are wrong.
MeeSeva, launched in 2011 in undivided AP, is the single-window service delivery platform. Amma Vodi, Rythu Bandhu and Navaratnalu are welfare schemes, not e-governance platforms.
Khajane is Karnataka's computerised treasury system, not land records; Bhoomi handles land records. So statement 1 is incorrect.
e-Pramaan is the National e-Authentication framework built under MeitY (then DeitY) by C-DAC. DigiLocker is a document locker, not the e-authentication service.
Sri Gupta was the founder of the Gupta dynasty; Chandragupta I is only the real founder of the empire, which makes option 2 tempting but wrong.
The Gupta Era (319-320 CE) was started by Chandragupta I, marking his accession. Later rulers like Chandragupta II did not found it.
The Prayag (Allahabad) Prashasti was composed by Harisena and records the achievements and conquests of Samudragupta, not the other Gupta kings.

The Allahabad Pillar carries Harisena's prashasti glorifying Samudragupta. Ashoka's edicts are also on it, but the Gupta eulogy is the inscription associated with Samudragupta, and the Mauryas and Nandas are not linked to it.
Samudragupta, called the Napoleon of India by V.A. Smith, has his conquests recorded on the Allahabad Pillar, not the Mehrauli Iron Pillar, which is of Chandragupta II.

Ujjain became Chandragupta II's second capital after his conquest of the Western Kshatrapas, while Pataliputra remained the first capital. Malwa and Saurashtra are regions, and Mehrauli is a pillar site.
Chandragupta II issued silver coins modelled on Saka coins after defeating the Western Kshatrapas. Chandragupta I and Samudragupta issued gold coins, so they are not the first to issue silver.
The notes record that on 28 June 2023 Canara Bank signed an MoU with the Ministry of Culture for veteran artists, so Canara Bank is correct.
Punjab National Bank won the Scotch Challenger Award in 2008, as noted; the other banks listed are not linked to it.

Chronic drug and alcohol use damages the liver (cirrhosis) and the nervous system. Leukaemias and lymphomas are cancers not typically caused this way, and the other options do not describe the characteristic effects.
Asia is the largest continent, with about 44.57 million sq km, or 29.8% of the world's land. 'America' is not a single continent in this list.
Asia's area is about 44,568,500 sq km, i.e. roughly 44 million sq km, so option 4 is correct.
Dakshin Gangotri was India's first Antarctic research station, set up in 1983-84 on the Antarctic ice shelf. It is not in Uttarakhand, the Himalayas or the Arctic.
By share of land, Africa (20.3%) > North America (16.2%) > South America (11.8%) > Europe (6.8%). That matches option 2. The other options put North America first or leave out South America.
Africa is called the 'Cradle of Mankind' because the earliest human fossils and ancestors have been found there, for example in East Africa and South Africa.
Asia is the largest continent by area (44.57 million sq km, 29.8% of land) and also the most populous.
The RBI sets the repo rate (through its six-member MPC); the other bodies listed have no role in it.
Bank Rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to or rediscounts bills of commercial banks, so it is the rate charged by the RBI on its loans.
The RBI is the custodian of forex and manages the forex reserves under FEMA 1999, so it maintains them, not SBI, the Finance Ministry or EXIM Bank.
The RBI controls credit creation by commercial banks through qualitative and quantitative measures. The banks themselves create the credit.
Monetary policy belongs to the RBI (the MPC since 2016), while fiscal policy belongs to the Ministry of Finance.
The repo rate is set and announced by the RBI through its MPC, not by the Government, the PM or the President.
The RBI, through its MPC, sets the repo rate. The CAG, the Finance Ministry and SBI do not.
Credit creation is done by commercial banks. The RBI only controls credit, so credit creation is not an RBI function.
The RBI is called the Banker's Bank because it holds the reserves of scheduled commercial banks and acts as their lender of last resort.
The RBI sets the repo rate, lends to commercial banks as lender of last resort and acts as banker to the Government, so all three are central bank functions.
The Reserve Bank of India is the central bank of India. The other banks listed are commercial banks.
Under the RBI Act, Section 26(2) gives the power of demonetisation, i.e. withdrawing notes as legal tender.

MILAN is the Indian Navy's multilateral exercise held at Visakhapatnam, which hosted MILAN 2020 (planned) and was the venue in other years. The notes do not state the 2020 venue, so Port Blair (the 1995 host) is the tempting but wrong option.
The first trilateral India-Singapore-Thailand naval exercise (SITMEX) was held at Port Blair in the Andaman Sea in 2019. The notes do not state this directly.

India signed the agreement in 2016 to develop Chabahar port in Iran (Sistan-Baluchestan), giving access to Afghanistan and Central Asia bypassing Pakistan. Gwadar and Hambantota are Chinese-linked String of Pearls ports, not India's.

India backs Chabahar because it gives access to Afghanistan and Central Asia bypassing Pakistan. US sanctions are the main issue for the port, and India's not subscribing to unilateral Western sanctions on Iran explains why it continues to support it, so R explains A.
Shankaracharya wrote commentaries (bhashyas) on the Prasthanatrayi: the Upanishads, Brahma Sutras and Bhagavad Gita. He did not comment on the Rigveda, a Samhita.
The word gotra first occurs in the Rigveda, where it means a cow shelter or herd of cows.
The Rigveda is the oldest Veda, while the Atharvaveda is the latest.
The Yajurveda's Brahmanas are the Taittiriya and Shatapatha. Gopatha belongs to the Atharvaveda, Panchavimsha and Jaiminiya to the Samaveda, and Aitareya and Kaushitaki to the Rigveda.
The Hotri priest is associated with the Rigveda, as Hotri-Udgatri-Adhvaryu-Brahman correspond to Rig-Sama-Yajur-Atharva.
The Gayatri Mantra is in the Rigveda, Mandala III, attributed to Vishvamitra.
The Purusha Sukta, describing the four varnas, is in Mandala X of the Rigveda.
The Rigveda is a collection of hymns, i.e. prayers to nature deities.
Phoenix was the NASA Mars lander (2008) that studied water ice near the Martian north pole; the other options are not Mars spacecraft names.

Statement I is correct: the first steel-slag road on a National Highway is on NH-66 (Mumbai-Goa). Statement II is wrong because the technology was by CSIR-CRRI, not IGBC. Statement III is not supported, so only I is correct.
Google's Bengaluru tech campus launched in February 2025 is called Ananta, so option 2 is correct.

The notes do not state the sign-language telecast fact. Punjab is the correct pair as given. The other pairs are wrong: Skyroot is known for the private orbital rocket Vikram-1, not a satellite constellation.
Cameroon (Jan 2024) was the first country to add a malaria vaccine (RTS,S) to routine child immunisation, so option 3 is correct.
HLL Lifecare Limited is the nodal agency for sourcing the Aarogya Maitri Cubes under Project BHISHM.
A normal human body (somatic) cell has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); 43-45 are not normal counts.
The medulla oblongata in the hindbrain houses reflex centres for swallowing, vomiting, breathing and heart rate; the cerebellum handles balance and the pons relays signals.
The brain (medulla) controls heartbeat and the cerebellum maintains body balance, so both statements are correct.

Acquired immunity is cell-mediated (and humoral), starts with a low-intensity primary response, and includes active and passive types. Polymorphonuclear leucocytes and NK cells belong to innate immunity, so IV is wrong.
Light enters the eye through the transparent cornea, which is the thin outer membrane; the pupil is only the opening and the iris controls its size.
Light enters the eye through the transparent cornea, which is the thin outer membrane; the pupil is only the opening and the iris controls its size.
Blood pressure is measured in mmHg, where Hg is the symbol of mercury used in the sphygmomanometer.
Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles, so glycogen is the storage form.
Gonads secrete progesterone (A-2), the pituitary secretes growth hormone (B-3), the pancreas secretes insulin (C-1) and the adrenal secretes cortisol (D-4), giving 2 3 1 4.
Normal blood pressure of a healthy adult is 120/80 mmHg (systolic/diastolic).
A healthy adult passes about 1.5 litres of urine per day.
The hypothalamus is the body's thermoregulatory centre, controlling body temperature.
Cowper's (bulbourethral) gland is part of the male reproductive system, not the intestine, so that pair is wrongly matched.
Blood sugar is regulated by insulin and glucagon from the pancreas, not by the kidney; the kidney regulates water, filters urea and secretes hormones like erythropoietin.

Statement 1 is wrong because clean blood returns via the renal vein, not the renal artery. Statement 2 is correct: filtrate from Bowman's capsule passes through tubules where glucose is reabsorbed into the blood.
Humans are homeothermic; body temperature stays about constant (37 °C) regardless of season.
The liver is the main detoxifying organ and metabolises alcohol.
Low blood oxygen is sensed by chemoreceptors, which stimulate the respiratory centre to raise the breathing rate.
The masseter muscle of the jaw is regarded as the strongest muscle in the human body for its size and bite force.
Patta (title deed) and qabuliyat (deed of acceptance) were introduced by Sher Shah as part of his land revenue settlement, not by Shivaji, Jahangir or Aurangzeb.
Sher Shah introduced the patta and qabuliyat as instruments of direct state-peasant settlement; the other rulers listed did not.
Sher Shah Suri restored/built the Sadak-e-Azam (Grand Trunk Road) running between the Indus and Sonargaon in Bengal.
The silver Rupiya (about 178 grains) was introduced by Sher Shah Suri in 1540-45 and remained a standard for centuries.
The rupiya, a silver coin, began with Sher Shah Suri, not with Tughluq, Alauddin Khalji or Akbar.
Islam Shah (Jalal Khan), Sher Shah's second son, succeeded him and ruled 1545-53; the other names are not his successor.
Rajkumar Shukla, not Rajendra Prasad, persuaded Gandhi to come to Champaran, so I is wrong. J.B. Kripalani accompanied Gandhi there, so II is correct.

The Champaran struggle was against forced indigo cultivation and illegal exactions by European planters, on behalf of the tenant cultivators. So I is correct. II is wrong because the planters oppressed the tenants, not the zamindars.
Champaran was launched to solve the problems of indigo workers, so II is correct. It was a localised movement; Gandhi's first all-India venture was the Rowlatt Satyagraha, so I is wrong.
Ram Manohar Lohia is not connected with Champaran. Kripalani, Rajkumar Shukla and Rajendra Prasad were all involved.
The Ahmedabad mill owners withdrew the plague bonus, which triggered the dispute and the strike.
The Ahmedabad struggle involved mill workers, i.e. industrial labour, unlike the peasant movements of Champaran and Kheda.

The dispute was over the plague bonus and wages, not hours of work, and the mill owners were led by Ambalal Sarabhai, an Indian, not European owners. So I is wrong. Gandhi did advise the workers on the strike, so II is correct.
The Ahmedabad Mill Strike involved mill workers, i.e. the industrial working class. Champaran and Kheda were peasant struggles.
The Ahmedabad Satyagraha was the struggle of mill workers, i.e. industrial labour. Champaran and Kheda concerned peasants.
Kheda was called off when the government agreed to collect revenue only from those able to pay, suspend it for poor peasants and return confiscated property.
The Kheda grievance was crop failure with the government refusing to remit or suspend land revenue, so I is correct. Nothing in the notes mentions a permanent settlement proposal, so II is wrong.
Dyer blocked the only exit and fired without warning for about 10 minutes on the crowd gathered in the garden, and he was the officer who ordered the firing. So I, II and III are all correct.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq began state-backed canal irrigation and levied the irrigation cess haq-i-sharb (one-tenth of produce). The other Sultans listed did not levy it.
Firoz Tughlaq began state-backed canal irrigation and charged haq-i-sharb, an irrigation cess of one-tenth of the produce, so he is the answer.
Dar-ul-Shifa (Dar-ul-Shafa) was Firoz Shah's free hospital, so a free hospital is correct, not an almshouse or library.
The employment bureau is traditionally credited to Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who took welfare measures for the jobless. The notes do not state this directly.
Jaunpur was founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq in memory of his cousin Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Jauna Khan), so the answer names Jauna Khan. The notes only list Jaunpur among Firoz's towns.
Fatehabad was one of the towns founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who named it after his son Fateh Khan. The other rulers did not found it.
Dar-ul-Shifa (Dar-ul-Shafa) was Firoz Shah's free hospital, so a free hospital is correct.
The Public Works Department is credited to Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who built canals, towns and buildings. Iltutmish, Balban and Alauddin are known for other measures.
Firoz Shah set up the Diwan-i-Bandagan, a separate department for slaves, so option 4 is correct. Dagh (horse branding) was Alauddin's, not Balban's.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq set up the Public Works Department, which handled canals, towns and buildings. The other Sultans are not linked to it.
The Wildlife Protection Act came in 1972, Project Tiger in 1973, Project Elephant in 1992 and the Biological Diversity Act in 2002, giving III, I, II, IV.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973, with Corbett as the first reserve.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973 to conserve tigers through a network of reserves, i.e. to save the tiger from extinction. Option 3 is the aim; the others are only partial or incidental activities.
The pugmark method was the traditional way of estimating tiger numbers from footprints, which is population estimation of wild animals. It has been replaced by camera trapping.
Project Elephant was launched in February 1992, not 1990, so statement 4 is incorrect.
The Ganges River Dolphin was declared India's National Aquatic Animal in 2009, so River Dolphin is correct.
Dolphins are cetaceans, which are warm-blooded, air-breathing mammals that suckle their young, not fish, amphibians or reptiles.
The National Dolphin Research Centre is at Patna. Bhagalpur is the site of the Vikramshila Dolphin Sanctuary, which is the tempting wrong option.
The notes give the Lorenz curve as developed by Max O. Lorenz in 1905.
The Gini coefficient measures inequality, running from 0 (perfect equality) to 1. It is therefore tied to income inequality, not inflation, a poverty index or personal income.
NSSO/NSO measure household inequality through MPCE, which is consumption expenditure, not income or wealth.
Adam Smith wrote The Wealth of Nations (1776). The other titles are by different authors.
Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by elected MLAs through proportional representation with the single transferable vote (Art 80(4)), so option 2 is correct.
The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha for special knowledge in literature, science, art and social service.
Chhattisgarh has 5 Rajya Sabha seats, so option 2 is correct. The notes do not give this figure.
Maharashtra has 19 Rajya Sabha seats, second only to Uttar Pradesh's 31.
Uttar Pradesh has the most Rajya Sabha seats, 31, so option 3 is correct.

After UP's 80, Maharashtra has 48 Lok Sabha seats. Among the options, Andhra Pradesh's 25 is the highest in the pair, so option 1 is the best choice, though the notes' table does not list Bihar, West Bengal or Karnataka.
Meghalaya has two Lok Sabha seats, whereas Nagaland, Sikkim and Mizoram have one each.
Maharashtra has 48 Lok Sabha seats, second only to Uttar Pradesh's 80. Tamil Nadu has 39.

NAPCC, launched on 30 June 2008, has 8 missions (Solar, Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge), so 8 is correct.
The Jharkhand State Action Plan on Climate Change was published in 2013, so option (1) is correct.

Market loans (G-Secs) are internal marketable debt of the Centre. Small savings, deposits and provident funds and reserve funds are other liabilities in the Public Account, and foreign borrowings are external debt.
Most external debt is non-sovereign (companies, banks), so statement I is wrong. Only about 54.8% is in US dollars, with rupee, yen and others making up the rest, so statement II is wrong too.

Statement I is right: the FRBM Review Committee recommended a general government debt of 60%, split 40% Centre and 20% States. Statement III follows the Art. 293 borrowing restrictions on States, which require Centre's consent where liabilities are outstanding. Statement II is not supported by the notes and is incorrect on the figures.

Non-financial debt is the debt of households and non-financial sectors, such as housing loans and credit card dues. Treasury bills are also counted here under the question's classification, so all three are included.

Madhya Pradesh is called the 'Ethiopia of India' because of its very high malnutrition; the notes record it with the highest share of malnourished children (about 60%, MoSPI 2011) and the highest underweight burden.
ICDS was launched on 2 October 1975, so 1975 is correct.
ICDS is run by the Ministry of Women and Child Development, which is the option closest to 'Women and Child Welfare'; Education and Finance do not run it.
ICDS covers supplementary nutrition, immunisation and nutrition and health education, but not family planning.
The Mid-Day Meal scheme was renamed PM POSHAN in 2021.
NP-NSPE (the Mid-Day Meal scheme) began on 15 August 1995.

Mission Investigation@75 Days was launched by Bihar Police (from 1 Jan 2024), requiring investigation and charge-sheet within 75 days of the FIR. Gujarat, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh are not associated with it.

The Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework (2014) was headed by Urjit Patel. Vaghul and Tarapore headed other committees (money market, capital account convertibility).
The Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee (1985) reviewed the working of the monetary system and recommended monetary targeting with feedback.
The RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016 inserted Sections 45Z-45ZO into the RBI Act, 1934, giving statutory backing to FIT and the MPC. The other Acts were not amended for this.
The RBI Act, 1934 was amended in May 2016 (RBI Amendment Act, 2016) to give statutory backing to flexible inflation targeting.
The inflation target is fixed by the Government of India in consultation with the RBI, not by the RBI or the MPC alone. The 4% target (with a 2% band) was notified for 2016-2021.
The target notified in August 2016 for the period up to 31 March 2021 was 4% CPI inflation (with a band of ±2%).
Only statement I is correct: the MPC fixes the policy repo rate. It has 6 members, not 12, and is chaired by the RBI Governor, not the Finance Minister.
The MPC fixes the policy repo rate, and its decisions are binding on the RBI. The Finance Ministry and SBI have no such role.
RTI is a legal right created by the RTI Act, 2005 (it is also read into Art. 19(1)(a)); among the options given, 'legal right' is the one that fits, not a political or social right.
Right to property was deleted from Part III by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now only a legal right under Art. 300A, so it is not a fundamental right. The others remain fundamental rights.
After the 44th Amendment (1978), property is a legal (constitutional) right under Art. 300A, not a fundamental right.
Since the 44th Amendment, property is a legal (constitutional) right under Art. 300A, not a fundamental right or a DPSP.
The right to property is the only fundamental right ever deleted; the 44th Amendment (1978) removed it from Part III and placed it in Art. 300A.

The lockdown rested on the Disaster Management Act 2005 (ordered by NDMA and MHA under it) and the Epidemic Diseases Act 1897, the legal framework used in COVID-19. The Mental Health Care Act and Enemy Property Act are unrelated.
GIS network analysis finds locations and the fastest routes to hospitals and fire stations in disasters like earthquakes. Real-time spatial mapping is instead the tool for vaccine distribution.
GIS real-time spatial mapping is the tool best suited to vaccine distribution in biological disasters such as COVID-19.

Geospatial technology supports contact tracing of exposed people and hotspot mapping, so statement I is correct. Administering medicines and performing surgery is not a geospatial function, so statement II is wrong.

Both statements are true: eruptions are commonly accompanied by earthquakes, and volcanoes emit water vapour (the commonest gas) and ash. But the emission of vapour and dust does not explain why earthquakes accompany eruptions, so II is not the explanation of I.

The Himalayas were formed by continental collision (Indian and Eurasian plates), not by subduction or hotspot volcanism, so they have no extrusive volcanoes. Alaska, the Rockies and the Andes are tied to the volcanic Pacific belt.
Cotopaxi is an active stratovolcano in the Andes of Ecuador, so Ecuador is correct. South America is a continent, not a country.
Barren Island is India's only active volcano. Narcondam is dormant and Dhinodhar is extinct.
Baratang in Middle Andaman has the mud volcanoes. Barren Island is a magmatic active volcano, not a mud volcano.
Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is a volcano, India's only active one, so it is of volcanic origin.

Infiltration is entry of water at the surface, percolation is movement down through the soil column, permeability is ease of movement, and saturated flow is when all pores are full. This gives I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B.
A soil profile is the vertical arrangement of horizons from the surface down (O, A, B, C) to the bedrock. Option 2 describes a single horizon, not the whole profile.
Zinc is the micronutrient most widely deficient in Indian soils, more than copper, iron or manganese.
Maharashtra has the large Deccan Trap black cotton tracts, so it has the largest area of regur soil. Assam, Bihar and Punjab are not black soil regions.
Alluvial soil is the most widespread in India, covering about 45.6% of the area, more than laterite, red or black soils.
Laterite soil is poor in nitrogen and is not mainly in Rajasthan or UP, so II and III are wrong. Tapioca and cashew grow well on it, and it is generally reddish, so I and IV are correct.
The Gangani region of West Bengal has laterite soil, which is the western upland of Bengal with laterite cover. Alluvial, saline and terai soils are not typical of it.

Red soil is found across Peninsular India, and it covers about 60% of the cultivated area in Andhra Pradesh. Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh are therefore correct, while Punjab and Haryana have alluvial soils.

Air masses form over uniform source regions (land or ocean) and are associated with anticyclonic high-pressure areas such as the Siberian and Canadian Highs, not with cyclonic conditions. So the statement that they develop in a cyclonic condition is false.

Maritime Equatorial (mE) air originates over equatorial oceans and is hot and very humid. The other pairs mismatch the source: mP forms over polar oceans, cT over hot deserts, and cP over cold continental land.
Under Article 219, a High Court judge takes the oath of office before the Governor (or a person appointed by him), not the President or the Chief Justice.
Under Article 222 the President transfers High Court judges from one High Court to another after consulting the CJI; the CJI or collegium only advises, and the Law Minister has no such power.
Leila Seth was the first woman Chief Justice of a High Court (Himachal Pradesh, 1991). The notes do not cover this fact.
High Court judges retire at 62 (15th Amendment, 1963); 65 is the Supreme Court age, and they do not serve at anyone's pleasure.
The Uttarakhand High Court declared the entire animal kingdom to be legal entities with the rights and duties of a living person.
The World Competitiveness Ranking is published by IMD (Institute for Management Development), Lausanne. WEF publishes the Global Competitiveness Report, which is the tempting wrong option.
The Rule of Law Index is published by the World Justice Project (WJP), so option 4 is correct.
India ranked 38th of 139 countries in the World Bank's LPI 2023, up from 44th in 2018.
India was 38th in the World Bank LPI 2023 (up from 44th in 2018), so 38 is correct.
The notes do not cover the Foundational Literacy and Numeracy index. West Bengal is the keyed answer, as the top larger state in primary education in that index.
The Aihole inscription, composed by Ravikirti for Pulakeshin II, records that Harsha was stopped at the Narmada. The Allahabad Pillar concerns Samudragupta.
Prakrit was the language of the earliest stone inscriptions (Ashokan edicts). Brahmi is a script, not a language, and is the tempting wrong option.
Prakrit was the language of the earliest stone inscriptions, the Ashokan edicts. Brahmi is the script, not the language.
James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837 from Ashokan inscriptions, which made the edicts readable.
James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837 using Ashokan inscriptions. Cunningham is known as the first Director General of the ASI.
The Kushanas are noted for large gold issues, so they issued gold coins regularly. The Satavahanas used lead, copper, bronze and potin, not gold.
Satavahana coins were of lead, copper, bronze and potin, so Satavahanas – Gold is the wrongly matched pair.
The usual sequence is urban culture (Harappan), then the iron plough, then punch-marked silver coins, then gold coins (Indo-Greek, Kushana and Gupta). So the order is IV, III, II, I.
Megasthenes, the Greek envoy at Chandragupta Maurya's court, wrote Indica.
The order is Megasthenes (4th c. BCE), Fa-Hien (Chandragupta II), Hiuen Tsang (Harsha, 7th c.), then I-Tsing (671–695 CE), which gives III, I, IV, II.
The CAG audits receipts and expenditure of the Consolidated Fund and also stores and stocks, so both statements are correct.
Article 149 deals with the duties and powers of the CAG; Art. 148 covers appointment, oath, term and removal.
The CAG does not control the entire financial system; he is only an auditor with no control over issue of money. The term (6 years or 65) and salary (equal to SC judge) statements are correct.
The CAG is described as the friend, philosopher and guide of the Public Accounts Committee, attending its meetings; not of the Estimates Committee or COPU.
CAG reports on Union accounts go first to the President (Art. 151(1)), who has them laid before Parliament; they do not go directly to the PAC or the Speaker.
Union audit reports are submitted to the President (Art. 151(1)), not to the CJI, PM or Vice President, so 'None of the above' is correct.
The notes state WED 2022 had the theme "Only One Earth"; the other options are themes of other years or not the 2022 theme.
The notes do not state when India set up the National Committee on Environment Planning and Coordination, so no line can be linked.
World Environment Day is observed on 5 June, the date the Stockholm Conference opened in 1972, so option 4 is correct.
The notes do not cover the International Nitrogen Initiative, so no line can be linked.
Rio+5 (Earth Summit +5) was held in 1997 as a UNGA special session in New York that reviewed Agenda 21.
UNEA-4 was held 11-15 March 2019 in Nairobi, Kenya, so option 4 is correct.
The notes do not mention the MIDORI Prize or Komal Bawa, so no line can be linked.
The notes state the World Wetlands Day 2017 theme was Wetlands for Disaster Risk Reduction.
Kolleru Lake is AP's only Ramsar site. Loktak is in Manipur and Chilika is in Odisha.
The Ramsar Convention (1971) is the Convention on Wetlands, so it deals with wetland conservation.
The notes do not describe Wetlands International, so no line can be linked.
CITES is the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species and regulates trade in them. CMS covers migratory species and WHC is the World Heritage Convention.
Masulipatnam under the Golconda (Qutb Shahi) kingdom was famous in the 1600s for textile and diamond trade, so diamonds is the precious material; silver, gold and platinum are not mentioned.
Motupalli (Desiyakondapattanam) was the most important Kakatiya port; Machilipatnam was the Qutb Shahi port, so it is the tempting wrong option.
The first English factory in South India was set up at Masulipatam in 1611. Vizagapatnam's English factory came much later, in 1682.
Rio+20 (2012) was the UN Conference on Sustainable Development (UNCSD), not a WTO, IPCC or CBD meeting.
The Rio+20 (2012) outcome document was 'The Future We Want'.
The 2030 Agenda adopted in 2015 contains 17 SDGs (169 targets, 232 indicators).
Agenda 2030 dimensions are economic, social and environmental; military, political, technological or cultural dimensions are not among them.
Andhra Pradesh adopted all 17 SDGs and identified 212 indicators to monitor progress to 2030.
The 2030 Agenda adopted in 2015 has 17 SDGs.
Sustainable development covers meeting present needs without harming future generations, and environmental conservation. Climatic changes over time are a natural phenomenon, not part of the concept.
The 2030 Agenda comprises 17 SDGs, with 169 targets.
SD balances economic growth, environmental protection and social equity. Growth with no concern for the environment, or conservation over all else, is not the goal.
The UN's three pillars are economic growth, environmental protection and social equity; the other options are not pillars.

The assertion is false, since economic sustainability does not mean maximising profits while ignoring social and environmental factors. The reason is true because SD balances economic, social and environmental concerns.
Natural capital is made up of resources created by nature such as air, water, land, minerals and forests. Roads are man-made, so they are not natural capital.
Ecological footprint is the productive land and sea needed to meet a person's consumption and absorb wastes. Biota, biome and niche are not measures of area required to sustain a person.

Statement I (President taking over State administration under emergency/Art. 356) is a unitary override of State powers, so it violates federal principles. Statement II is listed in the notes as a unitary feature but is not violative in the intended key, and III (three-list division of powers) is a federal feature. Hence II and III are not violative.
Local government, including panchayats and municipalities, is State List Entry 5, so Panchayati Raj is a State subject.
The Seventh Schedule contains the three Lists (Union, State, Concurrent) that divide powers between the Union and the States.
The Seventh Schedule with its three Lists distributes legislative powers between the Centre and States; the other schedules deal with different subjects.
Panchayats fall under local government, State List Entry 5, so the State List is correct.
Article 248 in Part XI (Chapter I) gives Parliament exclusive power over matters not in any List (residuary powers), so Part XI is correct.
Residuary powers are the matters enumerated in none of the lists, over which Parliament has exclusive power under Art. 248 and Entry 97 of List I.
The 42nd Amendment moved administration of justice (courts other than the SC and HCs) from the State List to the Concurrent List.
Advection is horizontal transfer, convection is vertical, insolation heats directly, and conduction heats the lower air layers in contact with the ground. This gives a-I, b-II, c-III, d-IV.
The troposphere is heated from below by long-wave radiation re-emitted by the earth's surface, not directly by the sun or by heat generated within it.
Wind on a hot day arises from convection: warm air rises, and cooler air flows in to replace it. Conduction only heats the thin layer of air touching the ground.
Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium, whereas conduction and convection need matter (solid or fluid) to carry heat.
Equatorial regions get direct rays and nearly constant day length all year, so their insolation varies least. Polar and high-latitude areas have large seasonal swings.
Insolation depends mainly on the angle of the sun's rays, which is set by latitude: it is highest where rays are direct and falls toward the poles.
Polar zones have the greatest seasonal contrast in insolation, with months of continuous daylight in summer and none in winter, whereas the equator is nearly constant.
Solar radiation is mostly visible light plus short-wavelength (near) infrared. Long-wave infrared is what the earth re-emits, not what comes from the sun.
The share of incoming radiation reflected back to space is the albedo; for the earth as a whole this is the planetary albedo, about 35 units of 100 (roughly 30%).
The earth receives sun's energy mostly as short-wave radiation (visible light) and re-radiates it as long-wave infrared, not ultraviolet. So both statements are wrong.
Without the atmosphere's greenhouse effect the earth's average temperature would be about -18°C instead of +15°C.
A nautical mile is defined internationally as exactly 1,852 metres, so option 2 is correct. The notes do not cover this fact.

The slope has canyons and trenches (b-I), and the deeps have volcanoes and earthquakes (d-II). The shelf is matched with sedimentary deposits (a-III) and the deep sea plain with fine-grained sediments (c-IV), which gives option 3.
The shelf is a submerged prolongation of land reaching about 200 m, which is roughly 100 fathoms (1 fathom = 6 ft), so I and II are correct. The notes do not support III or IV, so option 2 is right.
The Mariana Trench is in the Pacific, near the Northern Mariana Islands in the western Pacific, so option 2 is correct. The Atlantic options are wrong because it is a Pacific trench.
Bhimbetka is the rock shelter with the most paintings in India; Ghagharia, Lekhahia and Adamgarh are not noted for this.
Bhimbetka was discovered in 1957 by Dr. Vishnu S. Wakankar; Sankalia is linked to other work (rice in Andhra).
Bhimbetka is famous for prehistoric (Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic) rock paintings, unlike the others listed.
V. S. Wakankar discovered Bhimbetka in 1957 and recognised its rock art; the other archaeologists are not credited with it.
Graves with weapons, tools and pottery circled by big stones are megaliths (mega = large, lith = stone), not microliths or chalcoliths.
Burzahom in Kashmir is known for the dog buried with its master; Koldihwa is known for early rice.
Burzahom (Kashmir) is known for pit dwellings; Koldihwa is known for early rice, and Brahmagiri and Sanganakallu are not noted for pit dwellings.
Mehrgarh in Baluchistan has the earliest wheat and barley farming; Koldihwa's rice is later and Burzahom is known for pit dwellings.
Burzahom is known for a dog buried with its master; Chirand is known for bone and antler tools.

In a test tube baby (IVF), the egg is fertilised outside the body in a test tube and the embryo is then implanted in the uterus to develop. So option 2 is right; option 1 is wrong because development does not occur in the test tube.
Stem cells divide, self-renew and can become many cell types, so they can develop into any type of cell. Endodermal, ectodermal and muscle cells are already specialised.
Haemophilia is an inherited, sex-linked bleeding disorder. Cataract, pellagra (vitamin deficiency) and osteoporosis are not classic hereditary diseases.

RNAi works by small RNAs (like microRNA) silencing target genes after transcription, which supports gene-silencing therapies, cancer therapies and virus-resistant crops. It is not used for hormone replacement therapy, so statement III is wrong.
Royal haemophilia is an X-linked (sex-linked) recessive disorder. Tay-Sachs and cystic fibrosis are autosomal, and hypertension is not a single-gene sex-linked disease.
Haemophilia is an inherited genetic defect of blood clotting, not an infection caused by bacteria or viruses or by pollutants.
Vinegar is a dilute aqueous solution of acetic acid, produced by Acetobacter fermentation.
Sour milk products such as curd contain lactic acid, formed by bacterial fermentation of lactose.
Vinegar is chemically acetic acid (CH3COOH), made by Acetobacter.
Vinegar is acetic acid, produced by Acetobacter. It is not an alcohol such as methanol or ethanol.
Yeast and mushrooms are fungi because they lack chlorophyll. They are not algae, gymnosperms or roots.
Curd is formed when Lactobacillus bacteria convert lactose into lactic acid, souring and setting the milk. Vitamins and enzymes alone do not do this.

Mughal painting reached its zenith (golden period) under Jahangir, with naturalism, portraits and albums. Akbar's period built the atelier and Shah Jahan's was formal and gold-heavy, so they are not the peak.
Mughal painting covered battle scenes (Hamzanama), animals, birds and nature (Jahangir's studies), and formal court scenes (Shah Jahan), so all the options are true.

Akbar's period was dominated by illustrated manuscripts such as the Hamzanama and Akbarnama, with portraits too, so I is correct. The Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad founded the Mughal school (Persian fused with Indian), so II is correct.
European pictures reached Akbar's court through the Portuguese (Jesuit mission of 1580), so Akbar is the answer. Jahangir only later patronised European art further.
Humayun brought the Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad, who founded the Mughal school. Akbar expanded it but did not lay the foundation.
Humayun brought the Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad, who founded the Mughal school. Akbar expanded it but did not lay the foundation.
Ustad Mansur of Jahangir's court was the greatest painter of birds, animals and plants. Basawan belongs to Akbar, and the Persian masters Abdus Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali served Humayun and Akbar.
Ustad Mansur received the title Nadir-ul-Asr (Nadir-ul-Asra) from Jahangir. Abul Hasan got Nadir-uz-Zaman, while Bishandas and Manohar were portraitists.
Satyadoota (1835), started by Christian missionaries at Bellary, was the first Telugu paper. The other options (Desabhimani, Tattvabodhini, Andhra Patrika) were started later and elsewhere.
The English daily Swarajya, published from Madras, was started by Tanguturi Prakasam. Konda Venkatappayya is linked with Krishna Patrika, and the Telugu Swarajya belonged to Gadicherla.
Veeresalingam's journals include Satyasamvardhini (1891). Hitabodhini and Zanana are inexact names for his Sati Hitabodhini and Zenana Patrika, and Sanjivani is not among his journals.
Desabhimani argued that Telugu culture needs its own government, so it is the paper that made this remark.
Denmark, in financial difficulty, sold Serampore and Tranquebar to the British (English) in 1845, ending the Danish presence in India. The Portuguese, French and Dutch were not the buyers.

Article 51 directs the State to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration, so all three statements are correct.

Panchsheel comprises territorial integrity and sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful co-existence. Non-alignment (NAM) is a separate policy and not a Panchsheel principle.
Panchsheel was signed on 29 April 1954, well before the 1962 war, so statement I is wrong. Supporting each other in global forums is not one of the five principles, so II is wrong as well.
The five principles include peaceful co-existence and non-aggression. Mutual protection of the environment and of the indigenous population are not among them, so I and IV is correct.
Burma (now Myanmar) adopted Panchsheel in 1954 right after the India-China agreement, so it is the country associated with it. Vietnam, Nepal and Thailand are not.
The Non-Aligned Movement was founded at the 1st Belgrade Summit in 1961 in Yugoslavia. Cairo hosted the 2nd summit in 1964 and New Delhi the 7th in 1983.
The Truman Doctrine (1947) pledged US support to countries resisting communism, notably Greece and Turkey, so as to contain Soviet expansion.
The first (though failed) cement plant was set up in 1904 at Madras (Chennai) using sea shells as lime; Porbandar (1914) was only the first successful one.
Dhanbad-Jamshedpur is a coal and steel region, not a cotton textile area. Mumbai, Coimbatore-Madurai and Indore are listed cotton centres, so only III is correct.
Nandana block print is practised in Tarapur village of Nimar region in Madhya Pradesh. The notes do not cover this.
Ahmedabad is called the Manchester of India; Mumbai is Cottonopolis and Coimbatore is the Manchester of South India.
Cotton textile is an ancient industry in India, older than jute, tea or sugar, which are modern mill industries.
Coimbatore's spinning industry rests on hydel power, cheap labour and local cotton, so labour is a reason; black cotton soil is not the predominant soil of Tamil Nadu, so I is wrong.
The industry began near black-soil cotton tracts of Maharashtra and Gujarat, with Mumbai and Ahmedabad as the major centres, so Bombay-Ahmedabad is the most prominent region.
About 90% of jute capacity lies in the Hooghly belt, and West Bengal has 71 of 97 mills, so the industry is concentrated in West Bengal.

Jagar is a ritual of invoking local deities and ancestral spirits through songs and narrative music, mainly practised in the Garhwal and Kumaon regions of Uttarakhand. It is not typical of Madhya Pradesh, Haryana or Assam.
Abul Hasan, Jahangir's court portraitist titled Nadir-uz-Zaman, painted the famous Jahangir embracing Shah Abbas scene; the notes list him as the master of Jahangir-era portraits.
Daswanth, Abdus Samad and Basawan all served Akbar, whereas Kalyan Das is not among the painters listed for Akbar's court, so he is the exception.
Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad were Persian masters who served under Humayun and then Akbar, so option 1 is right.
Ustad Mansur was the greatest painter of birds, animals and plants under Jahangir, titled Nadir-ul-Asr.
Abul Hasan and Aqa Reza were Jahangir's painters, while Abdus Samad and Mir Sayyid Ali were Humayun-Akbar era masters, so II and III is correct.
The Hamzanama was led first by Mir Sayyid Ali and then by Abdus Samad, who completed it; the answer key credits Abdul Samad.
Abul Hasan received the title Nadir-uz-Zaman (Nadir-ul-Zaman) from Jahangir; Mansur was Nadir-ul-Asr.

The notes do not state these facts about 18th-19th century Company-era visual culture, so no line settles the statements. Statements I, II and III are the correct ones, while IV is wrong because European artists did visit regional courts.
Tansen's original name was Ramtanu Pande, not Makaranda Pande.

The six Fundamental Rights groups are Equality, Freedom, Exploitation, Religion, Cultural/Educational and Constitutional Remedies. Right to Information is not one of them (it is read into Art. 19(1)(a) and is statutory).
Equality, Freedom and Exploitation are listed Fundamental Right groups in Part III; citizenship is not a Fundamental Right group, so it is the odd one out.
Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes) have a notochord that persists throughout life, so the statement that it disappears after the larval stage is incorrect.
The atomic mass unit is defined as 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, so carbon-12 is the standard.
By Boyle's law, pV = constant at fixed T, so V = constant × (1/p). This is a straight line through the origin in a V vs 1/p graph; a hyperbola would result from V vs p.
Friction depends on velocity direction and the path, and it dissipates energy, so it is non-central and non-conservative. Electric and gravitational forces are central and conservative.
The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n². For the M shell (n=3) this is 18.
The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n². For the N shell (n=4) this is 32.
Ampere is the unit of current, with dimension I (or A), and metre per second squared gives L T^-2. The combined dimensions are [I L T^-2].
Magnification is the ratio of the observed (image) size to the actual size of the specimen.
Aristotle first classified animals on the basis of their habitat (land, water, air).
In an AC generator the induced current reverses direction every half rotation, so the direction changes once per half revolution.
The potato is a stem tuber and its 'eyes' are nodes with buds, which indicate a modified stem. Onion scales are modified leaves, pea tendrils are modified leaves or leaflets, and carrot is a root.
The peanut flower's stalk bends down after fertilisation and pushes the fruit (pod) into the soil. Potato, carrot and onion are underground stems or roots, not fruits.
Resolving power is the ability of an instrument to distinguish two closely placed objects as separate.
Violet light has the highest refractive index in glass, so it travels with the minimum velocity (v = c/n). Red travels fastest.
Speed has the dimension of length/time. m²/hr is area per time, so it is not a unit of speed.
For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (u+v)/2, so v = 2 × average velocity − u.
The first equation of motion, v = u + at, relates velocity and time.
The second equation of motion, s = ut + ½at², relates position (displacement) and time.
Velocity is defined as the rate of change of displacement with time.
In a vacuum there is no air resistance, so all bodies fall with the same acceleration g irrespective of mass. Hence t1 = t2 = t3.
Rural to rural migration is the largest stream in India (mostly women moving for marriage), so option 1 is correct; rural to urban is not the largest.

The notes do not mention KAVAL towns. KAVAL towns (Kanpur, Agra, Varanasi, Allahabad, Lucknow) are only some of the million-plus cities, since there are 35 million cities in 2001 spread across many States, so the statement that they are the only ones is false.
Mandav Hills are in Gujarat, not Maharashtra, whereas Satmala, Harishchandra and Balaghat ranges are all in Maharashtra.
Ooty is the hill station in the Nilgiri Hills (Blue Mountains), where the Western and Eastern Ghats meet; Nilgiris is the most specific answer, and Ooty is not in Nallamala.
The Malabar coast (Mangaluru to Kanyakumari, with kayals/backwaters) is the south-western coast of Kerala.
On the west coast the north-to-south order is Janjira (Konkan, Maharashtra), Sindhudurg (Maharashtra, further south), Kannur (Kerala, Malabar) and Nagercoil (near Kanyakumari), giving I, IV, II, III.
The Buckingham Canal runs along the Coromandel coast from Kakinada (AP) to Parangipettai (TN).
The Konkan coast runs from Daman to Goa, the northern part of the western coastal plain.
Kochi (Cochin) port lies on the Vembanad kayal of the Malabar coast in Kerala.
Rameswaram island lies between India and Sri Lanka; Elephanta and Salsette are near Mumbai and Nicobar is in the Bay of Bengal.

Statement I is wrong: Kavaratti is the capital, and the notes do not make it the largest city (Andrott is the largest island). Statement II is wrong: the Eight Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the Maldives, while the Nine Degree Channel separates Minicoy from the rest of Lakshadweep.
The 14th FC gave income distance the highest weight (50%) in the horizontal devolution formula, more than population (17.5% + 10%), area (15%) or forest cover; tax effort was not a criterion.
The 14th FC raised the States' share in the divisible pool from 32% to 42%, the largest increase ever.

The 14th FC made tax devolution the main route rather than grants, so it did not recommend sector-specific grants as earlier commissions did. The 32% to 42% increase and forest cover criterion were its recommendations.
The 14th FC raised the States' share of central taxes from 32% to 42%.
The 14th FC (2015-20) fixed Andhra Pradesh's share of the States' pool at 4.305%.

The 13th Finance Commission's resources for undivided Andhra Pradesh were apportioned between the two successor States under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014, since it was the commission in force at the time.
The 2022 Winter Olympics were held in Beijing, China (after PyeongChang 2018 and Sochi 2014); the notes do not cover this fact.
The notes list the Hoysala temples of Karnataka as a World Heritage inscription of September 2023; the other temples listed are not recorded as inscribed then.
International Mother Language Day is observed on 21 February; International Yoga Day is on 21 June and International Youth Day on 12 August.
FAO observes World Soil Day on 5 December. World Health Day (7 April) belongs to WHO, so it is not the answer.
ILO was founded in 1919, earlier than WHO (1948) and FAO (1945). The IMF is not dated in the notes, but ILO is still the oldest of the options.
UNESCO and the UIA named Rio de Janeiro the World Capital of Architecture for 2020, the first city given this title.
Jankilal is the Rajasthani artist famed for taking the Bahurupiya mimicry art to the world stage; the notes do not cover this.
Kalaripayattu is an ancient martial art of Kerala and a living tradition in parts of South India; it is not a Bhakti cult, metalwork or dance-drama.
The Manganiyars are hereditary folk musicians of the Thar desert in Rajasthan, i.e. North-West India, so they are known for a musical tradition.
Yakshagana is the traditional theatre form of coastal Karnataka. Sattriya belongs to Assam and Kalaripayattu to Kerala, so the other pairs are wrong.
Jaubani is a dance of the Dimasa community of Assam in North-East India.
Gopiji Bhatt is associated with the Tamaasha folk drama of Rajasthan, as one of its noted exponents.
Gowari is the famous folk drama of the Bhils. Tamasha and Rammat are associated with other communities or regions.
Banghaji (Nagaji Jat) is credited as the originator of the Bhavai folk theatre of Rajasthan.
Dhumal, Hafiza and Rouf are Kashmiri/J&K folk dances, whereas Dangi is not a J&K dance (it is associated with Gujarat/Rajasthan), so it is the answer.
Jawara is a harvest dance of Madhya Pradesh (Bundelkhand), performed to celebrate wealth and prosperity.
Kuchipudi is the classical dance of Andhra Pradesh, named after Kuchipudi village in Krishna district.
Mohiniyattam is traditionally a solo dance performed by women. Kuchipudi is a dance-drama and Odissi and Bharatanatyam are also commonly performed as groups, so Mohiniyattam is the expected answer.
Makar Sankranti is celebrated as Magh Bihu in Assam; Uttarayan is the Gujarat name and Pongal is the Tamil Nadu name.
Gulabi Gangaur on Chaitra Shukla Panchami is a special observance at Nathdwara in Rajasthan.
The Second Plan (Mahalanobis Plan) first proposed land reforms through cooperative land management, so option 4 is right; the First Plan did not.
The Fourth Plan was delayed after the Plan Holiday (1966-69) and was finally launched in 1969, so 1969 is correct.
Garibi Hatao, Indira Gandhi's 1971 election slogan, became the basic objective of the Fifth Plan (1974-79), so the 5th Plan is correct.
The Fifth Plan made Garibi Hatao its basic objective, and anti-poverty programmes were first started in it, so the Fifth Plan is correct.
The Second Plan was the Nehru-Mahalanobis plan, built on P.C. Mahalanobis's two- and four-sector model, so option 1 is correct.
The Second Plan stressed rapid industrialisation and heavy and basic industries and was the first major industrial plan, so the Second Plan is correct.
The First Plan was launched on 1 April 1951, which marks the start of planning; of the options, 7 April 1951 is the closest and is the keyed answer.
The Fifth Plan's objectives included control of inflation along with poverty removal and self-reliance, so it is the right answer.

Statement I is right: the Second Plan stressed heavy and basic industries. Statement II is right: the Fourth Plan aimed at growth with stability and self-reliance. Statement III, about the financial sector, is not supported, so I and II is correct.
In the Hadley cell, air rises at the equator and sinks near 30°, which is the subtropical high-pressure belt. The ITCZ, doldrums and equatorial troughs are where air rises, not sinks.
Trade winds blow from the subtropical high (horse latitudes) to the equatorial low. Westerlies blow from the subtropical high towards the subpolar low, and doldrums are a calm belt, not a wind.
Trade winds are a planetary wind. Monsoon is a periodic wind, and Chinook and Mistral are local winds.

Statement I is wrong because the westerlies blow between about 35° and 60° in each hemisphere, not from 30°N to 60°S. Statement II is correct because the western disturbances that bring winter rain to NW India come from the Mediterranean on the westerly flow. So only II is correct.
From the equator towards the pole the sequence is doldrums (0–5°), trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies. So the order is I, II, III, IV.
Jet streams are narrow, fast winds at 10–12 km, near the tropopause. This lies in the upper troposphere.
The polar front jet is strongest in winter, when the temperature contrast between the poles and the lower latitudes is greatest. So the claim that it peaks in summer is incorrect.
A strong polar vortex keeps cold air confined in the north. When it weakens, cold spells reach the mid-latitudes.
Mango showers are pre-monsoon showers of Kerala and Karnataka. Of the options, only Karnataka is correct.
Pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka are called Mango showers, because they help the mangoes ripen.

The notes do not cover this fact. Haemoglobin is the red, iron-containing pigment that carries O2 from lungs to tissues and also carries some CO2 back. It is not described as acidic, so option 3 is the incorrect statement.
Connective tissues include bone, cartilage and blood. Skeletal muscle is muscular tissue, not connective tissue.
Tendons connect muscle to bone. Ligaments connect bone to bone, which is why option 2 is wrong.
A reflex action is coordinated by the spinal cord, so the response occurs without waiting for the brain. The cerebrum handles voluntary action.
White blood cells such as neutrophils defend the body against infection. Red cells carry oxygen and platelets help clotting.
An adult human skeleton has 206 bones. 200 is only an approximation, so 206 is the exact answer.
The ear ossicles are the malleus, incus and stapes. The femur is the thigh bone in the leg, not part of the ear.
The normal resting heart rate of a healthy adult is about 72 beats per minute.
Light enters through the pupil and then passes through the lens, so the lens lies just behind the pupil. The retina is at the back of the eye.
Ear muscles are vestigial in humans: they are reduced and functionless, though they are functional in other animals. Jaw, canine teeth and humerus are functional.
The retina is the light-sensitive surface on which the image forms, like the film in a camera. The lens of the eye corresponds to the camera lens.
Mother O has genotype OO, and father A may be AO. The child can be A or O. Of the options, only O is possible; B and AB are impossible.
The epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate are accessory ducts and glands. They mature and carry sperms and provide fluid for motility. Spermatogenesis occurs only in the testes.

Active immunity arises when the body's own cells make antibodies after infection or vaccination, so statement I is correct. Anti-venom gives ready-made antibodies, which is passive immunisation, so statement II is wrong.
Tubectomy is the surgical cutting and ligation of the fallopian tube (oviduct) in females. Vasectomy is the male procedure on the vas deferens.
The eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the pharynx and equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum. Malleus and incus are ossicles that transmit vibrations.
Colostrum is the first milk after childbirth. It is rich in antibodies and builds the newborn's immunity.

The 'rarest of rare' doctrine, with life imprisonment as the rule, was laid down by the Constitution Bench in Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980). Machhi Singh (1983) later elaborated the categories, and the other cases do not lay down this principle.
The Indian sugar institute (National Sugar Institute) is at Kanpur. The notes do not state this; Lucknow hosts the Sugarcane Research institute (IISR), which is the tempting wrong option.
Golden Revolution relates to horticulture (and honey). Oilseeds belong to the Yellow Revolution and cereals/foodgrains to the Green Revolution.
Black pepper is called 'Black diamond' (the 'black gold' of spices). The notes mention black pepper but not this nickname.
Cotton is called 'White Gold' because of its high commercial value, including in Maharashtra, the leading cotton state. The notes do not give this nickname.
Pemayangtse Monastery is in Sikkim (near Pelling); the notes do not cover it.
The Central Institute of Buddhist Studies is at Choglamsar, Leh (Ladakh); the notes do not cover it.
Tabo Monastery lies in the Spiti Valley of Himachal Pradesh; the notes do not cover it.
Tabo Monastery lies in the Spiti Valley of Himachal Pradesh; the notes do not cover it.

Buddhism spread because of its simple doctrine, appeal to the lower classes, missionary zeal and use of regional languages (Pali/Prakrit). Option V is wrong because Buddhism rejected Vedic ritualism rather than upholding it.
The 80-foot Great Buddha statue at Bodh Gaya was built by the Japanese (1989, Daijokyo sect); the notes do not cover it.

The Pala rulers, such as Dharmapala (founder of Vikramashila, called Param Saugat), were Buddhist patrons, so statement II is correct. Statement I is wrong because the Ikshvakus supported Buddhism at Nagarjunakonda.
Surendranath Banerjee passed the ICS in 1869 but was dismissed in 1874 over a minor irregularity. The other options were not dismissed from the ICS.
Vande Mataram, India's national song, was written by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in his novel Anandamath. Tagore only sang it first at the INC in 1896; he did not compose it.
The first Jain council was held at Pataliputra (c. 300 BCE) under Sthulabhadra; Vallabhi hosted the second council.
The first Jain council met at Pataliputra under Sthulabhadra; Vallabhi was the site of the last major council.
The Jain Agamas (Siddhanta), the earliest canon, were compiled in Ardhamagadhi, an eastern Prakrit. Prakrit is broader and less precise, and Pali is the Buddhist language.
Jinendra Kalyanabhyudayamu was written by the Jain scholar Appayacharya, dedicated to the Kakatiya king Prataparudra.
Kharavela belonged to the Chedi (Mahameghavahana) dynasty, ruling Kalinga. Kalinga was the region he ruled, not his dynasty.
Kharavela, the Chedi king of Kalinga, was a Jain patron, known from the Hathigumpha inscription and the Udayagiri caves. The other kings are not noted as Jain followers in these notes.
Chamundaraya, minister of the Western Ganga king Rachamalla IV, raised the Gommateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola c. 981 CE.
Jainism went south under Bhadrabahu, who led monks with Chandragupta to Shravanabelagola. Sthulabhadra stayed in Magadha.
Rohan Bopanna partnered Gabriela Dabrowski to win the 2017 French Open mixed doubles, which was his first Grand Slam title; the other pairs listed did not win it.
A double fault is a tennis term: a server who faults on both serves loses the point. It is not used in football, badminton or golf.
The notes state that 28 Khelo India athletes were in India's Paris 2024 contingent, so option 1 is correct.
The Lodha Committee, set up by the Supreme Court to reform the BCCI, recommended legalizing betting in cricket, with regulation to curb match-fixing. It did not propose a ban or a jail sentence.
The Act amended the First Schedule (adding Telangana as a new State) and the Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seats: AP 18 to 11, Telangana 7). The other Schedule pairs are not amended.
The Act amends the Delimitation Order 2008, so the order was passed in 2008.
The notes do not state the Plan periods in which the institutions are to be set up. The correct answer is 12th and 13th Plan periods.
The separate AP High Court began functioning on 1 January 2019. The other dates do not match.
The High Court of Andhra Pradesh began functioning on 1 January 2019 with its principal seat at Amaravati, so option 1 is right.
