Schedule X covers continuance of facilities in State institutions and lists 107 institutions.
Gomti rises at Gomat Taal (Fulhar lake) near Pilibhit in the plains, making it the only Ganga tributary that rises in the plains; Son, Sharda and Ramganga rise in hills or the plateau.

Pindar meets the Alaknanda at Karnaprayag, so Alaknanda–Pindar is the correct pair. Kabini is not a Godavari tributary, Manjra is not on this basis a Krishna pair here, and Subansiri is a Brahmaputra tributary, not Indus.
Yamuna (Yamunotri), Alaknanda (Satopanth glacier) and Mandakini rise from glaciers, while the Kosi is a rain-fed river formed by Himalayan tributaries such as Sun Kosi, Arun and Tamur Kosi.
North Koel rises on the Ranchi plateau, flows through the northern part of Betla National Park (Palamu) and joins the Son; Mechi, Mahananda and Mahadayi do not fit.
The Kosi is known for the maximum shifting of its course and dangerous floods; its 2008 course change caused the Bihar calamity.
North Koel is a tributary of the Son, which joins the Ganga, so it is part of the Ganga basin. Barakar is a Damodar tributary and South Koel is not a Ganga tributary.
A is true, as the Yamuna is heavily abstracted and nearly dry between Delhi and Agra. R is false because the Yamuna is a perennial Himalayan river fed by rain and snowmelt.
In Tibet the Brahmaputra is called Tsangpo (Yarlung Zangbo/Sanpu); the other rivers listed are not known by this name.

Archaeological excavations are what revealed Harappan culture, since the script is unread and there are no religious books; seals found in digs are the main source, so excavation is the broad correct answer.

Seals were used for trade regulation and authentication, and uniform seals and weights prove standardised, regulated trade, so they indicate commercial and economic development; pottery and houses do not show this directly.
AI, machine learning, blockchain, IoT and geo-spatial mapping are listed as 4IR technologies, so they power the fourth industrial revolution, not the third (electronics/IT).
IoT stands for Internet of Things, covering smart homes and connected appliances; the other options are invented expansions.

Statement I is wrong because NAFRS is run by the NCRB, not the National Informatics Centre. Statement II is also wrong since the main concern is privacy, not an inability to identify people in real time. So neither is correct.
Zawar (Udaipur) is a lead-zinc mining area, not an iron ore area. Badampahar (Odisha), Bailadila (Chhattisgarh) and Anantapur (AP, first in haematite) are iron ore areas.
Iron ore occurs in Bihar (Jharkhand), MP and Odisha, but Punjab is not among the iron-ore regions of India, so Punjab is the answer.
Nathra-ki-Pal in Rajasthan is an iron ore occurrence (Rajasthan is among the other iron-ore areas), not lead-zinc, copper or manganese.
Uranium was first found at Jaduguda (Jharkhand) in 1951. Tummalapalle in Kadapa is only a large reserve, not the first discovery.
The Majhgawan mine at Panna in Madhya Pradesh is India's diamond mine, so it is famous for diamond mining.
There are 18 Mahapuranas, so option (1) is correct. The notes do not state the total number of Puranas.
Manusmriti is the Dharmashastra text that disapproves of widow remarriage. The Jataka, Yajnavalkya and Arthashastra are not the texts known for prohibiting it. The notes do not cover this.
The Nachiketa-Yama dialogue on death is found in the Katha Upanishad (Kathopanishad), which belongs to the Yajurveda. It is not in the Brihadaranyaka, which features Yajnavalkya, Gargi and Maitreyi.

Krishna, son of Devaki, is first mentioned in the Chandogya Upanishad, where he is a pupil of Ghora Angirasa. The Mahabharata and Bhagavata Purana are later and deal with him at length. The notes do not cover this.
Tabaqat-i-Nasiri by Minhaj-us-Siraj covers the Ghurids and Bakhtiyar Khalji, so it holds the earliest account of his Bihar invasion. Taj-ul-Maasir deals with the early Sultanate under Aibak.
Taj-ul-Maasir was written by Hasan Nizami, who was patronised by Aibak. Isami wrote Futuh-us-Salatin, and Sarhindi (Yahya bin Ahmad) wrote Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi.
Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (3), Hasan Nizami wrote Taj-ul-Maasir (4), Minhaj wrote Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (2), and Yahya bin Ahmad wrote Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi (1). This gives 3 4 2 1.
Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit and studied Indian religion and philosophy, including the Puranas, so he was the first Muslim to study them. The notes do not state this fact directly.
Al-Biruni came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni in the 11th century. Firishta, Ibn Battuta and Afif belonged to other periods.
Tahqiq-i-Hind (Kitab-ul-Hind) was written by Al-Biruni (Alberuni). Amir Khusrau wrote other works.
Ramacharitam by Sandhyakara Nandi is a double-meaning poem about the Ramayana and the Pala king Ramapala. It records the Kaivartha revolt against the Pala prince, so option 4 fits best.
Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini in the 12th century and was a contemporary of the Kashmir king Jayasimha (Jaisingh). The notes do not name this king.

Al-Biruni came from Khwarazm in present Uzbekistan (IV). Ibn Battuta was from Morocco (III), Mahmud Wali Balkhi from Afghanistan (I), and Seydi Ali Reis from Turkey (II). This gives A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.
IPR 1948 (6 April 1948) was the first industrial policy of independent India; the 1956 resolution came later and replaced it.
FERA (1973) was replaced by FEMA in 1999. The Competition Act replaced the MRTP Act, not FERA.

IPR 1948 laid the foundation of a mixed economy by defining the spheres of both public and private sectors, so option 3 is right. It did not nationalise everything or give private enterprise exclusive dominance.
The notes list licensing, expansion of the public sector and small and cottage industries as provisions of IPR 1956, so all three are correct.
The Industrial Policy Resolution of 30 April 1956 was announced after the First Plan, so 1956 is the answer.
The Industrial Licensing Policy Inquiry Committee (1967, report 1969) was headed by Subimal Dutt, and it led to the MRTP Act.
The 1977 Janata policy statement stressed small-scale, tiny and cottage industries and set up District Industries Centres, not heavy industry or FDI.
The New Industrial Policy 1991 abolished industrial licensing except for a few industries, ending the licence-permit-quota raj. The 1970 and 1980 policies did not do this.
The 1991 policy abolished the mandatory convertibility clause for term loans of new projects, so it no longer applies.
Balban set up the Diwan-i-Arz (army department) under the Ariz-i-Mumalik to maintain a large standing army against the Mongols. Alauddin is the tempting wrong option, but he did not found it.

The Satyakama Jabala story, where he takes his mother Jabala's name as she cannot name his father, is told in the Chhandogya Upanishad. The Jabala Upanishad is a different text, so option 1 is the tempting wrong choice.

The notes say gotra as descent from a single male ancestor was established in Later Vedic times, after the Rigvedic period, when it meant only a cow-pen. Of the given options, the post-Vedic period fits best.

The full set of four ashramas, including Sannyasa, is first found in the later Jabala Upanishad, which makes it the latest of these institutions. The four varnas appear in the Rigveda's Purusha Sukta and the gods in the options are Rigvedic.
Deodar is a temperate conifer of the moist temperate zone (about 1,500-3,000 m), which covers 1,800-2,600 m. Sal grows in the foothills and chir pine at lower sub-tropical altitudes.
Oak and rhododendron grow naturally in the temperate Himalayan zones. Sandalwood is a dry deciduous species of South India, not the Himalaya, so only I and II are correct.
Bhitarkanika lies in Odisha on the Brahmani-Baitarani delta (Kendrapada), not in the Vamsadhara-Subarnarekha delta or West Bengal. Both statements are therefore wrong.
India holds only about 3% of the world's mangrove cover, so 0.03 is the correct option.
Lok Adalats are statutory bodies set up under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, so option 1 is correct.

Judicial review is the power of the courts to test laws and executive orders against the Constitution and declare them void, so the SC can declare a State law invalid. It is not final authority over all issues, nor an appeal from HCs.

Judicial review lets courts strike down laws of Parliament and State legislatures that violate the Constitution, which checks legislative excesses. President/Governor intervention, no-confidence motions and elections are political checks, not the check on unconstitutional laws.
Basic structure, PIL and removal of handcuffs are genuine Supreme Court evolutions. Exemptions to fundamental rights (Arts 31A-31C, 33) are constitutional text, not SC evolutions.
Justice P.N. Bhagwati, with V.R. Krishna Iyer, pioneered Public Interest Litigation in India, so option 1 is correct.
PIL can be filed under Art. 32 in the Supreme Court or Art. 226 in the High Courts, so option 4 is correct. Tribunals like the CAT are not the forum for PIL.

At Wandiwash (22 January 1760) Eyre Coote of the English routed the French under Count de Lally, which ended French political power in India. The Portuguese, Danes and Dutch were not involved in this battle.
In 1767 Parliament made the Company pay £400,000 a year to the state for its territorial revenues (and capped its dividend at 10%), so option 3 is correct.
The Santhal Hul of 1855-56 was led by the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu against dikus; the other names are not associated with it.
Eklavya is the educational TV channel for engineering and technology subjects. The notes only cover Eklavya Model Residential Schools, which are unrelated, so no line is linked.
Maize is a C4 plant (it uses the Hatch-Slack pathway), whereas paddy, soybean and wheat are C3 plants. The notes do not cover photosynthetic pathways.

Statement I is right: black gram (urad) can be grown in both kharif and rabi/zaid seasons, and the notes confirm pulses are grown in both seasons. Statements II and III are false: pulse production is not dominated by green gram, and rabi pulses have not declined.
Rice needs rainfall above 100 cm, and the 100 cm isohyet is roughly the western limit of rice cultivation. So 100 cm is the correct option.
Macaroni (durum) wheat is hardy and suited to rainfed, low-moisture conditions, so rainfed is correct. The notes do not mention macaroni wheat.
Jonnavittula Gurunatham of Guntur wrote six articles in The Hindu in 1911 titled 'On the present position of the Telugu people'; Gurunadham is the same person.
The official language of the Madras Presidency was Tamil, even though Telugus were about 40% of the population.
B.N. Sarma presided at Bapatla and warned that the demand might do 'more harm than good'. Nyapati Subba Rao opposed the resolution but presided only at the 2nd session.
A separate Telugu university was first demanded at the first Andhra Mahasabha at Bapatla in 1913, while the province resolution was deferred.
Albania, Bosnia and Croatia all have Adriatic coastline, so I, II and III are correct. Macedonia is landlocked and has no Adriatic coast.
The Aral Sea has shrunk drastically because of irrigation diversion. The Black Sea and Lake Baikal have not dried up from human activity.
Indonesia renamed the part of the South China Sea within its EEZ north of the Natuna Islands as the North Natuna Sea in 2017. Malaysia, Brunei and the Philippines did not do this.
The Dead Sea is the lowest point on land at about 1,385 ft below sea level, which is the figure given in the APPSC key.
The Mediterranean lies between Europe to the north (Spain, France, Italy, Greece) and Africa to the south (Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco). So it separates Europe and Africa.
The Kiel Canal connects the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. None of the options (Baltic–Mediterranean, Red–Mediterranean, North–Black) gives this pair, so 'None of these' is correct.
The 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali, taking the Eighth Schedule from 18 to 22 languages.

Bodo was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Amendment (2003). Angika is not listed, Hindi is the official language rather than a national language, and a State cannot compel minorities on medium of instruction.
Bhojpuri is not in the Eighth Schedule, whereas Urdu, Nepali and Konkani are.
Article 345 lets the State Legislature adopt one or more languages as the State's official language(s). Article 343 concerns the Union, 344 the Commission, and 346 inter-State communication.
The first Official Language Commission under Article 344 was set up in 1955 under B.G. Kher.

Article 343 makes Hindi in Devanagari the official language of the Union, not a 'national language'. It does not provide for English within states or Hindi between states by agreement, so I, III and IV are not its central features.
Monpa is a Sino-Tibetan language of Arunachal Pradesh, not a principal language of Jammu and Kashmir, whereas Urdu, Gujari and Koshur (Kashmiri) are.
Sikkim's official languages are Nepali, Sikkimese (Bhutia), Lepcha and English, with Tibetan not among them, so the pair Sikkim-Tibetan is wrong.
Uttarakhand made Sanskrit its second official language in 2010, the first state to do so; the notes do not cover this.
Telugu is called the 'Italian of the East' because of its melodious, vowel-ending sound.
Kurukh (Oraon), a Dravidian tribal language, has official status in West Bengal and is regarded as endangered, whereas Santali is not considered endangered.
The Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) is located at Mysuru (Mysore).

The Allahabad-Haldia stretch (NW-1) and the Sadiya-Dhubri stretch of the Brahmaputra (NW-2) are declared National Waterways. The Godavari stretch is also a declared waterway (NW-4 covers the Godavari-Krishna system), so all three are correct.
NW-1 is the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly stretch from Haldia to Prayagraj (Allahabad). Sadiya-Dhubri is NW-2, Kakinada-Puducherry is NW-4, and Kollam-Kottapuram is NW-3.
Khajuraho, Jabalpur and Gwalior are operational airports of Madhya Pradesh, while Panna has no operational airport, so Panna is the answer.
Pakyong Airport is located near Gangtok in Sikkim, which was the state's first airport.
DigiYatra was launched on 1 December 2022 at Delhi, Varanasi and Bengaluru airports. Mumbai was not among the first three, so it is the answer.
Dibang, Lohit and Kameng (Jia Bharali) are all listed as Brahmaputra tributaries, so all three statements are correct.
Lohit and Subansiri are Brahmaputra tributaries that flow through Arunachal Pradesh. The Barak rises in the Manipur hills and is part of the Meghna system, so statement I is wrong.

Rangeet is the Teesta's largest tributary, so II is correct. Teesta rises from Tso Lhamo lake in Sikkim, not at the Brahmaputra source, so I is wrong. It joins the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) in Bangladesh and does not flow into the Bay of Bengal itself, so III is wrong.
The Brahmaputra (Tsangpo) turns south at Namche Barwa, making a sharp U-turn before entering India as the Dihang. The Ganga, Teesta and Barak do not.
Teesta is a right-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra. Ghaghara, Kali (Sharda) and Son belong to the Ganga system.
Pangong Tso is a brackish, high-altitude lake, not a freshwater one, so the statement that it is freshwater is incorrect.
Pangong Tso is a brackish, high-altitude lake, not a freshwater one, so the statement that it is freshwater is incorrect.
Pangong Tso and Tso Moriri are in Ladakh, and Tso Kar is also a Ladakh lake. Tsomgo (Changu) lake is in Sikkim, so III is wrong.
Loktak is a freshwater lake in Manipur, famous for its floating phumdis.
The floating islands of vegetation on Loktak Lake in Manipur are called phumdis.

The notes say the PMO is the PM's policy office, while the Cabinet Secretary heads the Cabinet Secretariat, not the PMO, so statement II is wrong. The notes do not give the PMO's 1977 origin, but the answer key treats statement I as the only correct one.
The Right to Food campaign (PUCL PIL 2001) led to the National Food Security Act 2013, which is the Right to Food Act. No Right to Health or Right of Shelter Act was passed.
Fasciola hepatica is the sheep liver fluke, a flatworm that lives in the liver and bile ducts of its host.
Taenia (tapeworm) and Fasciola (liver fluke) are flatworms, so they belong to phylum Platyhelminthes.
Sleeping sickness is caused by Trypanosoma brucei species and spread by the tsetse fly. Leishmania causes kala-azar instead.
Ascariasis is caused by the nematode Ascaris lumbricoides, a parasitic worm, so it is a parasitic infection rather than viral, bacterial or protozoan.
Ascaris lumbricoides is an intestinal nematode acquired by swallowing its eggs, which pass out in faeces. Wuchereria affects lymph vessels, while Epidermophyton and Microsporum are skin fungi.
Ringworm is caused by dermatophytes, which are fungi, and is treated with griseofulvin.
Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, caused by viruses such as hepatitis A and E, and it causes jaundice.
Typhoid, caused by Salmonella Typhi, is diagnosed with the Widal test. ESR, ELISA and DLC are not the specific test for typhoid.
Baking soda (NaHCO3) releases CO2 and works as a mild antacid, so options 1, 2 and 4 are true. It is a mild base, not a corrosive one, so option 3 is the incorrect statement.
Soap micelles are colloidal-sized particles that scatter light (the Tyndall effect), which makes the solution look cloudy.
A fuse works by the heating effect of current, so the wire must conduct and have a low melting point so that it melts and breaks the circuit when overloaded.
Fuse wire is made of a tin-lead alloy, which has a low melting point. Nichrome is a heater coil material, not fuse wire.
A fuse is connected in series so that the whole circuit current flows through it. It is placed on the live wire so the circuit is cut off from the supply when it blows.
Tungsten is used for bulb filaments because it has the highest melting point of the metals.
Tungsten has the highest melting point, so the filament can glow white-hot without melting.
Nichrome is used as the heater coil material. Tungsten is for bulb filaments.
The coil of nichrome wire in a heater is called the heating element. A filament is the term for a bulb's wire.
Ethylene glycol is mixed with water in automobile radiators as an antifreeze because it depresses the freezing point of water.
Electroplating deposits a thin film of gold on the jewellery when an electric current is passed through the gold salt solution.
Sodium calcium silicate is soft (soda-lime) glass. Hard glass and borosilicate glass are different types.
CaOCl2 (calcium oxychloride) is bleaching powder.
German silver contains nickel (A-2), solder contains tin (B-1), bleaching powder contains chlorine (C-4) and hypo is sodium thiosulphate (D-3), giving 2 1 4 3.
Solder is an Sn-Pb alloy, so it is made of lead and tin.
Rose metal is the alloy of bismuth, lead and tin. Solder has only tin and lead.
Brass is copper with zinc and bronze is copper with tin.
Natural rubber is a polymer of isoprene.
Soap molecules surround grease and break it into small droplets that disperse in water. This is emulsification.
Soap lowers the surface tension of water, so it wets the fabric and lifts dirt better. It is not a catalyst.
Chauri Chaura is in Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh (4 Feb 1922), not Bihar or the other states listed.
The movement was called off at Bardoli (11-12 Feb 1922) because of the Chauri Chaura violence, so both A and R are true and R explains A.
The sequence is police firing, then the police station burnt, then Gandhi postponed the movement, then he was arrested on 10 March 1922.
Gandhi withdrew the movement because of the violence at Chauri Chaura, not because of arrests or any British concession.
The NCM was called off by the Bardoli resolution of Feb 1922, so it was suspended in 1922.
Statement I is correct as the NCM made nationalism a mass movement. Statement II is wrong because the movement was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922), not after Jallianwala Bagh (1919).
Gandhi suspended the movement because of the Chauri Chaura violence, which went against his strict non-violence.
The NCM was launched on 1 Aug 1920, so the year is 1920.
Metformin is a standard oral anti-diabetic drug (it lowers blood glucose); zolpidem is a sleep aid, promethazine an antihistamine and hydralazine an antihypertensive.
Analgesics are pain-relieving drugs; antipyretics reduce fever, antibiotics kill bacteria and antiseptics are applied on living tissue to prevent infection.
Physalia is the Portuguese man of war (4), Taenia is a tapeworm (3), Fasciola is the liver fluke (1) and Scypha (Sycon) is a sponge (2), giving 4 3 1 2.
Bacteria, viruses and fungi multiply rapidly in large numbers, whereas worms reproduce sexually and much more slowly.
Mammals have a four-chambered heart; a three-chambered heart is found in amphibians and most reptiles. The other statements hold (hair, egg-laying monotremes, aquatic whales).
Length, time and mass are fundamental quantities; weight is a force (mg), a derived quantity that varies with gravity.
Iodine exists as diatomic I2 molecules, whereas copper, helium and barium occur as single atoms (monoatomic).
Morphine comes from the poppy plant, tetracycline from bacteria (Streptomyces), quinine from cinchona bark and penicillin from the fungus Penicillium, giving 2 4 1 3.

Pleiotropy is when a single gene affects two or more characters; apomixis is seed formation without fertilisation, polyploidy is extra chromosome sets and polyteny is repeated DNA strands in giant chromosomes.
Pulses (legumes) have two cotyledons so they are dicots; rice, wheat and maize are monocot cereals.
Vegetative propagation gives clones (I) and can be done through much of the year (III). It does not eliminate viruses, since the virus passes on to the offspring, so II is wrong.
In photosynthesis, water is split and oxygen is released as the by-product; sugar is the main product, and CO2 is a raw material.
Among the options, tungsten is the hardest metal; it also has the highest melting point.
Cloves are the dried unopened flower buds of the clove tree (Syzygium aromaticum).
Cro-Magnon man was the most recent of these and was essentially anatomically modern Homo sapiens; Java, Peking and Neanderthal men were earlier.
Starch gives a blue-black colour with iodine, but cellulose does not. Both are plant-origin glucose polymers.
Zoology is the study of animals, both living and dead (fossils, preserved specimens); botany deals with plants.
Evolutionary order of appearance: amphibian (salamander), then reptile (python), then mammal (kangaroo). The other sequences are not in evolutionary order.
Ice absorbs latent heat of fusion from the drink while melting, which lowers the drink's temperature, so R correctly explains A.
Jalaluddin Khalji ruled 1290-1296, Muhammad bin Tughlaq 1325-1351 (closest to 1324-1351), Khizr Khan 1414-1421 and Bahlol Lodi 1451-1489, which gives A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1.
The nobles of Alauddin included Ulugh Khan, Nusrat Khan, Zafar Khan, Ain-ul-Mulk Multani, Malik Kafur and Ghazi Malik. Munim Khan is not among them, so he is the answer.
The notes only place Ain-ul-Mulk Multani under Alauddin Khalji and say nothing of Iltutmish. Iltutmish ruled long before Alauddin, so Multani could not have served him.
Warangal's ruler was the Kakatiya Prataparudra II, not Shankar Dev, so that pair is wrong. Devagiri-Ramachandra, Hoysala-Vira Ballala and Madurai-Pandya princes are consistent with the notes.

The campaigns aimed at wealth and tribute, so returning with immense wealth (II) is a significance. Statement IV, Kafur's promotion to Malik-naib, is also a recognised result, which makes II and IV the answer. The notes do not support I and III as significance.
Malik Kafur led the Deccan campaigns against Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai. Nusrat Khan and Ulugh Khan commanded the Gujarat campaign instead.
Chengiz Khan only reached the Indus under Iltutmish while chasing Jalaluddin Mangbarni and did not invade India beyond it. Qutlugh Khwaja did attack at Kili in 1299.

Zafar Khan (the Jafar Khan of the option) was killed at the Battle of Kili in 1299 against Qutlugh Khwaja's Mongols, so he is the general killed, unlike Nusrat Khan, who died at Ranthambore. The notes do not number the invasions, so the 'third' label is not directly confirmed.
Jayasi wrote Padmavat in Awadhi, an early form of Hindi, so statement II is accepted as correct. Muhammad Shah (1719-48) patronised Urdu, so statement I is also correct, and the answer is both.
Ghazi Malik, a noble of Alauddin, killed Khusrau Khan in 1320 and founded the Tughlaq dynasty as Ghiyasuddin Tughluq.
Cripps (1942) came first, then the Wavell Plan (1945), then the Cabinet Mission (1946), and the Radcliffe Award (August 1947) came last, giving III, I, IV, II.
The C.R. Formula of 1944 was authored by C. Rajagopalachari, not Nehru, C.R. Das or V.P. Menon.
The notes do not state this fact. Wavell's 'Breakdown Plan' (1946) was a contingency plan for a phased British withdrawal from India, which is why the answer is Viceroy Wavell.

The Cabinet Mission proposed a Union of provinces with a weak Centre (a federal-type structure), so I is correct. The notes mention nothing about enlarging the powers of courts or more Indians in the ICS, so II and III are wrong.
Helle Thorning-Schmidt became Denmark's first woman Prime Minister after the September 2011 election; the other countries listed did not elect her.
Bibek Debroy was Chairman of the EAC-PM (appointed 2017), so option 2 is correct; the others are economists who have not held that chair.
In 2014 the Supreme Court barred CBI Director Ranjit Sinha from supervising the 2G case investigation after allegations about his meetings with accused persons.
Amitabh Bachchan was named Maharashtra's horticulture brand ambassador, so option 4 is correct; the other actors were not given that role.
Aparna Kumar, an IPS officer of the ITBP, was the first Indian woman IPS officer to reach the South Pole, so option 2 is correct.
Ann Daniels and Caroline Hamilton are British (English) polar explorers who became the first women to reach both poles.
Forbes 2019 listed Jeff Bezos as the world's richest person; Musk was not on top then and Gates was second.
HAZOP is a study that checks the adequacy of safety measures, so option 1 is right.

Non-structural mitigation is community awareness and public education, so public education is a mitigation example. Emergency exercises are preparedness, and search and rescue and temporary housing belong to response and recovery.
MAT stands for Mitigation Assessment Team.
A hazard-specific control activity targets one particular hazard, such as flood levees against floods. 'Non planning required' is not such an activity.
The first forest-fire disaster management exercise was held in Uttarakhand in April 2017.
Uttarakhand's Disaster Mitigation & Management Centre won the Subhash Chandra Bose Aapda Prabandhan Puraskar 2020.
In the IMD colour code, Orange means 'be prepared'. Green is all well, Yellow is be aware, and Red is take action.
Prakampana was the super-cyclone preparedness exercise at Visakhapatnam, run by the Eastern Naval Command with civil agencies.
Drop, Cover, Hold is the safest action indoors during an earthquake.
For earthquake safety the recommended action is Drop! Cover! Hold under a strong table. The other options are incorrect statements.
IMD is headquartered at New Delhi, as the notes list it under institutions and locations.
GIS stores, analyses, overlays and presents spatial data on disasters. It does not perform rescue or response itself, or predict exact timings.
GIS is used to plan camps, routes and resources, so the statement that it cannot be used for this is incorrect.
GIS maps flood damage, so mapping the extent of flood damage is a specific GIS application. Medical treatment and nutrition analysis are not GIS functions.
Earth observation and communication satellites detect and deliver early warnings. They cannot give individual-level data or eliminate disasters.
GIS cannot fully resolve social issues, so the statement that it can completely resolve them is incorrect.
GIS cannot give details of individual victims and their exact locations, so that statement is incorrect.

GIS supports floodplain zoning and vulnerability mapping, evacuation route planning, and damage assessment. Statement IV, that GIS is not effective for assessing flood damage, is false. So I, II and III are the accurate statements.

Statement I is wrong: the first woman president was Annie Besant (1917); Sarojini Naidu (1925) was the first Indian woman. Statement II is right: Badruddin Tyabji (1887) was the first Muslim president.
Gandhi presided over only one Congress session, Belgaum 1924, so he was President once.
Pattabhi Sitaramayya wrote the History of the Indian National Congress.
The Battle of Talikota was fought on 23 January 1565, so 1565 A.D. is correct; 1526 is the First Battle of Panipat.
Vijayanagara faced a confederacy of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar. The Bahmani kingdom had already broken up, so option 2 is wrong.
Bijapur's Adil Shahis (Ali Adil Shah) were part of the sultanate confederacy that fought Rama Raya. The other options name only one sultanate, or Berar, which stayed out.
Vijayanagara was defeated at Talikota in 1565, after which Hampi was looted; so 1565 AD is correct.
Kshetrayya, composer of padams with the mudra Muvva Gopala, was patronised by Vijayaraghava Nayaka, the last Nayaka king of Tanjore. Tirumala Nayaka of Madurai is a different person.
Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission on 1 May 1897, naming it after his guru Ramakrishna Paramahansa. Ramakrishna was the guru and inspiration, not the founder, so option 1 is wrong.
The 73rd Amendment inserted Part IX with Articles 243 to 243O, which is 16 Articles.

Direct election, a five-year term and one-third women's reservation are compulsory. Statement I is wrong because the three tiers are not compulsory in every State: the middle tier is optional for States with a population of 20 lakh or less.
The notes do not state what happens when a Zila Panchayat president is suspended. This is a matter of State Panchayat law, so no line is linked.
The minimum age for Panchayat membership is 21 years, not 25, so option 2 is the incorrect statement. The other statements match the rules on term and reconstitution.
Janpad Panchayat is Madhya Pradesh, Kshetra Panchayat is Uttar Pradesh, Taluka Parishad is Gujarat and Anchalik Parishad is West Bengal. This gives the code 3 4 2 1.
The notes do not cover nomination of representatives by ex-officio members or by a woman Sarpanch. The 'Sarpanch's husband' proxy practice is not legal, so option 4 is the answer.
The notes do not cover the composition of a Gram Panchayat under this State's Act, such as the number of panchs or nominated members. Nominated members cannot vote, so statement VI is wrong.

Only statement III is correct because Article 243B provides for a Panchayat at the intermediate level, subject to the 20 lakh population exception. Statement I is wrong: one-third of seats are reserved for women, not 50% for SC/ST women. Statement II is wrong: the Gram Sabha consists of registered voters, not all persons living in the village.

Seats are filled by direct election, the Gram Sabha consists of registered voters, and the State Legislature endows Panchayats with powers. Statement III is wrong because Panchayats do not work on a principle of constitutional autonomy.
Under Article 243(b), the Gram Sabha is the body of all persons registered as voters in the electoral rolls of a village within the Panchayat area.
India pledged at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) to reach Net Zero by 2070, so 2070 is correct; 2050 and 2060 are the commonly assumed but wrong years.
The MNRE mission covers all five aims: energy security, a larger share of clean power, availability and access, affordability, and equity. So 'All of the above' is correct.
The Renewables Integration in India 2021 report was a joint NITI Aayog and International Energy Agency publication, so option 2 is correct; the other pairings are not the publishers.
The first in-depth review of India's energy policies (Jan 2020) was released by the IEA together with NITI Aayog. World Energy Council, OPEC and IRENA are distractors.
Mawsynram (Mausimram) in Meghalaya has the highest average annual rainfall in India; Cherrapunji is the tempting but wrong option.
Leh in Ladakh lies behind the Great Himalaya and is the lowest-rainfall place, so it gets the least rain among these.
Shillong is in Meghalaya, a very heavy rainfall area, while Ajmer in Rajasthan is dry; the other pairs do not differ as sharply.
Heavy to very heavy rainfall occurs in the Western Ghats, Meghalaya and the Northeast; the other regions are moderate or scanty.
Both are correct: monsoon duration falls from south to north (over 120 days in the SW peninsula, under 75 in W Rajasthan), and plains rainfall falls from east to west.
The leeward (eastern) side of the Western Ghats lies in the rain shadow. Rajasthan's dryness is due to the Aravalli alignment, not a rain shadow, and the Nilgiri windward slopes are wet.
Pune and Bengaluru lie in the rain shadow east of the Western Ghats, and Leh is behind the Great Himalaya. Mangaluru is on the windward west coast.
Western Disturbances bring winter rain to north-west India, entering from the west, so rainfall decreases from west to east as the moisture is spent.
Western Rajasthan has high rainfall variability (CV over 50%), unlike Meghalaya, Kerala and West Bengal, which have low variability.
About 68% of India's agricultural land is drought-prone (33% chronic plus 35%).
Hydrological drought is based on falling river flow (reduced streamflow) and groundwater. Lack of rain is meteorological and lack of soil moisture is agricultural drought.
The notes give the first voyage (1602, James Lancaster, factory at Bantam) but do not name the ship, so no line supports Red Dragon. Red Dragon was Lancaster's flagship on the first voyage.

James I sent both Hawkins and Roe as envoys to Jahangir. Charles II is linked with Bombay as dowry, not with Roe.
In Child's War (1686-90) the Company led by Josiah/John Child attacked Mughal shipping and was crushed by Aurangzeb. The Company had to pay a fine to be pardoned, so Sir John Child is the answer.
Surat got the first permanent English factory in 1613 through Jahangir's farman. Masulipatnam (1611) was earlier but only temporary.
Surat was the early Western Presidency of the Company and was later replaced by Bombay.
The founding years were Surat 1613, Madras 1639, Bombay 1668 and Calcutta 1690. This gives the order Surat, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta.
Rammohan Roy is called the Father of Modern India (also Maker of Modern India and first 'Modern Man'); Nehru, Gandhi and Bonnerjee do not carry this title.
Rammohan Roy is traditionally called the prophet of Indian nationalism, which is why he is the answer, but the notes do not state this title.
David Hare worked with Roy in founding the Hindu College (1817), his educational venture. Derozio was a teacher there and Dwarkanath was a Brahmo Sabha associate, not an education collaborator.
The Hindu College in Calcutta was founded in 1817 with Roy's help to David Hare, so 1817 is correct.
Rammohan Roy founded the Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1821) to promote rational monotheism, though the notes do not mention it. Vidyasagar, Keshab and Tagore did not found it.
Chellavva, titled Samasta Gandharva Vidya Kovida, was the court singer and dancer of Chalukya Bhima I, who gave her Attili village. Gunaga Vijayaditya is the tempting wrong option.
Lodhi Gardens in Delhi was earlier called Lady Willingdon Park, after the wife of the Viceroy Lord Willingdon. The other options are not known by this name.

Atala Mosque, Jaunpur (1408) is earliest, then Sher Shah's tomb at Sasaram (finished under Islam Shah, c. 1545), then Humayun's tomb (1565-72), and Rabia-ud-Daurani's tomb (Bibi ka Maqbara) last, under Aurangzeb's reign. The order is IV, II, III, I.
Gobar gas is biogas from cattle dung, and its main component is methane.
Biogas is mostly methane (about 50-75%), with CO2 and only traces of other gases, so methane is the largest component.
Biogas is methane-rich (50-75%), and methane is the component that burns as fuel gas. Butane, propane and ethane are not biogas constituents.
Third-generation (3G) biofuels are made from algae or algal biomass. Food crops are 1G feedstock and wood residue is 2G.
Gasohol is petrol (gasoline) blended with ethanol, typically about 10% ethanol, so option 2 is correct.
Annie Besant led the Theosophical Society in India and became its President in 1907 after Olcott's death. Hume, Griffith and Dufferin had no leadership role in it.
The Central Hindu College at Benaras was founded by Annie Besant in 1898 and was the nucleus of BHU. Malaviya founded BHU itself, so he is the tempting wrong option.
Viceroy Lord Hardinge II laid the foundation stone of BHU on 4 Feb 1916 (Basant Panchami). Malaviya was the founder and Besant cooperated, but neither laid the stone.

The Shuddhi Movement, which reconverted people who had turned to Islam or Christianity, was launched by the Arya Samaj. The Brahmo Samaj, Satyashodhak Samaj and Ramakrishna Mission had no such programme.
Humans do not emit water vapour directly in significant amounts; they raise it only indirectly, because warmer air holds more water vapour.
Greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate the Earth's outgoing heat, trapping it and warming the surface. The ozone layer, ocean currents and wind patterns do not trap heat in this way.
The Earth's surface re-emits long-wave infrared radiation, which greenhouse gases absorb, and this heats the atmosphere. UV rays, gamma rays and X-rays are not the radiation involved.
Greenhouse gases, ozone depletion and pollution are all commonly cited as causes of climate change, so 'All of the above' is the accepted answer. The notes do not state this directly.
The greenhouse effect concept was first proposed by the French scientist Joseph Fourier in the 1820s.
Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) is the largest source of emissions, and CO2 is the main gas it produces. CH4 and N2O come mainly from farming.
The greenhouse effect is a rise in Earth's temperature due to the concentration of greenhouse gases. It is not about growing plants in glass houses.
The enhanced greenhouse effect arises from rising GHG concentrations, with CO2 the biggest contributor. The atmospheric change linked to it is therefore an increase in CO2 concentration.
The atmosphere is heated mainly by long-wave terrestrial radiation, which the surface re-emits and the gases absorb, rather than directly by short-wave solar radiation.
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of air but does not absorb infrared radiation, so it is not a greenhouse gas. CO2, N2O and water vapour are all greenhouse gases.

The Twelfth Plan stressed faster, sustainable and inclusive growth, health, education and skills, and social-sector PPPs. A 'gene revolution' is not among its objectives, so option 4 is the one that does not belong.
The Second Plan (Nehru-Mahalanobis model) stressed rapid industrialisation with heavy and basic industries. The Fourth, Fifth and Sixth Plans had other priorities.
The First Plan gave top priority to agriculture and irrigation, with about a third of spending going to them (Bhakra Nangal, Hirakud). The Second Plan shifted to heavy industry.
The First Plan spent about a third of its outlay on agriculture and irrigation, which was the highest agricultural share. Later plans, such as the Second, shifted emphasis to industry.
The Tenth Plan ran from 1 April 2002 to 31 March 2007, i.e. 2002-07.
The Minimum Needs Programme began in the first year of the Fifth Plan, and anti-poverty programmes were first started in the Fifth Plan. The Fourth Plan introduced target-group programmes instead.
NRHM was launched in 2005, which falls in the Tenth Plan (2002-07), not the Eleventh.

Quorum under Art 100(3) is one-tenth, i.e. 10 percent of the total members; 15 percent is a wrong figure.

The Houses are unequal in financial matters (Money Bill only in LS) and in accountability of the Council of Ministers (no-confidence only in LS). Constitutional amendment and the election of the President are matters where they have equal powers.
Constitutional amendment bills have equal treatment in both Houses, with no joint sitting. Creating All India Services is an RS power, and removing the government and money matters rest with the LS.
Article 249 lets the Rajya Sabha, by a two-thirds resolution, authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest.
Lawmaking is the primary legislative function of Parliament; the other options are secondary or not legislative functions.
Parliament legislates, controls the executive and amends the Constitution. Executing policy decisions is the executive's job, not Parliament's.
Under Article 106, members of Parliament receive salaries and allowances as determined by Parliament by law.

The Houses are not co-equal: the Lok Sabha is superior in money matters and the no-confidence motion, though they are equal in some areas. Only the Rajya Sabha is indirectly elected, so option 4 is wrong.
Article 243(b) defines the Gram Sabha as the body of persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village within the Panchayat area, which matches option 3.
PESA 1996 emerged from the Bhuria Committee (1995) report. The Mehta, Rao and Ashok Mehta committees dealt with general Panchayati Raj, not Scheduled Areas.
Article 243(b) defines the Gram Sabha as persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village in the Panchayat area, so the members are the registered voters, not all adults or residents.
Part IX does not apply to the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram under Article 243M. Assam and Tripura are not fully exempt (only their Sixth Schedule areas).
Meghalaya is one of the three States (with Nagaland and Mizoram) fully exempt under Article 243M. Tripura and Assam are only partly exempt, and Goa is covered.
Nagaland and Mizoram are exempt under Article 243M, and J&K was outside Part IX until 2019. The option listing all three matches the exam key.
By 2010, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh had provided 50% reservation for women in local bodies. Bihar was the first, in 2006.

The Eleventh Schedule lists primary and secondary education, not higher education. Non-conventional energy, roads and libraries are all listed.
APEDB's report puts AP's share of India's exports at about 5.8% in 2020-21, so 5.8 is correct.

AP got first position in GSDP growth in 2015-16, when it was also the only State with double-digit growth.

For 2022-23 the sector shares were agriculture 36.19%, industry 23.36% and services 40.45%, which matches option 1. The other options swap the figures.
Services contributed 42% of AP's GVA at current prices in 2021-22.
Services contributed 42% of AP's GVA at current prices in 2021-22.

The notes do not state the Veterinary Biological Research Institute devolving to Telangana. They mention the White Paper but not this fact.

Natural increase is births minus deaths, so it results from the crude birth rate and crude death rate. Migration is a separate component, and marriage is not one.

The Annual Financial Statement (Budget) is presented in the Lok Sabha and, like Money Bills, cannot originate in the Rajya Sabha. Constitutional Amendment Bills and Bills altering State boundaries (Art. 3) can start in either House.

If the President does not summon the joint sitting, the Bill comes to an end.

A joint sitting applies to ordinary bills (and Financial Bills). Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills are excluded, and the Vice-President is not elected at a joint sitting.
Under Art. 108 the President notifies his 'intention' to summon the joint sitting.

The Lok Sabha Speaker presides over a joint sitting (Art. 118(4)). The Deputy Speaker presides only in his absence, and the Vice-President does not preside.
The Lok Sabha Speaker presides over the joint sitting (Art. 118(4)); the Rajya Sabha Chairman does not.
The President summons the joint sitting under Art. 108.
A joint sitting applies to ordinary bills. Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills are excluded, and an Appropriation Bill is a Money Bill.

A joint sitting resolves a deadlock over a Bill that the two Houses disagree on. Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections are not held through joint sittings, and Constitution Amendment Bills are excluded.
Only ordinary legislation can go to a joint sitting. Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills are excluded.
The Lok Sabha Speaker presides over a joint sitting under Art. 118(4).
The government gave SEBI regulatory powers to prevent capital-market scams. RBI regulates banking and SBI and ICICI are banks, not regulators.
SEBI was given statutory regulatory powers to prevent capital-market scams. RBI is the banking regulator, while SBI and ICICI are commercial banks.
SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) is the main regulator of the capital and securities (stock) market. The Ministry of Finance is only its parent ministry.
The SEBI Act was passed in 1992 (April 1992, in force from 30 Jan 1992), giving SEBI statutory status.
SEBI regulates the capital and securities market, including the share market. FEMA and the MRTP Act do not control the working of the share market.
SRO stands for Self Regulatory Organisations, bodies such as stock exchanges that regulate their own members, so option 1 is correct.

Duns are longitudinal valleys between the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwalik, so A is true. R is also true, since Dehra Dun, Kotli Dun and Patli Dun are examples, but it only lists examples and does not explain why they are called Duns.
The notes do not cover the Dogras. They are the people of the Jammu region, from the southern Pir Panjal foothills to the Punjab plains.
The Kumaon Himalaya lies between the Sutlej and the Kali. The Punjab Himalaya lies west of the Sutlej, between the Indus and the Sutlej.
Godwin Austen is another name for K2, which lies in the Karakoram. Everest and Kanchenjunga are in the Himalayas.
Nanga Parbat, at the western end of the Himalaya, is 8,126 m high.
Stars such as the sun run on fusion (hydrogen → helium), not fission, so nuclear fusion is correct.
The hydrogen bomb works by uncontrolled fusion of deuterium/tritium into helium, triggered by a fission bomb. The atom bomb is the one based on fission.
Fission occurs when a neutron hits a heavy nucleus such as U-235, which splits and releases 2–3 more neutrons. Protons and electrons do not trigger fission.
In a reactor the chain reaction is controlled by moderators and control rods, while in an atom bomb it is uncontrolled. Both involve chain reactions.
The hydrogen bomb works by uncontrolled fusion of deuterium/tritium into helium, triggered by a fission bomb. The atom bomb is the one based on fission.
Stars such as the sun run on fusion (hydrogen → helium), not fission, so the fusion reaction is correct.
Breaking apart of a nucleus is fission, not fusion, so option 2 is the incorrect statement. Fusion is the joining of light nuclei.
Zirconium (Z = 40) is not radioactive, whereas elements above Z 80 are mostly radioactive. Astatine and francium are heavy radioactive elements, and tritium is a radioactive hydrogen isotope.
Beta rays are electrons (negative beta) or positrons (positive beta) emitted from the nucleus, so they are charged particles. They are not neutral and not electromagnetic radiation (that is gamma).
Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide by law for adjudicating inter-State river water disputes. The other articles do not deal with this.

The Apex Council under Sec. 84 has the Union Water Resources (Jal Shakti) Minister as chair and the Chief Ministers of AP and Telangana as members, and it supervises the GRMB and KRMB. It includes no Home Minister.
The KRMB is to install telemetry meters at about 47 points to monitor water use by both States, so 47 is correct.

AP's petition to notify the KRMB's jurisdiction was made under Section 87, which deals with Board jurisdiction over projects notified by the Centre. Section 85 only constitutes the Boards, and Sec. 89 concerns KWDT-II.
The notes do not state the 834 feet power-generation objection. Telangana's power generation at Srisailam was the reason for AP's protest, specifically generation below the 834 ft level.
In the 2014 ad hoc split of the Krishna waters, AP gets 512 TMC and Telangana 299 TMC (66:34). 299 is Telangana's share.
Statement 1 is wrong because KCC was launched in August 1998, not 2001. Statement 2 is right because the scheme aims at adequate and timely credit for cultivation needs, so only 2 is correct.
KCC was launched in August 1998 (1998-99) as a NABARD model scheme on the R.V. Gupta Committee recommendation.
KCC was launched in August 1998 (1998-99), not 2001.
The agency order of institutional agricultural credit is commercial banks > cooperative banks > RRBs, i.e. 3, 1, 2.
Commercial banks are the largest source of agricultural credit, about three-fourths of the total (73.86% in 2010-11), far ahead of cooperatives and RRBs.

Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta is the Sanskrit drama on the overthrow of the Nandas and the rise of Chandragupta Maurya. Arthashastra is a statecraft treatise and Indica is a foreign account, so neither has this plot.
Indica was written by the Greek envoy Megasthenes, who was at Chandragupta Maurya's court at Pataliputra. Diodorus, Strabo and Pliny only preserved fragments of it.
Indica was written by Megasthenes, the Greek envoy of Seleucus I to Chandragupta's court. Deimachus was a later envoy to Bindusara and Pliny only preserved fragments.

Megasthenes' Indica describes Pataliputra's administration by six committees of five members each, with town officials called Astynomoi. The Arthashastra and Ashokan inscriptions do not give this account.
Megasthenes' Indica claimed there was no slavery in India, which was wrong. The Arthashastra and Ashokan edicts actually mention dasas.

Megasthenes' Indica gives the account of city administration, with six committees of five members each for Pataliputra. This is not the focus of the Arthashastra, Mudrarakshasa or the Ashokan inscriptions.
Megasthenes' Indica described Indian society as seven classes rather than the fourfold varna system. The Arthashastra and the other sources do not give this seven-class division.
Megasthenes' Indica described society as seven classes rather than the fourfold varna. The Arthashastra, edicts and Puranas do not give this division.
Indica was written by Megasthenes, the Greek envoy at Chandragupta Maurya's court at Pataliputra. Plutarch, Justin and Herodotus did not write it.
James Prinsep first deciphered the Ashokan edicts in 1837. The other names listed are not credited with this.
James Prinsep, the British scholar, first deciphered the Ashokan edicts in 1837, so he is the answer.
James Prinsep first deciphered Ashoka's edicts in 1837. Buhler, Max Muller and William Jones are not credited with the first decipherment.

Article 249 lets the Rajya Sabha, by a resolution backed by two-thirds of members present and voting, empower Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest. Article 250 deals with National Emergency, so it is the tempting wrong option.

Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws on State List subjects to implement international treaties, agreements or conventions, without any State's consent. Articles 249, 250 and 252 cover other situations (Rajya Sabha resolution, Emergency, State consent).

Parliament may legislate on a State List subject if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution under Article 249 by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. The President's wish or the concerned State's request alone is not enough, and 'under any circumstances' is wrong because Parliament is otherwise barred.

Under Article 249, a Rajya Sabha resolution backed by two-thirds of members present and voting, declaring it necessary or expedient in the national interest, lets Parliament legislate on a State List matter. No order from the President, Supreme Court or Prime Minister can confer this power.

The doctrine of paramountcy resolves conflict where both Centre and States can legislate on the same matter (Concurrent List): the Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy (Art. 254).
VAT is a non-cascading tax on value added at all stages between production and final sale, so option 4 is right.
Service tax was introduced in 1994-95 on the advice of the Raja J. Chelliah Tax Reforms Committee, not the Kelkar committee.
The K.N. Raj Committee on Agricultural Wealth and Income Tax recommended an agricultural holding tax; the notes do not state this, and Chelliah dealt with general tax reform.
MODVAT, introduced in 1986 to ease cascading, is a Union excise duty credit scheme, so it relates to excise duty and not to sales, wealth or income tax.
CENVAT replaced MODVAT from 1 April 2000 and relates to Union excise duties, not customs or central sales tax.
Buddhacharita is a Sanskrit work by Ashvaghosha, the court poet of Kanishka.
Milindapanha records the dialogue of Nagasena and King Milinda and is a Pali text, not Sanskrit.
The Mahavamsa, a Pali Sri Lankan chronicle, records Ashoka and the third council. The Pitakas are canonical collections and not accounts of Ashoka.
Edwin Arnold's The Light of Asia drew on the Lalitavistara, a Sanskrit Buddha biography. The notes do not state this.
Pali was the language of the early Buddhist canon and its propagation. Sanskrit later replaced Pali, which contributed to Buddhism's decline.
Sthaviravadins are Hinayana, so statement I is wrong. Lokottaravadins were an offshoot of the Mahasanghikas, and Mahasanghika deification of the Buddha fostered Mahayana, so II and III are correct.
Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika school of Mahayana and its Sunyata doctrine, based on the Prajnaparamita texts. Kanishka was a patron, not a formulator of ideas.
Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika (Sunyavada) school, which teaches Shunyata. The other options are not linked to this doctrine.
In April 2022 NITI Aayog and UNICEF India signed the Statement of Intent on SDGs with a focus on children, so option (2) is correct.
The April 2022 NITI Aayog–UNICEF India Statement of Intent on SDGs focused on children, so option (2) is correct.
In August 2023 NITI Aayog signed an MoU with UNDP to fast-track the SDGs, so UNDP is correct.
SDG 14 (Life Below Water) is the goal on conserving and sustainably using oceans, seas and marine resources; SDG 15 is Life on Land.
SDG India Index is by NITI Aayog, Global SDG Report by the UN Statistics Division, VNR by UN Member States and EPI by Yale and Columbia, so A-i, B-ii, C-iii, D-iv is correct.
In the 2018 baseline SDG India Index, Kerala and Himachal Pradesh were the front runners with a score of 69.
Gujarat is not among the top-ranking States in the SDG India Index (2019-20 edition: Gujarat not in top five), so it is the answer.

The 2022 Global Index of SDGs ranked India 121st out of 163 countries, so option (3) is correct.
Magadhas were the bards/chroniclers who memorised and recited genealogies, dynastic histories and epic tales; Shramanas and Parivrajakas were ascetics, not chroniclers.
The Gathasaptasati (Gadhasapthasati) is a Prakrit anthology by King Hala that reflects Satavahana society, but it does not narrate the early history of the family as the other listed works do.
Rajatarangini, the chronicle of the kings of Kashmir, was written by Kalhana. Arthashastra is by Kautilya and Indica by Megasthenes.

Panini, author of the Ashtadhyayi, the earliest known Sanskrit grammar, is traditionally placed in the 6th-5th century BC, so option 2 is right.
Rajatarangini was written by Kalhana in the 12th century. Megasthenes, Al-Biruni and Herodotus were foreign writers.

The Dipavamsa is a Sri Lankan Pali chronicle, not a biography of a king, whereas Harshacharita, Vikramankadevacharita and Prithviraja Vijaya are biographies of kings. So only I is not a historical biography.
The Rigveda was composed in Vedic Sanskrit, the earliest form of Sanskrit. Pali and Prakrit are later languages, and Brahmi is a script, not a language.
National Parks are in-situ sites, conserving species within their natural habitat, so maintenance of genetic diversity there is in-situ conservation, not ex-situ.
A national park protects species and the ecosystem in their natural habitat, which is in-situ conservation; ex-situ means outside the habitat (zoos, gene banks).

Both statements are wrong: ESZs are notified under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, not WPA 1972. They prohibit only certain activities (mining, polluting industries) while regulating others and permitting ongoing agriculture.
Dibru-Saikhowa and Great Rann of Kutch are not in WNBR, and Cold Desert was not in it at the time the question was framed. Nokrek and Khangchendzonga are in WNBR, so option 4 is correct.

Biosphere reserves protect a whole ecosystem with core, buffer and transition zones, involving local communities. This makes them the key strategy, while botanical gardens are only ex-situ.
Biosphere reserves have a protected core with viable populations of all trophic levels, conserving biodiversity and genetic resources in situ. Genetic diversity is the best fit among the options.

e-PDS distributes food grains to BPL families through fair price shops using biometric authentication and stock tracking. The other options are unrelated to PDS.
Anantapuram had the most ration (fair price) shops as of Feb 2017, per the notes.
The 2017 white ration card ceiling is Rs 75,000 a year for urban families (Rs 60,000 rural); Rs 60,000 is the rural limit.
YSR Navodayam is an MSME debt restructuring scheme, not a transport-sector self-employment scheme, so pair 4 is incorrect. The Chedodu and Thodu descriptions match the notes.
APSHCL launched YSR Jagananna Housing on 3 June 2021 (Jagananna colonies), so option 2 is correct.
The notes state Badugu Vikasam is not a scheme to encourage OBCs and was not launched on 26 October 2022, so neither statement is correct.

Vidya Deevena gives 100% fee reimbursement to SC, ST, BC, Minorities, Kapu, EBC and Differently Abled students plus Rs 20,000 maintenance support, matching a and b; the notes do not give the 15.5 lakh figure, but the keyed answer includes c.
Dudekula, a Muslim community in the AP BC list, received special cover in the 2021-22 budget; Bohra and Mappila are not mentioned.
Dulhan gives Rs 50,000 to poor Muslim brides via the AP State Minorities Finance Corporation, so option 2 is correct. It is not a general uplift scheme for the whole community.
Lilavati, the famous mathematics treatise, was written by Bhaskaracharya (Bhaskara II). Ramanuja was a Vedanta philosopher, Kautilya wrote the Arthashastra and Amartya Sen is a modern economist.
Makkhali Gosala is the usual answer for founder of the Ajivika sect, as its most important leader and populariser. The other options are Buddhist scholars (Vasubandhu, Dignaga, Upagupta).
The Ajivikas believed in Niyati (fate): fate assigns everything and humans are incapable of changing it. Jains and Buddhists stress effort.
The Ajivikas believed in Niyati, with everything predetermined by fate before birth and no free will. Charvaka, Jainism and Buddhism do not hold this fatalism.
"Fate assigns everything, human is incapable" is the Ajivika doctrine of Niyati. Jains and Buddhists emphasise effort.
Gosala (Makkhali Gosala) was the leader of the Ajivika sect and taught Niyativada (fatalism). He is not linked with the Vajrayana, Sthaviravada or Mahasamghika Buddhist schools.
Lokayata is another name for the Charvaka school of materialism, so Charvaka is the answer.
Charvaka is a complete materialism whose highest value is Kama (material pleasure), not Dharma or Moksha.
The aphorism about living happily and drinking ghee even on debt is the Charvaka maxim, which rejects the afterlife. Ajivikas believed in fate, not this hedonism.
The NDC's ex-officio secretary is the Secretary of the Planning Commission, which serviced the Council. The notes do not state this fact.
The NDC linked the Planning Commission and the States, so it acted as the coordinator between them. The Finance Commission and the National Integration Council have no such role.
NITI Aayog does not allocate funds to States, unlike the Planning Commission; that work lies with the Finance Ministry and the Finance Commission. So option 4 is what it does not envisage.
Paradip port in Odisha lies at the mouth of the Mahanadi river, so Mahanadi is correct.
Kamarajar (Ennore) Port is the first major port registered as a company and corporatised, so it is not run by a Port Trust Board; Haldia, Paradip and Kandla are not.
Chennai is an artificial port, whereas Kandla is tidal and Haldia a riverine port.
Mumbai is treated as the biggest port (largest natural harbour) among the options; Visakhapatnam, Tuticorin and Kandla are not.
Haldia is a decongestion/outport port relieving Kolkata, a riverine port upstream; the other options are not outports.
JNPA (Nhava Sheva) was developed in 1989 to ease congestion at Mumbai port.
Mundra is in Gujarat (largest private port), not Andhra Pradesh, so the pair is wrong.
Going north to south: Kandla (Gujarat, west), Haldia (West Bengal), Paradip (Odisha), then Kochi (Kerala) at the southwest.
Visakhapatnam is a natural landlocked, protected harbour, whereas Chennai and Tuticorin are artificial and Haldia is riverine.
Reverse osmosis applies pressure on the concentrated (salt) side so salts are left behind, giving pure water (desalination).
A fuse works on the heating effect of electric current: the low-melting wire heats and melts when current is excessive, breaking the circuit.
In a pressure cooker the higher pressure raises the boiling point of water (~120 C), so food cooks faster. It is not because water boils at a lower temperature.
Bleaching powder is calcium oxychloride, so option 2 is correct; calcium hydroxide is only a reactant used to make it.
Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with chromium (plus some nickel), and the chromium gives corrosion resistance. Carbon is also in steel but is not the metal added for stainlessness.
The Coastal and Marine Ecosystem mission is not one of the eight NAPCC missions. Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency and Sustainable Habitat are all core missions.

The National Water Mission aims at a public water database, a focus on over-exploited areas and a 20% gain in water-use efficiency, which fits the recycling and desalination-type statements I and II. River interlinking of Himalayan and peninsular rivers (III) and full reimbursement of farmers' bore-well costs (IV) are not mission goals.
Nuclear/atomic energy is not among the eight NAPCC missions. Solar and Green India (afforestation) are missions, and the proposed Waste-to-Energy idea is the closest to the waste option.

Green India Mission aims to protect, restore and enhance forest cover and tackles both adaptation and mitigation, so only III is correct. Green accounting (I) and a second green revolution (II) are not its aims.
FFFAP stands for Fridays For Future Andhra Pradesh, the group that joined the first global climate strike in 2019.
Andhra Pradesh created its exclusive Climate Change Cell in November 2022.

Chemical energy is energy stored in the bonds of atoms and molecules, so statement II is correct. Statements I and III swap the definitions of sound (longitudinal waves) and radiant energy (electromagnetic transverse waves), so they are wrong.
In a hydro plant stored water (potential) falls, drives a turbine and generator, so the net conversion is potential to electrical energy.

Chemical, nuclear and other stored forms are potential energy, but electrical energy is not listed as stored here. The notes say electric, chemical and nuclear are stored forms, so this is tricky. The answer follows the key that electrical energy is the odd one out, being a transferred or flowing form rather than stored.
Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy. Heat (thermal) energy is internal molecular energy and is not part of it.
Energy of every form, including mechanical energy, is measured in joules. Watt is the unit of power.
Kinetic energy equals half mass times velocity squared, so it depends on mass and velocity.
A moving body has kinetic energy due to its motion. Friction and gravity are forces, not energy.
A raised hammer is at a height and holds stored energy of position, which is potential energy. It has no kinetic energy while at rest.
A released compressed slinky turns its stored potential energy into the energy of motion, which is kinetic energy.
A body rolling down a hill is moving, so it has kinetic energy, and it is still at a height above the bottom, so it has potential energy too. Together these make up its mechanical energy.
The Azamgarh proclamation of 25 August 1857 called for restoration of the Mughal Badshahi (Bahadur Shah's rule); it did not support the English or stress a Hindu-Muslim divide.
Mangal Pandey was a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry, which was disbanded after the Barrackpore incident; the other regiments named are not linked to him.
The notes do not mention Gandhi's naming of Catherine Mary Heilman as 'Saralaben'. She was a British disciple of Gandhi; Madeleine Slade was named 'Mirabehn' instead.
The notes record Diu being taken from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat by the Portuguese (1535), but not his death. He was killed in a conflict with the Portuguese in 1537, so Portuguese is correct.
Krishnadevaraya was on friendly terms with the Portuguese: he treated with Friar Luis and allowed Albuquerque to build a fort at Bhatkal for the horse trade.
William Hawkins was the envoy of James I who came to Jahangir's court in 1609. The other options were not the envoy of James I in the notes; Edward Terry was only Roe's chaplain.
Jahangir gave the title 'English Khan' to Captain William Hawkins, not to Roe or Terry.
The notes only identify Edward Terry as Roe's chaplain at Jahangir's court and do not state the Ganga water detail. Terry's account of the Mughal court records this, so he is the answer.
The Dutch first factory in Andhra was at Masulipatnam in 1605. Nizampatnam came later.
The notes say Andhra calico/Kalamkari was a major export. The cotton cloth from Calicut was called 'calico' in Europe, derived from the name Calicut.
TOFI stands for Trees Outside Forests in India, the programme launched by the AP Forest Department with USAID in Nov 2022.
TOFI stands for Trees Outside Forests in India, the programme launched by the AP Forest Department with USAID in Nov 2022.
ISFR 2019 reported forest plus tree cover of 24.56% of India's area, so option 3 is correct.
ISFR 2015 estimated about 36% of forest cover to be prone to frequent fires, with dry deciduous forests most vulnerable.

Silver iodide (AgI) is the standard cloud-seeding agent because its crystal shape mimics ice, so it is the substance used for artificial rain; silver bromide and ammonium nitrate are not the seeding agents listed.
Silver iodide is the chemical used in cloud seeding for artificial rain because its crystals resemble ice; the other options are not seeding agents.
A hygrometer measures humidity, i.e. the moisture in the air; barometer, anemometer and thermometer measure pressure, wind speed and temperature.
A wet and dry bulb thermometer (psychrometer) gives humidity from the difference between wet- and dry-bulb readings. The other instruments measure wind direction, pressure and temperature extremes.
An isoneph joins places with equal cloudiness, whereas an isobar joins equal pressure and an isohyet joins equal rainfall.
A hygrometer measures the moisture (humidity) of air; a hydrometer, the tempting option, measures the density of a liquid.
Rain washes dust and pollutants out of the air as precipitation, so it helps clean the polluted environment; oxygen, nitrogen and air do not do this.
The Speaker is chosen by the Lok Sabha from among its members (Art 93), not appointed by the President. The CJI and service chiefs are appointed by the President.

Only III is correct: the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker (Art 94(b)). He is chosen by the House and is not removable at the President's pleasure (I wrong). He must already be an elected member; the six-month grace applies only to Ministers (II wrong).
The notes do not cover the Warrant of Precedence. As per the Warrant, a Governor within his own State ranks immediately after the President, above the Deputy PM, former Presidents and the Speaker.

Statement I is right: the Speaker's salary is charged on the Consolidated Fund (Art 97). Statement II is also right under the Warrant of Precedence, where the Speaker ranks 7th, above Cabinet Ministers other than the PM, so both are correct.
The Speaker can be removed only by a Lok Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all the then members with 14 days' notice. The President, PM or Rajya Sabha has no role.
During his own removal resolution the Speaker cannot preside but may speak and vote in the first instance. He has no casting vote, so option 4 is the incorrect statement.
Under Art 94(b) the Speaker resigns by a letter addressed to the Deputy Speaker, not to the President or PM.
The Speaker is removed by a Lok Sabha resolution passed by an effective majority (a majority of all the then members) with 14 days' notice, not by two-thirds or by the President.

Stupa is a mound, the garbhagriha is where the deity's image is installed, and the pradakshina patha is the circular path around the stupa. The mandapa is the assembly place in temples, which gives 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c.
A chaitya is a prayer and assembly hall, often with a stupa at the far end, while a vihara is a monastery where monks live. So option 2 is right; option 1 reverses the two.
The Phanigiri Buddhist site in Suryapet, Telangana, yielded a life-size stucco sculpture, so the answer is Telangana.
Sachchidananda Sinha, as the eldest member, was temporary President and chaired the first sitting. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President only on 11 Dec 1946.
The National Flag's wheel is the Ashoka Chakra (Dharmachakra), which has 24 spokes.
The first meeting was chaired by Dr Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary President (eldest member). Rajendra Prasad became permanent President two days later.

Statements (i) and (iii) are correct: the first meeting was on 9 Dec 1946 and the Muslim League boycotted it. (ii) is wrong because Sinha was only the temporary President; the permanent President was Rajendra Prasad.
Rajendra Prasad was popularly called 'Deshratna'. The notes do not state this epithet.
Pherozeshah Mehta, with K.T. Telang and Badruddin Tyabji, founded the Bombay Presidency Association in 1885; Anandacharlu belonged to the Madras Mahajana Sabha and Banerjea to the Indian Association.
The East India Association was in London (not Calcutta) and the Indian Association was in Calcutta (not Bombay), so pairs II and IV do not match.
A.O. Hume, a retired ICS officer, organised the Congress and became its first General Secretary, so he is called its Father; the others did not found it.
The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885, with its first session held on 28-31 December 1885 in Bombay.
A.O. Hume, a retired British ICS officer, founded the Congress and became its first General Secretary; Tilak, Motilal Nehru and Banerjea were not its founders.

Rain water helps raise nitrogen content because lightning fixes atmospheric N2 into nitrates/ammonia that rain carries to the soil. Phosphorus, calcium and potassium are sedimentary cycle elements with no atmospheric phase.

All three statements are correct: agricultural soils (N fertiliser) emit nitrogen oxides such as nitrous oxide, and livestock (cattle) and poultry release ammonia and other reactive nitrogen compounds. The notes confirm soil N releases and human-driven nitrogen overload, so I, II and III are all correct.

Both statements are true: disturbance of seral stages produces sub-climax vegetation, and secondary succession is faster than primary because soil, seeds and roots remain. But the speed of secondary succession does not explain why disturbance leads to a sub-climax community, so R is not the explanation of A.

Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate (NO3−), ammonifying bacteria form NH4+/ammonia from organic nitrogen, denitrifying bacteria return N2 to the air, and Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen. This gives A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1.
The statement is not correct because the FD for 2019-20 was budgeted at 3.3% but the actual was 4.6%, so it did not match the Budget Estimates.

Neither statement is supported: the fiscal deficit did not rise steadily over the decade (it fell from about 5.9% to 3.5%, spiked in 2020-21, then fell again), and the notes give no steady-rise fact for tax revenue either.
Downsizing bureaucracy cuts spending and selling PSU shares (disinvestment) raises receipts, so III and IV reduce the deficit. FDI and privatising higher education are not deficit-control measures.
Reducing revenue expenditure and rationalising subsidies cut spending and so reduce the deficit. New welfare schemes add spending, and expanding industries is not a deficit-reduction measure.
Centrifugal force from rotation is greatest at the Equator and zero at the poles, so weight is least at the Equator and greatest at the poles. Weight is therefore not the same everywhere.
Two high tides occur each day, about 12 h 25 min apart, which is approximately 12 h 26 min. 24 h 52 min is the lunar day, the interval between two high tides on the same side.
Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth and Moon are in line, which happens at both new moon and full moon. So both days are correct, not just one.

Seasons arise mainly from the Earth's axial tilt together with revolution. With a circular orbit the varying Earth–Sun distance (perihelion and aphelion) would disappear, which would reduce the difference between seasons.

The Cabinet Mission proposed a Union with a weak Centre and groups of provinces (a federal-type structure); nothing in the plan enlarged the powers of the courts or increased Indians in the ICS, so only I is correct.
The Cabinet Mission arrived on 24 March 1946, so the year is 1946.
The members were Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps and A.V. Alexander. Wavell was the Viceroy, not a member of the Mission.
The plan envisaged a Union of provinces with a weak Centre (Defence, Foreign Affairs, Communications), so 'Union of States' fits best.
The Muslim League called for Direct Action, and 16 August 1946 was Direct Action Day (the Great Calcutta Killings).
The Constituent Assembly was envisaged by the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946, not by the Independence Act or a Congress resolution.
Acid rain is formed when SO2 and NOx react to give sulphuric acid (about two-thirds) and nitric acid (about one-third), so both HNO3 and H2SO4 are components. CO2 is not a component of acid rain.
Fly ash is the residue produced by coal-fired thermal power plants, so burning coal generates it. Charcoal, diesel/kerosene and CNG are not its source.
Asbestos dust affects the lung, lead damages the brain, mercury affects the stomach, and carbon monoxide affects the blood stream (forms carboxyhaemoglobin). This gives the code 3 1 2 4.

Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with 200–250 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. Carbon dioxide and the nitrogen oxides do not act this way.
Carbon monoxide is produced by incomplete combustion, as in vehicle exhaust, and is also present in cigarette smoke. CO2 is the product of complete combustion.

The C. Rangarajan Committee (1993) is the disinvestment committee, recommending 49% disinvestment in reserved PSUs and 74% in others. The tempting Arjun Sengupta committee dealt with MoUs, not disinvestment.

The AICC session at Vijayawada (31 March-1 April 1921) accepted Gandhi's leadership of the national struggle, so the year is 1921. The 1919 Vijayawada meeting was a different event, about Tilak and the Paris Peace Conference.
Kanneganti Hanumanthu, hero of the Palnadu satyagraha, was born in Guntur district.

The core challenge in managing India's oil consumption is supply-chain disruption and volatile global oil prices. Consistent prices, abundant reserves or low demand do not apply, since India has only 0.4% of world oil reserves and imports about 88.5% of its crude.
The Methanol Economy aims to cut the oil import bill, reduce GHG emissions and convert coal reserves and municipal solid waste into methanol, so all three statements are correct.

Landing a probe on a comet (ESA's Rosetta/Philae) lets scientists analyse its ice and organic material, so they can study whether comets brought organic matter and water to Earth. It does not reveal the age of the Sun or the universe, or any new atomic particle.
The Leonid meteor shower, debris of Comet Tempel-Tuttle, is an astronomical event, so it greatly attracted astronomers who study meteors and comets.
Cosmic dust is tiny particles of solid matter spread throughout space, not material specific to the Moon, the Sun or constellations.
OSIRIS-REx was renamed OSIRIS-APEX to study the asteroid Apophis, which passes close to Earth in 2029 (the 'God of Chaos' asteroid).
NASA's Juno mission was sent to orbit and study Jupiter, its atmosphere, magnetic field and interior, so the answer is Jupiter.
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory is located in Pasadena, California, not Houston (Johnson Space Center) or Cape Kennedy (launch site).

Evolved LISA (eLISA) is the gravitational-wave observatory planned as three spacecraft in an equilateral triangle with million-km sides linked by lasers. LISA Pathfinder was only a technology test with a much smaller setup.
Mir Mahbub Ali Khan (Asaf Jah VI) succeeded as an infant and is the youngest Asaf Jahi ruler; the other options were adult rulers.
Mir Mahbub Ali Khan (Asaf Jah VI) succeeded as an infant and is the youngest Asaf Jahi ruler; the other options were adult rulers.
The Salar Jung family rose to prominence under Nasir-ud-Daula, when Mir Turab Ali Khan became Diwan in 1853 (Salar Jung I).

Both statements are true: Afzal-ud-Daula was Nizam in 1857 and was loyal to the British. But the reason does not explain the assertion, which concerns the lack of local leaders in Andhra; Andhra lay largely under direct British rule, not under the Nizam.
Alessandro Volta isolated methane (marsh gas) in 1776 and showed that a methane-air mixture explodes with an electric spark. The notes do not cover this history.
Natural gas is a fossil fuel, formed over millions of years. Wood is not a fossil fuel, and coke and producer gas are manufactured fuels rather than natural fossil fuels.
Gobar gas (biogas) is mainly CH4. Coal gas is H2, CH4 and CO. Producer gas is CO with N2 (and H2). Water gas is CO + H2. This gives A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1.
India ranked 3rd in the Renewable Energy Country Attractiveness Index 2021.
SCCL is held by the Telangana government and the Centre in a 51:49 ratio, so option 4 is right.
SCCL is held by the Telangana government and the Centre in a 51:49 ratio, so option 4 is right.
The pupil is the opening whose size is adjusted by the iris to regulate the light entering the eye; the notes do not cover this.
The stapes, a middle-ear ossicle, is the smallest bone in the human body; the vomer and the other ossicles are larger.
