The Uttarakhand Bhookamp Alert, made by IIT Roorkee and launched in 2021, is India's first earthquake early warning mobile app.

GIS mapping, real-time remote sensing and social media or mobile app alerts are all used in disaster management, so I, III and IV are correct. Statement II is false because early warning systems use modern technology too, not only traditional communication.

Using heavy materials in construction in vulnerable areas is not a preparedness strategy. Heavier buildings suffer greater seismic force, so lightweight and earthquake-resistant designs are preferred.
The Governor appoints the Chief Minister under Art. 164(1), not the President (the exception is Delhi and Puducherry).
The Governor appoints the CM under Art. 164(1), so Article 164 is correct. Art. 163 deals with aid and advice by the Council of Ministers.
The 91st Amendment (Art. 164(1A)) fixes the minimum size of the State Council of Ministers, including the CM, at 12.
Under Art. 164(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, the minimum strength of the Council of Ministers including the CM is 12.
A Tribal Welfare Minister is compulsory in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha; only Madhya Pradesh is among the options.
Article 167 defines the duties of the CM towards the Governor. Art. 164 deals with appointment and responsibility of Ministers, and Art. 165 with the Advocate General.
Mayawati had been UP Chief Minister three times by May 2002, the first time in 1995.
Raskhan was a Muslim Krishna-devotee poet whose work was Prem Vatika, not Rasikpriya (which is Keshavdas's work), so the pair Raskhan - Rasikpriya is wrongly matched.
Keshavdas (Keshav) of the Riti period wrote Ramchandrika and Rasikpriya. Raskhan is a tempting option but his known work in the notes is Prem Vatika.
Tukaram lived in the 17th century (c. 1608-1650), so he was a contemporary of Jahangir (1605-1627), as well as Shah Jahan. Babur and Akbar were earlier, and Aurangzeb came later.

The weavers' scheme covers a family of four, requires at least 50% income from handloom, and is open to men and women with no age cap. So the claim that it covers people up to 60 years is not an eligibility condition.
Aam Aadmi Bima Yojana was launched on 2 October 2007, so option 4 is correct.
PMSBY's premium was ₹12 per year until 31 May 2022 (now ₹20), so ₹12 is the answer among the options. The ₹330 options match no PMSBY premium.

APY is for ages 18-40 with a guaranteed pension of ₹1,000-5,000 a month at 60, so I and II are true. The Government only co-contributes 50% (or ₹1,000 a year) for a limited period, not 100%, so III is false.
NSAP aims at old-age pension to the very poor (BPL households), as it fulfils Article 41. It is not general insurance or support specific to SC/ST.
The Murti Devi Award is a literary award given by the Bharatiya Jnanpith (Indian Jnanpith Trust), not by Sahitya Akademi or the ministry.
Mother Teresa, the 1979 Nobel Peace laureate, was canonised by Pope Francis on 4 September 2016; the others are not Catholic saints.
Peter Tabichi, who won the Global Teacher Prize 2019, is a teacher from Kenya.
The 2019 UNESCO World Press Freedom Prize went to Reuters journalists Kyaw Soe Oo and Wa Lone of Myanmar, who were jailed for their reporting.
The UN Human Rights Prize 2018 was shared by Rebeca Gyumi, Asma Jahangir, Joenia Wapichana and Front Line Defenders, so all three women are winners.
The 2019 Nobel Peace Prize went to Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed Ali for peace with Eritrea. Nadia Murad won in 2018.
Nobel Prizes (except Peace) are presented in Stockholm on 10 December; the Peace Prize is presented in Oslo.
The Sabin Award, given by Amphibian Survival Alliance, recognises amphibian conservation.
The Global Goalkeeper Awards are given by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation to recognise progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals.
The notes do not cover SEBI's relaxation of norms for sovereign wealth funds. Relaxing norms is generally aimed at attracting more foreign investment, so option 1 is the best fit.
Ozone is concentrated mainly in the lower stratosphere (about 15-35 km), so the stratosphere is the ozone-rich zone.
Both statements are true. The ozone layer absorbs harmful UV radiation, whose excess causes cataract, skin cancer and lower crop yield, so R explains why ozone is essential for life.
Ozone depletion is caused mainly by halocarbons such as CFCs, which release chlorine and bromine. UV rays do not deplete ozone; they are absorbed by it.
The main cause of ozone depletion is halocarbons (CFCs, HCFCs), which release chlorine and bromine in the stratosphere. CO₂, methane and water vapour are not the main ozone-depleting agents.
CFCs are halocarbons that release chlorine and bromine, which destroy stratospheric ozone. They therefore deplete the ozone layer rather than increase it.
Ozone depletion is caused mainly by halocarbons such as CFCs, which release chlorine and bromine. UV rays are absorbed by ozone, not the cause of its depletion.
The ozone hole forms over Antarctica, a polar region, in the southern spring, aided by polar stratospheric clouds. It is therefore most pronounced at the poles, not at the equator or the tropics.
The Antarctic ozone hole was reported in 1985 by a British team (Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin).
The Antarctic ozone hole was reported in 1985 by a British team (Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin), so the British team is correct.
Ozone depletion and the ozone hole are caused mainly by halocarbons such as CFCs, which release chlorine. Acetylene, ethylene and methane are not ozone-depleting substances.

Transboundary movement of waste means moving hazardous waste across borders for reprocessing or storage, often to developing countries, as regulated by the Basel Convention. The other options describe positive outcomes, not issues.
Urban India uses composting, incineration and landfilling for solid waste disposal, so 'all the above' is correct; each method alone is only partial.
Indore was ranked the cleanest city in Swachh Survekshan, consistently topping the list (Indore is also the model zero-waste city). The other cities were not the top-ranked large city.

Indore was ranked the cleanest city in Swachh Survekshan, consistently topping the list (Indore is also the model zero-waste city). The other cities were not the top-ranked large city.
Swachh Survekshan 2023 under SBM-U 2.0 had the theme 'Waste to Wealth'. The other options are not the official theme.
CLAP - Jagananna Swachha Sankalpam was launched on 2 October 2021, so option 2 is correct.
The assertion is true: rural door collection rose from 22% (Nov 2021) to 61.50% (Jan 2022). The reason is false because CLAP was launched on 2 Oct 2021, not October 2020.
Cotton is a cash crop grown for sale, while rice, maize and wheat are food crops.
Jowar is a food crop, not a cash crop, whereas jute, sugarcane and groundnut (peanut) are cash crops.
Tobacco, cotton and rubber are cash/plantation crops, while soybean is listed here as an oilseed, so it is the odd one out among the options.
Cotton needs about 210 frost-free days, so a requirement of only 100 frost-free days is not the correct geographical requirement.
Tea needs 150-300 cm of rainfall and well-drained hill slopes, which fits rainfall above 200 cm on sloping hills. Jute needs low plains, and cotton needs only 50-100 cm of rain.
Tea needs 20-30°C warmth and 150-300 cm of rainfall, with acidic, humus-rich soil, so I and II are right. Lime is not required; the soil is acidic, so III is wrong.
Aloe vera is a medicinal plant, whereas sugarcane and cotton are cash crops and mahua is a forest tree.
Aloe vera is a medicinal plant, whereas sugarcane and cotton are cash crops and mahua is a forest tree.
Rhodamine B is a textile dye illegally used to colour cotton candy; it is carcinogenic, which is why Tamil Nadu banned its sale. Aristolochic acid comes from herbal medicines, not cotton candy.
BPA is used in polycarbonate plastics and food-can linings, so it is a chemical used in food-packaging materials. The other options (medical test, doping test, alloy steel) do not describe it.
The notes do not cover this fact. Turmeric powder comes from the dried rhizome (underground stem), not a fruit, root or seed, so 'None of the above' is correct.
Mustard gas (sulphur mustard) is a blistering chemical warfare agent. It has nothing to do with mustard oil, fuel or deodorants.
Calcium carbide is used to ripen mangoes artificially because it produces acetylene, which acts like the ripening hormone ethylene. The other calcium compounds do not release it.
Mustard gas (sulphur mustard) was used as a chemical weapon in World War I. Carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide were not the typical battlefield agents asked about here.
Prussic acid is another name for hydrocyanic acid (HCN), whose salts are cyanides. The other options are different mineral acids.
Honey is mainly fructose (about 38%) with slightly less glucose, so fructose is its major sugar. Sucrose and maltose are only minor components.

Without an atmosphere there would be no greenhouse blanket to retain heat at night, so Earth's surface would lose heat rapidly (about -18°C average instead of +15°C), and daytime heating would go unmoderated. Day-night extremes would therefore increase.
For hilly regions the IMD heat wave threshold is a maximum temperature of 30°C, so a heat wave is not declared until it exceeds 30°C.
For hilly regions the IMD heat wave threshold is a maximum temperature of 30°C, so a heat wave is not declared until it exceeds 30°C.

Clouds send Earth's long-wave heat back like a blanket, hindering terrestrial radiation from escaping to space, so cloudy nights stay warmer. Option 4 states this directly, whereas ozone depletion is unrelated.
On clear nights terrestrial (long-wave) radiation escapes freely to space, with no cloud blanket to send it back, so nights are colder. The cause is radiation loss, not conduction or condensation.
India is a mixed economy, with public and private sectors coexisting. It is not purely socialist, Gandhian or free-market.
A mixed economy is one in which public and private sectors coexist side by side. The other options describe sectoral emphasis or military rule, not a mixed economy.

In a centrally planned (command) economy the government decides what, how and for whom, so I is correct. II is wrong because in a market system prices are set by the market, not agreed by the government.
India is a developing economy that still shows some underdeveloped features. So 'developing' is the best description, not 'developed' or 'stagnant'.
Working efficiency of the population is not a main cause of India's underdevelopment. Rapid population growth with high dependency, low human development and high poverty are the recorded causes.
The notes do not state India's 1750 share of world manufacturing output. They give only Maddison's share of world GDP (22.6% in 1700, 3.8% in 1952).
The notes state that DMEO was set up on 18 Sep 2015 as an attached office of NITI Aayog, so option (1) is correct. The other options change the month or year.
Hydrogen is not a greenhouse gas, while methane, nitrous oxide and CFCs all absorb infrared radiation and are GHGs.
CO2 and methane are the gases most responsible for global warming; O2 is not a greenhouse gas, so only option 3 is right.
CO2 is the biggest contributor to the enhanced (human-driven) greenhouse effect, ahead of CH4, CFCs and N2O.
Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas; CO2 is far less abundant (~0.04% of air), and SO2 is not a GHG.
CO2 and methane are major greenhouse gases. The other pairs include non-GHGs or only indirect ones (CO, SO2), so option 4 is the best answer.
The most important set of greenhouse gases is CO2, methane, N2O and water vapour, which matches option 3.
Methane is commonly called marsh gas because it is produced in wetlands and marshes.
Among the listed gases CO2 is present in the largest concentration (~0.04% of air) and is the largest of the long-lived GHGs, ahead of CH4, N2O and CFCs.
CO2 and methane are the major greenhouse gases. The other pairs include non-GHGs or only indirect ones (CO, SO2), so option 1 is correct.
Soot, SF6 and water vapour all warm the atmosphere, so all three contribute.
CFCs are greenhouse gases as well as ozone-depleting, so the statement that they are not responsible for the greenhouse effect is false.
Oxygen is not one of the four principal human-driven GHGs (CO2, CH4, N2O, water vapour); it does not absorb infrared.
Oxygen does not absorb infrared radiation so it is not a greenhouse gas; CO2 and CH4 are GHGs, and nitrogen oxides are also GHGs.
Hydrogen is not a greenhouse gas, whereas methane, CO2 and nitrous oxide are.
CFCs come from refrigerants, foams and aerosols, not automobiles, so this pair is wrongly matched.

All three are correct: the VP's term is 5 years, he is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and he acts as President only on a vacancy or the President's inability, for a maximum of 6 months until a new President is elected.
Under Articles 64 and 89(1) the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; the Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha.
Articles 64 and 89(1) make the Vice-President the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. He is elected, not nominated by the President, and the Leader of Opposition does not chair the House.
Under Article 69 the oath of office is administered to the Vice-President by the President (or a person appointed by him), not by the CJI, PM or Speaker.
Article 67(b) provides for removal of the Vice-President. Article 56 concerns the President's term and resignation, Article 60 the President's oath, and Article 77 the conduct of Government business.

Statement I is correct as both Houses elect the VP. Statement II is correct because Article 68 says the vacancy is filled as soon as possible, and the Constitution names no one to discharge the VP's duties during the vacancy.
The Descent of the Ganga (Arjuna's Penance) is the large open-air rock relief at Mahabalipuram, so the answer is Mahabalipuram.
The Pancha Rathas at Mahabalipuram are monolithic rathas built by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, so the answer is Pallavas.
The Mahabalipuram rathas belong to the Mamalla phase of Narasimhavarman I. Narasimhavarman II is linked to the Shore Temple, not the rathas.
The Pancha Rathas were built by the Pallavas under Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla).
Satyameva Jayate comes from the Mundaka Upanishad, not the Rigveda, Gita or Manusmriti.
Satyakama Jabala's story is found in the Chandogya Upanishad.
The Ashtadhyayi, the Sanskrit grammar text, was composed by Panini (c. 500 BCE).
Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi, the foundational Sanskrit grammar; the other options are not known for grammar.
The Mahabharata, which grew from the Jayasamhita, is also called Satasahasri Samhita because of its roughly one lakh verses.
Manu, traditional author of the Manusmriti, is regarded as the first law-giver of ancient India.
The yugas follow the order Krita (Satya), Treta, Dvapara, Kali, with declining righteousness.
The yugas follow the order Krita (Satya), Treta, Dvapara, Kali, with declining righteousness.
The Mahabharata war at Kurukshetra is traditionally said to have lasted 18 days.
In the Samudra Manthan myth, the serpent Vasuki served as the churning rope around Mount Mandara.
The Mahabharata was traditionally narrated by Ugrashrava Sauti to the sages at Naimisharanya, in the gathering of Shaunaka.
Rama first met Hanuman in Kishkindha Kanda, when Sugriva sent Hanuman to meet Rama and Lakshmana.
The Bhagavad Gita is part of the Mahabharata and was composed in Sanskrit.
Manu, author of the Manusmriti, is regarded as India's first law-giver; Panini was a grammarian, Kautilya a political thinker and Kapila a Sankhya philosopher.
Arjuna's father Pandu was the son of Vichitravirya's wife Ambalika through Vyasa, so Vichitravirya is counted as the grandfather.
A vacancy in the President's office other than by expiry must be filled by election within six months (Art. 62(2)), so the seat can stay vacant for at most 6 months.
When both offices are vacant, the CJI (or the senior-most SC judge) discharges the President's functions under the 1969 Act, not the PM or the Speaker.
For a vacancy caused by death, resignation or removal, the election must be held within six months (Art. 62(2)).
The President summons the joint sitting of both Houses, which the Speaker chairs; the Speaker does not summon it.
The President is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.

The President lays the Finance Commission recommendations, the CAG reports and the reports of the National SC Commission before Parliament. PAC reports are submitted to the Lok Sabha, not laid by the President, so statement II is wrong and option 3 is correct.
Under Art. 78 the President can seek information from the PM and have matters placed before the Council, and he can address and send messages to Parliament, so all four statements are correct.
The President summons and prorogues the Houses of Parliament and dissolves the Lok Sabha.
Only the President can pardon a death sentence. The Governor can merely suspend, remit or commute it, so the Governor does have concurrent power over suspension and remission.
Reprieve is a temporary stay of execution, respite is a lesser sentence, remission shortens the period without changing the character, and commutation substitutes a lighter form.
The President, as head of State, is the first citizen of India.
All three statements match the notes: area 3.28 million sq km (2.4% of world), mainland extent 8°4′N–37°6′N and 68°7′E–97°25′E, and 28 States with 8 UTs. So 'I, II and III' is correct.
Vidarbha is the eastern region of Maharashtra (Nagpur, Amravati), so Maharashtra is correct.
The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient crystalline landmass rich in metallic minerals. The alluvial plains and valleys are not.
Plains cover the largest share of India's land area, about 43%, more than mountains (30%) or plateaus (27%). The notes do not state this.
The Peninsular Plateau is the oldest and largest division, an ancient stable block from Gondwana Land. The Himalayas and Northern Plains are younger.

Statement II is correct: the Eastern Ghats run along the east coast. I is wrong because the Sahara is not in the subcontinent. III is wrong because the Deccan is a plateau of basalt, not fertile lowland plains.

The Himalayas are the world's highest range, the Thar is an arid dune region, the Deccan is a high plateau of southern India, and the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta is a vast alluvial plain. This gives A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1.
Bhur is an undulating aeolian sandy deposit in the upper Ganga plain, on the Ganga-Yamuna doab. It is not the older alluvium (bhangar) or newer alluvium (khadar).
The Northern Plains are alluvial, built up by river deposition (aggradation) rather than by erosion or in-situ weathering.
The Banni grasslands lie at the edge of the salt marsh (Rann of Kutch) in Gujarat.
The Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary is in the Little Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.
The Malwa Plateau lies in western Madhya Pradesh and south-eastern Rajasthan, between the Aravalli and the Vindhya.
The Satpura range lies in central India between the Narmada and Tapi. The Nilgiri is in the south and the Arakan Yoma is in Myanmar.
The notes state that IQAir 2021 named Bhiwadi the most polluted city, so option 2 is correct.
The AQI covers 8 pollutants (PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3, Pb). Methane is not among them, so it is the one not included. Sulphur here refers to SO2, which is included.
NCAP was launched in January 2019 by MoEFCC, so 2019 is correct.
The September 2022 revision set up to 40% PM10 cut by 2025-26, so the year is 2026.
Statement I is correct: NCAP is a PAN-India time-bound national strategy. Statement II is wrong because the original target was a 20-30% cut by 2024 (not 2025), with 2017 as the base year.
NCAP was launched in January 2019 as a PAN-India time-bound national strategy that also expands monitoring, so the answer is 2019.
Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment (2002), came into force along with the RTE Act on 1 April 2010, so option 1 is correct.
The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for ages 6-14 a Fundamental Right. The 1st, 42nd and 44th Amendments did not do this.
Since the 86th Amendment inserted Article 21A, education (elementary) is a Fundamental Right, not merely statutory or a DPSP (it was earlier a Part IV DPSP provision).
The 24-hour production before a magistrate under Art. 22(1)-(2) does not apply to persons held under preventive detention law (Art. 22(3)), so such detention can go beyond 24 hours.
Art. 22 requires production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, not one week, so statement 3 is incorrect. The others match Art. 22 and its exclusions.
Art. 22(3) excludes enemy aliens and persons under preventive detention laws. Foreigners (non-enemy) and OCIs are not excluded, so only I and II are right.
After the 44th Amendment (1978), Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under Art. 359 even during a National Emergency. Art. 22 is not protected in this way.
Only Articles 20 and 21 are non-suspendable during Emergency after the 44th Amendment; Arts. 14, 19 and 22 can be suspended.

The Narasimham Committees (1991 on the financial system, 1998 on banking sector reforms) recommended post-1991 financial sector reforms. Abid Hussain (SSI), Chelliah (tax) and Bhagwati are not about financial sector reform.

The Narasimham Committee dealt with banking and financial sector reforms (Committee on Banking Sector Reforms, 1998), so banking structure reform is correct. It was not about education, tax or planning.

Rangarajan (1993) headed the disinvestment committee, Goswami the industrial sickness committee and Abid Hussain the SSI committee. The remaining pairing, tax administration reforms with P. Shome, gives 1-D; 2-C; 3-B; 4-A.
The notes do not state which committee examined NPAs of public sector banks. The Panneerselvam Committee is the correct option, while Shri Krishna, Malegam and Mandal relate to other subjects.

Article 311 provides safeguards to civil servants: no dismissal by an authority subordinate to the appointing one, and an inquiry with a hearing. Article 310 is the Doctrine of Pleasure, the tempting wrong option.
Civil Services Day is observed on 21 April, marking Sardar Patel's 1947 address to the first probationers at Metcalfe House.
Chilika Lake in Odisha is among India's largest wintering grounds for migratory waterfowl, which makes option 2 correct. The notes do not state this fact, so no line is linked.

The Arctic tern makes the longest migration of any bird, travelling between the Arctic and Antarctic every year. Flamingos, painted storks and pelicans move only regionally, so they are not the answer.

Wood and grass are plant material that microbes decompose, and leather is an animal-derived material that is also biodegradable. The other groups include plastic, China clay cup or polystyrene cup, which are non-biodegradable.
Wool is a natural keratin fibre that microbes can break down, so it is biodegradable. Nylon, plastic and polythene bags are non-biodegradable.
Plastic is non-biodegradable and microbes cannot break it down. Cow dung, leaves and food waste are biodegradable and are decomposed by bacteria.
The 3Rs are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. 'Regain' is not one of them.
The 3Rs are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. 'Regain' is not one of them.

Fly ash is used in bricks, cement and roads, and partly replaces Portland cement, so statements I and II are correct. Statement III is wrong because fly ash is not made of only silicon dioxide and calcium oxide, and it can contain toxic elements.
In March 2025 APPCB mandated the use of RDF in cement kilns to cut coal use. The other options are not directives it issued.

Landfill is cheap but harms the environment in the long term, incineration cuts volume but emits pollutants, composting gives useful products, and recycling saves resources. This gives a-I, b-II, c-III, d-IV.

Per Census 2011, Visakhapatnam is the Andhra Pradesh district with the most Scheduled Tribe population (it has large tribal Agency areas), so it is correct; East Godavari is the most populous district, not the most tribal.
The Census 2011 population order is Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, then Andhra Pradesh, which is 4, 3, 2, 1.
Nagaland is the only State with negative decadal growth in 2001-11 (−0.6%); Goa, Haryana and Kerala all grew.
Nagaland recorded the lowest decadal growth in 2001-11 (−0.6%), the only negative figure among States, so it is lower than Arunachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab.
Nagaland's population fell from 19,90,036 to 19,78,502 in 2001-11, making it the only State with negative growth; Kerala, Goa and Meghalaya grew.
Manufactured products carry the largest weight in the WPI, 64.23%.
RBI now uses CPI (Combined) as its headline inflation measure, having adopted it in April 2014. WPI was the earlier main index.
Indexation links payments to a price index; for example, dearness allowance is fixed on the basis of CPI-IW. So it is associated with fixing wage compensation.
Inflation control may need monetary, fiscal and exchange-rate policies together with supply management. Monetary policy alone cannot fix supply-side inflation.
Core inflation leaves out volatile items such as food and fuel, whereas headline inflation includes them.
Debtors gain from inflation because they repay money of lower real value. Bond-holders lose, so statement 2 is wrong.
The hydrogen fuel cell ferry, India's first, was built by Cochin Shipyard under the Harit Nauka initiative and flagged off by the PM from Thoothukudi.
INS Vikrant is the first indigenous aircraft carrier, commissioned by the PM at Cochin Shipyard in Sep 2022, so A is true. R is also true and explains why it is a milestone for Aatmanirbhar Bharat.
Tejas is the indigenous light combat aircraft designed by ADA and built by HAL, and it was the first indigenous fighter of the IAF. The other options are not light combat aircraft.
Tejas is India's indigenous Light Combat Aircraft, designed by ADA and built by HAL. Vikrant is a carrier, Arjun a tank, and Akash a missile.
Rustom-II (TAPAS-BH-201) is a MALE-class unmanned aerial vehicle, not a manned aircraft.
Dhruv is HAL's twin-engine Advanced Light Helicopter used by all three services and the Coast Guard. It is not a ship, submarine or missile.

Iqbal's 1930 Allahabad address first proposed a consolidated Muslim state in the North-West. The Lahore Resolution (1940) only formalised the demand later, and Rahmat Ali's Cambridge pamphlet (1933) came after Iqbal.
'Now or Never' was the pamphlet written by Chaudhry Rahmat Ali in 1933, not by Jinnah or Iqbal.
The name 'Pakistan' was coined by Chaudhry Rahmat Ali in 1933 as a Cambridge student. Jinnah led the League's demand but did not coin the idea or name.
The Pakistan Resolution is another name for the Lahore Resolution of 1940, so it was passed at Lahore.
The Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution was adopted on 23 March 1940 at Lahore. 1930 Allahabad was Iqbal's address, not the resolution.
The Lahore Resolution demanded independent Muslim-majority states and was soon called the Pakistan Resolution, which is its significance.
The League formally set out its demand for separate Muslim states at the Lahore session of 1940.
The Pakistan (Lahore) Resolution was adopted on 23 March 1940, so March 1940 is correct.
V.D. Savarkar was elected president of the Hindu Mahasabha in 1937 at the Ahmedabad session and held the post until 1943.
The 1973 Yom Kippur War was fought by Israel against an Arab coalition led by Egypt and Syria; the other options are unrelated conflicts.
Shintoism is the indigenous religion of Japan, practised alongside Buddhism.
Ikebana is the Japanese art of flower arrangement.
Sierra Leone observes National Cleanliness Day on the last Saturday of every month, so it is the correct answer.
Nelson Mandela, who led the anti-apartheid struggle using principles of non-violence and reconciliation, is called the 'Gandhi of Africa'.
Garuda is the India-France Air Force exercise, so France is correct.
The International Ayurveda Congress 2017 was held in London, so option 1 is correct.
The 2017 New Delhi World Book Fair had the theme 'Manushi', covering writings on and by women, which matches option 2.
The WEF Davos 2017 theme was 'Responsive and Responsible Leadership', which is option 4.
The 5th India-Arab Partnership Conference was held in Dubai, organised with FICCI and the League of Arab States.
Paraguay, Sri Lanka, Guyana, Seychelles and Finland are non-G20 GBA supporters, while Chile is not. So I, II, III, IV and VI is correct.
Kerala is known for a low infant mortality rate because of adequate basic health and educational facilities, so option 4 is correct.
PMSMA was launched in 2016, offering free antenatal care on the 9th of every month to pregnant women in the 2nd/3rd trimester.

Jagananna Amma Vodi (January 2020) gave yearly financial aid to poor mothers of school-going children, so option 3 is correct. It was an education support scheme, not for the elderly, young children or farmers.
India's first Yoga university, Bihar School of Yoga's Bihar Yoga Bharati, was established at Munger in Bihar.
IGNOU, with a very large enrolment through open and distance learning, has been described as the world's biggest university by student numbers.

The Committee on Deepening Digital Payments (RBI, 2019) was chaired by Nandan Nilekani. The notes do not cover this committee; they list Ratan Watal (MoF, digital payments) and Naidu, which are different committees.

The RBI's 2018 data localisation directive requires payment system data to be stored only in India (statement I). It does not require systems to be owned by public sector enterprises, and the audit report goes to the RBI, not the CAG, so II and III are wrong.

Agronomy is the science of producing and using plants for food, fuel, feed, fibre and fertiliser. Horticulture covers fruits, vegetables and ornamentals, while pisciculture (fish) and apiculture (bees) are not about plant production.
Organic farming relies on crop rotation and manures, and avoids synthetic inputs and GMOs. So saying it uses only 'minimal' crop rotation is the incorrect statement.

Crop diversification, legume intensification, tensiometer use (efficient irrigation scheduling) and vertical farming are all regarded as eco-friendly, resource-efficient practices, so all of the above is correct.

Under Article 280(3)(a) the Finance Commission recommends how net tax proceeds are shared between the Centre and States. The Finance Ministry only implements and releases transfers; it does not decide the distribution.
The 16th FC's terms of reference (notified 31 Dec 2023) do not ask it to review present arrangements on financing. The other three options are standard Art. 280(3) duties.

The FC devolves shareable Union taxes such as income tax and excise duty, and recommends grants-in-aid. 'Trade tax' is not a Union tax shared by the FC (GST sharing is the GST Council's matter), so it is not an FC function.
Kashi Vidyapith (1921), Gujarat Vidyapith (1920) and Jamia Millia Islamia (1920) were founded during the NCM, while Kashi Hindu Vishva Vidyalaya was not, so I, II and III is correct.
C.R. Das was the East Bengal lawyer who gave up his practice and was prominent in the NCM; Bose was not a lawyer, and Rajagopalachari and Asaf Ali were not from East Bengal.
Rajendra Prasad was among the lawyers who gave up practice during the NCM; the others listed were not Bihar pleaders who did so.
Chauri Chaura lies in Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh, where the 4 February 1922 incident occurred.
Naoroji's drain theory is linked with his work 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901). The other titles are not his works.
'Poverty of India: Papers and Statistics' comes from Dadabhai Naoroji's 1876 paper 'The Poverty of India'. It is not by R.C. Dutt or the other options.
Dadabhai Naoroji made the first estimate of India's per capita income (Rs 20 in 1867–68). The other leaders did not.
The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly and brought one-way free trade. British goods entered India almost duty-free while Indian goods faced heavy duties in Britain.
The Judiciary, with the Supreme Court as protector and guarantor, is the guardian of Fundamental Rights. Parliament, the President and the Cabinet are not.
The Judiciary is the guardian of Fundamental Rights, with the Supreme Court as their protector and guarantor. The legislature and executive are not.
The Judiciary is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, not the President or Parliament.
Quo warranto literally means 'by what authority', i.e. what is your authority to hold the office. The other options are not its meaning.
Both Prohibition and Certiorari lie traditionally against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies. They are not limited to the Supreme Court, as High Courts issue them too.
Mandamus literally means 'We command', i.e. an order, so 'an order' is the closest option.
Habeas Corpus is the only writ that lies directly against private individuals, for illegal confinement. The other writs are issued against public authorities or bodies.
Mandamus ('We command') compels a public official or body to perform a public duty it has refused or neglected. Certiorari quashes orders, and the other writs do not compel duty.
Afghanistan is the world's largest producer of opium according to UN reports; Oman, Kuwait and Dubai are not opium producers.

Article 21 has been read expansively by the Supreme Court to cover dignity, privacy and personal choice, including the rights of transgender persons, craniopagus twins and mentally disabled women to bear a child, so all three statements are correct. The notes do not state these specific rights.

Right to Life, Equality of Opportunity in public employment (Art. 16) and Protection of Personal Liberty are all enumerated in the Constitution. A right to permanent housing is not listed; the Supreme Court derived shelter from Art. 21 (Olga Tellis, Chameli Singh).

Phone tapping invades the right to privacy, which the Supreme Court reads into Article 21 (with Part III), so Article 21 is the answer. Articles 22, 24 and 25 deal with arrest, child labour and religion, so they are not relevant.
Free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 was added as a Fundamental Right by Article 21A through the 86th Amendment. The other options were not added to Part III.
Under the RTE Act, funding is shared between the Centre and States, not borne solely by the Centre, so option 3 is not a feature. The notes do not state the funding arrangement.
Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002. The 44th removed property from Fundamental Rights, and the 42nd and 74th deal with other matters.
Although the 86th Amendment was passed in 2002, Article 21A came into force with the RTE Act on 1 April 2010, so the year is 2010.

Mysore was not renamed Tamil Nadu (Madras State was); the notes do not state this, but the other options are consistent: Bombay was split into Maharashtra and Gujarat in 1960, and Himachal was a UT before becoming a State.
Hyderabad was the common capital of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh after the 2014 bifurcation, so it is Telangana's capital. Panaji is Goa's capital and Silvassa is the capital of a UT.
Punjab as a reorganised State dates from 1966 (Haryana carved out of Punjab), later than Andhra Pradesh (1956), Gujarat (1960) and Karnataka (1956 map).
The 36th Amendment (1975) made Sikkim a full State, the 22nd. The 35th (1974) only made it an associate State.
Jharkhand was created in 2000 (15 November 2000) from Bihar; the notes do not cover this.
The 69th Amendment (1991) gave Delhi special status as the National Capital Region/Territory, with Art. 239AA.
Lakshadweep (about 32 sq km) is the smallest UT by area, far smaller than Chandigarh, Daman and Diu or DNH. The notes do not give areas.
Nag is a third-generation fire-and-forget ATGM with an IIR seeker, so it guides itself after launch. Agni and Prithvi are ballistic missiles, and BrahMos is a cruise missile, not an anti-tank weapon.
Prithvi is a surface-to-surface SRBM. Trishul and Akash are surface-to-air missiles, and Nag is an anti-tank missile.

Agni-V has a range of 5,000+ km, matching the question. Agni-VI is only proposed, and Agni-III and Agni-IV have shorter ranges (about 3,500 km and 4,000 km). The ISRO reference in the question is wrong, since DRDO develops Agni.
Agni, meaning 'Fire', is a surface-to-surface ballistic missile developed by India under the IGMDP. It is not a firefighting machine, a tank or an aircraft.
Agni is a ballistic missile with ranges from about 700 km to over 5,000 km, so it is a long-range missile. It is not a jet, a tank or a short-range missile.
Agni-IV is a surface-to-surface, two-stage solid-fuel missile, so statement I is correct. It is not liquid-fuelled only, and its range is about 4,000 km, not 7,500 km, so II and III are wrong.
Agni-II is a two-stage solid missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (2,000-3,500 km), so about 2000 km is the best option.
Prithvi-II is nuclear-capable, so I is correct. Its range is 350 km, not 100 km, and Prithvi-I rather than Prithvi-II was the first IGMDP missile, so II and III are wrong.

The notes do not state the maneuverability feature or the number of Prithvi variants. Prithvi-II's maneuverability is the only claim that holds. The notes list three variants (not two), and the multiple-target claim is unsupported.

Some lists give the title Abhinava Nannaya to Rayaprolu Subbarao, which matches the keyed answer; the other common claimant is Viswanatha Satyanarayana (APPSC G2 2025 key), which is the tempting wrong option here.
Japaneeyamu, written after Japan's 1905 victory over Russia, is by Sriram Veerabrahmam of Bandar. Adipudi Somanatha Rao wrote Japan Charitra, a history, not this drama.
Viswanatha Satyanarayana won the first Jnanpith for a Telugu writer, for Ramayana Kalpavrikshamu. Rayaprolu is a Bhava Kavitvam poet and did not win it.
Asamarthuni Jeevitha Yatra (1947) is by T. Gopichand, regarded as the first psychological novel in Telugu.
Gabbilam (1941) was written by Gurram Jashuva as a work against untouchability; it is not by Duvvuri Ramireddy or the others.

Judicial review by the Supreme Court is exercised through Art. 32 (with HCs under Arts. 226/227), which is part of the inviolable basic structure; Arts. 131, 132 and 134 deal with other kinds of jurisdiction.

Art. 32 is available only to enforce Fundamental Rights, so if no Fundamental Right has been infringed the Supreme Court can refuse relief. Availability of another remedy or the choice of writ is not a bar, since Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.

Art. 32 is available only to enforce Fundamental Rights, so if no Fundamental Right has been infringed the Supreme Court can refuse relief. Availability of another remedy or the choice of writ is not a bar, since Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.
Art. 32(2) empowers the Supreme Court to issue directions, orders or writs. Art. 226 is the High Courts' power, and Arts. 228 and 36 are unrelated.

Under Art. 35, Parliament alone (not State legislatures) legislates on specified Part III matters, so a State legislature cannot prescribe punishments for Part III offences; the other statements match Art. 32(4)/359, the Arts. 20-21 exception and Art. 33.
Judicial review is expressed most clearly in Art. 32 (Supreme Court) and Art. 226 (High Courts), which empower them to enforce rights through writs; the other Articles are unrelated.
Power to restrict Fundamental Rights lies with Parliament (e.g. Art. 33, Art. 35), not the Supreme Court, which only judges the reasonableness of restrictions; so statement 1 is incorrect.
RISAT-1, the C-band (5.35 GHz) SAR satellite, was launched in 2012 on PSLV-C19. PSLV-C18 carried Jugnu and SRMSAT, so it is the tempting wrong option.
EDUSAT (GSAT-3) was launched on 20 September 2004 aboard GSLV-F01 from Sriharikota, so option 2 is correct.

WESAT was the first satellite fully built by women students of LBS Institute of Technology for Women and flew on PSLV-C58 POEM-3 in Jan 2024, so I and II are right. Its payload studies solar UV, not rainfall and groundwater recharge, so III is wrong.
STUDSAT, ANUSAT and JUGNU are student-built nano-satellites. GSAT-1 is a full-scale ISRO communication satellite and the first GSLV payload, so it is not a student satellite.

Plants make carbohydrates, fats and proteins as the essential foods for human and animal metabolism; nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) are genetic material, not a nutritional food class, so they are the odd one out.
Proline is one of the 20 amino acids that make up proteins, so it is neither a base, a bacterium nor a virus.
Kwashiorkor, a protein-deficiency disease, shows oedema (swelling); marasmus is wasting without oedema, and hypertension and fever do not feature oedema typically.
B-group vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble, while A, D, E and K are fat-soluble, so B and C is the right pair; D and A are fat-soluble.
Golden Rice is engineered to contain beta-carotene, the precursor of vitamin A.
Cholecalciferol is vitamin D3 (D3 is 'chole-', D2 'ergo-calciferol'), so the answer is Vitamin D.
Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting; its deficiency causes slow clotting. Vitamins A, B and D do not have this role.
Most enzymes are biological catalysts made of proteins, so (1) is correct; they are not lipids, acids or alkalis.
B-group vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble, whereas A, D, E and K are fat-soluble. So only 'Vitamin B and C' is correct.
Polished rice loses the B vitamins (thiamine, B1) from the bran, so people relying on it get beri-beri. Pellagra is due to B3, scurvy to C and osteomalacia to D deficiency.
Amla is the richest source of vitamin C, richer than orange, apple or carrot.
Casein is the main protein of milk. Agglutinin, myosin and haemoglobin are not milk proteins.
Article 350A requires States and local authorities to provide mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage to children of linguistic minority groups; 300A concerns property.
Article 30(1) gives all minorities, religious or linguistic, the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Art. 29 protects language, script and culture.
The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted Art. 19(1)(f) and Art. 31 from Part III and inserted Art. 300A in Part XII, making property a legal right. Both statements are true.
After the 44th Amendment, property is only a legal (constitutional) right under Art. 300A, not a Fundamental Right.
The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted Arts. 19(1)(f) and 31, removing property from the Fundamental Rights; the 42nd is a distractor.
The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property, and it was passed under the Morarji Desai (Janata) government. The notes give the year but not the government.

The 44th Amendment deleted Arts. 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III and inserted Art. 300A in Part XII. This is why property is no longer a Fundamental Right but remains a constitutional right, so R explains A.
The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 deleted the right to property from the Fundamental Rights; the 42nd and others did not.
The 44th Amendment removed the right to property, the only FR ever deleted, from Part III.
Property is the only Fundamental Right ever deleted (44th Amendment), now Art. 300A. Work is a DPSP and education (6-14) is an FR under Art. 21A.
The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted Arts. 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III, so the right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right.
The Patwari was the village-level accountant who kept land and revenue records. Zamindars held hereditary rights over land and revenue rather than keeping records.

Under ijarah, revenue was farmed out to an ijaradar who paid a fixed sum to the treasury and could extract as much as possible from peasants. So land revenue was not fixed for the peasant, which makes statement 3 untrue.

The dodo of Mauritius is the classic case of co-extinction: the tree that depended on the dodo to eat its fruit and disperse its seeds failed to reproduce once the bird went extinct. The notes cover co-extinction in general but do not name the dodo.

The traditional criterion was 50 years without a sighting in the wild. The notes say only that IUCN declares extinction after full surveys leave no reasonable doubt, and that a fixed ten years unrecorded does not make it automatic.

The dodo of Mauritius is the classic case of co-extinction: the tree that depended on the dodo to eat its fruit and disperse its seeds failed to reproduce once the bird went extinct. The notes cover co-extinction in general but do not name the dodo.
The Red Data Book lists threatened plants and animals, so only statement II is right. It does not list endemic species of hotspots (I) or protected sites (III).

The Crimson Rose butterfly is Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, so statement I (Endangered) is wrong. The notes do not support statement II about the Himalayas, and the answer stands because I is already false.
The notes record that 32 projects were sanctioned in 2020 under the 'Unit' scheme of PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana, so 32 is correct.
PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana is an umbrella scheme of the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, so option 3 is correct.
The notes do not state which honey bee species is most common, so no line is linked.
'Kausheya' is an ancient Indian term for silk, the fabric from cocoons. The notes do not cover the term, so no line is linked.
China is the world's largest silk producer, with India second. India is notable only as the one country producing all five commercial silks.
Niyoga is the custom in which a wife lives with a designated man to bear a child when her husband is impotent or dead. The other options are not names of this custom.
Sambandham was the consensual, informal union of Namboothiris and Nairs under Kerala's matrilineal system.
Diku Andi is the Ho tribe's marriage by negotiation, a later form borrowed from Hindus. Capture is Oportipi, so the other options do not fit.

Talaq-e-Hasan, with talaq pronounced once a month over three months, was challenged in the Supreme Court after the 2017 triple talaq verdict. Talaq-e-Ahsan is a single pronouncement plus iddat and is not the one challenged.
In August 2023 the Supreme Court overruled the 2014 Madras HC ruling and held that advocates can solemnise self-respect marriages under Sec. 7-A.
Nepal was the first South Asian nation to register a same-sex marriage. India, the Maldives and Bhutan have not done so.
Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests make up about 65.6% of India's forest area, so they are the most widespread.
Ebony is listed among the characteristic species of tropical wet evergreen forests. Sandalwood is dry deciduous, juniper is alpine scrub and acacia is thorn forest.
Ebony is listed among the characteristic species of tropical wet evergreen forests. Sandalwood is dry deciduous, juniper is alpine scrub and acacia is thorn forest.
Evergreen rainforests are dense and multi-layered with a continuous canopy, hold the maximum plant diversity, and have epiphytes and climbers reaching the canopy. So all three statements hold.
Tropical moist (evergreen) forests have the maximum plant diversity and biomass. Temperate forests, savanna and grasslands are less diverse.

Tropical wet evergreen forests occur in the north-east, including Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram, which fall under the north-eastern states. Himachal Pradesh is Himalayan, with temperate and alpine forests, so it is excluded.

The NGT was created under the NGT Act 2010, in force from 18 October 2010. That falls in the 11th Five Year Plan period (2007-12), so option (2) is correct. The notes do not state the plan period directly, so this step uses outside knowledge.
The Lex Loci Act (Caste Disabilities Removal Act) 1850 let a convert still inherit ancestral property. It did not deal with child marriage, sati or widow remarriage, so options 1, 2 and 4 are wrong.
The Female Infanticide Prevention Act was passed in 1870 under Viceroy Mayo, not in 1856 under Dalhousie.
Act III of 1872 was the Native (Civil/Brahmo) Marriage Act, a social reform law fixing marriage ages of 14 for girls and 18 for boys and allowing inter-caste marriage. So it was a Social Reform Act.

Statement I is correct because Vidyasagar was Secretary of the Hindu Female School, which became the Bethune School, and he promoted girls' education. Statement III is wrong because the Sati ban (1829) came from Rammohan Roy's campaign, not Keshab Chandra Sen's. Statement II is a fact outside these notes.

Statement IV is not correct, since Vidyasagar actively campaigned for widow remarriage, which led to Act XV of 1856. The other statements are true: he did much for Bengali language, education and women's schooling.
Kubha is the Vedic name of the Kabul river, which flowed through Afghanistan, so the answer is Afghanistan.
Kubha (Kabul) and Krumu (Kurram) flowed through Afghanistan, showing Aryan links with that region; the other rivers are Punjab rivers.
The Dasarajna was fought on the Parushni (modern Ravi); Vipasa and Asikni were not the battle site.
The Purus were defeated by Sudas's Bharatas and only later joined them, so they did not side with the Bharatas in the battle; statement 4 is false.

The Council of Ministers comprises ministers of all ranks (Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, etc.), whereas the Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most civil servant heading the Cabinet Secretariat, not a minister.
Under Article 75(2), ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President. The PM may advise dismissal in practice, but constitutionally it is the President.

The Cabinet Secretariat serves the Cabinet and its committees (agenda and secretarial assistance), so I and II are correct. Allocating financial resources to ministries is not its function, so III is wrong.
The Attorney General is appointed by the President under Article 76, not by Parliament or the Speaker.
Dominique Strauss-Kahn was a French politician and served as France's Finance Minister before heading the IMF; the notes do not cover this fact.
The World Development Report is a World Bank publication, not one from the UN, ADB or WTO.
The World Economic Outlook is published by the IMF; the World Bank's flagship reports are the Global Economic Prospects and the World Development Report.
The BRICS countries set up the New Development Bank (NDB) under the 2014 Fortaleza agreement, with its headquarters in Shanghai, China.
AIIB and the World Bank are backing the ₹7,500 crore Mission School of Excellence in Gujarat.
The chronological order is Balwant Rai Mehta (1957), Ashok Mehta (1977-78), G.V.K. Rao (1985), then L.M. Singhvi (1986), which is III, IV, I, II.
The 73rd Amendment inserted Part IX (Articles 243-243O) into the Constitution to deal with Panchayats, so option 4 is correct.
White clothes reflect heat and light, so they suit summer, not winter, when darker clothes that absorb heat are preferred. So (A) is false, while (R) is true.
Banana is propagated vegetatively by suckers (side shoots from the underground rhizome), since cultivated bananas are seedless.
At night trees do not photosynthesise but keep respiring, releasing carbon dioxide and taking in oxygen. Sleeping under one can raise CO2 levels around you, which is why it is considered harmful.
On the 13-district map used in Census 2011, Vizianagaram had the lowest literacy rate (58.89%). Alluri Sitarama Raju is the least literate only on the newer 26/28-district maps.
West Godavari, a delta paddy district, has the highest share of agricultural labourers among workers, so it is the correct option over the other districts listed.
Max Muller popularised the 'Aryan' idea, and he is the European credited in this question with designating Aryan as a race. The others (Jones, Wilson, Cunningham) are not linked with this.

The Boghazkoi inscription (Asia Minor, c. 1400 BCE), a Hittite–Mitanni treaty, names the Vedic gods Indra, Mitra, Varuna and Nasatyas. Mansehra, Shahbazgarhi and Junagarh are Ashokan/Rudradaman sites with no such mention.

Statements I and III are correct: Rigvedic people used coat of mail and helmet and domesticated the horse, while the Harappans show no horse evidence. Statement II is wrong because Indus people knew gold, silver and copper, and iron was not known to them.

Statements I and III are correct: Rigvedic people used coat of mail and helmet and domesticated the horse, while the Harappans show no horse evidence. Statement II is wrong because Indus people knew gold, silver and copper, and iron was not known to them.

MWCD's schemes are grouped under three umbrella missions: Mission Poshan 2.0, Mission Shakti (with its Sambal and Samarthya parts) and Mission Vatsalya. The notes also list Sambal and Samarthya as separate rows, which is the tempting source of a higher count.
The WTO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, so (3) is correct; Montreal, Seattle and The Hague are not its seat.

Statements I, II and III correctly describe the WTO as the rule-setting body for trade, set up after the Uruguay Round to replace GATT. Statement IV is wrong because the WTO does frame IPR rules through the TRIPS agreement, so (1) is correct.
TRIPS sets minimum standards for all intellectual property rights, so it deals with intellectual property protection, not tariffs, trade facilitation or property taxation.
Bt brinjal is a genetically modified (transgenic) brinjal carrying the Cry1Ac gene from Bacillus thuringiensis, so it is not a conventional new variety or a wild type.
The insect-resistance toxin (Cry) gene in Bt cotton comes from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, not the other Bacillus species listed.
Bt brinjal carries the Cry1Ac gene giving resistance to the fruit and shoot borer, i.e. insect resistance, not drought, bacterial or fungal resistance.
Genetic modification is flagged for biodiversity concerns (e.g. gene flow, genetic homogenisation), whereas solar panels, wind turbines and rainwater harvesting are not.

Statement 1 is wrong because the Bt gene comes from a soil bacterium, not a fungus. Statement 2 is wrong because Bt brinjal is not a terminator (GURT) seed. Health and biodiversity concerns are the real objections, so only 3 and 4 are correct.
Cartagena, after which the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety is named, is in Colombia.

The Nuremberg Code was the set of ethical principles for human experimentation that emerged from the Nuremberg trials of Nazi war criminals by the International Military Tribunal; the other codes listed are not the ones.
Gout is caused by high uric acid levels in the blood, which deposit as crystals in the joints. The notes do not cover this.
Phenylketonuria is a genetic disorder in which phenylalanine cannot be metabolised. It accumulates and damages the brain, causing mental retardation (idiocy). The notes do not cover this.

The hypothalamus forms the basal part of the diencephalon in the forebrain. The pons is part of the hindbrain. Schwann cells and synaptic knobs are neuron-related structures. The notes do not cover this.
Sonography uses ultrasound, which is sound above 20 kHz whose echoes form the image. Ordinary audible sound is not used, so option 3 is not the best answer.
ARTSENS was developed by IIT Madras and measures arterial stiffness or vascular age, not neuron health. So statements I and II are incorrect, and III is not disputed.
Ultrasound, which is sound above 20 kHz, is safe for the foetus and is used to image fetal growth. X-rays are ionising and therefore not used.
An electrocardiogram (ECG) records the electrical activity of the heart. It does not record the cornea, kidney or brain, which would be EEG for the brain. The notes do not cover this.
CT stands for Computerised Tomography. A CT scan uses X-rays plus a computer to produce cross-sectional images of the body.
Foot-and-mouth disease affects cloven-hoofed animals including cattle, sheep, goat and pig, so all the listed pairs are affected and 'All of these' is correct.
Leptospirosis is caused by a bacterium (Leptospira), not a virus, fungus or protozoan, so 'None of these' is right. The notes only mention it as a flood-related disease and do not state its cause.
Swine flu (H1N1) is the disease spread by pigs. Zika is mosquito-borne and plague is spread by rat fleas, while Nipah mainly comes from fruit bats with pigs only as an intermediate host.
Swine flu is caused by the H1N1 influenza virus, so the answer is virus. It is not bacterial, fungal or a tapeworm.
Brucellosis is a bacterial disease, so 'bacteria' is correct.
The State of Global Air 2020 report found that air pollution killed more than 116,000 Indian infants within a month of birth in 2019.
The UNFCCC entered into force on 21 March 1994, so option (1) is correct.

Only pair III is correct: the CDM is a Kyoto Protocol mechanism. Annex-I is a Kyoto grouping, not from the Cartagena Protocol, and CERs are issued by the CDM Executive Board, not under the Nagoya Protocol.
The Kyoto Protocol set binding targets for Annex I countries to cut greenhouse gas emissions. It is not about poverty, nuclear arms or agricultural subsidies.

Statement I is right: Kyoto came into force on 16 Feb 2005. Statement II is wrong: Kyoto targets greenhouse gases, while ozone depletion is the Montreal Protocol's subject. Statement III is taken as correct, since methane has a greater warming effect per unit than CO2.
The CDM under Kyoto Article 12 lets an Annex I party run emission-reduction projects in developing countries and earn CERs, so it is the market-based device described.
The CDM is the mechanism by which Annex I parties run projects in developing countries, so it encourages rather than prohibits such investment. Statement 4 is therefore not true.

Statement I is correct: CDM is one of the Kyoto flexible mechanisms. Statement II is wrong: CDM projects are run in developing countries, whereas Joint Implementation covers projects between Annex I countries.
India's INDC of 2015 was a 33-35% cut in emissions intensity from the 2005 base by 2030.
Paris NDC targets are not legally binding on any party, including the USA, China, India or the EU. Only the procedural obligations are binding, so the answer is None of these.
Paris moved from INDCs to Nationally Determined Contributions, which each country sets itself. The other options are not part of the agreement.
Haryana has no notified Scheduled Tribes, whereas Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka do.
Mizoram has the highest ST share (94.4%) among the options; Nagaland, Meghalaya and Arunachal have lower shares.
The Tharu is the largest tribe of Uttarakhand, living in the Terai; Jaunsari, Bhotia and Bhoksa are smaller.
The Blue Mountains are the Nilgiris, home of the Toda tribe (buffalo herders). Gonds, Lambadas and Jarawas live elsewhere.
Malaviya Chamatkar is a high-yielding pigeon pea (arhar) variety, so option 2 is correct. The notes do not cover crop varieties.
Aparna is a leafless (semi-leafless, afila type) pea variety, so option 3 is correct. The notes do not cover pea varieties.
International Day for Biological Diversity is observed on 22 May, so option 2 is correct. 22 March is World Water Day, so it is not the answer.
JRY merged NREP and RLEGP and is a labour-oriented additional employment programme, so the emphasis is on creating labour-oriented additional employment.
Barley's leading producer is Uttar Pradesh, groundnut's is Gujarat, ragi's is Karnataka, and West Bengal is the 'Rice Bowl' and a top rice producer in older keys. This gives a-II, b-III, c-I, d-IV.

The Gulf Stream is a warm current of the North Atlantic, so it cannot sustain coral reefs on the West Pacific coast. The Kuroshio is the warm current of the North Pacific, which makes option 4 the incorrect statement.
The Kamchatka (Kamchatka) current is a cold current of the North Pacific Ocean, flowing south along the Kamchatka coast, so the answer is Pacific Ocean.

The North Atlantic Drift gives NW Europe mild winters and ice-free ports, so I is correct, and II is also correct. III is wrong because the Labrador and Gulf Stream currents meet at the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, not near Vancouver Island.
Fish are most abundant where warm and cold currents meet, because the mixing brings nutrients and plankton, as at the Grand Banks. The other options are not locations of this mixing.

The cold Humboldt (Peru) Current flows along the Peru-Chile coast and causes upwelling there. The Canary and Agulhas currents are in other regions, and El Nino is a warm episode, not this cold current.
ITEWS uses bottom pressure recorders in the deep ocean to confirm that a tsunami has been triggered. Seismic stations only detect the earthquake, and tide gauges are coastal.
Kuroshio is a warm Pacific current, Peru (Humboldt) is a cold Pacific current, Labrador is a cold Atlantic current, and the Florida current is a warm Atlantic current. This gives A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1.
Nelson Mandela wrote 'The Struggle Is My Life' (a collection of his writings and speeches); the notes do not cover it.
'I Do What I Do' is by Raghuram G. Rajan, the former RBI Governor; the other options are not its author.
'Rights of Man' (1791) was written by Thomas Paine in defence of the French Revolution, replying to Burke.
'Termites in the Trading System' is by economist Jagdish Bhagwati, on protectionism and preferential trade agreements.
The book is attributed to Dr APJ Abdul Kalam, who wrote several books on youth and action; the notes do not cover it.
'Turning Points: A Journey Through Challenges' was written by APJ Abdul Kalam as a sequel to 'Wings of Fire'.
'The Audacity of Hope' (2006) is by Barack Obama, later US President.
'Dreams from My Father' (1995) is Barack Obama's memoir about race and his family heritage.
'An Era of Darkness: The British Empire in India' (2016) is by Shashi Tharoor, not Romesh Dutt.
Shashi Tharoor won the 2019 Sahitya Akademi Award (non-fiction) for 'An Era of Darkness'.
'The Sellout' won the 2016 Man Booker Prize and was written by American author Paul Beatty.
'The Namesake' (2003) is by Jhumpa Lahiri; Kiran Desai wrote 'The Inheritance of Loss'.
'Maila Aanchal' (1954) is the famous regional novel by Phanishwar Nath Renu; Raag Darbari is by Shrilal Shukla.
'An Area of Darkness' (1964) is by V.S. Naipaul; the other three are Rushdie's works.
'Arms and the Man' is a play by George Bernard Shaw; Death of a Salesman is Arthur Miller's and Murder in the Cathedral is T.S. Eliot's.
The Sarvodaya Plan (1950) was proposed by Jayaprakash Narayan, not by Nehru, Gokhale or Radhakrishnan.
The National Development Council was set up on 6 August 1952, not in 1950, which is when the Planning Commission was set up.
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
Planning is a conscious effort by the state to achieve a set of goals using a set of means within a specific time period, so all of the options apply.
Planned development began with the First Five Year Plan from 1 April 1951, not at Independence or the Republic's start.
The rolling plan for backward countries was suggested by Gunnar Myrdal.
The rolling plan combines a current-year plan, a plan for 3-5 years revised every year, and a long-term perspective plan of 10-20 years, so all four statements hold.
The Janata Party government introduced the rolling plan in 1978, ending the Fifth Plan a year early.
The notes do not credit Lakdawala with introducing the rolling plan; they attribute the idea to Myrdal and its introduction to the Janata government, and the keyed answer is not supported by them.

Duggirala led the Chirala-Perala movement, Veeresalingam is called Gadya Tikkana, Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Rampa rebellion, and Bipin Chandra Pal is linked with the Vande Mataram movement. This matches option 1.
Ramadandu was the volunteer corps of Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya in 1921. The others listed are not linked to it; Shanti Sena belonged to Parvataneni Veeraiah Chowdary.

The Chipko movement (1973, Uttarakhand) was led by Sunderlal Bahuguna, along with Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Gaura Devi. Medha Patkar and Baba Amte are linked to the Narmada Bachao Andolan, so they are wrong.
The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) was founded in 1961, so (3) is correct. The notes do not cover this fact.

In floods, GIS analyses flood patterns and the topography of affected areas, which enables proactive action. Options 2 and 3 wrongly say it does only one of these, and option 4 is wrong because GIS cannot give details of individual victims.
DEM stands for Digital Elevation Model, a digital representation of terrain. The other expansions are not standard terms.
IMBEX (India-Myanmar Bilateral Exercise) is the regular army exercise between India and Myanmar; the notes do not cover it.
Bhutan has constitutionally committed to keep at least 60% of its land under forest cover; the notes do not cover this.

The IFC-IOR at IMAC, Gurugram is aimed at maritime domain awareness and security through information sharing, so a is right and it is not for a joint satellite mission, so b is wrong. The notes say it is hosted by the Indian Navy, and statement c is accepted as correct per the given answer.

The Gadgil formula (1969) is the formula for distributing Central Plan assistance to States, i.e. devolution of funds. It has nothing to do with the line of control, forex regulation or river water sharing.

Bobbili Raja was Madras Chief Minister in 1932-37, so he is the 1932 CM; the other options held office at different times. The notes do not state his stand on a separate Andhra state, only the office.
Panagal Raja (Panaganti Ramarayaningar) was CM 1921-26, which fits the early 1920s. The notes do not mention the Cooum River boundary remark.
The Self-Respect Movement was founded by Periyar (E.V. Ramasamy Naicker) in Tamil Nadu in 1925; Ambedkar and the others did not found it.
E.V. Ramasamy Naicker was popularly called Periyar. The notes use the name Periyar for him but do not state it explicitly.
E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker was popularly known as Periyar. The notes use the name Periyar for him but do not state it explicitly.
INS Sarvekshak, a hydrographic survey ship, was the first Indian Navy ship to install a solar power system (Green Initiative, February 2017), with 18 flexible 300 W panels.
The Dhar (Linguistic Provinces) Commission was appointed by the Constituent Assembly President on 17 June 1948 under Justice S.K. Dhar, and was to examine Andhra, Karnataka, Kerala and Maharashtra.
Potti Sriramulu spent about three years at Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram; the other options (Swami Sitaram, Pattabhi) are not noted for this.
Andhra State, formed 1 Oct 1953, had Kurnool as its capital (inaugurated by Nehru); Guntur was only the High Court seat, while Vijayawada and Tirupati were rival proposals.
Cochin was the Portuguese base from 1503 and the first HQ of the Estado da India. Anjediva (1505) and Goa (1510) came later, so Cochin is the answer.

The Blue Water Policy, aiming at naval mastery of the Indian Ocean, was introduced by the first Viceroy Francisco de Almeida. Albuquerque, the tempting option, reversed it by pursuing territorial conquest.
Albuquerque (1509-15) is regarded as the real founder of Portuguese power in India, having conquered Goa in 1510. Almeida was only the first Viceroy.
Hooghly was the Portuguese base for piracy in the Bay of Bengal, together with Arakanese pirates, until Shah Jahan's forces took it in 1632.
Chilli is a New World crop brought to India by the Portuguese. Opium, coffee and betel leaf are not in the list of Portuguese introductions.
Kudgi is in Karnataka, Kahalgaon in Bihar, Sipat in Chhattisgarh and Dadri in UP, which gives a-II, b-IV, c-I, d-III.
Salal hydroelectric project is on the Chenab river in Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir, so J&K is correct.

The notes say Sidrapong, Darjeeling (1897) was the first hydropower station and Shivasamudram the second oldest. Of the options given, Shivanasamudra in Karnataka is the one treated as the answer, since the others are not mentioned.
The first hydropower station in India was Sidrapong, Darjeeling (1897). Shivasamudra is only the second oldest.
Kandla in Gujarat, set up in 1965, was India's and Asia's first Export Processing Zone; the other options were set up later.
The SEZ Act was passed in 2005 but the Act and SEZ Rules came into force on 10 February 2006, so 2006 is correct.
SEZs are export-oriented duty-free enclaves, so the claim that they are set up primarily to generate employment is false; the other statements match the Act's features.
The SEZ Act's objectives include promoting investment from domestic and foreign sources, so discouraging foreign investment cannot be an objective.
Infrastructure development and promotion of foreign investment are listed objectives; 'exports of services only' is not (the objective covers goods and services), so 1 and 2 only.
Infrastructure development and promotion of foreign investment are listed objectives; 'export of services only' is not (the objective covers goods and services), so I and II.
Mercury is the smallest planet (diameter 4,879 km), so it has the least mass among the options; Neptune, Jupiter and Mars are all larger.
Terrestrial planets are the rocky inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars); Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus are outer giant planets, so Mercury is the answer.
Only Mercury and Venus have no natural satellites; Mars has two moons (Phobos, Deimos) and Earth, Jupiter and Saturn also have moons.
The inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) lie between the Sun and the asteroid belt, which is located between Mars and Jupiter.
The July 2018 discovery of a large subsurface lake (under the south polar ice cap) was on Mars; the notes mention only Mars's subsurface ice, not the lake.

A is false because the Sun is not the only brighter body: the Moon is brighter than Venus, so Venus is not the brightest object after the Sun. R is true because Venus is the second planet from the Sun (108.2 million km).
Venus (12,104 km) is smaller than Earth (12,756 km), whereas Neptune, Saturn and Uranus are all larger.
By diameter: Mercury (4,879) < Mars (6,792) < Venus (12,104) < Earth (12,756) < Uranus (51,118).
Distances from the Sun: Earth 149.6, Jupiter 778.5, Uranus 2,867, Neptune 4,515 million km, giving II, III, IV, I.
Saturn takes about 29.4 years to revolve once around the Sun, so about 29 years (the question wording 'around the Earth' is loose).
Mercury is nearest the Sun and has the fastest orbit (88-day revolution), so it moves around the Sun at the highest speed.
Malthus's Principle of Population (1798) argued that population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, so the theory relates to population.
The growth rate from natural increase is the birth rate minus the death rate, so option 4 is right. Birth rate alone (option 3) is only one component.
IMR measures infant deaths before age 1 per 1,000 live births, so before the age of 1 is correct; the other ages are wrong.
The notes give IMR of 47 in 2010 and 24 in 2024, but no figure for 2020 from the National Health Profile 2021, so the answer of 28 is not stated in the notes.

Methane in Mars' air has been measured (by Mars Express and Curiosity), and together with water and gypsum it is cited as evidence for possible life, so the combination of water, gypsum and methane is correct.
VENµS, the environmental research satellite launched in 2017, was a joint Israel-France mission, so Israel is correct; the notes do not cover it.
JAXA launched the world's smallest satellite-carrying rocket (SS-520 series), so JAXA is correct; the notes do not state this.
Sputnik-1, launched by the USSR in 1957, was the first artificial satellite. Soyuz, Salyut and Vostok came later.
Messenger mapped Mercury and Voyager 1 and 2 explored the outer solar system, so II and III are correct. Cassini-Huygens studied Saturn, not Venus, so I is wrong.
Kalpana Chawla flew on Columbia STS-107 as a Mission Specialist (flight engineer), not as commander or pilot. The notes confirm only the Columbia disaster and her death.
Valentina Tereshkova of the USSR flew on Vostok 6 in 1963 and was the first woman in space. Sally Ride and Chawla were later, and Savitskaya was the second woman.
Valentina Tereshkova of the USSR flew on Vostok 6 in 1963 and was the first woman in space. Sally Ride and Chawla were later, and Savitskaya was the second woman.
The Moon's escape velocity is below the RMS speed of gas molecules, so gases escape and it has no atmosphere. Distance from Earth, revolving around Earth or sunlight are not the reason.
Yusuf Adil Shah founded the Adil Shahi dynasty of Bijapur, not Ahmadnagar (the Nizam Shahi capital, founded by Malik Ahmad). So the pair is wrongly matched; the other pairs are correct.
Adil Shahi–Bijapur (4), Barid Shahi–Bidar (3), Imad Shahi–Berar (2), Nizam Shahi–Ahmadnagar (1), Qutb Shahi–Golconda (5), which gives 4 3 2 1 5.
Malkibharama was the title given to Ibrahim Qutb Shah by his subjects for his tolerant rule, so option 1 is right. Muhammad Quli is known by the pen name Maani.
Mahasibs/Mustasibs were the officials in charge of public morals, similar to the Mughal Muhtasib. They were not judges or Taraf heads.
The main source of state income under the Qutb Shahis was land revenue, collected through tax farming. Customs and other taxes were secondary sources.
Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV-B) radiation, protecting the biosphere; it does not screen infra-red, X-rays or gamma rays in this role.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) aims to phase out production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances. Basel deals with hazardous waste, Kyoto with GHGs and Cartagena with biosafety.
The Montreal Protocol is a treaty under the Vienna Convention to phase out ozone-depleting substances, so it relates to protection of the ozone layer.
The Basel Convention (1989) controls transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal. The other options concern carbon emissions, wetlands and forests, which are different treaties.
The Kigali Amendment (2016) amends the Montreal Protocol to phase down HFCs. It does not modify Kyoto, which belongs to the UNFCCC.
Nallapoddu, the first collection of Dalit women's writing, was edited by Gogu Syamala, so option (3) Shyamala is correct.
In Jashuva's Gabbilam, modelled on Kalidasa's Meghaduta, a bat carries the hungry Dalit's message to Lord Shiva. The bat stands for the untouchable, who is kept outside the temple.
Veyi Padagalu by Viswanatha Satyanarayana was translated into Hindi as Sahasraphan by P.V. Narasimha Rao. Tulasidalam, Mahaprasthanam and Vennello Aadapilla are distractors.
Markandeshwar temple in Markanda (Gadchiroli, Vidarbha) is called the Khajuraho of Vidarbha for its carved temples; the notes do not cover this.
Chandrahasini Devi temple at Chandrapur (Chhattisgarh) stands at the Mand-Mahanadi confluence; the notes do not cover this.
Sadaiv Atal is the memorial of Atal Bihari Vajpayee, with a nine-square black granite platform; Shakti Sthal, Shantivan and Veer Bhumi are other leaders' samadhis.
The Naropa festival is a Buddhist festival held every 12 years at Hemis/Lamayuru in Ladakh, not in the other listed regions.
The Naropa festival is a Buddhist festival held every 12 years at Hemis/Lamayuru in Ladakh, not in the other listed regions.
Biraja (Jajpur), Rajarani (Bhubaneswar) and Samaleswari (Sambalpur) temples are all in Odisha.
The Kanha Baba fair is held at Sodalpur in Madhya Pradesh; the other options are not its venue.
The Vivekananda Rock Memorial is on a rock off Kanyakumari in Tamil Nadu, at India's southern tip.
Chail is a hill station in Solan district of Himachal Pradesh, so option 2 is correct.
Kumbh Mela rotates among Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain; Varanasi is not a venue.
Bavikonda is in Visakhapatnam, Guntupalli in Eluru, and Yaganti in Nandyal, so a-2, b-1, c-3.
Araku Valley is in the Alluri Sitharama Raju district, in the hills near Visakhapatnam, so Visakhapatnam is the nearest listed city.
The Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya, the national museum of mankind, is in Bhopal on the Shamla Hills.
The notes state that 20 new sites were identified for the national importance tag in 2022, as per Culture Minister G Kishan Reddy in the Lok Sabha.
The notes state that the gharial, Indian wild ass and wild buffalo cannot be hunted except as the law permits, so all three statements are correct.
The notes record 3,474.57 ha of forest land diverted in AP between 1 Jan 2015 and 5 Feb 2019.
The notes place the Animal Welfare Board at Ballabhgarh, Haryana, not Chennai. The notes do not support the given answer, so no line is linked.
The WCCB is headquartered in New Delhi (it has regional offices in Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Chennai and Jabalpur), so New Delhi is correct.
The WCCB is headquartered in New Delhi (it has regional offices in Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Chennai and Jabalpur), so New Delhi is correct.
The National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources is located in New Delhi (Pusa). The notes do not cover this, so no line is linked.
Kushinagar Airport in Uttar Pradesh was given international airport status by the Union Cabinet on 24 June 2020; the notes do not state this fact.
Cochin International Airport (CIAL) was the first Indian airport set up as a public limited company. The notes mention Cochin only as the first fully solar-powered airport, which is a different fact.

Lhasa Gonggar (~3,570 m) is far higher than Kathmandu, Tehran or Tashkent, so it is the correct choice among the options. The world's highest airport overall is Daocheng Yading, but it is not among the options.
Rayagajakesari was the title of Rudrama Devi, earned by her victory over the Yadavas of Devagiri. Prataparudra is wrong because he is the answer only if she is not among the options.
Marco Polo, the Venetian traveller, visited during Rudramadevi's reign and landed at Motupalli. The other travellers listed are not associated with her reign.

Demographic dividend, demographic bonus and demographic window are used for the same phenomenon: the economic growth potential from a rising share of working-age population. So 'All of these' is correct.
The Muslim League observed the Day of Deliverance on 22 December 1939, so 1939 is correct.
The Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed harsh, humiliating terms on Germany, which fed resentment that helped cause WWII. The other options were not WWII-linked settlements.

At Ramgarh (March 1940) Congress offered to help in the war if a provisional national government was formed at the Centre, i.e. cooperation conditional on a political assurance, not unconditional support or neutrality.
The Nuremberg Trials (1945-46) tried the major Nazi war criminals of WWII. The other options are not trial sites.
The US dropped the first atom bomb on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 (Nagasaki followed on 9 August). Options 1 and 4 are identical.
Fascism is linked to Mussolini, democracy to Woodrow Wilson, Nazism to Hitler and socialism to Lenin, giving the code 3 4 1 2.
Mussolini founded and championed Fascism in Italy. Hitler's ideology was Nazism, a related but distinct movement.
The Axis powers were Germany, Italy and Japan. China fought against Japan on the Allied side, so it was not an Axis power.
World War II ran from 1939 to 1945; the notes place India's entry in September 1939, which fits the start date.
